News.title: Amazon plane crashes on to motorway after overshooting runway at Miami Airport with ‘multiple patients’ being treated
News.content:
AN AMAZON plane has crashed on a motorway after missing Miami Airport’s runway, leaving “multiple” people injured.

The crash has sparked a full shutdown of the airport and grounded all flights – as plumes of thick smoke were seen billowing from the site of the smash.



Authorities said “multiple patients” are currently being treated at the scene.

The Boeing 767-300 overshot the airport runway before smashing into the road.



It was arriving at Miami-Dade International Airport after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Authorities said they “arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing”.

Footage on social media showed columns of smoke rising from the aircraft.

Jaw-dropping pictures also showed the hulking aircraft lodged into the ground as shocked bystanders watched on.



Miami Dade Fire Rescue says crews “received reports of a hazardous situation involving a plane that overran a runway and struck multiple vehicles” at 1.55pm local time.

The airport has confirmed the jet was an Amazon cargo jet.

They also said the closure was due to a “disabled aircraft,” according to the Federal Aviation Administration.



According to FlightRadar24 data, no planes have left or arrived at the airport since the crash.

Miami Airport said: “At approximately 2 p.m. today, Prime Air flight 7598 overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport.

“All runways and taxiways at [Miami International Airport] are currently closed as of 3.00pm and a ground stop is in effect.”

The Federal Aviation Authority is set to start a probe to investigate the full circumstances of the crash.

News.title: Mudslide death toll in China rises to three with nine others still missing after heavy rain from Typhoon Saudel
News.content:
THREE people are dead and 11 are missing after devastating mudslide tore through a village in China following days of torrential rain.

Shocking footage shows a huge wall of mud and debris hurtling down a hillside at terrifying speeds before smashing into homes and sending clouds of dirt billowing into the air.



The disaster struck Mingkeng Village in Gaoping Town, Suichuan County, Jiangxi Province, in the early hours of Saturday.

The violent torrent damaged around a dozen houses and left a trail of destruction through the village.



Desperate search and rescue operations are continuing as crews scour the wreckage for survivors.

More than 640 rescuers have poured into the disaster zone, battling treacherous conditions and wrecked roads to reach those still unaccounted for.

Search teams reportedly found two victims on Saturday and a third victim was found on Sunday.

The mudslide completely obliterated a road leading into the affected area, severely hampering the frantic rescue effort.



Wan Qiang, an on-site rescuer with state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, said the destroyed road was making it difficult for teams to reach the stricken area.

Nearly 200 villagers from Mingkeng have been evacuated to a safe site, where they are receiving food and medical care.

More than 5,300 people in neighbouring areas have also been moved to safety amid fears of further disasters.

The catastrophe was unleashed after days of relentless rain battered the region in the wake of Typhoon Saudel.



A staggering 161,500 people across Jiangxi have been affected by the typhoon’s punishing downpours.

The Ministry of Natural Resources raised Jiangxi’s geological disaster response from Level IV to Level III on Saturday as the threat intensified.

A government work team has been dispatched to the scene to help direct the rescue operation, while 20 million yuan (£2.2million) has been released from central disaster relief funds.

China operates a four-tier emergency response system, with Level I representing the most severe threat.



The deadly devastation has also spread beyond Jiangxi.

Two people were killed in neighbouring Hunan Province following torrential downpours brought by Saudel, according to state broadcaster CCTV.

The rain triggered landslides and other disasters across the region, although the precise cause of those two deaths was not specified.

Saudel first slammed into Zhejiang Province on August 28 before making a third landfall as a tropical storm in Fujian Province on September 3.

Both provinces neighbour Jiangxi, which has since been battered by the storm’s punishing aftermath.



In Fujian, around 600,000 residents had been evacuated by Friday night as floodwaters and landslides wreaked havoc.

More than 100 homes were destroyed in Huating Town, Putian, while a breached dam unleashed a torrent of floodwater into surrounding villages.

Rescuers were forced to deploy inflatable boats through streets transformed into raging rivers as they searched for trapped residents.



Images showed bricks and timber from smashed homes floating through filthy floodwater, with other buildings left partially collapsed and torn open.

The latest disaster comes amid a wider wave of deadly flooding across the region.

Days earlier, catastrophic flash floods ripped through communities along the Nepal-Tibet border, killing more than 1,200 people – including Brits – and leaving thousands missing.

Entire settlements were swallowed by torrents of water, mud and debris, leaving behind scenes of almost unimaginable devastation.

The sheer scale of the destruction has also crippled rescue efforts, with landslides and obliterated roads cutting off remote communities.



Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped inside tunnels at hydropower projects in Nepal after floodwaters and landslides ripped through the sites.

Around 900 workers are missing from 12 projects, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped underground.

Three workers have been pulled alive from the Trishuli project in Rasuwa district since Friday.

Huge boulders and surging floodwaters have blocked tunnel entrances and buried sections beneath tonnes of mud and debris.

At the Trishuli facility, rescuers took six days to locate the tunnels and are now pumping air inside while desperately working to drain the floodwater.

News.title: Two cyclists killed and another injured after car crashes into riders in UK village – as three arrested
News.content:
SMASH HORROR Two cyclists killed and another injured after car crashes into riders in UK village – as three arrested

TWO cyclists have been killed and a third injured after a car crashed into riders, as the cops make three arrests.

The incident occurred in the village of Cobham near Gravesend at around 7.47am on Sunday, when a white Ford Focus travelling along Sole Street towards Meopham collided with the cyclists, Kent Police said.

Two of them – a man in his 60s and a woman in her 50s – were confirmed dead by paramedics attending the scene near the junction with Round Street.



The third rider was taken to hospital for treatment to injuries police said were minor.



Two men aged 20 and 21 were subsequently arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

A 19-year-old woman was also detained on suspicion of assisting an offender, according to Kent Police.

The force’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit (SCIU) is now appealing for anyone who has either witnessed the collision, or saw the car or cyclists prior to the incident, to come forward.



Motorists with dashcam equipment or residents with private CCTV have also been urged to get in touch with the force.

Members of the public with relevant information can contact the Kent Police SCIU by calling their appeal line on 01622 798538, quoting reference RY/KA/071/26.

News.title: Huge blaze erupts at scrapyard with plumes of black smoke billowing across the sky
News.content:
FIREFIGHTERS battled through the night to bring a blaze ripping through a scrapyard under control.

The huge fire broke out at a site packed with scrap metal and tyres in Barnsley at around 1.15am.



Ten fire engines and several crews from South Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service raced to the scene on Saturday.

Firefighters battled to fight the flames into the early hours of this morning.



An aerial ladder platform and several operational support vehicles were also deployed as the blaze reached its peak.

The towering plumes could be seen for miles around as flames swirled viciously through the scrapyard.

Firefighters could be seen blasting the inferno with powerful jets of water as they fought to bring it under control.

The fire service urged nearby residents to keep their doors and windows shut because of the large amount of smoke.



Members of the public were also warned to avoid the area while crews continued tackling the blaze.

In an update at 1.15pm, the fire service said Boulder Bridge Road was closed.

They added it would be “for several hours”, adding that drivers should avoid the area if possible.

News.title: Migrant mega-dinghy carrying 140 people reaches UK from Normandy after ‘longest-ever Channel crossing’
News.content:
A MIGRANT mega-dinghy carrying 140 people has reached the UK after it was launched from the furthest ever point in the Channel yesterday.

It comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed a crackdown on crossings.



The mega-dinghy was launched from the Jobourg region in Normandy, 180 miles west of Calais.

Despite launching six boats and two helicopters to monitor the boat, French cops allowed it to carry on, noting in a press release on Sunday morning: “The vessel is currently continuing its journey towards the United Kingdom.”



They said that despite the departure location being “unusual for the area”, they were still available to provide “rapid and robust assistance”.

The boat was then met by two RNLI lifeboats with the migrants taken ashore at Portsmouth before being transferred to the processing centre at Manston.



RNLI boats carrying migrants docked in Langstone Harbour near Portsmouth yesterday evening.

It comes after the PM met with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron with the small boats issue a focal point of talks.

A new surge team of 45 officers has been deployed – but drew criticism as it emerged, they would have to seek permission in order to enter the water.

The crossings were the first in nine days after more than a week of no migrant dinghies, according to Home Office data.



It comes after masked protesters chanting “stop the boats” were able to bring chaos to the Port of Dover on Saturday.

Cars were stuck in huge queues after the balaclava-clad group blocked off roads from 7am.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, criticised Kent Police for being “slow” to react to the far-right group, who were “exceptionally well organised”.

He said the force “appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing”.

“The protesters knew what they were doing, I’m not sure the police did know what was going to happen.



“But then I accept that the police resource is stretched.”

Kent Police said no arrests had been made and labelled the demonstration as “spontaneous”.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds criticised the protest but declined to comment “on the security and policing side of it”.

He told Sky News: “I do think our police forces deal with a great deal across British towns and cities.

“And these days, people can use modern communications in ways that do make things happen quickly.



“I think on the whole, the police handle it very well. But look, peaceful protest, yes. Those kinds of scenes, absolutely not.”

Reform UK politician Robert Jenrick said he had “always hated people obstructing other people doing their daily life, whether it’s Just Stop Oil or whatever”.

He added: “And I don’t like people going around in balaclavas, which is obviously very intimidating. In fact, our party’s policy is to ban face coverings like that.

“But do I understand why people are extremely frustrated? Yes, absolutely. This needs to end. This farce of the small boats has been going on for far too long.

“And in fact you saw at our conference Nigel Farage and (National Rally president) Jordan Bardella, the likely next Prime Minister of France, signing an agreement which has the prospect of ending this once and for all.”



A Government spokesperson said on Saturday that it condemned the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it caused.

News.title: Huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia sends ash cloud 15km into sky closing 8 airports & leaving 170k passengers stranded
News.content:
AT LEAST 170,000 air passengers have been left stranded after after a furious Indonesian volcano blasted enormous plumes of ash 15km into the sky.

Eight airports have been forced to close as vast clouds of volcanic ash billowed across the atmosphere.



Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was among those locked off, with officials warning that the ash could pose a serious danger to aircraft engines.

A staggering 1,558 flights have been delayed, with the affected airports expected to remain closed until midnight as authorities scramble to assess the fallout.





The eruption began late on Friday and has continued to rumble ominously.

Lava fountains and relentless seismic tremors have also been reported.

Its booming eruptions have echoed across surrounding regions, with authorities warning of continued volcanic activity.

Two further eruptions struck in the early hours of Sunday, swelling the colossal clouds of volcanic ash.



The health minister has urged people living in ash-hit areas to stay indoors and wear face masks.

Officials warn the fallout could cause respiratory problems as well as irritation to the eyes and skin.

The ash has already begun causing misery on the ground, with several schools cancelling activities after students and residents complained of sore, irritated eyes.

Some fisherman were also forced to abandon trips out to sea after reporting similar problems.



One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told local newspaper Kompas that the ash had left his eyes feeling as though they were filled with “small grains of sand”.

He said he had been forced to use eye drops to ease the irritation, while the layer of volcanic dust was so thick that he had to sweep his front yard every five minutes.

There has been no tsunami warning linked to the latest eruptions, and officials have reported no casualties or ordered any evacuations.

But authorities have warned people to stay at least 3km from the volcano’s active crater, with the nearest settlement more than 16km away.



Anak Krakatau – meaning “Child of Krakatoa” – rose from the sea in the early 20th century inside the enormous underwater caldera left behind by the catastrophic eruption of Mount Krakatoa in 1883.

That eruption was one of the most powerful in recorded history, with explosions heard thousands of miles away and vast quantities of ash blasted into the atmosphere.

More recently, Anak Krakatau itself made headlines when a section of the volcano collapsed into the sea in December 2018, triggering a devastating tsunami that swept into coastal communities on Java and Sumatra.

At least 430 people were killed and thousands more were injured or displaced as huge waves slammed into the shoreline.



Researchers later found that some of the chunks of rock involved in the collapse were an astonishing 70 to 90 metres high.

The island was left at only around a quarter of its previous size.

The latest activity has been building since July, according to Indonesia’s Geological Agency, with Sunday’s eruptions described as the strongest during that period.

Lana Saria, head of the Geological Agency, said the repeated blasts suggested magma and volcanic gases were continuing to rise beneath the volcano.



But she warned there was no way of knowing whether the heightened activity would develop into something far larger.

Officials say the immediate dangers include thick ash, high concentrations of volcanic gases and chunks of scorching rock being hurled from the crater.

And with the volcano sitting in the Sunda Strait between two of Indonesia’s most heavily populated islands, authorities are continuing to monitor every movement beneath the restless peak.

Indonesia lies on the notorious Pacific “Ring of Fire” – a vast 25,000-mile horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquake zones encircling the Pacific.

Around 90 per cent of the world’s earthquakes occur along the belt, which is also home to roughly 75 per cent of the planet’s active volcanoes.

News.title: Germany’s far-Right AfD party set for big win in state election, exit polls show
News.content:
GERMANY’s far-right party is set to win a historic landslide in a key state election, exit polls show.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is projected gain a whopping 44.5 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt.



The ultra conservative party soared past German Chancellor Frierich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) who are set to take just 18.5 per cent.

The AfD – who have faced probes and accusations by Berlin for right-wing extremism – need to reach 50 per cent to control the state parliament.



If they don’t manage the threshold, it could force several mainstream parties – who have balked at the idea of the AfD in power – to make a coalition with them.

The AfD wants closer ties with Vladimir Putin‘s Russia and a hardline approach to immigration.



The party’s co-leader Alice Weidel hailed it as a “historic” result which had given the AfD a clear mandate to govern.

The projected results mark a political earthquake in Germany – no far-right party has won control of a state in the nation since World War Two.



Should they gain full control of local authorities, they will have power over policing, education and culture.

Saxony-Anhalt, which has a population of 2.1 million, and its AfD officials have been called “far-right extremist” by German intelligence.

The party rejects this label.

Germany’s history with Nazism has fuelled fears of a rising far-right party, and prompted establishment groups to shy away from cooperation.

Some parties have outright refused to form coaltions with the AfD – a policy known as the “firewall”.



The CDU’s secretary general Franziska Hoppermann said her party “does not collaborate with extremists” in response to the exit poll.

She said: “Above all, not with right-wing extremists.”

Sunday’s result also marks another blow to Merz – with the German leader’s popularity seeing sharp declines since the beginning of his tenure.

The AfD has not only dominated the local election campaign – it is also sending political shock waves across the country.

It is now Germany’s most popular party and the latest victory will fuel belief among its millions of supporters.

News.title: Tributes to ‘beloved’ mum, 38, who died after car hit wall in UK city
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH TRAGEDY Tributes to ‘beloved’ mum, 38, who died after car hit wall in UK city

THE heartbroken family of a woman killed in a horrific car crash have paid a moving tribute to their “gorgeous” daughter, mum, sister and aunty.

Kelly Marie Lundie, 38, died after the red Nissan Juke she was travelling in left the road and smashed into a brick wall.



Emergency services rushed to the scene shortly after 11.30pm on Friday, September 4.

Kelly was tragically pronounced dead at the scene.



Her devastated family have now described her as “outgoing and full of life”, saying her presence could “light up a room”.

In a moving tribute, they said: “Kelly Marie Lundie was gorgeous, inside and out.



“She was outgoing and full of life.

“Her presence could light up a room, and her smile and personality will remain in the hearts of those who knew her.

“Above all, Kelly was a devoted and beloved mother to her son, Caleb.

“He was her world, and the love she had for him was immeasurable.



“She was also the best aunty to her nephews, who adored her and shared a very special bond with her.

“She brought so much fun, affection and happiness into their lives.

“Kelly was a cherished daughter, a much-loved sister, a wonderful aunty and a loyal friend.

“She meant something different and special to so many people, and her loss has left an enormous space in the lives of everyone who loved her.”

The family added: “There are no words that can truly express how deeply Kelly will be missed.”



Cops are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the fatal smash.

They are asking anybody with information to get in touch, quoting reference 26000727021.

News.title: Minister to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
News.content:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.

JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.

Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change.

"If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."

He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.

The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.

The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk".

"This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.

News.title: Jamaica to bring slavery reparations petition to King Charles
News.content:
The Jamaican government will hand a petition to King Charles over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said.

It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".

She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era.

The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress.

The petition, which is not a demand for payment, goes to the King who then refers it to the JCPC.

King Charles has no personal discretion in deciding whether to make a referral.

Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined."

Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition is correctly lodged.

A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today."

News.title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel
News.content:
Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel.

The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast overnight, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said. They will now be taken to shore in the UK.

It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.

The dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.

It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.

French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.

Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy.

A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.

"Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election."

They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".

It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

News.title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
News.content:
As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.

What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.

The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.

The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.

Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.

He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.

"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.

"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes withâ¦ to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".

Such a scenario, he thinks, would make the disruption for passengers caused by the incident in June seem relatively minor â and could even put lives at risk. But how likely is it?

News.title: Fifa president Infantino will stand for re-election
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election in March, says football's world governing body.

Infantino, who has filled the role since 2016, has been under pressure following his scrapped plan to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment firms.

Infantino's lucrative plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

"The Fifa president announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027," read a Fifa statement.

"Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election."

Infantino refused to answer questions about his future when asked by reporters at the Women's Under-20 World Cup in Poland on Saturday.

It is the first time Fifa has said he will run for a new term since the plan was announced following the summer's World Cup.

Should the 56-year-old Swiss be re-elected, he will serve until 2031.

Fifa this week accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership", in a challenge to litigation over Infantino's plan.

Last week Uefa filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

News.title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
News.content:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

News.title: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'
News.content:
When it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion.

"I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says.

"If I'm sat in a chair, I get nothing.

"So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"

Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.

Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.

On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause.

"It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness.

"I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."

Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger.

"You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'

"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."

News.title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
News.content:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

News.title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
News.content:
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.

Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.

Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".

Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".

"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.

"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."

The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".

"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.

Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".

Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".

Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.

News.title: Baby girl dies while camping with family in woods
News.content:
A three-month-old girl has died while camping in woodland with her family, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to land off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at 08:45 BST on Saturday, to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

"While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident," Det Insp Katie Gregory said. "The death is being treated as unexplained at this time."

People living in the close-knit community, a village of around 7,000 people, have been left shocked by the child's death.

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Swinney suggests Scots will not travel further for health care under reforms
News.content:
Scots should not have to travel further for health care under the government's plans to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two, John Swinney has suggested.

The BBC asked the first minister about the impact of such changes for people who are already travelling long distances - such as women living in the far north who have to travel 100 miles down the A9 to give birth in Inverness.

Swinney said it would "not be my intention" for people to travel further, with initial modelling showing the country divided into two east and west health boards.

He also said he could not put a "specific figure" on NHS job losses, but he had been "open about the fact that public sector employment will fall".

News.title: Three charged with attempted murder after shooting
News.content:
Two adults and a teenager have been charged with attempted murder after a shotgun was fired in a town centre.

Police were called to Market Place in Braintree, Essex, at about 22:10 BST on Monday following what officers described as a "targeted attack".

Two teenagers sustained serious injuries to their face and upper body, while a third person was also injured.

Destiny Ema, 23, of Meadgate Avenue, Chelmsford, Kayden Brown, 18, of Noaks Avenue, Chelmsford, and a 17-year-old from Braintree who cannot be named for legal reasons are due to appear at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A 16-year-old boy previously arrested in connection with the incident has been released on police bail until 30 November.

Ema was also charged with numerous other offences connected to separate investigations including:

Attempted grievous bodily harm with intent

Possession of a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence

Possession of a firearm while committing an indictable offence

Possession of a firearm while prohibited for life

Harassment

Malicious communications

Possession of a shotgun with intent to cause fear of violence

News.title: Two killed as car hits group of cyclists
News.content:
Three people have been arrested after a car crashed into a group of cyclists, killing two riders.

Kent Police said a white Ford Focus was travelling along Sole Street in Cobham near Gravesend just before 07:50 BST on Sunday when it was involved in a collision with three cyclists.

Two of the cyclists - a man in his 60s and woman in her 50s - were confirmed dead by emergency services on the scene, the force added.

Their next of kin have been informed.

A third cyclist was taken to a local hospital for treatment with minor injuries, according to officers.

Two men aged 20 and 21 were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

A 19-year-old woman was also detained on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Kent Police said the road was closed while an investigation took place.

The force is now appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident or saw the car or cyclists before the crash to contact them.

News.title: Body-worn cameras given to school crossing wardens
News.content:
Lollipop men and women in Sheffield have been given body-worn cameras in an effort to combat abuse and aggressive behaviour from drivers.

Sheffield City Council said school crossing wardens at several unspecified locations across the city would be given the cameras, which will record interactions, as part of a new initiative.

The local authority said the measure would create a safer environment for families walking to school in the new academic year and provide reassurance to staff working alone.

Wardens have been subjected to "unacceptable behaviour" and dangerous driving by a "small" number of motorists, the council added.

Jefferson Nwokeoma, the authority's assistant director of city transport said: "These body-worn cameras will help protect our staff, provide valuable evidence when incidents occur and encourage motorists to follow the rules of the road.

"Ultimately, this is about making the journey to school safer for everyone."

Drivers who fail to stop for a school crossing warden can be fined up to Â£1,000 and have three penalty points added to their licence.

News.title: Police investigate Bielik fan clash at Portsmouth
News.content:
Police are investigating an incident between Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik and home supporters during Portsmouth's 2-0 Championship win on Saturday.

Bielik was involved in a physical altercation with a fan as he went to retrieve a ball from the crowd late in the second half.

Hampshire Police were notified of the incident during the match and launched an investigation immediately afterwards.

"We can confirm that we are investigating an incident in which a teenage boy was reportedly the victim of a common assault during the football match at Fratton Park. Our enquiries are ongoing," the police said.

Several Portsmouth supporters made gestures that indicated they believed the fan had been grabbed by the throat.

Cardiff head coach Brian Barry-Murphy claimed afterwards that Bielik "got slapped in the face", while clips circulating on social media appeared to show the Poland international grabbing a young fan around his upper body.

In the aftermath, another fan threw a ball at the head of Cardiff defender Perry Ng. Both supporters were ejected from the stadium.

After the game Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho apologised to Cardiff City's players.

Pompey added in a statement:, external "Portsmouth Football Club are aware of supporter concerns regarding the incident involving a young fan and an opposition player at yesterday's match at Fratton Park.

"As this remains a safeguarding matter and is currently under investigation by both the club and the police, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further on the circumstances at this time.

"However, we are aware that a number of claims and assertions are circulating on social media. We would urge caution against speculation while enquiries are ongoing.

"The welfare and safeguarding of young people are of paramount importance to Portsmouth Football Club. We will continue to liaise with the relevant parties as enquiries progress.

"No further comment will be made at this stage while investigations remain ongoing."

The Football Association is aware of the matter and will review the details in the referee's match report before deciding whether any action should be taken.

Cardiff City said: "We are satisfied with the way that match officials dealt with the situation during the game, having been in full view of it. Player protection will always be of paramount importance to us."

President Donald Trump has already changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario, and now he’s targeting a US state for a rebrand.

Trump is spending the holiday weekend dreaming up his next demand to relabel America’s geography. He posted a map on Truth Social Sunday afternoon of New Mexico, but the word Mexico was crossed out and replaced with America.

Relabeling the southwestern state on the U.S.-Mexico border as New America is reminiscent of an executive order he signed early in his second term, in which he changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has already changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario, and now he’s targeting a US state for a rebrand ( Getty Images )

In that January 2025 executive order titled “Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness,” Trump also changed the name of North America’s tallest peak, Denali in Alaska, back to Mount McKinley.

Trump’s controversial relabeling of America’s geography didn’t stop there. The president signed an executive order late last month changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America amid an escalating trade war with Canada.

Despite Trump repeatedly suggesting Canada become the nation’s 51st state, he recently told Fox News, “They think they’re a state, but they’re not a state. Why should we be subsidizing Canada?”

Like Trump’s previous name changes on the U.S. map, his latest push to relabel New Mexico is sure to receive a wave of backlash.

The group Republicans Against Trump was quick to post on X following Trump’s suggested name change of New Mexico, writing, “WTF is wrong with him?”

open image in gallery The president posted a map on Truth Social Sunday of New Mexico, but the word Mexico has been crossed out and replaced with the word America ( Donald Trump via Truth Social )

When the president relabeled Lake Ontario, MapQuest refused to change its navigation app, writing on X, “We’re not changing it.”

MapQuest then saw a surge in App Store rankings, with the company’s general manager Doug Berger saying, “We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they're familiar with.

“Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app.”

But tech giants Apple and Google caved to Trump, switching the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America for U.S. users of their maps apps, just as they did when the president demanded that the Gulf of Mexico be changed to the Gulf of America.

Conservative journalist Eric Daugherty, however, was seemingly on board with the relabeling of New Mexico, writing on X, “This man is on a roll!”

Trump’s ambitions to remake Washington, D.C., and the rest of the U.S. as he sees fit apparently go beyond the country, and even the world.

open image in gallery Shortly after Trump’s post about relabeling New Mexico, he shared an image of the moon on Truth Social, with the caption 'The moon is ours' ( Donald Trump via Truth Social )

Shortly after Trump’s post about relabeling New Mexico, he shared an image of the moon on Truth Social, with the caption “The moon is ours.”

The 80-year-old leader has been heavily focused on his legacy during his second term, not just with changes to the map, but with renovations to the White House, including his massive and expensive ballroom, and the broader D.C. area.

He’s also slapped his name and face on several buildings in the nation’s capital, most notably the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. But a federal judge demanded his name be taken down from the center, and it was removed.

Meanwhile, 73 percent of Americans say Trump hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important problems, according to a CNN poll conducted by research firm SSRS and published in late July.

For many Americans, Labor Day weekend signifies the start of a new school year — and sadly, the end of summer fun.

As kids head back to school, most amusement parks across the country close their doors for the season before picking back up again the following year.

However, some beloved amusement parks are saying goodbye for the last time this summer as they plan to shut down for good.

That includes the long-standing Wild Waves park in Federal Way, Washington, which is closing its doors for good following its 50th summer season.

“A lot of people have been flooding back to the park to relive the memories, make new ones, and say goodbye,” Wes Petree, the park’s director of sales and marketing, told KIRO. “The community has really shown up in support of Wild Waves.”

open image in gallery Wild Waves Theme & Water Park in Federal Way, Washington, will close in November after its 50th summer season ( Google Maps )

The park’s operator, Oklahoma-based Premier Parks, announced its closure in December, citing growing costs associated with running the park.

Wild Waves employs 35 full-time staff and 800 to 900 seasonal workers. While its water park plans to shut down for good after Labor Day, its theme park side will stay open for various Halloween-themed events until it also closes for good November 1.

Another longtime amusement park, Fun Spot America in Fayetteville, Georgia, also closed down this summer after 36 years.

The park, which opened in 1990 as Dixieland Fun Park and then became Fun Junction USA, had go-karts and some of the best-rated roller coasters in the world — but still had low attendance, its owner told WSB-TV.

“We tried our best here, and it just didn’t work,” owner John Arie told the outlet.

More than 200 people, mainly teens and college students, lost their jobs when the park closed this past August, according to the report. Fun Spots locations in Orlando and Kissimmee, Florida, will both remain open.

Keaira Stanley, who visited the park as a child, came back this summer to say goodbye, telling the news station, “Even when I came awhile ago, that’s how it was. It was real slow.”

open image in gallery Fiesta Fun Park in Califronia ended its run over the summer after first opening in 1974 ( Fiesta Village Family Fun Park/Facebook )

Another amusement park, the family-owned Fiesta Village in Colton, California, closed for good this past July due to rising costs and declining attendance.

“For decades, Fiesta Village has been a place where families gathered, friendships grew and memories were made,” the park said in a social media post.

“When we were given the opportunity 25 years ago to carry forward the tradition that began in 1974, our goal was to preserve that spirit and create a welcoming space for connection, celebration and joy, while also providing meaningful employment for the people who helped bring it all to life.”

The confirmed, full results in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt regional election are likely to be a major political headache for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) have governed the eastern state for more than 20 years.

Sunday evening’s exit poll showing the far-right, pro-Russian, Alternative for Germany (AfD) potentially gaining 44.5 per cent of the vote is beyond the 40 per cent recent opinion polls had been showing and well in excess of the 20.8 per cent the party secured in 2021. Mr Merz’s CDU fell to 18.5 per cent in the exit poll from 37.1 per cent in 2021. The CDU currently leads a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the free-market Free Democrats (FDP).

About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents. Participation was at a record high of 76.5 per cent.

AfD had been looking to secure an absolute majority of above 50 per cent, to ensure they could try and implement their own radical agenda.

So what happens now?

1. AfD seizes power

If AfD were to take control of the regional parliament, they would be the first far-right party to have power in either a regional or the national parliament since the Second World War. If this were to happen, what is known in Germany as the “firewall” – where parties create coalitions to keep far-right parties from power – would be breached for the first time.

open image in gallery Ulrich Siegmund, top candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ( AFP/Getty )

AfD has been clear about what it would do if it were to take power. It seeks to restrict immigration, quit the Euro and restore ties with Russia as most of Europe rallies around Ukraine.

Based on the party’s “Vision 2026” election manifesto, victory in Saxony-Anhalt could invite sweeping reforms around state policy on migration, education, culture and the family.

Under Germany’s federal system, state governments sit in the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, and also have wide powers in education, domestic security and culture.

An AfD-led state would launch a crackdown on migration, with a task force set up to coordinate quicker deportations.

The children of refugees would be placed in separate classes at school to prevent what the party claims are “stresses” on the other children from being around different cultures.

Meanwhile, children with disabilities would no longer be taught in the same classroom as those without, instead being sent to new schools.

Schools would also be banned from flying rainbow flags, and the government would exhaust “all legal avenues” to limit Islamic expression.

The party has claimed greater acceptance of what it offensively labels as “sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles” has contributed to sinking birth rates and promises to aggressively promote “traditional” family structures consisting of a mother, father and children. An AfD government would see major changes to the school curriculum around a “patriotic cultural policy”, extended to raising the German national flag daily and singing the national anthem at school celebrations.

open image in gallery Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel ( AFP/Getty )

It would also advocate for removing war refugee status for Ukrainians in Germany as long as the conflict remains concentrated in eastern Ukraine, arguing they should seek refuge in western Ukraine.

The current structure of the public broadcasting system would be dismantled and funding withdrawn for some cultural institutions.

In terms of domestic security in Saxony, AfD in the state is assessed by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency as a “far-right extremist” group, which would create concerns about the intelligence AfD would be able to see if it was in charge of the regional parliament.

However, AfD will likely need the support of another party, depending on how many smaller parties pass the five per cent threshold needed to get seats. In Saxony-Anhalt, all the parties except the small far-left BSW party have ruled out joining a coalition with AfD.

If some smaller parties do not pass the threshold though, it would make AfD’s job easier, as it would make the chance of a coalition against it less likely.

The party will talk to any sensible party with whom it can find common ground on policy positions, said AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel after the exit poll

2. The CDU pulls together a coalition

The CDU has been hit hard, but may yet be able to pull together a “firewall coalition”. That is what happened in the state of Thuringia in 2024, where AfD gained more than 30 per cent of the vote, but not enough for an absolute majority.

However, American think tank the Brookings Institution believes this will be difficult. “The task of organising a CDU-led governing majority faces almost insurmountable difficulties,” it said in a recent briefing note, exacerbated by the CDU’s ruling out of any coalition with the staunchly socialist party Die Linke (The Left). With exit polls predicting a 9.4 per cent share of the vote for The Left behind the CDU’s 18.4 per cent, the party leadership has indicated it would be open to an arrangement formalising support for a CDU-led government over AfD. But the CDU faces internal divisions over a possible alliance with a party on what it regards as the far left.

open image in gallery German Chancellor and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party leader Friedrich Merz ( Reuters )

Mr Merz said ahead of the election last Sunday that they would “assess the situation in light of the election results” and “do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt from falling into the hands of the radicals”.

State premier Sven Schulze congratulated AfD in the wake of the exit poll and acknowledged the result showed it was the strongest party. If AfD is unable to rule outright, it could trigger a protracted process of coalition building by mainstream parties who are determined to keep a party under investigation for right-wing extremism by Germany’s domestic intelligence service.

3. The German government takes a hit regardless

However the political wrangling in the wake of the Saxony result ends up, it is clear that the manner of AfD’s win is important for their national standing and a blow to Mr Merz’s coalition government.

Nationwide, AfD has swollen to become the most popular party, polling at 29 per cent, while Mr Merz has become the most unpopular chancellor since the founding of the Federal Republic, with 85 per cent of voters dissatisfied.

Lars Klingbeil, co-leader of Germany’s centre-left SPD party and vice chancellor in Mr Merz’s governing coalition, said after the exit poll that the result of the Saxony-Anhalt state election is a signal for Berlin politics. The result is ⁠a reason to reflect on the federal government’s policies, Mr Klingbeil told public ‌broadcaster ZDF. “And ​rest ‌assured, that ⁠is what ⁠we will ‌do.”

Mr Merz has already sought to create a harder line on immigration, in a move designed to try and stem the rise of AfD. There will no doubt be a greater push from AfD to try and move the needle on national policy, while their pro-Russia stance could be an issue when it comes to European support for Ukraine, given the nation has previously been accused of moving cautiously when it comes to handing Ukraine weapons to fight off Russia's invasion.

Mr Merz will face an increasing level of political pressure about his own job and government, something AfD will be all too happy to try and press home in both future regional elections and the wider national polls.

Hang on. We’d seen that goal before, hadn’t we? We’d seen Martin Odegaard just there, lurking undetected in a pocket of space between defence and midfield. We’d seen Christos Tzolis drive inside and fire that exact pass into the centre. We’d seen Riccardo Calafiori’s decoy run and Kai Havertz intelligently leave it. We’d seen Odegaard’s little dart, the velcro control, the poise as he waited just a beat before pulling the trigger.

If Odegaard’s winning goal against Chelsea felt familiar, that’s because he’d scored a carbon copy against Manchester City in the Community Shield four weeks earlier. The same players, the same movements, the same outcome, with a world-class goalkeeper – then Gianluigi Donnarumma, now Emiliano Martinez – left beaten on the ground as the ball hit the net.

The prevailing question at the start of the season was not who would win the league so much as how Arsenal would win it. Will they roll out the 2025/26 blueprint, bludgeoning teams to death by a thousand corners, strangling possession, smothering all routes to xG? Or would we see something altogether more free-flowing and spontaneous now the weight of a 22-year wait had been lifted?

You can already feel a buzz in the air outside the Emirates, a sense that the brittleness of past years has disappeared in the wind. Music blaring from the megastore DJ could be heard down every road leading to Armoury Square three hours before kick-off. Inside, hundreds queued to buy an Arsenal scarf or pyjamas or a cushion with Declan Rice’s face on. Outside, content creators jostled for space while fans videoed fellow fans being interviewed by other fans on YouTube.

It is that strange time of the season when the leaves are still green and summer is clinging on. The transfer frenzy has only just ended and, really, we don’t know anything yet. The sample sizes are small and in this twilight window, we inevitably draw bad judgments. At exactly the same stage last year, three games in, the champions Liverpool beat the pretenders Arsenal and the title race was surely over.

But, defending their title, what sort of Arsenal might we get? The first few games of the season had not served up a definitive answer, but this game felt different. It was no doubt influenced by Chelsea’s decision to play basketball, by Morgan Rogers’ early goal which forced Arsenal to show urgency, by Martinez, chief s***house of the Premier League, whose presence poked the Emirates into furious noise. Even so, this was a performance full of roving positions, slick interchanges and seamless rotations which felt thrilling at times, and Chelsea struggled to follow them.

open image in gallery Martin Odegaard fires home Arsenal's winning goal against Chelsea ( PA )

open image in gallery Martin Odegaard scored the winner as the Gunners maintained their 100% record ( Reuters )

There was a moment late in the first half when Havertz was on the right wing, Calafiori was galloping into the right half-space, Odegaard was the striker and Bukayo Saka was inside as the No 10. Only David Raya, Ezri Konsa and Gabriel Magalhaes could claim to have been at their stations. And Odegaard’s goal was a product of a higher tempo that this Arsenal side had at times abandoned in the final months of last season, understandably so through tension, through fatigue, perhaps even through sheer fear at what they might lose.

It didn’t help that Arsenal played without this version of Odegaard last season, a campaign derailed by injury. He rediscovered his flow captaining Norway at the World Cup and has continued that form with three goals in four Arsenal games, if you like to count the Community Shield as a game. Where he has sometimes fallen into a rhythm of taking the easy option, being Arsenal’s playmaker on the fringe of a match, here there was a boldness to his runs, getting closer to Havertz, nearer the goal, demanding the ball in tight spaces where his close control can hurt opponents.

“He’s fit, his confidence is one of the highest that I’ve seen him and he has a point to prove,” said Arteta. “Kai the same, Bukayo the same. We missed so many attacking players last season for long, long periods, and I don’t know how many times they’ve played together, those three, in the last few years. Probably not much. You feel the chemistry that they have between them and what they can produce. You have to play with real intent and that’s what I loved seeing today. He was running forward, he took shots, he created so many situations for his teammates.”

Are Arsenal about to unleash a season of wild, entertaining chaos-ball? Probably not. Arteta is not about to abandon the positional principles that have served his coaching career so well. Arsenal will not play a team as frantic as this Chelsea side every week. But there is a paradox here, that the cohesion and connections in this team are so well honed by now, so sharply refined, that Arsenal can produce pre-planned patterns as mesmerising to watch and difficult to defend as anything off the cuff.

Perhaps this is the next evolution of Arteta’s team, to be as meticulously well-drilled in the disorder of open play as they are standing over the certainty of a set-piece. The fact Odegaard scored the same goal twice in a month suggests that, even within the confines of their manager’s highly tuned system, Arsenal might be unlocking some new attacking verve.

News.content:

Ohio governor hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy was mocked online after attending Ohio State’s home opener in what commenters described as a “knockoff” jersey.

The Trump-endorsed Republican nominee watched Saturday’s game against Ball State in Columbus and later posted photos of himself gladhanding fans in the crowd. “Great start to the season. Let’s go Bucks,” he wrote on X.

The post quickly went viral, drawing 3 million views and hundreds of comments. College football fans homed in on Ramaswamy’s black jersey — which featured the Ohio State logo and the number 1 — noting it did not match the team’s official red jerseys with striped sleeves.

According to critics, Ramaswamy’s outfit resembled a “Temu knockoff,” the “generic CVS” version, and something “fresh off the rack at Walmart.” One even said that the clothing choice could impact his decision at the ballot box, writing: “I can’t vote for you with that jersey on I’m sorry man.”

The Independent has contacted Ramaswamy’s campaign for comment.

open image in gallery Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP nominee for Ohio governor, was mocked online for wearing a 'knockoff' Ohio State jersey to the Buckeyes' home opener ( @VivekGRamaswamy, X )

The backlash appeared to hinge less on fashion than on optics: the gubernatorial candidate has a massive fortune and could easily afford an authentic jersey – or hundreds. Ramaswamy, an Ohio native, Harvard graduate and founder of a drug development company, has an estimated net worth of $3 billion, according to Forbes.

“You’re a billionaire, why don’t you own an officially licensed OSU jersey?” wrote one X user, while another chimed in: “A billionaire in a knockoff jersey. That seems fitting.”

Others sought to paint Ramaswamy — who won the GOP primary in May — as an out-of-touch member of the coastal elite, noting that he appeared to have attended the U.S. Open in New York City the previous day.

“This loser flies in late from NY tennis match, slaps on a $19.99 Walmart special OSU jersey, probably given to him by handlers, cuz, you know, optics, and does his kissing babies routine,” one X user wrote.

Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for Ohio governor, slammed her opponent for attending the tennis tournament in a Saturday social media post.

“Vivek Ramaswamy thinks he is too good to spend Labor Day Weekend in Ohio, instead jetting off in his private plane to watch the U.S. Open in VIP seating with his billionaire friends,” she wrote on X.

open image in gallery ‘You’re a billionaire, why don’t you own an officially licensed OSU jersey?’ wrote one X user ( @VivekGRamaswamy, X )

Still other commenters seized on a viral 2024 post by Ramaswamy in which he wrote that American culture venerates “mediocrity” over excellence. “A culture that celebrates the prom queen over the math olympiad champ, or the jock over the valedictorian, will not produce the best engineers,” he wrote at the time.

“I thought celebrating sports was dumb?” wrote one X user, while another added:“Man, mimicking the culture you mock… interesting.”

Some commenters, however, came to Ramaswamy’s defense.

“Hilarious how many people think claiming that Vivek's jersey is ‘fake’ or ‘cheap’ is a gotcha,” wrote one user. “THE next governor of O H I O! Ladies and gentlemen,” wrote another.

Ramaswamy will face off against Acton on November 3. Polls indicate it is shaping up to be a close race.

England completed a series clean sweep against Ireland with a dominant victory in the third one-day international at Worcester.

Sophia Dunkley starred with a century as England finished their innings on 291 all out, and Ireland were never close to threatening that total, going down by 114 runs.

Ireland won the toss and chose to bowl, and Orla Prendergast thought she had trapped Dunkley in front with the score on just two, but England reviewed the decision and the replay showed the ball had hit the bat.

Dunkley emphatically made the most of her second chance, going on to make 119, her highest one-day international score.

The 28-year-old and fellow opener Maia Bouchier put on 61 in the first power play before Bouchier gave a catch to Gaby Lewis off the bowling of Kia McCartney when she looked set on 39.

Dunkley reached her second ODI century off exactly 100 balls, dominating a partnership of 110 with Jodi Grewcock, who fell for 35 to a soft caught-and-bowled from Cara Murray.

open image in gallery Sophia Dunkley made her highest one-day international score ( PA Wire )

Alice Capsey was then unfortunate to be run out after McCartney deflected Dunkley’s drive onto the stumps.

Dunkley’s innings came to an end with England on 214 when Prendergast caught her on the boundary, and the home side’s innings began to unravel after Freya Kemp was caught by Lewis at long-off.

They lost their final six wickets for just 31 runs, including Dani Gibson for 41, with Murray finishing with four wickets for 56 runs from her 10 overs.

Arlene Kelly, meanwhile, claimed a wicket in her final international for Ireland, with Ryana MacDonald-Gay picking out Murray.

A smattering of rain in the interval did not disrupt the contest, and England were in the ascendancy throughout Ireland’s reply.

Ireland managed only 39 from the first power play and lost Lewis, who gave Lauren Filer her 50th international wicket when she picked out MacDonald-Gay at fine leg.

Ireland progressed cautiously to 80 for one before Tilly Corteen-Coleman bowled Alice Tector for 29, and Mady Villiers was next among the wickets, with Capsey stumping Amy Hunter for 39.

Another stumping left the visitors on 127 for four, Rebecca Stokell coming down the wicket but missing a short ball from MacDonald-Gay, and Prendergast sent a skier off Villiers into the hands of Bouchier.

The Ireland tail offered little resistance, with their final five wickets falling for just 10 runs.

That included Kelly managing just two runs, the 32-year-old’s 110th and final match for Ireland ending when she chipped Charlie Dean to MacDonald-Gay.

Filer and Villiers were particularly effective, finishing with three wickets apiece, while Tilly Corteen-Coleman took two for 34 from her eight overs as Ireland were bowled out with more than five overs remaining.
