Sports.title: Huge crash knocks Leclerc out of F1 Italian GP
Sports.content:
Ferrari Formula 1 driver Charles Leclerc crashed out of the Italian Grand Prix, bringing out the red flag after two racing laps at Monza.

At the end of the second lap, Leclerc was defending fourth position from McLaren's Oscar Piastri when the Ferrari driver suffered a snap of oversteer and lost the rear of his Ferrari through the fast Parabolica right-hander.

Leclerc spun in the outside barriers at high speed, but walked away unhurt. But a safety car turned into a full red flag so race officials could repair the barriers.

It was a huge blow for Ferrari at his home race, which had already suffered a poor start when Leclerc pushed team-mate Lewis Hamilton wide at the start. Hamilton was demoted to eighth, with Mercedes' George Russell taking over the lead from surprise polesitter Pierre Gasly in the Alpine.

On the team radio Hamilton fumed that "Charles pushed me off", an incident that was noted by the stewards but no investigation was called for.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Drivers are expected to take a standing restart at 15:39 local time, with teams allowed to make a tyre change during the stoppage.

Russell will lead the restart from Gasly, Max Verstappen, Franco Colapinto and Piastri, championship leader Kimi Antonelli worked his way up to 12th after starting down in 19th due to an engine penalty.

Given the severity of the impact, Leclerc headed to the medical centre for precautionary checks, but was cleared and released without injuries.

Sports.title: Alpine brings back folding rear wing at Italian GP as Gasly grabs pole
Sports.content:
There are magical days, but there are also special places. Monza is one of them for Pierre Gasly. Six years after his triumph with AlphaTauri, in what was one of the most unpredictable Formula 1 races ever, the Frenchman took the first pole position of his career in the most unexpected way possible.

Even Alpine itself had not predicted that it could get involved in the fight for the very top positions, especially considering that the target at the start of Saturday had been to make the top 10 in qualifying. That was a more than realistic and achievable goal based on what was seen in practice, with the team fighting Racing Bulls and, albeit inconsistently, Audi.

The final classification was much more favourable than anyone could have expected, but this was not a pole position produced by chance. It was deserved and earned on track. Certainly, the slipstreaming games played their part, and it cannot be denied that Mercedes realistically had more margin with George Russell had he not been involved in a fracas with Max Verstappen on his final attempt. But you have to capitalise on such opportunities.

That is exactly what Alpine did. The A526 is a car that, particularly in the configuration brought to Monza, generates relatively little aerodynamic drag compared with other teams, and that undoubtedly helps on the long straights. Even in practice, it was possible to see that the Enstone team was recording excellent top speeds on the straights. The challenge was finding the right balance through the corners without giving too much away.

There is, however, an interesting aspect to this weekend’s pole position, because the low-downforce package also featured an old acquaintance: the rear wing that opens in reverse, causing the two flaps to collapse. This solution had been seen in testing and during the first three races of the season – Australia, China and Suzuka – before being set aside in favour of a more conventional opening mechanism similar to last year’s DRS.

Alpine novel rear wing assembly made a comeback in Monza Photo by: Marcel van Dorst / EYE4images / NurPhoto via Getty Images

The low-downforce package has therefore brought back the early-season wing, while all the additional elements on the wing actuator have been removed. Alpine was actually the first team this season to introduce dedicated structures around the wing-opening mechanism at Suzuka in order to find more aerodynamic load, starting a trend that was subsequently adopted by all the other teams.

On a circuit like Monza, however, all those additional elements aimed at generating more downforce were not considered necessary and were removed, effectively returning to the very first specification from the beginning of the year. That version was considered more efficient, including in its interaction with the diffuser.

It is worth remembering that at Zandvoort two weeks ago, Alpine introduced a major package of long-awaited technical upgrades. With it, the A526 found some of the downforce it had been lacking, and this was particularly useful in the high-speed corners.

That does not mean that Alpine has suddenly become a benchmark car in terms of cornering performance. Rather, it has managed to find those few extra km/h needed to avoid throwing away what it gains on the straights.

“The new package we put on is not very draggy, which is good here. Our top speed is no secret. You can see that. It's competitive. So, who knows? Let's see what we can do,” explained Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen.

Sports.title: "We don't need to be respectful" - Alpine bullish about Italian GP win after Gasly’s shock pole
Sports.content:
Going into the Italian Grand Prix, of all the storylines and narratives being composed, absolutely none of them involved Pierre Gasly and Alpine.

That’s not dismissive of the French driver or the Enstone team, but Ferrari competing on home soil with a decent chance of victory and an Italian in Kimi Antonelli leading the championship was always going to take every column inch available this weekend.

So, when the FIA Court of Appeal report dropped at the start of first practice at Monza to inform the world that Gasly had lost his Monaco GP podium, a new and unexpected theme emerged. And then it snowballed.

First there was Flavio Briatore’s questioning of the integrity of one of the judges, Filippo Marchino, about connections to McLaren – one of the lead proponents in the appeal – which McLaren team principal Andrea Stella vehemently took offence to, then there was the FIA Court of Appeal statement to dismiss comments of impartiality.

It all overshadowed the Alpine message of ‘we’re disappointed but we’re going to fight back on track’ that the team initially released as it looked to move on from the saga. And to Alpine’s credit, it has done exactly that.

Having been in with a reasonable shout of reaching Q3 amongst the congested midfield on practice pace showing, Gasly topped Q1 to trigger the first sign of something special building and then duly grabbed a shock maiden pole by 0.060s from heavy favourite George Russell and Mercedes.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Dom Gibbons / Formula 1 via Getty Images

From the mechanics jumping around the Alpine garage to Gasly’s screams of delight over the team radio, it was clear this one meant more than perhaps it would’ve done before Friday’s appeal outcome. It was the perfect reaction – unlike Briatore’s show in the FIA press conference.

For Alpine and Gasly to truly put the Monaco GP appeal saga behind them, following up pole with a big haul of points – say, the 13-point swing inflicted on Alpine on Friday – would ensure the 2026 Italian GP storyline would end on a real high for the Enstone squad.

Alpine to target Italian GP victory: “Why not?”

But Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen feels Gasly can aim for something even bigger. When asked what the goal is for Sunday, he replied: “Try and win it.

“I think we're going to try [to win]. Why not? We don't need to be respectful of anybody. We're on pole on merit. Let's see what we can do.”

Reflecting on a whirlwind two days, Nielsen feels a strong result on Sunday regardless will be the ideal ending to a challenging few days.

“We had a blur a couple of days ago with the Monaco decision being turned around,” he said. “But I'm looking forward to stopping talking about that.

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director, Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“It's amazing. It's the best feeling we could have. And like I said, we're going to aim high tomorrow and leave here [with] as much points as we can get.”

Gasly has taken a more pragmatic approach, acknowledging the reality of Alpine lacking the pure pace and performance of the likes of Mercedes and Ferrari, but he also didn’t dampen his victory hopes.

“My plan is to stay first as long as I can,” Gasly said. “How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.

“I’m really hoping we can stick to that position [in the lead], but as we know, it’s racing. Time will tell and I’m just going to make sure I do my work as I always do, and come as prepared as I can and give it my best chance.”

Throughout Monza’s storied F1 history, surprise wins have been a theme, particularly in the modern era; Sebastian Vettel’s maiden win for Toro Rosso in 2008 (from pole), Gasly’s own first F1 win in 2020 and Daniel Ricciardo’s shock McLaren triumph in 2021 spring to mind.

Having been reportedly 1000-1 for pole, what are the odds of Gasly and Alpine taking Italian GP victory and dominating the headlines again? At the time of writing, 10-1…

Sports.title: How Piastri's Q3 mistake denied Norris "half a second" in Italian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
Lando Norris believes he could have set a quicker lap in Monza qualifying had his team-mate Oscar Piastri not made a mistake in the closing moments of Italian Grand Prix qualifying, which may effectively have cost the defending Formula 1 world champion a few positions on the grid.

Norris was ninth in qualifying, with his best Q3 lap coming on his first attempt. His 1m22.256s put him seventh in the order after the first runs, but he was unable to improve on his second attempt.

This was largely down to the fact that, he reckons, he ended up effectively first on the road in the closing stages of the session.

Norris later explained that McLaren's plan was for Piastri to run ahead of him on that attempt to provide him with a tow. The McLaren drivers were the first to leave the pits for the final runs, with Piastri leading Norris. But Piastri, who was third after the first runs, made a mistake into Turn 1, locked up and aborted his lap, leaving Norris without the assistance of a slipstream, which is particularly valuable at Monza.

On the first run, Norris had been ahead of Piastri but still had a slipstream from George Russell in front. His time was three tenths slower than his team-mate's, before he was left without the planned tow on the second run because of Piastri's mistake.

"I had priority in terms of I had to go out first of the pitlane on Q3 run one, which meant Oscar had a couple of cars ahead of him and I just had the one [of Russell] and most of my time loss is just in the straights," Norris said.

"So it's nothing I can do, it wasn't my best lap either, I'm not going to deny that, but the majority of my time is just lost in the straights - and of course on the second run, it's my time to go behind and get a bit of a slipstream and that certainly didn't go as I'd hoped."





Watch: Pierre on Pole, Ferrari Flounders - F1 Italian GP

Norris explained that because McLaren is still struggling with straightline speed, he and his team-mate needed to follow other cars particularly closely, with a gap of around two seconds required to optimise their laps.

Indeed, when Piastri crossed the line to start his final lap in qualifying, Norris followed just 2.3 seconds later. But the Australian locked his right-front tyre on the approach to Turn 1 and took to the escape road. By the time he rejoined the track, Norris was already coming through and passed his team-mate.

Piastri explained that McLaren's position in the pitlane, with the team's garage being far from pit exit, was behind the decision to send its cars out first. Waiting longer risked leaving both drivers at the back of the queue and potentially without enough time to complete their final laps.

"The slipstream is really important, obviously," the Australian said. "We kind of knew going into the into the session that where we are in the pitlane, we often have to leave the garage first, because if we don't, we end up being last. There was a fair bit of mess behind us, behind me and Lando.

"And if you don't go early enough, you get stuck right at the back of that and you don't get a lap."

Piastri also admitted he had been too ambitious under braking for Turn 1 as he tried to make up time.

"So the second lap, yeah, I was leading the train around," he said. "I think I was already like two tenths down into Turn 1. So I tried to compensate. Your braking point changes quite a lot with that speed difference. So I tried to probably be a bit too ambitious, locked the front and that was it."

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

That left Norris without a tow, and his second lap was a 1m22.573s, around three tenths slower than his first.

When asked whether a slipstream could be worth two or three tenths, Norris insisted its value was considerably greater: “No, it's more like half a second, maybe even more.”

An improvement of half a second on his final lap could potentially have put Norris in the fight with the Ferraris and Max Verstappen, who occupied positions from fourth to sixth in the qualifying order.

"It cost me because I have no slipstream, that's it," he said. "It doesn't matter, we're useless as a car, we're so slow in the straight, we have to have a good slipstream otherwise we're not quick enough.

"Oscar made use of a good slipstream and he could make it work. My chance never came around, so I just have to take it on the chin."

Norris will still gain one position thanks to Kimi Antonelli's grid penalty, meaning he is set to start eighth, with the Italian dropping to the back of the grid after taking new power unit components this weekend.

Still, the McLaren driver believes he was never in the fight for pole because of his car's straightline speed deficit compared to the opposition.

"I think the most painful thing this weekend is just the straightline speed deficit," he said. "Kimi could do a 22.1s or a 22.0s pretty much with no slipstream. With a slipstream he [would be] doing a 21.6s or something.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"I think we needed to be incredibly close to someone. I had a one car tow and I lose two tenths to Oscar who had a two-car tow [on the first run]. It's painful in that sense, but otherwise it's just what we've got to live with for now."

After winning the last two races in Hungary and the Netherlands, Norris is aware it will be difficult to repeat that result at Monza - not only because of his starting position, but because the track is less favourable to McLaren's characteristics.

"The people who were quick are because they're quick, not because they got lucky. They were quick from Q1 run one," he said. "They're quick because they're very good in the straights, they're good in low-speed corners, they completely deserve to be where they are, they didn't get lucky in any way.

"For us, we're probably one of the slowest in the straights. We have to start a lap two seconds behind someone, which is pretty insane. Otherwise, we're just not quick at all. We'll see what we can do tomorrow, but I think in any situation, if we get to [be in] clean air, we're not going to be very good at all. Really, I think we're quite a long way off.

"It's just that Oscar did a good job today and I never had that opportunity."

Piastri ended up third in qualifying, but will start Sunday's race from sixth after receiving a three-place grid penalty for impeding Lawson in Q2.

Sports.title: Domenicali hails F1’s ‘incredible racing’, Norris says it’s ‘just who presses a button when’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali and reigning world champion Lando Norris gave strikingly different assessments of the racing in today’s Italian Grand Prix.

Prior to the race, several F1 drivers predicted they would see “yo-yo racing” at Monza . This was expected as their energy-starved cars would swap positions repeatedly on the high-speed track while the Overtake Mode boost button would hand a valuable advantage to those following within a second of another car.

However Domenicali claimed the opposite, insisting there had been pre-race predictions of a processional race. He said the repeated positions swaps therefore represented a welcome surprise.

“In Monza, a lot of people yesterday were saying, maybe we’re going to have a lot of trains, one behind the other,” Domenicali told Sky. “And actually we had incredible racing.”

Several drivers have criticised the “yo-yo racing” produced by the current cars at some tracks, particularly the quicker ones. Norris gave a candid assessment of the racing today when asked by the official Formula 1 channel whether he enjoyed it.

“It’s good fun in parts,” Norris replied, “of course a lot of it’s just who presses a button when and so forth.”

His team mate Oscar Piastri agreed it had been “a very different race in Monza compared to what we’ve seen previously.”

Piastri repeatedly swapped positions with Lewis Hamilton during the race. He said that made it difficult to make progress.

“A lot of yo-yo battling, which [made it] quite difficult to know what exactly the right thing to do was. Because obviously you can’t just give up an easy overtake, but you also don’t want to be losing race time, you want to just going with whoever you’re racing.

“So that was quite difficult to manage. Definitely some lessons learned from that one.”

Sports.title: 2026 Italian Grand Prix interactive data: lap charts, times and tyres | 2026 Italian Grand Prix interactive data
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid – one of the lowest positions a race has ever been won from.

Jump to: Lap chart – Gaps chart – Lap times – Tyre strategies

Mercedes prepared Antonelli to run a long way into the race before making his first pit stop, putting him on a set of hard tyres. However an early red flag meant they quickly changed that strategy.

Antonelli gained five places at the original start, passing Lance Stroll , Carlos Sainz Jnr, Yuki Tsunoda and both Cadillacs. He overtook Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi on the next lap and picked up another place when Charles Leclerc crashed, leaving him 12th.

He took the restart from that position on a set of medium compound tyres and made up four places this time. He passed the Haas pair, Gabriel Bortoleto and Franco Colapinto, who went off at Lesmo One.

He was up to sixth place by lap seven as he passed Arvid Lindblad and Lando Norris. It was three laps until he gained another place, from pole-winner Pierre Gasly, and from there on he was fighting against the other leading cars.

The moment which won him the race arguably came on lap 28. After yo-yoing back and forth with team mate George Russell for several laps, swapping the lead, Mercedes opted to pit Antonelli during a Virtual Safety Car period, while leaving Russell on his original set of hard tyres.

The second pit stop proved effective as Antonelli easily re-passed the cars he dropped behind and caught Russell with five laps to go. He won by 3.8 seconds, but lost a significant amount of time when he went off at the Rettifilo. Without that, his winning margin would surely have been even greater.

Sports.title: Colapinto left in tears after mistake which cost him 11 places at restart | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Franco Colapinto was moved to tears by his mistake at the restart of the Italian Grand Prix.

The Alpine driver took the restart in fourth place but skidded off at Lesmo one and fell to 15th.

He recovered to finish ninth, just two places behind his team mate Pierre Gasly. But after the race Colapinto was clearly distraught still about his mistake and wept while speaking to the media afterwards.

“It was a difficult race with a few things and then a big mistake, I just lost the car completely.” he said. “I don’t really understand how I lost it so aggressively.

“I was very frustrated. It was a great opportunity for me and for the team, we’re second and third and I threw away a nice chance. So I’m very frustrated, of course, with myself.”

Despite recovering to finish inside the top 10 Colapinto said he should have done better.

“Of course I did some good things but I didn’t really put anything together,” he said. “I should have had more points and it’s a big disappointment.

“I think when you are there and you feel strong you want to go forward. Maybe it [was] not really our fight either and taking risks for no reason as well is not so smart, so I think on my side I’ll just try to learn from it and move on.”

The team showed strong pace at Monza as Gasly took pole position for the race. Colapinto admitted it was a “very positive” weekend for the team. “That’s why I’m frustrated because the team gave me a very good car and a very good opportunity and I didn’t make the most of that.”

Sports.title: Leclerc says car felt “weird” at Parabolica on lap before crash | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc was at a loss to explain the heavy crash which put him out of the Italian Grand Prix on lap two.

The Ferrari driver lost control of his car at the exit of Parabolica. He suffered a heavy impact with the barrier but was able to climb out of his car unaided.

However damage to the barrier was so substantial the race had to be red-flagged while it was repaired.

Leclerc said his car did not feel right in the corner when he went through it on the first lap.

“I went on throttle on the first lap and it felt kind of weird,” Leclerc explained. “I had to go back off and on throttle.

“On that second lap, I tried to do the same thing, but I don’t know, it just felt a little bit weird. So we’ll look into it.”

Leclerc also had a run-in with his team mate at the start of the race. Lewis Hamilton was forced into the run-off area after the pair went through the Rettifilo side-by-side.

Leclerc said he did not intend to hold up his team mate.

“It was way too close into turn one,” he said. “Unfortunately in turn two then – I don’t know if we had contact or whatsoever – I was quite a lot on the inside curve and tried to make the corner. I didn’t do it tight enough and then I obviously only saw in the mirrors what happened which is never what you want between two cars from the same team.”

Sports.title: Antonelli cruises past Russell and rivals to win at home from 19th on the grid | 2026 Italian Grand Prix report
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli extended his championship lead by winning his home race from 19th on the grid.

The Mercedes driver passed his team mate George Russell , who led much of the race, with three laps remaining. He is the first Italian driver to win the Italian Grand Prix since Ludovico Scarfiotti 60 years ago

Antonelli rose to the front so quickly thanks in part to an early red-flag following a major crash for Charles Leclerc, who was unhurt. Already up to 12th before the day’s second standing start, Antonelli immediately vaulted into the points-paying positions and began picking off the remaining cars between him and his team mate.

He and Max Verstappen, who also switched to mediums before the restart, soon closed on leader Russell. First Verstappen moved ahead temporarily before Russell yo-yoed back ahead.

As Verstappen’s tyres faded, Antonelli moved within range of Russell. The Mercedes pair yo-yoed back and forth repeatedly for many laps, until a Virtual Safety Car period changed the complexion of the race.

The earlier red flag gave most drivers a chance to switch to the hard tyres, satisfying their mandatory change of compounds, from where they could run to the end of the race. That included Russell, who had taken the lead from surprise pole-winner Pierre Gasly on lap two.

However Antonelli started on the hards, so Mercedes switched him to mediums during the stoppage. A mid-race VSC period caused by Lance Stroll’s retirement handed him the perfect opportunity to change tyres.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

While Russell pressed on, Antonelli and Verstappen rejoined in sixth and eighth respectively. With the added benefit of fresher tyres, they moved past the midfielders with even greater ease than before.

By the time Antonelli had the race leader back in his sights, Russell was struggling badly with his tyres. The outcome looked inevitable, yet Antonelli came dangerously close to blowing his chance.

He avoided diving past Russell into Parabolica as his team mate avoided using up his remaining energy. Instead Antonelli drew alongside as they approached the Rettifilo chicane. Russell braked deep into the corner and Antonelli scrambled ahead.

But he ran wide in the left-hand turn two, strayed onto the discarded tyre rubber, and speared off into the gravel trap. By the time he rejoined, Russell was over a second and out of the Overtake Mode danger zone.

Russell’s tyres were exhausted, however, and soon afterwards Antonelli drove past at the exit of Lesmo two with total ease.

Verstappen collected third while Lando Norris made a late attack on his team mate for fourth place. Oscar Piastri took fifth ahead of Lewis Hamilton: the pair repeatedly swapped places early on as drivers’ predictions of constant ‘yo-yo racing’ were borne out.

The Racing Bulls and Alpines completed the top 10: Gasly taking seventh ahead of Arvid Lindblad, Franco Colapinto and Yuki Tsunoda. Colapinto held fourth at the original restart but spoiled his afternoon by skidding off at Lesmo One.

The two Aston Martin drivers were the only retirements besides Leclerc. The stewards chose not to investigate the Ferrari driver for forcing his team mate off the track at the Rettifilo on the first lap.

Sports.title: Hearn Says TKO Gave Joshua 90 Minutes for America
Sports.content:
“Yesterday, TKO went around the back again to try and offer Joshua money to do the fight in America,” Hearn told DAZN. “It’s a dirty, dirty game, mate, to be honest with you. It’s made it even harder for them because Josh just ain’t about that. You’ve got an hour and a half to make your decision. Mate, what don’t you understand? I signed to fight in Britain. I want the fight in Britain.”

The 90-minute demand is the major addition to Hearn’s story. A deadline that short would leave Joshua little time to study revised terms, consult his lawyers, or calculate the financial consequences of moving the event from Britain.

It sounds like an attempt to place a large number in front of AJ and force an immediate decision. No amount has been disclosed, but TKO presumably understood that a modest increase would not persuade him to surrender Wembley Stadium, his home support, and the protection Hearn says was written into the signed agreement.

“You can’t buy everybody,” Hearn continued. “Especially the ones who it means something to.”

Hearn said the approach strengthened Joshua’s determination to keep the Fury fight in Britain. The growing public support has also changed the tone of the venue negotiations. A week earlier, Hearn said there was “zero interest” in London and that New York was being treated as the only destination. He now claims Sela has asked him about contacting London Mayor Sadiq Khan to help make the British event possible.

The conflict with TKO has not ended. When asked if Matchroom would take action over the direct approach, Hearn said his team had already written to the company.

“What are you doing?” Hearn said. “You guys are on the New York Stock Exchange. What is this? Just coming around the back trying to bung someone a few quid. Come on. It doesn’t have to be like that. But it’s pushing the fight further away because of their behavior.”

That is the danger behind TKO’s alleged tactic. The company may have believed a quick financial offer would settle the American venue, but Hearn says it produced the opposite response. Joshua is now more committed to Britain, Matchroom has contacted TKO in writing, and the relationship between the parties has deteriorated.

Hearn placed the likelihood of Fury and Joshua fighting in Britain at 64%. That oddly precise estimate still leaves New York in contention, but it is more optimistic than his position a week ago.

The missing financial figure remains fascinating. If TKO wanted Joshua’s answer within 90 minutes, it must have believed the offer was large enough to make him reconsider everything he had signed for.

Sports.title: Muhammad Ali, Richard Dunn, And The AccuPunch
Sports.content:
Both stood 6’3″, but nearly everything else separated them. Ali traveled with an international promotional circus and commanded million-dollar purses. Dunn was a former paratrooper and working scaffolder who balanced his trade with professional boxing. Their meeting was not part of the original plan.

German promoters anticipated that Bernd August would win the vacant European championship and provide Ali with a German challenger. Dunn ruined the arrangement by stopping August in the third round at London’s Royal Albert Hall seven weeks before the Munich date.

That victory sent Bradford’s working-class champion into a fight with the most famous athlete in the world.

Dunn was Ali’s third championship opponent in barely three months. Ali stopped Jean Pierre Coopman in February, struggled through 15 rounds with Jimmy Young in April, and returned against Dunn only 24 days later.

The champion traveled between Puerto Rico, Maryland, and West Germany while completing three training camps and fulfilling three promotional commitments. Money helped drive the pace. His large entourage, expensive lifestyle, and business obligations required a steady supply of purses.

Ali’s performance against Young showed what the schedule was costing him. He looked slow, poorly conditioned, and frustrated as Young made him miss before leaning through the ropes to escape exchanges.

The judges awarded Ali a unanimous decision, but the scores did not erase the criticism. Young had exposed how much of the champion’s timing and movement had disappeared since his physical peak.

Munich gave Ali an opportunity to look dominant again. Dunn held three respected championships, but his direct, aggressive style offered fewer complications than Young’s movement and defensive tricks.

The promotion struggled before either boxer reached the ring. A dispute involving $225,000 from Ali’s purse and German taxes placed the event in danger only days before the fight.

A late compromise kept the card alive. Ali’s purse was reported at approximately $1.6 million after adjustments, while Dunn received about $100,000, easily the largest payday of his career. Ali also helped cover a shortage in the challenger’s money.

The champion spent another $100,000 purchasing 2,000 tickets for American servicemen stationed near Munich. Even that gesture did not rescue the live gate.

The main event began around 3 a.m. local time to place it on NBC during American primetime. That decision served the television audience but punished German ticket buyers. High prices and the brutal starting hour helped leave thousands of seats unsold.

Roughly 11,000 people were inside the 12,700-seat Olympiahalle, but about 4,000 reportedly attended with complimentary tickets. Estimates placed the promoters’ losses between $300,000 and $500,000. Ali and Dunn received their money. The local backers were left with the bill.

Ali frequently described southpaws as awkward opponents. Karl Mildenberger had given him uncomfortable moments from the left-handed stance during their 1966 championship fight, creating the belief that the alignment itself caused Ali trouble. Dunn demonstrated the limits of that theory. A southpaw stance changes punching angles, but it does not automatically provide timing or defense. Dunn approached Ali upright, followed him instead of cutting off the ring, and often began his attacks with looping punches.

Those wide shots gave Ali time to recognize what was coming. Dunn also advanced without consistent head movement, leaving a direct lane for the champion’s right hand.

A quicker and more deceptive southpaw might have punished Ali’s low left hand and tendency to pull away from punches. Dunn lacked the speed and disguise required to take advantage. His stance altered the angles, but his technical flaws gave Ali the solution.

Ali waited for Dunn to square himself and drove short rights through the opening. The fight showed that his difficulties were not caused by southpaws alone. They came against opponents who knew how to use the stance.

Dunn pressed forward from the opening bell and tried to force a physical contest. His activity kept Ali from treating the bout as an exhibition, but much of his work struck gloves, arms, or empty space.

The challenger’s bravery soon worked against him. He continued marching forward after Ali established his advantages in speed, timing, and power. Instead of changing his approach, Dunn kept presenting the same openings.

Ali was more than 10 pounds lighter than he had been against Young. He remained heavier and less mobile than the dazzling fighter of the 1960s, but the lower weight helped him look sharper.

The champion stayed patient during the early rounds, studied Dunn’s attacks, and gradually began sitting down on his punches. Once he committed to the right hand, Dunn lacked the defensive reactions to protect himself.

Ali dropped him three times in the fourth round. Each knockdown exposed the difference between determination and defensive ability at championship level.

Dunn rose from another knockdown in the fifth, but a short right sent him to the canvas again. Referee Herbert Tomser stopped the fight at 2:05 as Ali theatrically wound up his right arm from a neutral corner.

Ali later credited taekwondo instructor Jhoon Rhee for teaching him the short right used in the finish. Rhee called it the “AccuPunch” and said its quick delivery was based on a technique Bruce Lee had shown him.

The punch was designed to remove the physical warnings that normally precede a power shot. Instead of drawing back the hand or first rotating the shoulder, the boxer sent the fist directly toward the target and brought the rest of the body behind it.

That approach suited the opening against Dunn. The challenger was advancing with his head high and his guard separated. Ali released the right from close range before Dunn recognized the attack.

The exaggerated arm motion came afterward, when Ali knew the contest was finished and began performing for the crowd.

It gave him the 37th knockout of his professional career. Ali never stopped or officially knocked down another opponent.

The Dunn victory was the last time Ali increased the pressure, repeatedly floored an opponent, and ended a fight before the final bell.

His later victories depended more heavily on endurance, clinching, defense, and carefully rationed attacks. Ken Norton forced him through another punishing 15 rounds. Earnie Shavers hurt him badly before Ali rallied in the final round. Leon Spinks outworked him in their first fight and pushed him through 15 more rounds in the rematch.

Ali retained the ability to produce combinations and fight through exhaustion, but he was no longer an offensive finisher. His legs moved less, his punches carried less force, and too many rounds were spent on the ropes while opponents worked.

Dunn became the final opponent Ali was able to erase once he decided to attack.

Ali had little time to recover. Just 33 days after beating Dunn, he faced Japanese professional wrestler Antonio Inoki in a mixed rules exhibition at Tokyo’s Nippon Budokan.

Inoki spent much of the 15-round contest on the canvas, repeatedly kicking Ali’s legs while remaining outside punching range. Ali absorbed more than 100 kicks and left with severe swelling, bleeding, an infection, and two blood clots.

Three months later, he defended his championship against Norton at Yankee Stadium and escaped with a disputed decision after another exhausting 15 rounds.

The sequence captured the reckless pace of Ali’s career. He fought Young in April, Dunn in May, Inoki in June, and Norton in September. His body received little opportunity to recover between major events.

Thousands of people lined the streets of Bradford to welcome Dunn home. They honored a working scaffolder who had risen to challenge the most famous boxer in the world.

His championship run ended five months later when Joe Bugner stopped him in the first round. Dunn retired after a 1977 knockout loss to Kallie Knoetze.

The Munich promotion lost money, but the fight gained historical importance. Dunn became the final opponent Ali stopped, permanently linking the Bradford heavyweight to The Greatest.

Sports.title: Dave Allen’s 40 Fight Plan Gets Bizarre Twist
Sports.content:
Officials had several possible outcomes to consider after watching the replay. Allen could not receive a stoppage victory because the punch was ruled an accidental foul rather than a legal blow. A disqualification would have required the referee to treat the foul as intentional.

Trainer Jamie Moore accepted the no contest despite Allen’s visible unhappiness inside the ring. “He’s gone to hit him in the side of the head. He’s turned his head, he’s hit him in the back of the head, and he’s fallen out of the ring,” Moore told IFL TV. “Dave can’t win on an unintentional foul, but he can’t lose either. So it’s got to be a no contest. By the rules, they’ve done the right thing.”

Under the unified rules commonly used in professional boxing, a fighter knocked out of the ring receives 20 seconds to return without assistance. An injury caused by an accidental foul before four completed rounds generally produces a no contest or technical draw, depending on the governing commission. There were no completed rounds available for a technical decision.

Consequently, neither boxer could be awarded a win from such an unusual sequence. The brief fight was erased competitively, leaving both men without a satisfactory result after completing full training camps.

Falling outside the ring also carried more danger than an ordinary knockdown. Carty dropped from the elevated platform into an area containing chairs and other ringside equipment. Medical personnel therefore had to consider the impact outside the ropes rather than judging his condition solely by the punch.

Before the ending, Carty had used his southpaw jab and attempted to press Allen. Moore was encouraged by how quickly his fighter closed the distance. Allen reached Carty at close range earlier than anticipated and forced the type of physical exchanges that suited him.

“I thought he hurt him a couple of times,” Moore said. “I was over the moon with the way it was going up until that point. It was just over way too quickly to tell anything.” Allen now has one appearance remaining under his 40-fight limit. The Carty contest counts as his 39th professional bout even though it ended without a winner.

A rematch would settle the unfinished business, but it would also require Allen to use his intended last appearance on another meeting with a tricky southpaw. He could instead pursue a larger domestic payday and leave Carty as one of the strangest opponents listed on his record.

Sports.title: Katie Taylor Defeats Flora Pili!
Sports.content:
The two-time undisputed champion controlled the opening rounds with her jab, speed, and movement. Pili made the third round competitive, but Taylor continued landing the cleaner punches as the fight progressed.

The action increased during the seventh, with Taylor getting the better of the exchanges. Pili switched to southpaw in the ninth and remained in that stance during the final round, but Taylor adjusted and finished strongly.

The judges scored the fight 100-90, 100-90, and 98-91. David Irving was the referee.

Paddy “The Real Deal” Donovan (16-2, 12 KOs) stopped Tyrone “The Mighty Celt” McKenna (25-7-1, 8 KOs) at 2:33 of the fourth round in their welterweight contest.

A body shot from Donovan dropped McKenna in the second round, with referee Paul McCullagh administering an eight-count. McKenna suffered a cut over his right eyebrow during the final minute of the fourth, and the ringside physician stopped the fight.

Taylor Bevan (10-0, 9 KOs) stopped Emmet Brennan (6-1, 1 KO) just 36 seconds into the sixth round of their super middleweight bout.

Bevan dropped Brennan near the end of the third round and put him down again with a left to the body at the bell in the fifth. Two more knockdowns followed early in the sixth before referee Padraig O’Reachtagain stopped the contest.

Joe McGrail (14-0, 7 KOs) stopped Matthew “Bam Bam” Boreland (7-1, 2 KOs) at 3:03 of the fifth round in their super bantamweight fight.

McGrail dropped Boreland with a combination in the closing seconds of the round. Boreland failed to beat referee Padraig O’Reachtagain’s count.

The heavyweight fight between Dave “White Rhino” Allen (27-9-2, 20 KOs) and Thomas “No Carty No Party” Carty (11-1, 9 KOs) ended in a first-round no contest.

Allen landed a right hand to the back of Carty’s head, sending him through the ropes and out of the ring. Carty was unable to continue, and the contest was ruled a no contest at 1:22. Emile Tiedt was the referee.

Molly “Meatball” McCann (5-0, 1 KO) defeated Sylwia Doligala by unanimous decision after eight two-minute rounds in their bantamweight bout.

McCann controlled the fight with her pressure and work rate. The judges scored it 80-72, 80-73, and 79-73. Paul McCullagh was the referee.

Paul “Ravishing” Ryan (12-2, 4 KOs) defeated Paddy “Pat-Man” Gallagher (17-7-1, 10 KOs) over six rounds in their middleweight contest.

Gallagher hurt Ryan badly in the fifth and had him leaning halfway through the ropes. Gallagher suffered a cut over his right eyebrow during an action-packed final round, but Ryan had done enough to receive the decision. Referee Paul McCoy scored the fight 58-55.

Heavyweight Adam Olaniyan (4-0, 4 KOs) stopped Matej Hudak (6-3, 6 KOs) at 2:59 of the first round.

Olaniyan landed a right hand to the chin in the closing seconds of the round. Hudak took the count on one knee before referee Emile Tiedt waved off the fight.

Bobby Flood (4-0, 2 KOs) defeated Jack “Mad Dog” Swallow (4-14-1, 1 KO) by decision in their four-round super welterweight bout.

Flood controlled the contest from start to finish. Referee David Irving scored it 40-36.

Mikey Sheehan and David Diamante served as the ring announcers.

Sports.title: Damian Knyba Is Anthony Joshua’s Perfect Fury Test
Sports.content:
He lacks Wladimir’s speed, timing, defense, and destructive power, but the basic construction is similar. That familiarity should benefit Joshua, who spent years studying Wladimir, training alongside him, and eventually fighting him at Wembley in 2017.

Facing Knyba would not reproduce Fury’s movement, feints, stance changes, or ability to invent his way through a difficult fight. It would give Joshua experience against another towering heavyweight who knows how to keep the action at long range and smother opponents once they get inside.

The matchup becomes more appealing because Knyba is not harmless. His power is respectable enough to test the weakness that now defines Joshua’s career.

Joshua’s punch resistance and recovery can no longer be trusted after his fights against Daniel Dubois and Kristian Prenga.

The younger AJ survived a crushing right hand from Wladimir, regained control, and stopped him in the eleventh round. He had the physical resilience and confidence to fight his way through a crisis. That version of Joshua is gone.

Against Dubois, the consequences of catching AJ cleanly and denying him time to recover were obvious. Once hurt, Joshua became rigid, lost track of incoming shots, and struggled to restore order.

His fight with Prenga provided more evidence that Joshua no longer processes hard punches as well as he once did.

Although Knyba does not punch like Dubois, he hits hard enough to stop Joshua. His height allows him to generate leverage on the straight right, particularly when an opponent remains directly in front of him or pulls back without changing angles.

AJ would have to close the distance behind his jab, keep his head moving, and remain defensively responsible after throwing. One lazy exit or mistimed entry might give Knyba the opening needed to wreck the Fury fight.

That danger is precisely what makes Knyba a worthwhile warm up. A harmless opponent would tell Eddie Hearn nothing about Joshua’s readiness.

The blueprint for beating Knyba was supplied by Agit Kabayel, who stopped him inside three rounds in January. Kabayel refused to conduct the fight from the outside, where Knyba’s 86 inch reach gave him the advantage. He applied pressure, shortened the distance, and forced the taller man to work at an uncomfortable pace.

There is little doubt that Joshua possesses the strength and power to follow that approach, but his recent habits create doubts.

Under Ben Davison, AJ has often settled into cautious outside boxing built around the jab and isolated right hands. That approach may suit him against shorter opponents who must cross open space to reach him. It makes less sense against Knyba, who owns the longer reach and wants a slow fight at the end of his jab.

AJ cannot afford to admire Knyba’s size from the outside. He would need to attack the body, force him backward, and make him reset his feet. Knyba becomes much less effective when denied the time and space required to extend his punches.

That would test Joshua’s willingness to take calculated chances. Moving into mid range places him closer to Knyba’s right hand, but remaining outside allows the Polish heavyweight to dictate the pace. Finding the balance between aggression and recklessness has repeatedly escaped AJ.

Reaching Knyba would solve only the first part of the problem. Against Andy Ruiz Jr., he regularly wrapped up and smothered the shorter fighter whenever Ruiz crossed the distance.

Fury uses that tactic even more effectively. He leans his weight across an opponent’s shoulders, forces him to carry the load, and drains his legs during long clinches. It is not glamorous, but it has become a vital part of his heavyweight style.

While Knyba cannot match Fury’s inside craft, he can give Joshua a physical rehearsal for those wrestling exchanges. AJ would have to keep his arms free, create enough room to punch, and avoid wasting energy trying to overpower a taller man in static clinches.

Too much muscular weight has caused Joshua to burn energy unnecessarily in previous fights. Continually wrestling with a heavyweight of Knyba’s size would test both his conditioning and his patience.

Frustration with the holding may tempt Joshua into lunging from too far away. That is where the straight right becomes dangerous.

Knyba’s victory over Andy Ruiz Jr. supplies more than a recognizable name for the promotion. It connects him directly to the most damaging defeat of Joshua’s career.

The loss to Ruiz destroyed Joshua’s aura at Madison Square Garden in 2019. Although AJ comfortably won the rematch, questions about his confidence and punch resistance followed him from that night onward.

By beating Ruiz, dropping him in the seventh round, and controlling much of the fight with his jab and reach, Knyba added a former unified champion to his record. The official scores were 117-110 and 114-113 twice, although the two narrow cards understated his control.

That creates an easy promotional story. Joshua would be fighting the man who just dominated his old conqueror while testing himself against the physical dimensions he will encounter against Fury.

The psychological angle should not be exaggerated. Beating Knyba would not erase what happened against Ruiz. It would still allow Joshua to show that he can dominate the fighter who just reduced Ruiz to a fading former champion.

Hearn cannot treat Knyba as an opponent controlled entirely by Matchroom. The Polish heavyweight signed a multiyear promotional agreement with Bob Arum’s Top Rank in 2023 and remains listed on the company’s roster. That introduces promotional politics.

From Top Rank’s perspective, the money and exposure attached to a Joshua fight may be tempting, especially after Knyba rebuilt himself by beating Ruiz. The company would also know that his size and right hand give him a genuine chance to spoil the larger plan.

Calling Knyba a warm up sacrifice would undersell his value. He has already fought Kabayel for an interim heavyweight title and now owns a win over Ruiz. Top Rank would likely want proper compensation and a favorable arrangement before placing him across the ring from one of Matchroom’s most valuable fighters.

Warren’s connection to Fury adds another consideration, although he does not control Knyba’s contract. Anyone invested in Fury versus Joshua must decide if the preparation value justifies placing AJ in another dangerous fight first. The financial calculation may ultimately kill the idea.

Heavy investment from Turki Alalshikh in both Joshua and Fury has helped keep their fight alive as one of the largest events available in British boxing. Sending Joshua against a towering heavyweight with a hard right hand creates a direct threat to that investment.

If Knyba knocks out AJ, the Fury fight loses much of its commercial power. It may still happen because of the names involved, but it would no longer carry the same sporting value or sense of occasion.

That gives the match its central contradiction. Knyba is the ideal warm up for Fury because he reproduces several of the physical problems Joshua must solve. He is also the wrong warm up from a business perspective because he carries enough power to destroy the entire plan.

On experience and technical development, Joshua should be able to pressure Knyba, attack his body, and exploit the weaknesses Kabayel exposed. But “should” offers little comfort with Joshua now.

Winning would not require Knyba to outbox him for 12 rounds. He would only need to survive long enough to land one clean right hand on a fighter whose recovery has badly deteriorated.

That is why the fight works. Knyba can prepare Joshua for Fury’s dimensions, force him to solve the clinching problem, and test the punch resistance Fury would attack. If AJ cannot safely handle that assignment, he has no business moving directly into the Fury fight.

Sports.title: Taylor Retires Undisputed After Dominating Flora Pili
Sports.content:
Before retiring in front of more than 80,000 fans, Taylor (26-1, 6 KOs) added the vacant WBC title to her WBA, IBF, WBO, and Ring championships. Pili (12-1, 2 KOs) suffered her first professional defeat after struggling to match Taylor’s speed, timing, and work rate.

There were no knockdowns, and Taylor was rarely in serious danger. It was a controlled farewell rather than another punishing war, with the 40-year-old boxing intelligently and refusing to give Pili the exchanges she needed.

From the opening bell, Taylor took the center of the ring and began setting the distance with her jab. She pressed behind the lead hand, landed the right hook, and put together quick combinations before Pili could answer.

During the opening two rounds, Pili looked tentative. She waited too long for Taylor to finish punching and then found the target had already disappeared. Taylor moved her head, changed position, and made the French challenger reset before beginning another attack.

Four-punch combinations allowed Taylor to score without remaining in front of Pili. Whenever the challenger attempted to close the distance, Taylor either countered her coming forward or tied her up before she could build any offense.

The difference in hand speed was clear. Pili had difficulty timing Taylor’s entries, while Taylor repeatedly beat her to the punch and moved away before the return fire arrived.

That pattern continued through the third round. Taylor stabbed with the jab, stepped into range with combinations, and smothered Pili’s attempts to respond. She did not need to take unnecessary chances because Pili was giving away rounds with her low output.

More urgency came from Pili in the fourth as she tried to push Taylor backward. Her pressure briefly made the fight more physical, but she still struggled to land cleanly. Taylor met her with counters and refused to remain trapped along the ropes.

The challenger continued advancing in the fifth, only to run into Taylor’s sharper punches. A clean left hook from Taylor closed the round and reinforced her control of the fight.

One of Pili’s better jabs snapped Taylor’s head back early in the sixth. Taylor responded quickly with punches through the middle and a counter right hand, preventing Pili from building on the moment.

The Frenchwoman’s punches looked slower, and her attacks usually came one shot at a time. That made it easier for Taylor to read what was coming and answer with combinations. Pili remained durable and willing, but she could not produce enough offense to change the direction of the contest.

Her best work came in the seventh and eighth rounds. Pili connected during a flurry in the seventh after Taylor had attacked the body, while the referee warned Taylor for using her head.

In the eighth, Pili crowded Taylor more effectively and landed a short right hand inside. The closer distance made the action rougher and took away some of Taylor’s room to operate. Those were the only rounds that offered Pili a reasonable argument on the scorecards.

Even during that stretch, Taylor continued finding openings with the jab and combinations. When Pili forced her toward a corner, Taylor punched her way out or held before the challenger could extend the exchange.

A more disciplined approach returned from Taylor in the ninth. She stayed near the edge of Pili’s range, slipped in a right hand, and changed levels with attacks to the body and head.

Despite continuing to come forward, Pili was following rather than cutting off the ring. Taylor controlled where the exchanges took place and rarely allowed her challenger to plant her feet long enough to throw sustained combinations.

The crowd rose as Taylor opened up in the 10th. She increased her output, fired fast combinations, and exchanged with Pili through the closing seconds. Taylor finished as the stronger and busier fighter before receiving a standing ovation at the final bell.

The wide scores accurately reflected the action. Pili had brief moments when her pressure made Taylor uncomfortable, but she never consistently solved the champion’s jab or timing.

It was a smart way for Katie to end a career filled with demanding fights. She did not chase a dramatic knockout or allow the emotion of the night to pull her into a reckless exchange. Instead, she relied on the speed, movement, combination punching, and experience that carried her to championships in two divisions.

The victory gave Taylor every major title at 140 pounds and a third reign as an undisputed champion. More importantly, it allowed her to leave boxing with her belts, her record intact apart from one defeat, and the final image of a packed Croke Park standing in appreciation.

Sports.title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili Live Results and Fight Updates
Sports.content:
Undercard action

Paddy Donovan stopped Tyrone McKenna in the fourth round after a cut forced the doctor to end their welterweight contest at Croke Park. Donovan dropped McKenna with a body shot in the second and continued targeting him with sharp, accurate punches. A damaging blow also opened a severe cut over McKenna’s right eye. Blood poured from the wound in the fourth, leaving the ringside doctor with little choice but to wave it off. The Limerick southpaw was patient behind his lead right hand, body attack, and head movement while McKenna struggled to catch him cleanly. .

Dave Allen’s heavyweight fight against Thomas Carty was ruled a no contest following a frightening incident in the opening round. Allen landed a short punch during a clinch near the ropes approximately 1:22 into the contest. Replays showed the shot catching Carty around the back of the head as the Irish heavyweight lost his balance. Carty tumbled through the ropes, landed awkwardly at ringside, and caught his foot in a chair. Medical personnel administered oxygen before determining that he could not continue, and officials treated the incident as an accidental foul. The crowd booed the ruling.

Taylor Bevan stopped Emmet Brennan 36 seconds into the sixth round after scoring five knockdowns in their super middleweight contest. Brennan had some early success, but Bevan’s sharper combinations and heavier punches soon took control. The Welsh prospect dropped Brennan twice during a punishing third round. A left hook to the body sent the Dublin fighter down again in the fifth. Bevan registered two more knockdowns at the beginning of the sixth before Brennan’s corner threw in the towel.

Molly McCann (5-0) defeated Sylwia Doligala (8-3-2) by unanimous decision after eight rounds in their super bantamweight bout. The judges scored the fight 80-72, 80-73, and 79-73. McCann controlled the action from the opening bell with steady pressure, a high work rate, and combinations to the head and body. Doligala remained durable but spent much of the contest moving backward and struggling to establish her offense. The accumulated punches left Doligala with swelling beneath one eye and blood on her vest by the later rounds. McCann completed the eight-round distance comfortably and earned her fifth win since leaving mixed martial arts for professional boxing.

Super bantamweight Joe McGrail (14-0, 7 KOs) stopped Matthew Boreland (7-1) with a left hook to the body in the fifth round of a 10-round scheduled bout. The win earned McGrail the vacant WBA Continental Gold title. Boreland fought competitively from the opening bell and began building momentum as the rounds progressed. McGrail remained composed, worked to the body, and found the decisive opening late in the fifth. His sharp left hook dropped Boreland, who remained down for the referee’s full count. The stoppage gave the 23-year-old Liverpool southpaw his seventh knockout and handed Boreland his first professional defeat.

Paddy Gallagher (17-6-1 entering) was initially announced as the majority decision winner over Paul Ryan (11-2 entering) after six competitive middleweight rounds. The score was given as 58-55 for Gallagher, but later reports stated that the referee’s card had been read incorrectly. The actual score was reported as 58-56 for Ryan, leaving the announced result subject to an official correction. Gallagher applied steady pressure and used his experience to force exchanges throughout the fight. The taller Ryan worked from his southpaw stance, boxing at range and looking to counter the advancing Belfast veteran. There were no knockdowns, and the result remained in question while the fighters’ official records were being updated.

Bobbi Flood (4-0, 2 KOs) defeated Jack Swallow (4-14-1) by unanimous decision over four rounds in a junior middleweight fight. The referee scored the contest 40-36, giving Flood every round. The 21-year-old Dublin native controlled the action from the opening bell with his cleaner and more consistent punching. Flood used his amateur experience to outbox Swallow, who remained durable but offered little effective offense. No knockdowns occurred as Flood continued piling up points without placing himself in unnecessary exchanges. The Croke Park crowd supported the local prospect throughout his comfortable points win.

Heavyweight prospect Adam Olaniyan (4-0, 4 KOs) overwhelmed Matej Hudak (6-3, 6 KOs) for a first-round stoppage on the preliminary card. The aggressive 20-year-old immediately closed the distance, established his jab, and hurt the much heavier Hudak with combinations upstairs.

A flurry sent Hudak to a knee as blood flowed from his nose and face. Referee Emile Tiedt stopped the fight after Hudak covered up without returning fire. Eddie Hearn is extremely high on Olaniyan, who has the raw talent and marketability to become Matchroom’s flagship heavyweight after Anthony Joshua retires.

Sports.title: WBO Orders Denzel Bentley–Yoenli Hernandez, Blocking McKenna Unification
Sports.content:
“OFFICIAL 🚨 WBO orders negotiations for Denzel Bentley vs. Yoenli Hernandez in the middleweight division. Both teams have 20 days to reach an agreement,” the WBO announced.

Bentley and McKenna had agreed to an IBF and WBO unification targeted for late 2026, but the fight still needed approval from both organizations. The WBO’s decision to enforce Hernandez’s mandatory removes the most important piece of that plan.

McKenna captured the vacant IBF title by defeating Etinosa Oliha in Dublin last month. Bentley became the full WBO champion in July after Janibek Alimkhanuly relinquished the belt before going up to super middleweight.

That created an opportunity to bring two titles together, and the Bentley–McKenna matchup made sense for both champions. Neither man is tied to one of the division’s established stars, while a unification would have given the winner a stronger negotiating position against WBC champion Carlos Adames or WBA champion Erislandy Lara.

Hernandez was never likely to step aside quietly. The Cuban contender earned his position and had already petitioned the WBO to enforce his title opportunity. Once the organization recognized him as Bentley’s mandatory, approving McKenna as a voluntary opponent became much harder to justify.

The WBO order does not permanently kill Bentley–McKenna. Bentley can face Hernandez first and return to the unification if he keeps his title. Hernandez would inherit that opportunity if he wins.

Bentley’s team can also request an exception allowing him to fight McKenna first, but the organization’s decision to order negotiations suggests it wants the mandatory completed without another delay. A unification agreement between the champions does not automatically override Hernandez’s rights.

The worst outcome for Bentley would be surrendering the WBO belt to preserve the McKenna fight. That would turn a two belt unification into a defense of McKenna’s IBF title and remove much of the contest’s value.

Postponement is more likely. Bentley can deal with Hernandez and revisit McKenna afterward, provided both champions still have their belts and their promoters remain interested.

For McKenna, the order forces him to find another opponent or remain inactive while Bentley fulfills his obligation. His own IBF mandatory situation may create another obstacle if the delay lasts too long.

The Bentley–McKenna agreement arrived before either organization had sanctioned the fight. The WBO has now made its position clear: Hernandez has the first claim on Bentley, and the unification must wait unless an exception is granted.

Ghana News.title: 2026 U-20 WWC: Black Princesses fall to Ecuador in opening game
Ghana News.content:
Ghana's U-20 women's national team had a troubling start to their FIFA Women's World Cup after losing to Ecuador.

The Black Princesses suffered a 3-0 loss to debutants Ecuador in their opening game of the tournament, which is being played in Poland.

Head coach Charles Sampson was without centre-back Margaret Agyapomaa, who was sent off in the final qualifier against Uganda.

Ecuador settled into the competition, brilliantly scoring after just two minutes to open the scoring against Ghana.

The Black Princesses struggled to break down the South Americans, as they were unable to string passes together.

Just when Sampson's side seemed to be settling into the game, Ecuador struck against just before the break to double their lead in the fixture.

The Black Princesses went into the break trailing by two goals, with hopes of fighting back to secure a point at least.

However, they were punished once again as Ecuador netted inside 24 minutes after the recess to wrap up all three points in their opening fixture.

The defeat leaves Ghana with just one win in their opening games at the World Cup since making their debut in 2010.

The Princesses will face South Korea and France in their next two games with the two teams playing out a 1-1 draw in the other Group C fixture.

Ghana News.title: GPL 2026/27: Hearts of Oak start new season with emphatic win over Berekum Chelsea
Ghana News.content:
Hearts of Oak kicked off their 2026/27 Ghana Premier League (GPL) campaign with a statement win over Berekum Chelsea at the University of Ghana Stadium.

John Antwi scored on his debut for the Phobians as they recorded a 4-0 victory in their first game of the new season.

The former Dreams FC forward didn't take long to settle as he got Hearts to a flying start after five minutes played from close range to make it 1-0.

While Chelsea pressed for the equaliser, Antwi scored once again in the 37th minute to double his side's lead at the University of Ghana Stadium, giving Hearts a 2-0 lead at the break.

After the recess, Hearts continued to press for more goals to stretch their advantage, but they had to wait until the 86th minute when Abdul Kader Kourama netted to make it 3-0.

As if the three goals were not enough, Ali Mohammed scored three minutes later from the penalty spot to make it four for the Accra-based side, running way with all three points.

Ghana News.title: GPL 2026/27: Asante Kotoko held by debutants Debibi United in four-goal thriller
Ghana News.content:
Newly promoted Debibi United produced a spirited performance to hold Asante Kotoko to a 2-2 draw in their opening Ghana Premier League fixture at the Berekum Golden City Park.

Kotoko looked set to begin the 2026-27 campaign with a victory after taking the lead through Yakubu Dogo, but Debibi United fought back twice to secure a point in their first-ever top-flight match.

The visitors made the brighter start and took the lead in the 15th minute.

Yakubu Dogo finished clinically after receiving a through ball from Hubert Gyau.

The forward took a touch before calmly placing his effort into the right corner to give Kotoko a 1-0 advantage.

The Porcupine Warriors went into half-time ahead and appeared on course to claim maximum points from their opening fixture.

But Debibi returned from the break with renewed purpose and levelled four minutes into the second half.

Richard Owusu stepped up to take a free-kick in the 49th minute and found the target, bringing the home side back into the contest at 1-1.

Kotoko were then forced to rely on goalkeeper Ibrahim Danlad to prevent Debibi from completing their comeback.

The pressure eventually paid off for Debibi in the 73rd minute.

Owusu struck again to complete his brace and put the home side in front for the first time in the match.

The turnaround gave Debibi United a 2-1 lead and put them within sight of a memorable victory over one of Ghana's biggest clubs.

However, just six minutes after Debibi had taken the lead, Hubert Gyau restored parity for the visitors in the 79th minute.

The Kotoko attacker reacted quickest to a goal-mouth scramble and found the back of the net to make it 2-2.

Neither side could find a decisive third goal in the closing stages, leaving the points shared after an entertaining encounter.

The result gives Debibi United an encouraging start to life in the league following their promotion from the Division One League.

The draw for Kotoko means new head coach Eric Tinkler begins his first competitive league game in charge with a point rather than a victory.

After the opening round of matches, Kotoko sit sixth in the league table, with Debibi United immediately behind them.

Kotoko will now turn their attention to their next fixture, when they host Heart of Lions.

Debibi United, meanwhile, face another challenge against Bechem United in their next league outing.

Ghana Premier League champions Medeama SC suffered a first-leg disappointment in the preliminary stage of the CAF Champions League following their defeat to TP Mazembe.

Medeama fell to a 1-0 loss to the DR Congo side at the TNA Stadium in Tarkwa as they began their quest to play in the continental club competition.

The Tarkwa-based side had control of the game in the opening 15 minutes and held Mazembe at bay for the majority of the opening half.

They also had chances to get in front in the game but were unable to breach the backline of the visitors as the first half ended goalless.

After the recess, the two teams had a go at each other in search of the opening goal.

It was TP Mazembe who came the closest to breaking the deadlock until they eventually did in the 86th minute to break the hearts of Medeama.

Medeama now have an uphill task of turning the tie around in the second leg when the two teams meet again.

Ghana News.title: Kumawu MP calls for urgent action on SHS infrastructure deficits
Ghana News.content:
The Member of Parliament for Kumawu, Ernest Yaw Anim, has appealed to the government and the Ministry of Education to urgently address infrastructure deficits confronting schools across the country.

He said inadequate classrooms, congestion and insufficient accommodation facilities continued to affect teaching and learning in some senior high schools.

Mr Anim made the call while supporting 500 BECE candidates in the Sekyere Kumawu District with essential items to prepare them for senior high school.

He noted that some students were confronted with inadequate sleeping facilities, including situations where available beds were insufficient to accommodate all students.

He therefore called for increased investment in educational infrastructure to provide students with safe and conducive environments for learning.

The MP also appealed to the government, the Ministry of Education and the Ghana Education Service to strengthen measures to motivate teachers and improve their working conditions.

He said motivated teachers were essential to delivering quality education and preparing students to become responsible and productive citizens.

Mr Anim further condemned sexual relationships between teachers and students, describing such conduct as unacceptable.

He called on teachers to desist from all forms of sexual misconduct involving students and urged the Ghana Education Service and the Ministry of Education to strengthen monitoring and supervision in schools.

He said headteachers, supervisors and other education authorities must ensure that teachers entrusted with the care of children acted professionally and protected the welfare and future of students.

Mr Anim said investing in human capital remained one of his major priorities, explaining that the ultimate goal was to see young people from the constituency become professionals who would contribute to the development of the district and Ghana.

He expressed the hope that beneficiaries of his educational support would eventually become doctors, nurses, engineers, lawyers, teachers and other professionals.

The MP said producing educated, productive and financially independent young people would constitute one of the greatest legacies of his service to the constituency.

Ghana News.title: Vice President urges Methodist Church to add digital skills to women’s training programmes
Ghana News.content:
Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang has urged the Methodist Church Ghana to incorporate digital skills training into its programmes for women to better prepare them for the changing world of work.

She said digital skills, financial literacy and entrepreneurship training were critical to reducing women’s economic dependence and equipping them to take advantage of emerging opportunities.

Professor Opoku-Agyemang made the call at the 3rd Biennial Conference of the Methodist Church Ghana, Northern Accra Diocese Women’s Fellowship, held at the Most Rev. Kwesi Dickson Memorial Methodist Church.

She said creating opportunities for women had significant benefits for the broader economy, noting that financial support and mentorship could help them turn their knowledge and skills into sustainable livelihoods while creating opportunities for others.

The Vice President highlighted the government’s efforts to expand technical and vocational training opportunities for women, as well as plans to launch the Women’s Development Bank, which is expected to provide financial support to women and women-led businesses.

She encouraged the women to extend the support they receive to others by sharing their knowledge, creating opportunities for others and responding to the needs of people in distress.

Professor Opoku-Agyemang also commended the Women’s Fellowship for its response to the Kantamanto Market fire, describing the intervention as an expression of the Methodist tradition of putting faith into service.

She further acknowledged the Methodist Church’s contribution to Ghana’s development through education, healthcare and moral formation, and urged the women to deepen that tradition of service.

The conference was held under the theme, “Walking in the Word, Equipped for Every Good Work.”

It brought together members of the Women’s Fellowship and other participants for worship, reflection and discussions focused on faith, service and personal development.

Ghana News.title: Forestry Commission arrests 12 illegal miners in Atewa Forest
Ghana News.content:
The Forestry Commission’s Rapid Response Unit (RRU) has arrested 12 persons suspected of engaging in illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, in the Atewa Range Forest Reserve in the Eastern Region.

The arrests were made during a dawn operation on Friday, September 4, 2026, around the Sagyimase community in Compartments 61 and 62 of the reserve, within the Kyebi Forest District.

According to the Forestry Commission, 17 personnel drawn from the Assin Fosu, Akim Oda and Juaso Forest Districts were deployed at about 1:30 a.m. for the covert operation aimed at clamping down on illegal mining in the reserve.

The team encountered a group of miners actively operating at the site and arrested 12 suspects, while others escaped into the surrounding bush.

The operation also led to the seizure of five motorbikes — three Royal motorbikes, one Apsonic Aloba and one Apsonic Paul Sport — as well as 11 shovels, water hoses, blankets used for washing gold and three gallons of petrol.

The Forestry Commission said the 12 suspects, together with two of the motorbikes and other exhibits, had been handed over to the Kyebi District Police Command for further investigation and prosecution.

The remaining three motorbikes have been kept at the Kyebi District Office of the Forest Services Division for safekeeping.

The Commission said the operation was conducted successfully without casualties and described the arrests and seizure of equipment as a deterrent to illegal mining activities within forest reserves.

The Atewa Range Forest Reserve is a major biodiversity hotspot and critical watershed, serving as the headwaters of the Birim, Densu and Ayensu rivers.

These rivers provide water to millions of people, including residents of Accra and surrounding communities.

However, the reserve has come under increasing pressure from illegal mining and logging, raising concerns over the potential threat to Ghana’s water security and biodiversity.

The Forestry Commission has vowed to sustain its operations to flush out illegal miners who continue to invade forest reserves.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.
