World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Connects Climate Solutions From Field To Factory
World.content:
As rainfall becomes less predictable, researchers are developing improved seed, testing more efficient irrigation and using digital tools to track water losses. Getting these solutions to farmers could protect harvests and provide Ethiopia’s textile factories with more locally grown fibre.

When the rains arrive late or stop too soon, cotton farmer Debalkie Abate can no longer depend on the planting calendar he once knew. But researchers and water specialists are working on an alternative: improved seed, better-timed irrigation and more accurate climate information that could help farmers continue producing despite increasingly unpredictable weather.

“The weather has become much less predictable than it was a decade ago,” Abate says. “Sometimes the rains arrive late, sometimes they stop too early. Without irrigation we cannot rely on rainfall alone.”

Ethiopia already possesses tools that could reduce that risk. Research in its cotton-growing lowlands shows how carefully timed irrigation can make better use of limited water. New assessments are identifying irrigation losses, while researchers develop varieties intended to improve productivity and fibre quality.



The challenge is to move those solutions from research centres into farmers’ fields, protecting livelihoods and providing Ethiopia’s textile industry with a more reliable supply of locally grown fibre.

The work reflects a wider continental shift. In February 2026, the African Union called for greater support to help smallholders—particularly women—access climate-resilient seed, irrigation and insurance. It also urged countries to share research and solutions involving digital agriculture, climate information and resilient infrastructure.

Using less water more effectively

The need to adapt is becoming more urgent. The Ethiopian Meteorological Institute’s 2025 climate projections anticipate continued warming under both medium- and high-emissions scenarios. Rainfall outcomes differ by region and season, with some areas potentially receiving more rain while others experience greater variability.

For farmers, the problem is not simply less rain. It is rain that can no longer be assumed to arrive when the crop most needs it.

At an AGRA agrifood-systems retreat in April 2026 , Ethiopia highlighted lessons from cluster-based approaches and digital advisory systems. It also identified stronger agricultural financing and greater climate finance for smallholders as priorities—support needed to move adaptation tools into farmers’ hands.

Research at Melka Werer in the semi-arid Middle Awash offers one possible response. Trials examined how cotton grown on heavy Vertisol soils performed under different irrigation schedules.

The study, available through the UN Food and Agriculture Organization , found that three strategically timed irrigations—at planting, flowering and boll formation—could produce a yield comparable with a far more intensive schedule while using about 40% less irrigation water, provided seasonal rain was normal and well distributed.

The research does not offer a ready-made prescription. The trials were conducted in the 1980s, relied partly on unpublished research-station data and involved specific varieties and soil conditions. Researchers would need to test the approach with current seed, weather patterns and farm conditions before recommending it widely.

Its value lies in showing what may be possible: improving productivity does not necessarily mean applying more water. Timing can matter as much as volume.

Finding where the water goes

More recent work is identifying another part of the solution—reducing losses before water reaches the field.

A 2025 International Water Management Institute assessment found that the Amibara irrigation scheme in the Awash River Basin was operating at just 32% overall efficiency, down from its original 49%.

Researchers combined remote-sensing information, digital mapping and field measurements to identify leakage, poor distribution and operational problems. They found that although water was available at the diversion point, supplies often fell short of crop needs farther along the scheme because of internal bottlenecks.

Digital water accounting can guide repairs and investment. It also shifts some responsibility away from farmers: advice on when to irrigate has limited value if ageing or silted canals cannot deliver water reliably.

IWMI says measures such as canal lining, improved furrows, low-cost moisture sensors and precision irrigation could raise efficiency. These interventions require investment, but could allow farmers to produce more with the water already available.

Getting improved seed to farmers

Water alone will not build resilience. Farmers also need varieties that can cope with heat, drought, pests and, in some irrigated areas, salinity without sacrificing the fibre quality manufacturers require.

At the Werer Agricultural Research Center in Afar, researchers have developed improved cotton varieties intended to raise yields and fibre quality. But limited capacity to multiply the seed has slowed distribution.

“Financial shortages and limited human resources have prevented multiplication of these improved varieties, leaving valuable research results underutilised,” says Berhanu Megersa, director general of the centre.

Recent research illustrates why seed access matters. A 2024 study of irrigated cotton in Ethiopia found that seed source, variety and planting rate significantly affected yields.

But a promising variety at a research station cannot protect Abate’s harvest. Seed must be multiplied and distributed, while extension officers help farmers select the right variety for local conditions. Seasonal forecasts also need to reach producers before planting and be translated into practical decisions about planting dates and irrigation.

Connecting farms and factories

Close 

The benefits could extend along Ethiopia’s value chain. Cotton must be ginned, spun into yarn, woven or knitted, and finished before a clothing factory can use it.

“If farmers cannot produce enough quality cotton, the entire manufacturing chain feels the impact,” Megersa says.

Abeje Menegesha, procurement manager at Amibara Agricultural Development PLC, says local fibre is preferred but its supply remains inconsistent.

“Our first choice is always Ethiopian cotton because it shortens supply chains and supports local farmers,” Menegesha says. “However, domestic production still does not consistently meet our requirements in quantity and quality.”

The work underway suggests Ethiopia does not need to wait for one transformative invention. It needs to connect several practical responses: repair irrigation systems, retest efficient watering schedules, multiply improved seed, deliver usable forecasts and give farmers a predictable market.

Farmer Abeje Selelew sees the opportunity in generational terms.

“I hope my children will see Ethiopian cotton processed into Ethiopian textiles and clothing sold across Africa and beyond,” he says. “When farmers receive fair prices and industries buy more local cotton, everyone along the value chain benefits.”

For Abate, the starting point remains his next planting season. The weather may be less predictable, but Ethiopia’s response does not have to be. Much of the knowledge already exists. The test now is whether it can reach his field in time.

World.title: Fisherman captures a crazy video of an alligator chasing a bear across a Florida river
World.content:
Let's head down to Florida where anything can and does take place. If you can dream it up, there's a good chance it will go down in the Sunshine State. That goes for both people and animals.

The latest example to prove that point comes from a fisherman out on the Kissimmee river near Lake Okeechobee. Captain Justin Morgan, who runs a fishing guide service, captured the crazy video.

The clip shows a scene that you don't see every day, a bear swimming across the river with an alligator hot on its trail chasing it towards the shore.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"Alligator tracking down a bear across the Kissimmee river near Lake Okeechobee," the captain captioned the action.

"We were out bluegill fishing when what from a distance looked like a wild hog was a black bear swimming across the Kissimmee with a gator not far behind! Not something we get to see everyday but really cool to watch!"

SON OF FLORIDA ALLIGATOR ATTACK VICTIM SAYS TOURISTS AND TIKTOKERS ARE EMBOLDENING THE GATORS

This was close to giving us a straight out of a nature documentary look at what would happen if an alligator and a black bear ever went at it in the wild.

That begs the question. What would happen? Did the alligator give chase after mistaking the bear for something else it could easily take down?

Does the advantage lean towards the alligator in the water and the bear on land? That's what I would assume.

GEAR UP FOR FALL WITH LABOR DAY DEALS ON HUNTING, FISHING, CAMPING AND OUTDOOR LIVING ESSENTIALS

World.title: Raskin calls Piker’s rhetoric 'irrelevant distraction' after the streamer said he'd vote for Hamas over Israel
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., dismissed scrutiny of far-left streamer Hasan Piker's rhetoric about Hamas as an "irrelevant distraction" Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," as host Kristen Welker pressed him over Democratic divisions surrounding Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's relationship with the controversial online personality.

Welker played Raskin a clip of Piker saying he would vote Hamas over Israel "every single time" and asked whether the Democratic Party’s tent was large enough to include the streamer.

"I don’t even know if Hasan Piker considers himself a Democrat. I know he attacked me for campaigning with Callie Barr and Sean McCann and other Democrats in Michigan. I think all of that is an irrelevant distraction," Raskin said. "Obviously, nobody supports Hamas, a terrorist organization which brutally attacked Israel on Oct. 7."

STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’

Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the RNC, pointed to Piker’s growing role in Democratic politics and his support for socialist candidates as she warned that his influence could become a broader liability for the party heading into November.

"The Democrat Party is being driven off [a] cliff by socialists who are driving blindfolded while arguing about the view," Baldassarre said in a recent statement to Fox News Digital. "Unless Democrats hit the brakes, every candidate on the ballot will have to answer for socialists’ outrageous beliefs that will bankrupt our country and strip every American of safety, sanity, and freedom."

Raskin's comments came after he campaigned alongside El-Sayed in Michigan in late August. El-Sayed has continued to face questions over his ties to Piker as some Democrats have publicly distanced themselves from the streamer.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA BACKS 'OUR TWITCH STREAMER' HASAN PIKER, RIPS ANTI-SOCIALISM HOUSE RESOLUTION

Piker, who endorsed El-Sayed and appeared at multiple campaign events during the Democratic primary, reiterated his comparison between Hamas and Israel during an April appearance on "Pod Save America."

"I’ve also said I’m a harm reduction voter. I’m a lesser evil voter, and therefore I would vote for Hamas over Israel every single time," Piker said in the clip played for Raskin on Sunday.

Piker has also faced renewed criticism for comments involving American Jews. Fox News Digital reported that he warned on a livestream that if American Jews continued presenting themselves as "singularly invested in Israel," someone could eventually "take action" against them.

HASAN PIKER INSISTS ABDUL EL-SAYED ASKED HIM TO 'STUMP' FOR MICHIGAN CAMPAIGN AMID BACKLASH

El-Sayed responded to that controversy by stressing that the streamer was not a spokesman for his campaign.

"I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople," El-Sayed said.

El-Sayed has nevertheless resisted calls to fully disavow Piker. During a recent interview with Stephen A. Smith, he said his goal was to bring the streamer's millions of listeners into the electoral process rather than abandon them over disagreements.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"What I’m saying is there are 3 million people who listen to Hasan," El-Sayed said. "I want to offer them a pathway into an electoral movement."

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., called the attention devoted to Piker "absolutely ludicrous," while Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash, said Democrats should engage his audience even if they disagree with some of his views. Other Democrats have urged the party to distance itself from him.

Fox News Digital reached out to Piker for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

World.title: Army combat veteran challenging Mike Lawler calls Hegseth national security 'hazard,' backs impeachment
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democratic congressional candidate Cait Conley, a 16-year Army combat veteran challenging Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in New York's 17th Congressional District, said Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" that she would support impeaching War Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of endangering U.S. national security.

Anchor Dana Bash asked Conley whether, if elected to Congress, she would support removing Hegseth from office amid recent scrutiny of his leadership at the Pentagon.

"I believe he has been a hazard to American national security and a disgrace to the office," Conley said. "I would absolutely support removing him from office because his actions and decisions are failing service members who have sworn an oath to this country and deserve respect."

DEM CANDIDATE CLEARS CROWDED FIELD TO FACE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT IN NY

Bash pressed Conley to clarify whether "removing" Hegseth meant she would actually vote for articles of impeachment against the Pentagon chief.

"Against Pete Hegseth for his failure to protect America? Yes," Conley replied.

Lawler campaign manager Ciro Riccardi seized on the impeachment declaration in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday, linking it to his campaign’s broader criticism of Conley following her appearance on CNN.

"Cait Conley’s refusal to disavow Zohran Mamdani and the DSA is disqualifying. She is just as extreme as the rest and that was exposed today for all to see, including embracing impeachment," Riccardi said.

TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS

Conley's declaration came months after House Democrats formally introduced six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of high crimes and misdemeanors over his handling of the Iran war, military strikes on alleged drug vessels, his use of Signal to discuss military operations, congressional oversight and other matters.

Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson dismissed that effort in an April statement to Fox News Digital and said Hegseth would remain focused on the department’s mission.

"This is just another Democrat trying to make headlines as the Department of War decisively and overwhelmingly achieved the president's objectives in Iran," Wilson said. "Secretary Hegseth will continue to protect the homeland and project peace through strength. This is just another charade in an attempt to distract the American people from the major successes we have had here at the Department of War."

Hegseth has also rejected previous waves of criticism surrounding his leadership. Amid calls for his removal following scrutiny of his use of Signal in 2025, Hegseth accused critics and the media of relying on disgruntled former employees to damage his reputation.

HEGSETH TURNS TABLES ON DEMS AS SPARKS FLY DURING HEARING CLASH: 'I PUT THIS ON YOU'

"This is what the media does. They take anonymous sources from disgruntled former employees, and then they try to slash and burn people and ruin their reputations," Hegseth said at the time. "It’s not going to work with me."

Pressure on Hegseth has more recently crossed party lines. Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., called on President Donald Trump last week to replace Hegseth following Army Secretary Dan Driscoll's resignation.

"I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it," Tillis said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

The White House pushed back on Tillis’ criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying Trump remained firmly behind Hegseth.

"The President has complete trust in Secretary Hegseth, who is doing an incredible job leading the Pentagon," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said.

Driscoll’s departure followed reported tensions with Hegseth over Army leadership and modernization. A source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital that Driscoll had raised concerns about Hegseth blocking Army transformation efforts by removing generals involved in them. Driscoll, however, publicly praised Hegseth upon leaving office, saying the Army’s progress would not have been possible without his support.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital reached out to Hegseth's office, the White House and Conley for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

World.title: James Franklin questions 'un-American' Virginia Tech penalty for high-fiving military cadets after touchdown
World.content:
The James Franklin era at Virginia Tech got off to an emphatic start on Saturday with the Hokies trouncing VMI by a count of 73-3. It was very much a celebration in Blacksburg, and as stress-free a day as the Hokies will have all season, but Franklin did have a small bone to pick with the officiating crew after the final whistle.

A coach on the winning side of a 70-point blowout shouldn't have any complaints, but Franklin's issue appears to be well warranted.

"We got a penalty for high-fiving one of our members of the core," Franklin said. "Not a huge fan. I don’t know why we can’t high-five somebody in the military; it seems somewhat un-American to me."

MICHIGAN-WESTERN MICHIGAN CLOCK CONTROVERSY LEAVES PLAYERS, FANS AND A RULES ANALYST PUZZLED

Unlike in the NFL, where there are essentially no limitations on what players can do in terms of celebrating, there is a set of rules for excessive celebrations in college football. Apparently, those rules are strictly applied, even when the player in question is celebrating with cadets seated in the front row.

Virginia Tech running back Marcellous Hawkins Jr. was the player flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct after scoring what was his third touchdown of the evening.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

After punching it into the end zone with 6:59 left in the third quarter, Hawkins immediately ran over to the large group of cadets and high-fived a number of them, which is what drew the penalty from an official in the end zone.

According to NCAA Rule 9-2, players are prohibited from any "delayed, excessive, prolonged or choreographed act by which a player (or players) attempts to focus attention upon himself (or themselves)."

Players are also mandated to immediately return the football to an official after scoring. Hawkins held onto the football while celebrating with the cadets, which very well could have led to the penalty flag being thrown.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Despite the "un-American" penalty that Franklin very much did not appreciate, it was a big-time Saturday for the Hokies as they picked up 619 yards and held VMI to just 83 of its own.

Virginia Tech's Corps of Cadets dates back to 1872, and the school remains one of a select few public universities with both an active cadet corps and a civilian campus lifestyle today.

World.title: NFL signs Roger Goodell through 2030 season as serious issues over antitrust exemption and ongoing growth loom
World.content:
Roger Goodell will remain the commissioner of America's strongest and most popular professional sports league at least through March of 2031, following an NFL announcement that he has signed a contract extension.

The league's Compensation Committee on Sunday notified the league's owners that it reached a four-season extension with Goodell.

The deal will carry Goodell through the end of the 2030 season and expire just prior to the 2031 NFL Draft when he will be 71 years old.

Terms of the new extension are not known and won't be announced as they are between an individual and a privately held company.

But one industry compensation consultant source told OutKick that Goodell was expected to reach $300 million over the four-year term if he meets the top tier of his deal's incentive thresholds.

Compensation Committee Chairman Robert Kraft, the New England Patriots owner and ally of Goodell, sent a memo to the rest of the league's 31 owners announcing the deal:

"As members of the Compensation Committee, we’re pleased to announce that we have reached agreement with Roger to remain as Commissioner through the 2030 League Season, ending on March 31, 2031.

"Throughout the negotiation process, the Committee worked closely with an independent third-party compensation consultant and outside counsel to structure a deal that aligns Roger’s compensation with the League’s long-term interests and success.

"To that end, the agreement is heavily performance based, with more than 95% of the total compensation tied to Roger’s and the NFL’s performance measured against various metrics and at the discretion of the Compensation Committee.

"We believe we are very fortunate to have Roger at the helm for the next four years. If any of you has any questions, please reach out to any of us."

The memo is from Kraft, New York Giants owner John Mara, Jacksonville Jaguars owner Shad Khan, Cleveland Browns owner Jimmy Haslam, Arizona Cardinals owner Michael Bidwill, and Denver Broncos owner Greg Penner – all of whom make up the committee.

This is Goodell's fifth contract extension since he became commissioner in September 2006.

At the end of this extension, Goodell will have served 24 years in his role. That would make him the second-longest serving commissioner in league history behind only Pete Rozelle who served 29 years and 10 months from 1960 to 1989.

NFL COMMISSIONER ROGER GOODELL CONFIRMS LEAGUE WANTS MULTIPLE TEAMS BASED OUTSIDE THE US: 'NO DOUBT'

The NFL's current collective bargaining agreement, which Goodell helped finalize in 2020, expires in March 2031, when Goodell's new extension will expire.

Goodell's tenure has been defined by aggressive commercial growth, enormous media-rights agreements, games expanding to international markets, increased emphasis on player safety and labor peace after the 2011 lockout.

The valuation of franchises under Goodell has skyrocketed with the Seattle Seahawks being the latest example in a sale worth $9.612 billion.

Those past victories and the possibility of new television contract coming online around 2029 and perhaps expansion of the business model to include flag football, more international revenue and games, and perhaps even expansion, obviously gave Goodell confidence to tie his compensation to performance incentives.

CONGRESS TARGETS NFL'S $110B BROADCAST MODEL AS JIM JORDAN REQUESTS GOODELL TESTIFY AT JUNE 10 HEARING

Simply: If he continues to author significant growth, he'll benefit.

And if he doesn't, which would be highly improbable given the NFL's history, then he won't.

Goodell, by the way, has not been without controversy during his tenure.

He has guided the league through controversies such as Spygate, Deflategate, an apparent rise in domestic-violence cases, concussion concerns, protests by players during the national anthem, lawsuits, and criticism that league discipline can be inconsistent.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Kraft recently outlined how the commissioner and, indeed, the entire league is facing enormous pressure from Congress and other government entities tied to its 65-year-old antitrust exemption.

There are serious questions whether the league is abusing it to gouge fans and force games behind paywalled streaming services and Goodell was even recently invited to testify on the subject before Congress.

He declined. But with his new term now secured, the question remains when, rather than if, he'll have to answer for the league's polices before fans and lawmakers.

World.title: Trump admin’s mail-in ballot fight lands back at Supreme Court
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration filed a new appeal with the Supreme Court on Sunday seeking to enforce restrictions on mail ballots, as the ballots begin entering states across the country ahead of the midterm elections.

The filing asks the high court to stay a preliminary injunction issued Friday by U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani that prevents the U.S. Postal Service from enforcing several requirements for ballot mail in the November elections.

"Ballots have already begun to be mailed in North Carolina, and more States will begin the mailing process as the injunction remains in place — including Alabama on September 9 and at least five States the week of September 13," Solicitor General John Sauer wrote.

FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS

"Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them," he added.

Sauer argued that allowing the injunction to remain in place risks "sowing confusion and chaos" as more states begin mailing ballots because preparations to comply with the Postal Service rule remain voluntary rather than mandatory.

The administration maintains the rule is "a lawful and modest exercise of rulemaking authority delegated by Congress to the Postal Service" and "regulates the U.S. Mail, not federal elections."

The rule requires federal election ballots sent through the mail to use envelopes that include the official Election Mail logo, meet automation requirements and carry unique barcodes, according to the filing. State election officials would also have to submit envelope designs for review and provide the Postal Service with information about intended ballot recipients.

The administration says the requirements are intended to improve the handling and delivery of ballot mail and protect the mail system from being used to facilitate voter fraud.

MAIL-VOTING CRACKDOWN MOVES AHEAD AS TRUMP COURT WIN OPENS DOOR TO FEDERAL ACTION

The rule would not give the Postal Service authority to determine who is eligible to vote by mail or whether ballots should be counted, responsibilities that would remain with state and local election officials.

Democratic-led states and voting rights groups challenging the restrictions contend the changes are unconstitutional, while election officials have argued there is not enough time to revise their systems to comply before November.

The administration disputes those arguments, saying Congress gave the Postal Service broad authority to regulate the handling and delivery of mail and that the rule does not dictate ballot content, determine voter eligibility, establish election deadlines or govern how ballots are counted.

The filing marks the third time the administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene in the dispute. The high court previously allowed the administration’s plan to move forward but has not ruled on whether the restrictions themselves are legal.

The battle could have major ramifications for the November elections, when control of Congress is at stake. Nearly one-third of U.S. voters cast ballots by mail.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: US-backed effort to disarm Iraq’s Iran-linked militias hits setback, experts say
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration’s push to compel the new Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to dismantle pro-Iran terrorist militias is moving forward — even with some setbacks.

As Mideast experts are taking a wait-and-see approach tinged with mild optimism, a senior Iraqi official announced in late August that Baghdad will not treat Sept. 30 as a deadline to disarm the pro-Iran groups known as the Popular Mobilization Units (PMU), also called the Popular Mobilization Forces.

The Iraqi government is seeking to exercise control over the rogue state-affiliated militias with a strategy to integrate them into the state apparatus. The radical Iraqi Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, who leads Saraya al-Salam armed group, said in May that he favored integration. Some of the more hardline pro-Iranian regime militias, like Kataeb Hezbollah and Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, declared that they will not disarm or integrate into the state.

The official, Qasim al-Araji, security advisor to the prime minister, told Al Iraqiya on Aug. 23, "Sept. 30 is the date for the international coalition to depart, not the deadline to hand over weapons." The international coalition is the U.S.-led force that defeated the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria during President Trump’s first term. It is unclear why Iraq’s government is walking back the disarmament deadline for the PMU.

IRAN'S WAR ON AMERICANS BEGAN DECADES AGO. THESE FAMILIES STILL CARRY THE SCARS

A spokesman for the Iraqi embassy declined to comment on the mixed messaging from Iraq’s government and on the timetable for dissolving or integrating the PMU.

Just days before al-Araji’s announcement, a representative of the Iraqi government sent Fox News Digital a statement: "Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi: All political forces fully agree on moving forward with restricting weapons to state control, and work is underway on mechanisms for surrendering weapons and bringing this issue to a complete end."

Al-Zaidi told the Baghdad Dialogue Conference at the same time that "all political forces agree on moving forward to ensure that all arms remain under state authority and on developing mechanisms for the handover of weapons. There are no intentions or prospects of any military confrontation, and we will not allow Iraq’s enemies to exploit any opportunity. The presence of weapons outside state authority creates an environment that discourages investment, which is unacceptable because it does not serve the interests of Iraqis."

In May, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Ali Maarij Al-Bahadly, Iraq’s deputy minister of oil, because he, according to the designation, "abuses his position to facilitate the diversion of oil to be sold for the benefit of the Iranian regime and its proxy militias in Iraq." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time, "Like a rogue gang, the Iranian regime is pillaging resources that rightfully belong to the Iraqi people," adding "Treasury will not stand idly by as Iran's military exploits Iraqi oil to fund terrorism against the United States and our partners."

In late August, the UAE's The National paper reported that "Iraq's anti-corruption body announced that deputy oil minister, Al-Bahadly, was sentenced to seven years in prison and fined millions of dollars for corruption.

Reacting to reports that Iran approved passage of Iraqi oil tankers via the Strait of Hormuz, Alberto Fernandez, former U.S. ambassador and Mideast analyst, claimed that "the profit from that Iraqi oil goes, in part, to pay for Iran’s own Iraqi militias/death squads on the Iraqi government’s payroll."

An Iraqi government spokesman dismissed Fernandez's comments, telling Fox News Digital, "That is not accurate."

TRUMP’S COUNTERTERRORISM STRATEGY SCORES BIG WINS AGAINST GLOBAL TERROR THREATS

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "Iraq has embarked on a new direction under the leadership of Prime Minister Al-Zaidi in full partnership with the United States. As President Trump made clear when he hosted Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s historic July 14 visit, the United States strongly supports his vision to ensure a brighter future for all Iraqis free from terrorism, to prevent attacks in and from Iraqi territory, and to deliver a strong and mutually beneficial U.S.-Iraq partnership."

Entifadh Qanbar, a former spokesman for the deputy prime minister of Iraq during the George W. Bush administration, told Fox News Digital: "We were all hoping that Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi would take decisive action against the militias, especially after his visit to the White House and the widespread praise he received from President Trump. I was always skeptical, very skeptical, but I believed he deserved a chance."

Qanbar added, "Initially, some militias such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Imam Ali (sanctioned by the U.S.) merely issued statements claiming they would hand over their weapons. There has been no credible evidence that they have actually disarmed."

IRAN’S GUTTED RANKS LEAVE LOYALISTS FILLING CRITICAL POSTS — WITH ONE GLARING PROBLEM

Qanbar claimed that "any remaining hope was further diminished after IRGC [Islamic Republic Guard Corps] Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani visited Baghdad. According to multiple reports, he instructed militia leaders to slow down any discussion of disarmament, reject the September 30 deadline, and maintain their weapons as part of Iran’s broader regional deterrence strategy."

When asked about Iraqi state efforts to dismantle the PMU, Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior non-resident fellow at the New Lines Institute in Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital, "The Iraqi government is trying. It genuinely carried out some moves. Unfortunately, because the militias are extremely willing to use force against their own people, including against security forces, the government finds itself in a position of backing down in the face of these militias."

She noted, "The militias have penetrated most state institutions… and you see repeated situations of the state backing down." Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iran-backed group designated by the U.S. as a terrorist organization, kidnapped Tsurkov in 2023 and held her hostage for nearly two years. The Trump administration secured her release in 2025.

The power of the PMU was demonstrated in a recent setback for the Iraqi government.

Both Qanbar and Tsurkov cited the case of the Iraqi Counter Terrorism Service (CTS), which arrested Abbas al-Yaqubi, the head of intelligence for the Popular Mobilization Forces’ Baghdad Belt Operations Command.

A few days after al-Yaqubi’s arrest, he was transferred to the PMU intelligence branch. Qanbar said: "Al-Yaqubi has long been involved in violence against Iraqi activists, and many viewed his arrest as an important signal that the government was finally willing to confront powerful militia figures. What seemed like a significant step forward turned into a major setback."

World.title: As Trump pushes for data centers, voters in key midterm races say they don’t want them
World.content:
DES MOINES, Iowa — Dawn Vogel, a Republican county supervisor in rural Buchanan County, Iowa, doesn’t have a lot in common with the leading democratic socialists in Congress. But on this bit of policy they agree: Data centers are proliferating across the American landscape too fast.

Vogel voted earlier this year for a moratorium that temporarily bans data centers from setting up shop in her heavily Republican county, which favored President Donald Trump 63%-35% in 2024. In Washington, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. — the nation’s two most prominent democratic socialists — have proposed a similar moratorium that would cover the entire country.

“I don’t think this is a Republican or Democratic issue,” Vogel said on the sidelines of the Iowa State Association of Counties’ annual conference here in late August, adding that she hasn’t talked to a single voter at home who wants data centers.

Dawn Vogel, a Republican supervisor in Buchanan County, Iowa, voted for a temporary moratorium on data centers in the county. Frank Thorp V for NBC News

“It’s an issue of what’s the best use for the land, what’s the best use for our natural resources,” she said. “You can have all the data you want to in the world, but if you don’t have water to drink, you don’t have humans to use the data.”

That point of view places Vogel in a loose, but very large, populist coalition that is fighting the rise of data centers at the ballot box, with yard signs, in courts and at all levels of government as November’s midterm elections approach.

An NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey, conducted from Aug. 20 through Sept. 1, found that 69% of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their local area, with 45% saying they “strongly oppose” the idea.

They are all at odds with President Donald Trump.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the end of August. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

But it’s more about backyards than being seen as backward, according to voters who spoke to NBC News on a recent road trip along Interstate 80 from Nebraska to New Jersey — a swath that includes eight swing districts key to determining which party will control the House next year and two marquee Senate races. These voters, who span the political spectrum, said they don’t want data centers anywhere near their communities.

For some, the issue has become a touchstone for the feeling that the powerful are taking advantage of the powerless.

“All of the data centers that are starting to pop up in areas, I find that troublesome because it drives utility costs for citizens in the area,” said Tamara Clark, 49, a Democratic voter who works in the healthcare industry. “I don’t feel like the rich should continuously get rich while we have to grovel for what we need in our everyday necessities.”

In Clark’s congressional district, Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, a 22-term incumbent, is using the issue against her rival, Republican Derek Merrin, who cast a 2017 vote in the state Legislature that helped extend tax breaks to companies that build data centers in the state.

Tamara Clark, an Ohio Democrat, said she finds it "troublesome" that data centers drive up utility costs for nearby citizens. Frank Thorp V for NBC News

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is seeking to hold his seat against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown, was a full-throated advocate for data centers when he was the state’s lieutenant governor. But in July, he introduced legislation in the Senate that would require utility companies to charge large-scale data center operators enough money to cover the costs of increased electricity and water use.

His change of tune reflects a broader shift among elected officials who embraced data centers as a way to bring jobs and tax revenue to their cities, counties and states. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, D-Pa., who is on the ballot in November, signed a new batch of data center regulations in August after having encouraged companies to locate them in his state.

While Republican voters are more supportive of data centers than Democrats and independents, the majority of them remain opposed — 57% to 43% — according to the NBC News Decision Desk poll. The survey found that 81% of Democrats and 71% of independents are against data centers being built in their communities.

While supporters have been less demonstrative, their ranks extend beyond the AI companies building data centers and the politicians who have looked to them as economic development engines.

National and local labor unions involved in the construction and maintenance of data centers tout them as a boon for workers, both as a source of jobs and for high rates of pay. Several data center workers in Ohio spoke to NBC News about those benefits on the condition of anonymity because, according to one of them, they have agreed not to discuss their jobs with the media.

That worker said he can make as much as $5,000 in a week, including overtime, at a relatively low-level union job.

“It’s helping a lot of people — a lot of work going on, a lot of people benefiting from it,” the data center worker said, adding that he was warned by friends about problems, from overuse of water resources to weird ringing sounds, that he has not witnessed at his workplace.

“It’s scary,” he said. “You got a lot of people that say all these horrific things. I was told all these negative things about data centers, and then I started working at one, and I didn’t see any of the things I was told about.”

He said he would like to see proponents and critics work together to fix any problems with data centers so that they can continue to be built and operate without disruption to the surrounding communities.

Jordan Cloe, an electrician, is concerned about a data center's water consumption in Altoona, Iowa. Frank Thorp V for NBC News

But Jordan Cloe, 47, an electrician from Bondurant, in Iowa’s hotly contested 3rd Congressional District, said he’s worried about the resources used by a data center in neighboring Altoona.

“Did we have any data on what the implications were about water consumption or anything? Like, we just built a power grid where that thing sits,” he said. “Did we get to use that? No, they gobbled that up.”

Cloe, who said he aligns more with Democrats, said he doesn’t know anything about Sarah Trone Garriott, the Democratic challenger to Republican Rep. Zach Nunn, but that he plans to vote for her in November.

For Vogel, the county supervisor, the unresolved questions are enough reason to keep data centers out of her county — at least for now.

“We need to do what’s best for Buchanan County and then, you know, if the companies want to come knock on the door,” she said, “then we’ll talk.”

World.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow mail ballot restrictions to move forward for a third time
World.content:
The Trump administration on Sunday asked the Supreme Court to temporarily allow the U.S. Postal Service to exert some control over mail-in voting in the upcoming midterm elections, just two days after a federal judge blocked the USPS from doing so.

It’s the third time the Trump administration has escalated this matter to the Supreme Court, as North Carolina last week became the first state to begin sending mail-in ballots to voters less than 60 days before the midterm elections.

On Friday, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani issued an order preventing the administration from carrying out the Trump-directed USPS regulation on mail-in ballots.

The directive is the president’s latest attempt to impose new forms of federal control over elections, which are typically run by states.

It would allow the USPS to track mail-in ballots and potentially reject ballots that are sent to and from voters not included in a federal database.

This application to the court comes after Talwani issued a preliminary block on enforcing the USPS rule, saying it’s likely unlawful and unconstitutional for the federal government to dictate how mail-in ballots are handled.

In her order Friday, Talwani also cited the rushed nature of the rule, writing that the “immediate implementation of the Final Rule issued less than seventy days before the November 2026 election threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.”

In Sunday’s filing to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued: “Contrary to the claims of the district court and respondents that the Postal Service is trying to federalize the rules for mail-in voting, the Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots sent via U.S. Mail.”

Specifically, the filing argues, the rule “requires States to upload the name, address, and barcode information of intended recipients of ballot mail in an online portal — information that election officials would necessarily already possess to send ballot mail under the Rule to those recipients.”

“The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures. The Rule thus plainly does not seize control of States’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail,” the filing adds.

Sunday’s application to the Supreme Court comes after the Trump administration already twice asked the highest court to intervene in this case. The Justice Department withdrew its previous pending request after submitting this morning’s application related to Talwani’s most recent order.

The rule stems from a March executive order signed by President Donald Trump.

It came just weeks after the president suggested that Republicans should “nationalize” elections, a comment that drew criticism from local election officials and lawmakers from Trump’s own party.

World.title: Plane with Amazon logo crashes outside Miami airport
World.content:
A plane with Amazon’s logo on its tail crashed just outside Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon.

Details of the crash were not immediately available, but video showed plumes of smoke billowing from the site. It appears that the aircraft crashed onto a road outside the airport.

A Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. ET while landing in Miami, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. The plane was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The FAA identified the aircraft as a 21 Air flight. A spokesperson for Miami International Airport identified it as a Prime Air flight.

The website for 21 Air lists Prime Air, an Amazon company, as one of its customers. Amazon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

All runways and taxiways at the Miami airport were closed due to a ground stop following the incident, the airport spokesperson said in a statement.

More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the scene, and firefighters are working to extinguish a fire that broke out as a result of the crash, the agency said in a statement. There are “multiple patients” involved in the incident, it added.

Open a few tabs and search for the exact same product at a handful of retailers to weigh which one offers the lowest price and lowest shipping fee. You can also shop through cash back apps and browser extensions online, which help you find additional promo codes and rewards, she says.

Shipping fees add up, especially if you’re placing online orders at numerous retailers or buying big-ticket products that require installation. If your total goes up drastically once you consider shipping fees, see if you can buy online and pick up in store instead. When do Labor Day sales start? Labor Day sales have already started. Retailers typically consider the Friday before the official holiday, which lands on Monday, Sept. 7 this year, the start of the long weekend, so all sales are now live. When do Labor Day sales end? Plan for most Labor Day sales to end on the holiday, Monday, Sept. 7. Some may extend longer into the week, but don’t plan on it — aim to get all your shopping done by Labor Day, but shop sooner if you can, says Carls. “Summer clearance is already working with fewer sizes, colors and models, so the thing you actually want can disappear before the promotion does,” she says. “The discount may hang around, but your exact patio set, for example, may not.” How can you save the most money during Labor Day sales? All the experts I talked to agree that the best way to save the most money during Labor Day sales is to stack your savings. That means looking at the deal price as the starting point and combining it with additional offers to save even more, says Gerstley. For example, search for promo codes to lower prices further, shop through cash back apps and browsers to put money back in your pocket, and pay with credit cards that let you earn rewards as you spend. Additionally, make sure you’re comparing prices across retailers before buying anything, says Porwal. Since so many retailers are hosting sales right now, they’re all competing for your attention, and you never know when one might lower prices just a little bit more to give themselves an edge, or throw in extras that make a purchase more worthwhile, like free shipping, delivery, install or haul-away. Don’t be afraid to ask about price matching, too, says Carls. If a retailer really wants your business, they’ll be open to negotiating with you. Last but not least, don’t feel like you absolutely have to buy something if deals aren’t compelling, says Gerstley. As we enter the final quarter of the year, sales are plentiful with early Black Friday and Cyber Monday offers starting in October, and Amazon Prime Big Deal Days might be around the corner (it hasn’t been confirmed yet, however). There will be more promotional moments in the near future, and waiting might be key to maximizing your savings.

Why are these Labor Day sales worth it?

Labor Day sales historically offer strong deals across key categories like summer clothing and shoes, outdoor goods, furniture, mattresses and bedding, and appliances. Shoppers can save online and in stores throughout the holiday weekend at almost every major retailer. Labor Day sales are typically the last summer clearance events, causing brands to drop prices extra low to get rid of inventory before the fall.

World.title: Andrew Williams, Every Time I Die guitarist known to wrestling fans as ‘The Butcher,’ dies
World.content:
Andrew Williams, the longtime rhythm guitarist for metalcore band Every Time I Die, who went by “The Butcher” in his other career as a professional wrestler, has died, All Elite Wrestling has confirmed. He was 48.

Williams’ death was announced hours after he collapsed during an independent wrestling show in Millvale, Pennsylvania, and was rushed to a hospital by ambulance Saturday night.

“Andy collapsed at the end of his match this evening,” Enjoy Wrestling, the promoter putting on Saturday’s event, said on X. “Our doctors on staff tended to him immediately, administering CPR until the ambulance arrived.”

Williams grew up in the Buffalo, New York, area, thinking he was going to follow his father’s and uncles’ footsteps and work at a factory when he got older. “I remember being like, ‘Oh, my God, I got to get out of here,’” he told Renee Paquette in a 2022 interview.

Williams recalled living with learning disabilities, including dyslexia, which prevented him from learning how to read music. But, he told Paquette, “I just picked up a guitar and it just made sense.”

Williams played with Every Time I Die from the group’s inception in 1998 to it’s disbandment in 2022.

“The band became known for turning chaos into catharsis, pairing breakneck intensity with anthemic hooks and off-kilter grooves,” according to Epitaph Records, which signed the group in 2008.

In 2025, Williams’ new band, Atomic Rule, released a demo EP. On Saturday, just hours before his collapse, Williams spoke in a video on the group’s Instagram page, saying they’d just wrapped up writing new music and would be appearing on tour with Gwar in November and December.

“Get ready, because Atomic Rule is going to be coming and smashing it,” Williams said in the video.

Between the ropes, Williams dispensed with his soft-spoken, easygoing demeanor and instead went by “The Butcher,” putting his burly, heavily tattooed body to hard-hitting use as one half of the tag team “The Butcher and The Blade.”

Though he’d loved pro wrestling as a child, he told the “HardLore” podcast in 2025 that it wasn’t until he attended a show held by Southern California indie promotion Pro Wrestling Guerrilla around 2014 that the idea of becoming a wrestler himself finally crystalized in his mind.

In 2015, at age 37, he finally wrestled his first full match. Four years later, he’d debut on All Elite Wrestling, performing on television until his contract expired in 2026.

Williams described the similarities between music and wrestling to “HardLore.”

“Anyone who’s written a song can wrestle a wrestling match,” he said. “It’s very similar to like — putting a song together is just like putting a wrestling match together. There’s ups and downs, there’s peaks and valleys.”

Despite his talents in two different arenas, Williams told interviewer and wrestling personality Alicia Atout in a 2017 interview that his “true life calling is just to make my friends laugh.”

“That makes me feel like a million bucks, if I can get dudes rolling,” he said.

Former colleagues and fans began paying tribute to Williams on Sunday.

Josh Eppard, the drummer for rock band Coheed and Cambria, called Williams’ death “beyond heartbreaking” and recalled his kindness, saying he met Williams during a 2019 tour.

“Peace to Andy, the kind giant who I thought was doing some backyard wrestling s--- with his buddies until one day I saw his mug on the TV and was in stunned disbelief,” Eppard said. “Andy was not only a pillar of one of the most true and influential bands in heavy music, he was also pulling double duty as a pro wrestler????”

Wrestler Matt Hardy, who worked with Williams at AEW, called him a “kind, funny & deep individual who was an extremely talented musician & wrestler.”

RJ City, an AEW interviewer and member of the company’s creative team, highlighted Williams’ intellect.

“Andy Williams was so smart and cultured that it made both his chosen careers all the more insane,” City said. “He was the opposite of how he looked, we were lucky to know him.”

Former AEW women’s world champion Willow Nightingale recalled Williams encouraging her, raising her confidence and advocating for her before she’d been signed to the company.

“He had every right to have an ego, but he didn’t,” Nightingale said. “He reached his hand out and did what he could to help others.”

Wrestler Josh Alexander called Williams “one of the best people I ever met.”

“I’ll remember Andy for what he was,” Alexander wrote on X. “A dude with an enormous heart that could always put a smile on my face.”

World.title: Sen. John Kennedy criticizes the Trump administration’s approach to Putin amid latest peace talks
World.content:
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., criticized Republican leadership on a number of issues including the Trump administration’s handling of the Ukraine peace process and Senate leaders’ response to inflation woes.

Kennedy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday he believes the Trump administration should take a different approach to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“This guy’s a pirate. He’s got blood under his fingernails. He doesn’t care about a bunch of pretty talk,” Kennedy said Sunday, as U.S. envoys meet with leaders on both sides of the conflict. “You don’t get any credit for kissing his ass. You’ve got to show him you mean business.”

Last week, the House failed to pass a Russian sanctions bill that the Senate approved in August.

“We should have passed that Russian sanctions bill, and we’ve got another chance to do it,” the Louisiana senator said. “Then we ought to help Ukraine and help Europe. They’re doing OK on their own, but we can provide them intelligence.”

Kennedy’s comments come as President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the president’s special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in Russia and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv this weekend.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomes U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner prior to their talks in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sunday. Genya Savilov / AFP via Getty Images

“We got Putin down. We’re choking him to death. We’re choking him. We’ve got to choke him to death. That’s what he understands,” the senator added. “I’m not putting down any of the talk, and I think talk is good and it can be helpful. But I won’t faint with surprise if our guys don’t come out of there without a deal.”

Kennedy also weighed in on the ongoing military conflict with Iran, telling “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker that the war will “probably not” end before the upcoming midterm elections.

Still, he praised the Trump administration’s decision to launch the military conflict, telling Welker: “We have accomplished all of our objectives in Iran. ... There’s just one problem: the Strait [of Hormuz] is semi-closed.”

The senator said that with the strait still blockaded by the U.S. military, gas prices in the U.S. likely won’t drop soon.

“The blockade was a smart play. It’s hurting the Iranians badly. It’s hurting the government,” Kennedy said. “I think we ought to leave it on for a few more months if we can stand the pain at the pump.”

Kennedy on Sunday also expressed doubt that Republicans in Congress would be able to do anything to lower costs or tackle inflation before November’s midterm elections, lightly criticizing his own leadership for not dealing with the issue sooner.

He described the economy as “solid” and pointed to “low” unemployment numbers, but said that inflation is “a big if.”

“It’s gutting people like a fish. Inflation is pernicious. And we’ve had it for a few years now. It’s been up and down since President Biden’s administration,” Kennedy said. “What we ought to do is something about it. I’m not blaming it on the president or the House. The Senate Republicans, about five months ago, for a reconciliation bill, we should have addressed it. We didn’t for a couple reasons. Number one, I couldn’t convince the majority leader to put a bill like that on the floor. And number two, we’re probably three or four votes short.”

Asked whether Republicans have enough time to address inflation before the midterm elections, Kennedy said, “We can do anything we want to in reconciliation and ask the House to come back and do it.”

Kennedy highlighted a procedural move Senate Republicans could use to pass some legislation without support from Senate Democrats but cast doubt on whether they would. “I’m not saying we will do that, certainly based on our record the last five or six months. It’s not likely.”

World.title: Notable Deaths in 2026
World.content:
Gloria Steinem is pictured at the office of Ms. Magazine in New York, Nov. 24, 1980. | Mel Finkelstein/New York Daily News via Getty Images A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity. By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery. Journalist, activist, and author Gloria Steinem (March 25, 1934-Sept. 2, 2026) was a trailblazing figure of the women's liberation movement, and a co-founder of Ms. Magazine, the first major publication to be owned, run, and written by women. Ms. was a spearhead for the promotion of equal rights, helping to raise awareness about issues of inclusion, media representation and social justice affecting women and girls. As a journalist, Steinem exploded the notions that "women's issues" were confined to women. She was also a tireless advocate for women's voices in politics – at the ballot box, and in the halls of power – by fighting for voting rights, and promoting female candidates for office. Steinem told "Sunday Morning" in 2023 that, as the women's liberation movement picked up steam, the very word "feminism" seemed to threaten people for two reasons: "One, because they didn't understand it, and two, because they did understand it!" Born in Toledo, Ohio, to a traveling salesman, Steinem lived an itinerant life as her family moved about, until her parents' separation and divorce when she was a teenager. Steinem ended up caring for her mom, who suffered from mental illness. Steinem's career as a journalist began in New York City, where she contributed to several publications, including The New York Times and Esquire. She made a splash with her two-part 1963 exposé in Show magazine, for which she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny at Hugh Hefner's Playboy Club. The article, which exposed sexual harassment on the club's floor and the toll on female employees behind the scenes (including mandatory blood tests and gynecological exams), was a sensation. After helping found New York Magazine (a news, pop culture and style publication), publisher Clay Felker volunteered to publish a sample issue of Ms. within the pages of New York magazine in 1971. The issue promptly sold out. The publication's first full issue appeared on newsstands on July 1, 1972. In addition to having Wonder Woman on its cover, the issue featured a petition signed by women of various backgrounds announcing that they had had an abortion and were demanding that it become safe and legal. [It would be another year before the Supreme Court's decision in Roe v. Wade.] The magazine courted controversy (a cover photo advertising a story about sexual harassment on the job, depicting a man fondling a doll, got the magazine pulled off newsstands), while some advertisers shied away (the head of a major cosmetics company told Steinem that women who read Ms. don't buy makeup). Still, the magazine persisted, while Steinem also helped nurture groups and publications dedicated to advancing civil rights, from the Ms. Foundation for Women (which created the Take Our Daughters to Work Day initiative, later expanded to include sons), to the Women's Action Alliance, and the National Women's Political Caucus. She was president and co-founder of Voters for Choice (which later merged with the Planned Parenthood Action Fund), and was co-founder of the reproductive rights organization Choice USA (now URGE). In 1999, Steinem was asked by the "CBS Evening News" whether technological advances were responsible for women's advancement. Steinem discounted that: "There's nothing automatic about political change, about liberation," she said. "There's no substitute for self-respect, banding together with other people, standing up for ourselves. Liberation does not come from outside. Power can't be given to you. The process of taking it is part of the empowerment." In 2000, Steinem (who once thought marriage was demeaning) did the unexpected: she married David Bale, a human rights activist and father of actor Christian Bale. But their life together ended three years later, when Bale died of lymphoma of the brain. In 2006, she told "Sunday Morning" that losing her husband made her understand the difference between sadness and depression. "Yes, because people would say to me, 'Aren't you depressed?' And I realized that in depression, nothing matters. And in sadness, everything matters. It makes everything poignant." Steinem continued writing and lecturing into her 90s, as some of the topics introduced long ago by Ms. Magazine, such as sexual harassment in the workplace and domestic violence, took on new force with the rise of the #MeToo movement. Steinem told "Sunday Morning" that the revolution for women's equality is still being fought today. "There's a barrier that has moved, but there's still a barrier," she said. "So, what used to be you couldn't get a job, now you hit a ceiling after a few years. What used to be an unequal marriage is now unequal after children are born. The barrier has moved, thank goodness. So, there's more room back here that's liberated. But the barrier is still there to be pushed.

Cassandra Wilson Frans Schellekens/Redferns via Getty Images Two-time Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer Cassandra Wilson (Dec. 4, 1955-Sept 1, 2026) was once called America's best singer by Time magazine. The daughter of musician Herman Fowlkes (who stopped going on the road when Cassandra was born) and teacher Mary Fowlkes, Cassandra studied piano from age 6 until 13, at which point her father encouraged her on the guitar. In addition to her love of Motown, Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk, she was also exposed to folk and rock music. "That was the beginning of my interest in people like Joni Mitchell and Judy Collins, Richie Haven," she told "Sunday Morning" in 1997. "It allowed me to step outside of the box, so to speak. You're placed in a box naturally – I think most of us are. And listening to this music gave me an opportunity to see possibilities." She performed at coffeehouses and in cover bands while studying at Millsaps College and Jackson State University, and mentored under jazz greats in New Orleans before moving to New York City, where she joined Steve Coleman's M-Base collective. Wilson's art, and her contralto, crossed folk, pop, R&B, and country. She recorded 20 albums, and was also a featured performer with Wynton Marsalis, Greg Osby, The Roots, Terence Blanchard, Elvis Costello, Luther Vandross and the Count Basie Orchestra, among others. She earned four Grammy nominations and won two for best jazz vocal album (for "New Moon Daughter" and "Loverly"). She released her last album, "Coming Forth by Day," an homage to Billie Holiday, in 2015. In 2022, Wilson was named a National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master. Though she was most frequently described as a jazz artist, Wilson called labels mostly stifling and altogether unnecessary. "It's a matter of testing yourself, pushing yourself, challenging yourself and not accepting the status quo, not accepting what everyone says you should be doing," she told "Sunday Morning."

Tim Curry A 1974 portrait of English actor Tim Curry. | Evening Standard/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Actor Tim Curry (April 19, 1946-Aug. 25, 2026) was famed for a roster of entertaining miscreants and villains, from a campy cross-dresser in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," to the manipulative butler Wadsworth in "Clue," to Pennywise, the sinister, murderous clown, in the Stephen King thriller "It." The fact that even his most devilish characters were crowd-pleasers was a testament to Curry's overpowering charisma. Acting, he told "Sunday Morning" in 2025, gave him "the freedom of being somebody else, and I think that I was (like everybody else) drawn to the idea of fame probably, although I came to kind of rather despise it." Curry's first professional stage role was in the London production of "Hair." But it was the cult favorite "Rocky Horror" that lit up his career. He said that what made the role of Dr. Frank-N-Furter unique was his power: "He gave a lot of teenagers permission to be different, and I'm very happy that he did have that power," Curry said. Other roles included a prince of darkness opposite Tom Cruise in "Legend"; Carol Burnett's scheming and duplicitous brother in "Annie"; a put-upon hotel concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York"; a Soviet officer in "The Hunt for Red October"; Cardinal Richelieu in "The Three Musketeers"; and Long John Silver in "Muppets Treasure Island." He was also the voice of Nigel Thornberry in the Nickelodeon series "The Wild Thornberrys" and its movie spin-offs. Curry also starred on Broadway in "The Rocky Horror Show," Tom Stoppard's "Travesties," "Amadeus," "My Favorite Year," and "Monty Python's Spamalot," earning him three Tony Award nominations. His life went sideways when, in 2012, he suffered a stroke (the same malady that his father had suffered before dying when Curry was 10), and a paralysis on his left side. He underwent invasive brain surgery, and had rehabilitation to learn how to speak again. "That was very weird," Curry said. "I hated not being able to speak." In 2025 he told "Sunday Morning" he was not remotely afraid of dying. "I don't fear death," he said. "I try to avoid it, as I think we all do! But I suspect that in the end, I will welcome it." Why? "Well, I think it may be very comforting to go bye-bye – and I want to earn it!" he laughed.

Dolly Parton A publicity photo of Dolly Parton for the 1988 CMA Awards. | CBS via Getty Images She was a singer-songwriter who lit up stages and screens for decades – who, beginning as a child, composed more than 3,000 songs and sold more than 100 million records. But Dolly Parton (Jan. 19, 1946-Aug. 25, 2026) was remembered for gifts beyond her sheer talent: as a philanthropist who donated millions of books to children, and whose charities benefited local communities, graduating seniors, and public health; and as a savvy businesswoman whose enterprises included her own recording company, theme parks, a chain of dinner theaters, and a downtown Nashville hotel, which includes a "Life of Many Colors Museum." Born in the foothills of the Smoky Mountains in eastern Tennessee, Parton grew up dirt-poor, the fourth of 12 children raised in a cabin with no electricity or indoor plumbing. But Parton's family was rich with music, and she showed a talent for it early on. "When I started writing these songs, my mom was real impressed with how I could write," Parton told "Sunday Morning?" in 2019. "And she would say, 'Oh honey, go get that guitar. I want you to sing them.' And she'd say to people, 'I want you to hear this song this little thing wrote.' And so I thought, Ooh, I'm getting a whole lot of attention now! "But also, I loved the sound of that music. I loved the sound of the instruments. I loved being able to create something, and it gave me a little space, and a little world of my own that I could just live in, and be creative in." The first of her family to finish high school, Parton graduated on a Friday, headed to Nashville on Saturday, and never looked back. Her first big hit, released in 1966, was "Dumb Blonde," which was not an apt description of Parton herself: "I'm pretty sharp," she told "Sunday Morning" in 2004. "I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. I'm country smart. You know how they say somebody's street smart? I feel like, you know, if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart." Those country smarts led her from her big break, in 1967, as a regular on a popular local music program, "The Porter Wagoner Show," to when she left Wagoner in 1974 to make it on her own. She turned the heartache of her professional split into art, penning the song "I Will Always Love You." "So I just started, you know, writing what was coming out, like, 'If I should stay, I would only be in your way. So I'll go, but I know I'll think of you...,'" Parton said. "So that song just flowed completely out. It just came out … I'll bet that song didn't take me more than an hour to write." Writing, to Parton, was seemingly effortless: "I mean, I've got boxes, dresser drawers, chests, trunks, Army trunks. I write something almost every day. Things just come to me, funny things, sad things. Depending on my mood, I have to write that. It's like my therapy. It's like my doctor." Songs like "Jolene," written in response to a bank teller's flirtatious behavior towards Parton's husband, Carl Dean; or "If You Hadn't Been There," released shortly after Dean's death, in 2025, ending their 59-year marriage. Parton's songs – of memory, love, painful wounds, and fierce humanity – included "Just Because I'm a Woman," "Yellow Roses," "In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad)," "My Tennessee Mountain Home," "Coat Of Many Colors," "Love Is Like a Butterfly," "The Bargain Store," and "9 to 5," which she recorded for her first film role, a comedy about female workers fighting back against a chauvinistic boss. She appeared in other films, including "Steel Magnolias," and recently co-wrote a biographical musical, "Dolly," set to begin previews on Broadway in December. Parton won 11 Grammy Awards, 13 Academy of Country Music Awards (including Entertainer of the Year in 1978), 14 CMT Music Awards, 10 Country Music Association Awards (including its lifetime achievement award in 2016), and an Emmy (for the TV movie "Dolly Parton's Christmas on the Square"). She was nominated for two Oscars (for best original song, for "9 to 5" and "Travelin' Thru"), and a Tony (for the 2009 stage musical based on "9 to 5"). Parton was Ms. Magazine's Woman of the Year in 1986, and was made a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2006. But her most inspiring accomplishment was to champion literacy through her Imagination Library, which has donated more than 300 million books to children in five countries. It was, she said, a response to her own father's illiteracy – and to the larger-than-life role that books played for her while growing up. For her philanthropy, Parton received the motion picture academy's Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award in 2025. And through it all, Parton maintained an embracing, big-hearted outlook that was as invigorating as her music – and she did it with lots of humor, too. When asked how she wanted people to remember her 100 years from now, she replied, "I want 'em to say, 'God, don't she look good for her age!'"

Bill Rasmussen Bill Rasmussen, the co-founder of ESPN, in 2018. | John Woike, Hartford Courant/Tribune News Service via Getty Images Bill Rasmussen (Oct. 15, 1932-Aug. 18, 2026) worked in the advertising services business, and in radio and television broadcasting, before serving as the public relations director for the New England Whalers, a World Hockey Association team, in Hartford, Connecticut. Fired along with other front-office staff in 1978 when the Whalers didn't make the playoffs, Rasmussen was sitting in idled traffic when he came up with the idea of a 24-hour sports network on cable TV with his son, Scott. The nascent channel secured 24-hour satellite time, which was initially planned to air Connecticut college sports. Backers were hard to come by. The head of one broadcasting company rejected his proposal to carry 24-hours sports, pronouncing that cable would be dead in a few years. After Rasmussen maxed out his credit card for a $9,000 advance, he received financial backing from Getty Oil; the channel also worked out a deal with the NCAA for exclusive rights to selected games, which expanded the range of their offerings. The Entertainment and Sports Programming Network — EPSN — went on the air on Sept. 7, 1979, while their Bristol, Conn., studio was still under construction. "SportsCenter" debuted, as the channel carried college football, basketball, soccer, tennis, bowling, and exhibition games in advance of the 1980 Winter Olympics. You want American Legion baseball? Sprint car racing? Full contact karate? The Royal International Horse Show? ESPN had you covered. The network began televising the NFL draft in 1980; inaugurated the ESPY Awards in 1993; and in 1995 launched the X Games competition. Over time, sports schedules were shifted to accommodate viewers, who in 2011 numbered more than 100 million. The number of postseason bowl games exploded. Rasmussen was ESPN's first president and CEO, but he and his son were forced out in 1980 by Getty, which owned 85% of the network. (The controlling interest was later sold to ABC.) Rasmussen and ESPN were estranged until 1999, when company executives invited him to the 20th anniversary celebration. He has since been recognized for his innovation, and has toured the country speaking at events for ESPN and the Walt Disney Company (the network's current owner). He was inducted into the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame in 2025. "A salesman once told me that every sale starts with a 'no.' We knew we were going to be really big because we got lots of 'no's' in the beginning," Rasmussen told Forbes in 2012. "Now there are over six U.S. networks and 46 international networks that have grown from the original ESPN."

Frank Beard An undated photo of drummer Frank Beard of the band ZZ Top. | Ed Spinelli for CBS News In the summer of 1969, drummer Frank Beard (June 11, 1949-Aug. 17, 2026), then 20, and guitarist Billy Gibbons got together to audition bass players at a Houston club called the Catacombs. When Dusty Hill strode in and began playing, "we wound up playing one song for about three hours straight!" Gibbons told "Sunday Morning" in 2019. The three would perform together for more than 50 years as the band ZZ Top. "I'm dumbfounded!" laughed Beard, the only member of the band without a beard. "It's longer than we've been married, by a long shot." Known for hits like "Legs" and "Sharp Dressed Man," ZZ Top had six No. 1 singles on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Airplay chart, and sold more than 50 million records. They earned three Grammy Award nominations, and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Beard, originally from Frankston, Texas, met Gibbons in a band called The Moving Sidewalks. With Hill (who died in 2021), they released their debut album in 1970, called "ZZ Top's First Album," a mix of hard rock, Southern rock, boogie and blues. Their heavy touring schedule — as many as 300 concerts a year — featured elaborate stage shows involving Texas longhorn steers, rattlesnakes and buzzards. By 1983, ZZ Top released their eighth album, "Eliminator," which featured three Top 10 hits: "Gimme All Your Lovin'," "Sharp Dressed Man" and "Legs." Their success was driven in part by their music videos on MTV, featuring a hot rod, pretty girls and catchy tunes, while sporting their signature look: fulsome beards (except for Beard himself), dark glasses, and flashy playing. Of the early music videos, Beard told "Sunday Morning," "We started out with some simple ideas. One, we thought, okay, the three of us are not, like, prima donna-looking rock stars, you know? So, let's be the ones watching what's goin' on in the background." Their video for "Legs" won them the MTV Video Music Award. Other ZZ Top hits included "La Grange," "I Thank You," "Sleeping Bag," "Tush," "Stages," "Doubleback," "My Head's in Mississippi," "Burger Man," "Give It Up," "Pincushion," and "What's Up with That."

Hayden Panettiere A 2013 photo of Hayden Panettiere as Juliette Barnes in the TV series "Nashville." | Bob D'Amico/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images Hayden Panettiere (Aug. 21, 1989-Aug. 16, 2026) was best known for starring in the TV series "Heroes" and "Nashville," and for the films "Remember the Titans," "I Love You Beth Cooper," "Bring It On: All or Nothing," two entries in the "Scream" franchise," and the 2011 biopic "Amanda Knox." Panettiere began her acting career as a child, appearing in 50 commercials by the time she was 5. At age 4 she was on the soap opera "One Life to Life." She later played recurring characters on "Guiding Light," "Ally McBeal," and "Malcolm in the Middle." She also voiced the character of Dot in Pixar's animated "A Bug's Life." Her breakout role was the 2006 TV series "Heroes," in which she played a high school cheerleader, Claire Bennet, who possessed the superhuman power of indestructability. In 2008 Panettiere told the Associated Press that the sci-fi series' appeal was that audiences could dream of something bigger: "And at the core of it are these human stories that people can relate to, very rugged. And it's just grabbed everyone in every age group." Panettiere won two Teen Choice Awards for "Heroes." In 2012 Panettiere starred in the series "Nashville," playing rising country singer Juliette Barnes. Over six seasons, Panettiere did her own singing, earning two Golden Globe nominations and hitting the Billboard country charts. (She'd earlier earned a Grammy nomination for the children's spoken word album, "A Bug's Life: Read-Along.") Meanwhile, she was struggling with mental health, addiction and postpartum depression following the 2014 birth of her daughter.
