Panettiere entered rehab in 2015 while filming "Nashville," putting herself into a treatment center. "I was drowning," she told Women's Health magazine in 2023. In her 2026 memoir "This Is Me: A Reckoning," she was candid about her long struggles with mental health and addiction, and her issues with paparazzi. Panettiere told "CBS Mornings" that the emotional challenges began as a young actress: "Once people figured out that I could cry on cue the way that I did, it was in everything, literally every scene," she said. "And it went from being a kid and having to imagine just that your pet passed away or something, but then as I got older, the imagery became darker and darker and darker, and the emotion that I had to hold within me in order to get those trigger tears going, it became harder and harder to jump out of it. I didn't know where my character started and where I ended … I was, you know, feeling just this deep sadness, and then the people were so happy afterwards. And you do that over such a long period of time — years after years after years — that of course it's going to take its toll on you emotionally." She credited finding the right therapist to helping her heal. She also served as an activist for environment causes, including protesting the hunting of dolphins and whales, and advocating for the victims of domestic violence. In her memoir, Panettiere described herself as an "optimist to the core" who refused to be defined by tragedy. She told "CBS Mornings" that her impetus to write the book was to address the stigma of postpartum depression and the backlash she received when she gave up custody of her daughter to the girl's father, Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko. "I had spent so many years trying to hide as much of my life as I could that it was just, you know, a habit," she said. "I really wanted to share with the world that they don't have to be afraid, that they can live their truth, that they can be imperfect, that being perfectly imperfect is being brave, and it's okay."

Tommy John Tommy John, of the Los Angeles Dodgers, pitching in the 1970s against the Phillies at Veterans Stadium in Philadelphia. | Focus on Sport/Getty Images During his 26 seasons in the majors, four-time All-Star pitcher Tommy John (May 22, 1943-Aug. 15, 2026) won 288 games, most while wearing the uniform of the Chicago White Sox, New York Yankees and Los Angeles Dodgers. But despite a career ERA of 3.34, notching 2,245 strikeouts and the second-highest number of wins of any pitcher since 1900 not yet elected to the Hall of Fame, John was perhaps best remembered for the groundbreaking elbow surgery that came to bear his name. Born in Terre Haute, Indiana, he was a top athlete in high school, and was recruited by the University of Kentucky to play basketball. However, John chose baseball and signed with the Cleveland Indians. In 1974, while playing for the Dodgers, the left-hander, then 31, tore the ulnar collateral ligament, or UCL, in his pitching elbow. At the time it was considered the death knell for pitchers' careers — that is, until Frank Jobe, the Dodgers' team physician, invented a procedure to fix John's arm, changing baseball forever. "I just said, 'You do what you have to do to get me back playing baseball again,'" John recalled for "Sunday Morning" in 2024. John allowed Dr. Jobe to replace the ligament with a tendon from his right forearm. The procedure had been done on others before, although it was usually performed on wrists and hands; John was the first pitcher to have it done on his elbow. Jobe gave the surgery 100-to-1 odds of being successful. John became the first pitcher to successfully return after undergoing the procedure — which is now called Tommy John surgery. He won 124 games before his UCL repair, and 164 after, with his final appearance in 1989, just days after his 46th birthday. Since John's return to the mound, more than 2,600 big leaguers and thousands more amateurs have had UCL reconstructions. Among active MLB pitchers, an astonishing 35% have had the surgery, including Shohei Ohtani and three-time Cy Young Award-winner Justin Verlander. But with advanced training methods, pitchers of all ages are throwing harder than ever, with the average speed of a major league fastball now close to 95 mph — about 6 mph faster than it was in 2002. And just as MLB pitchers are throwing harder, so are Little League pitchers. Today, about 60% of Tommy John surgery recipients are under 19. "I am sick my name is attached to a surgery happening in kids more than pros," John tweeted in July 2018.

Yayoi Kusama Visions of artist Yayoi Kusama (left, second from top, in 2013 in New York City). Pictured, clockwise from top left: "My Soul Blooms Forever" (2019) at the New York Botanical Garden; "With All My Love for the Tulips, I Pray Forever" (2017); "Infinity Room-Gleaming Lights of Souls" (2017); The Yayoi Kusama Retrospective Exhibition at The Whitney Museum of American Art (2012); "Pumpkin" (2019); the Yayoi Kusama exhibition at National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne, Australia (2024). | All photos via Getty Images: Timothy A. Clary/AFP; Roslan Rahman/AFP; Suhaimi Abdullah; J. Countess; Francois Goudier/Gamma-Rapho; Graham Denholm for NGV; Andrew Toth Pop artist Yayoi Kusama (March 22, 1929-Aug. 14, 2026) had an instantly identifiable style: a prodigious use of polka dots – on paintings, sculptures, even the human body. Her fixation with polka dots, she told "Sunday Morning" in 2012, stemmed from lifelong hallucinations. "I had a very miserable childhood and have been fighting against mental stress that comes from that," she said. "Producing art has been my cure for many years. I feel better when I make things and draw. So, I make more." Raised in a conservative, dysfunctional family on a flower farm in Matsumoto, Japan, Kusama was frustrated by the traditions of the Japanese art world. At 27, she wrote to artist Georgia O'Keeffe, whose words of encouragement were enough to set Kusama off for New York City. There, her vast "Infinity Net" paintings, along with her art "happenings," gained her notoriety within the avant garde world. She returned to Japan in the early 1970s, and lived voluntarily for decades in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital, where she continued to produce artwork that was noted for its obsessiveness. Whitney Museum curator David Kiehl described to "Sunday Morning" the "amazing control" of her art, which he held as extraordinary as a drip painting by Jackson Pollock: "She's repeating over and over again gestures or filling up all the spaces. The idea of layering something, and also the constant repetition as you repeat that gesture over and over again, you're saying, I am here, I am here." Kusama's artwork, sculptures and installations were featured in exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York City, and the Museum Ludwig in Germany. She also joined with fashion brand Louis Vuitton to design dotted fashion accessories. For a time, Kusama's paintings auctioned at the highest prices ever paid for a living female artist. In 2014, Christie's New York auctioned her "Infinity Net" painting "White No. 28" for $7.1 million, while in 2019 another "Infinity Net" painting went for $7.9 million. In 2022, Phillips New York sold her "Untitled (Nets)," from 1959, for $10.4 million. Kusama told "Sunday Morning" she still wore polka dots all the time, though, interestingly enough, never to bed. "When I go to sleep, I take off my polka dots nightgown," she said. "In the morning, I wake up, I see polka dots again, and it makes me happy."

Glen Hansard Irish musician Glen Hansard photographed at the Auditorium Parco della Musica, Rome, Nov. 12, 2019. | Luciano Viti/Getty Images Singer-songwriter Glen Hansard (April 21, 1970-July 29, 2026) started playing Dublin street corners at age 13 — just him and his guitar. But at least he had the permission of his grade school principal, Frankie Byrne, to quit school in order to pursue music. "So for me, that was just, you know, the wings I needed," Hansard told "Sunday Morning" in 2013. "So I went home, and basically announced to Ma, 'Listen, it's OK. Frankie told me it's OK!'" Busking led Hansard, at 18, to form a band, The Frames (named after the piles of bicycle frames in Hansard's backyard). Their music video for the 1995 song "Revelate," made using a post office security camera for less than $5, was picked up by MTV. Over the next 24 years, The Frames released nine studio and live albums, but while Hansard maintained ties with the group, he also worked with Czech singer-musician Markéta Irglová, forming another collaboration called The Swell Season. At the same time he was recording his first album with Swell Season, Hansard was asked by one of his former Frames bandmates ,John Carney, to help with a small film he was making, "Once," about a songwriter recording a demo and the tentative relationship he develops with a fellow musician. During filming, Hansard and Irglová became romantically involved. "I think part of what made 'Once' on the screen kind of work was that there was always this energy between us," Hansard told "Sunday Morning." "You'd be a fool to deny it." The film became an international hit, and Hansard and Irglová shared the Academy Award for writing the best original song, "Falling Slowly." "When we won that award, it was just, like, the most amazing thing," Hansard said. "And then my thing was like, 'OK, thanks, now let's get on with our lives.' And then when there was talk of it going to Broadway, I remember being very nervous, and honestly I was against it. "For me, Broadway meant sort of hamming it up," he said. "'Course, you're tempted by the idea of people saying, whispering in your ear, going, 'Do you know if this does well, like, you're gonna be seriously rich?' And going like, 'That was never why we did this.'" But Hansard relented, and the musical "Once" won eight Tony Awards, including best musical. Hansard and Irglová continued touring as The Swell Season and releasing new recordings, even after they broke up. "It was hard, and it was something we addressed all the time," Hansard said. "If you said to me, you could have all this success or you could just have a great relationship with Mar, I'd have took the relationship," Hansard said, "because it was the most profound and beautiful thing I had been through." The two were featured in a 2011 documentary, "The Swell Season," which examined the media attention on them following the success of "Once," and traced how the couple's romantic relationship ended. Each went on to marry others and have children; their most recent album was 2025's "Forward. In 2013, Hansard released the first of five solo albums, "Rhythm and Repose." And he continued busking for charity in Dublin with other Irish artists, like Sinead O'Connor and Bono. Playing music in the streets was, he said, a constant reminder of his origins. "You can climb all the levels of success and of celebrity or fame. But you're never more than a step away from the guy who's just making his money for the day," he said.

Charles Gaines Charles Gaines, co-creator of the sport of paintball. | adkisaac/Wikipedia Charles Gaines (Jan. 6, 1942-July 21, 2026) was a writer, documentarian, teacher, bodybuilder and outdoorsman, who studied creative writing at the University of Iowa under Kurt Vonnegut. His 1972 novel, "Stay Hungry," about the world of bodybuilding, was adapted to a film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger. Gaines also wrote and narrated the 1977 documentary, "Pumping Iron," based on his bestselling photo book. Over his career he wrote 25 books and more than 300 magazine articles. An avid fisherman, Gaines also helped found the U.S. Fly Fishing Team, and wrote and directed segments for ABC's "American Sportsman." But it was a disagreement over survival that led to his most notable innovation. Gaines, who'd grown up in the woods in the South, had long argued with his friend and tennis rival Hayes Noel, a New York City stockbroker, about whom would more likely survive in the wilderness. This led to a cat-and-mouse hunt in the woods, each wielding a paint gun used by farmers to mark livestock. What followed was devising structured gameplay out of their duel. On June 27, 1981, in Henniker, New Hampshire, Gaines and Noel, along with Bob Gurnsey, a local ski shop manager, put their challenge to the test by organizing the first paintball game. With 100 acres of forest staked out, and referees keeping score, a dozen camouflaged participants, armed with CO2-powered guns, paint pellets, goggles, and a compass and map, had to capture colored flags without being painted themselves. Players ran the gamut from hunters, an ex-Green Beret and a trauma surgeon, to a New York venture capitalist, a film producer, and an amateur boxer. Some played aggressively, racing through the course, snapped twigs be damned. Others stalked through the woods quietly, or set up defensive positions in abandoned buildings. "How people played the game reflected who they were," Gaines told NPR Boston in 2018. Ritchie White, a certified forester, stealthily accumulated four flags and exited the course first in just over two hours, without ever having fired a shot. Gaines, Noel and Gurnsey later commercialized the sport by forming the National Survival Game. Today, paintball and its variations (including speedball) have been played by millions, in amateur, professional and tournament competitions, in a market valued at greater than $1 billion. As the sport's co-creator, Gaines was inducted into the Paintball Hall of Fame in 2024.

Peter Lassally Producer Peter Lassally is photographed at CBS Television City in Los Angeles in 2013. | Liz O. Baylen/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Fabled TV executive Peter Lassally (Oct. 14, 1932-July 19, 2026) was the executive producer for such late-night stars as Johnny Carson, Tom Snyder, David Letterman and Craig Ferguson. He also championed many rising comedians, from the duo of Mike Nichols and Elaine May, to Mort Sahl, Garry Shandling and Steven Wright (who, Lassally said, would call him every year on the anniversary of Wright's first "Tonight Show" appearance to thank him). Despite being a kingmaker of late-night comedy, Lassally's background was exceedingly dark. Born in Hamburg, Germany, his Jewish family fled the Nazis to Holland. For a time, he attended the same grade school as Anne Frank. When he was 10, Lassally's father died. Soon after, he and his sister and mother were sent to the first of two concentration camps, witnessing terrifying brutality and enduring psychological torture. After the war. Lassally emigrated to the United States. He started out as a Radio City Music Hall usher (alongside Regis Philbin), and then as an NBC page. By the mid-1950s, he was working for America's biggest TV star, Arthur Godfrey. He served as a producer of "The Tonight Show" for more than two decades, as well as "Late Night With David Letterman." Lassally told "Sunday Morning" in 2018 that Johnny Carson, the king of late-night talk shows, was very uncomfortable with people: "If he'd have to go to a party, he'd sit at the end of the couch, wouldn't talk to anybody," Lassally said. "He was not a social animal." Lassally said that once Carson retired in 1992, the former star was finally able to relax — but missed giving a monologue every night. "He loved the monologue," Lassally told David Letterman in 2005. "And he would pick up the papers in the morning and write jokes from the paper for his own amusement, and then he would call me. It's true! He would call me and read them to me over the phone. And I thought they were hysterical, and I'd laugh like crazy." In 1993, after Letterman was passed over as "Tonight Show" host for Jay Leno, Lassally transitioned with Letterman from NBC to CBS, where they created the network's late-night programming block. Lassally was also executive producer of "The Late Late Show." His decades guiding TV's late-night stars earned Lassally the nickname "The Host Whisperer." In a 2009 interview for the Television Academy Foundation, Lassally said, "The most important thing for a talk show host is to listen. If they don't listen they're going to miss great opportunities. Try to make the guest look good, not necessarily make yourself look good."

Jennifer Finch Jennifer Finch performs with the punk band L7 in Belgium, 1992. | Gie Knaeps/Getty Images Punk musician Jennifer Finch (Aug. 5, 1966-July 18, 2026) played in bands alongside Courtney Love and Kat Bjelland, and was a member of the 1980s group L7, often performing bass while barefoot. As a teenager Finch began photographing Los Angeles punk bands; an exhibition of her pictures of such acts as Red Hot Chili Peppers and Bad Religion appeared at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 1986 she joined L7, which had formed as a duo the prior year with Donita Sparks and Suzi Gardner. With drummer Roy Koutsky, they recorded their first eponymous album in 1987. By 1989, when drummer Demetra "Dee" Plakas came on board, L7 had become one of the leading all-female punk groups, their songs "Pretend We're Dead," "Everglade," "Monster" and "Andres" charting in the U.S. and U.K. Fearless renegades and feminist icons, L7's music was dubbed by Vice magazine "unforgiving, aggressive, and chaotic." In 1991 the band founded Rock For Choice, which produced pro-choice benefit concerts that ran for 10 years. Finch recorded three more albums, and appeared in the "Doll Parts" music video with Hole, before leaving L7 in 1996. She formed OtherStarPeople with Xander Smith, then founded the bands The Shocker and Sex in Progress. In 2014 she reteamed with Gardner, Sparks and Plakas to record another L7 album, "Scatter the Rats." In a 2025 Guitar World interview, Finch said, "L7 ain't over yet. I'm in my 50s now and we still get to be examples. But also we get to fail publicly in a way that we couldn't do in our 20s. I've never felt directly responsible for anyone picking up a guitar — pick up your own f****** guitar! It's a thing you gotta do or do not. I'm very heart-warmed when particularly women say, 'Because of you, I got into politics,' or 'I got my medical degree because of you.' You know, fighting for housing rights — that's awesome."

Pat Oliphant Cartoonist Pat Oliphant at his drawing desk in Washington, D.C. in 1980. | Diana Walker, Getty Images; Maansi Srivastava, The Washington Post via Getty Pulitzer Prize-winning cartoonist Pat Oliphant (July 24, 1935-July 13, 2026) skewered the high and the mighty in cartoons syndicated to hundreds of publications around the world. Hailed for his acid humor and unforgiving pen, Oliphant once remarked to The New York Times about the politicians that were his frequent target, "They're all guilty until proven innocent." Born in Australia, he began working as a teenager at newspapers in Adelaide, producing cartoons and illustrations. By focusing his attention on international figures rather than locals, he managed to avoid censorship. In the early 1960s, eager to emigrate to the United States, he sent his portfolio to the Denver Post and was hired. His work lampooning President Lyndon Johnson, Barry Goldwater, Ho Chi Minh and others was soon syndicated internationally. In 1975 he moved to the Washington Star, positioned in the locus of American and global politics. Republicans, Democrats, military officers, pedophile priests — all were fair game to Oliphant, who was frequently criticized for offending segments of the public with his caricatures. "I usually stay away from presidents or politicians in general, because I might like them," Oliphant told an audience at the Yale University Art Gallery in 2014. "I did meet, after he was in office, Gerald [Ford]. He was a very good fellow, nice fellow. And that really gave me pause. You shouldn't hobnob with the enemy!"

Sam Neill Sam Neill as Dr. Alan Grant in Steven Spielberg's "Jurassic Park" (1993). | Murray Close/Getty Images Actor Sam Neill (Sept. 14, 1947-July 13, 2026) exuded suave, Old Hollywood glamour, which he displayed in some of his best-known roles, from blockbusters like "Jurassic Park" and "The Hunt for Red October" to "The Piano" and "Dead Calm." Born Nigel Neill in Northern Ireland to a New Zealander officer in the British Army, he emigrated to New Zealand as a child, and called himself Sam because, he said, there were too many Nigels at his school. At a boarding school in Christchurch, he developed a love for acting. He had roles in local productions, including the thriller "Sleeping Dogs" (which helped revive the dormant New Zealand movie industry), before his breakout Australian film alongside another rising star, Judy Davis, 1979's "My Brilliant Career." Neill spent subsequent years gliding among Australian, European and American films and TV, receiving a Golden Globe nomination for the series "Reilly: Ace of Spies." He portrayed Damien the Antichrist in the third "Omen" film, "The Final Conflict," and Cardinal Thomas Wolsey in the miniseries "The Tudors." Starring alongside Sean Connery, Neill played a Soviet submarine officer in "The Hunt for Red October" who dreams of living in Montana, or maybe Arizona. Neill also starred opposite Meryl Streep twice, in "Plenty" and "A Cry in the Dark." In Jane Campion's "The Piano," his character's jealousy over his wife's affair — abetted by her beloved piano — is so consuming he commits a particularly nasty act of revenge.



"With 'The Piano,' you know, I had terribly mixed reactions," Neill told "CBS This Morning" in 1999. "Some people would come up and say, 'I really loved the character that you play and I understood him and I bled for him.' And that's the way I felt about him. But on the other hand, a lot of people said, 'I hated you in 'The Piano.' People have this odd way of confusing you with the character that you play. A guy that chops off his wife's finger isn't going to make a lot of friends with those sort of people." Neill won over all audiences, however, in Steven Spielberg's "Jurassic Park" (1993), as paleontologist Dr. Alan Grant, whose visit to an island containing cloned dinosaurs sets the stage for deadly dinosaur-human clashes. He came back to the role in the sequels "Jurassic Park III" and "Jurassic World: Dominion." Along with his acting career, Neill was a country farmer. His organic winery, Two Paddocks, on New Zealand's South Island, produced pinot noir and riesling wines, while his social media account featured pictures of his farm animals named after his actor friends, such as Laura Dern the chicken. In a 2010 interview with Country Life, Neill said what he loved, more than anything, was planting things, "in particular, trees. Then I wander about them and take great satisfaction from their growth. … I do admire and emulate those who plant knowing they will never see the full fruits of their labor in their lifetime."

Bonnie Tyler Singer Bonnie Tyler performs c. 1980. | Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler (June 8, 1951-July 8, 2026) was best known for her chart-topping hit "Total Eclipse of the Heart," and "Holding Out For a Hero" from the "Footloose" soundtrack. Her trademark powerful and husky voice came about following surgery to remove nodules from her vocal cords. Ordered to rest her voice, she altered it permanently by screaming. The result: a gravelly sound reminiscent of Rod Stewart that carried her first major hit, 1978's "It's a Heartache," to worldwide acclaim. Born Gaynor Hopkins, in a small town outside Swansea, she was a coal miner's daughter living in public housing, who recorded "Top of the Pops" on her dad's reel-to-reel tape recorder. She also emulated her musical idols like Janis Joplin, Nina Simone and Tina Turner by singing into her hairbrush. "I fell in love with singing just from doing that," she wrote in her autobiography, "Straight from the Heart." "Looking back, even then my voice had a husky tone to it, but I didn't think much of it. I thought everyone's voices were different from each other's." Her debut album, 1977's "The World Starts Tonight," featured "Lost in France," and earned her a breakthrough artists nomination at the Brit Awards. Working with Meat Loaf songwriter-producer Jim Steinman, she recorded "Total Eclipse of the Heart," the debut single for her fifth studio album, "Faster Than the Speed of Night." "Eclipse" hit No. 1 on the U.S. Billboard chart in 1983 (and over time accumulated more than 1 billion streams). The following year her "Holding Out For a Hero" was a standout on the bestselling soundtrack to the movie "Footloose." Later releases included 1984's "Here She Comes" (from Giorgio Moroder's reimagining of "Metropolis"). She also recorded duets with Rod Stewart ("Battle of the Sexes"), Cliff Richard ("Taking Control"), Francis Rossi ("Someone's Rockin' Your Heart"), Vince Gill ("What You Need From Me"), and Mike Oldfield ("Islands"). Her 2013 album, "Rocks and Honey," a country album recorded in Nashville, featured the ballad "Believe in Me," which Tyler sung as the U.K.'s entry in that year's Eurovision Song Contest. Over the course of her career, Tyler recorded 22 studio and live albums, earning three Grammy nominations. In 2023 Tyler told the BBC she never got fed up with singing "Total Eclipse of the Heart." "Of course I don't! I love it!" she said.

Wally Funk Wally Funk speaks at a press conference following her flight aboard the Blue Origin spacecraft, July 20, 2021. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images Aviation pioneer Wally Funk (Feb. 1, 1939-July 8, 2026) spent her life in the clouds. After getting her first flight lesson at age nine, she became a licensed pilot at 17, and logged more than 19,000 flying hours. But her lifelong dream of going to space eluded her, until 2021, when – at age 82 – Funk became the oldest woman to travel beyond the Earth's atmosphere. In the early 1960s, Funk was a member of the Mercury 13 – female pilots who were put through the same training program with NASA as the all-male astronaut corps. "We had no idea what we were going through; we didn't know where it was taking us," Funk told "CBS This Morning: Saturday" in 2021. Among the strenuous tests they were forced to endure: "X-raying all over your body, every bone, every tooth, sticking water into your ears. I had to drink radioactive water." The women of Mercury 13 met, and often surpassed, the results of the men. But NASA required astronauts to be military test pilots, and at the time the military did not allow women to fly. [It wasn't until 1983 that an American woman, Sally Ride, flew into space.] Funk became the first female inspector for the Federal Aviation Administration, and the first female air safety investigator for the National Transportation Safety Board. But the dream of going into space never died. "That is my quest. ... I love flying, that's my job, that's what I love. And I'm not a quitter," Funk said. In 2021, she got her chance aboard Blue Origin's New Shepherd rocket, riding alongside Amazon founder Jess Bezos and two others (including 18-year-old Oliver Daemon, who became the youngest person to fly into space). There was a delay at Blue Origin's Texas launch site; Funk, sitting in the capsule, grew impatient. "Time's passing, and so I hit the button, I said, 'What's the holdup?'" she told CBS News Texas. But shortly after, the six-decade wait was over. "We're lifting off, and we're going up, and I'm looking out the window, I said, 'Wow! There goes the ground!'" Then came capsule separation, and weightlessness. "Oh, I love it, I love it," she exclaimed, as she floated in zero G. After landing in the Texas desert, she said, "I feel so lucky that my dream has come true." But she was eager for another invitation: "I want to go back up in space. That's where my brain has been, in space, ever since I came back."

Louise Lasser Louise Lasser as the title character of the 1970s TV satire "Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman." | Hulton Archive/Getty Images Actress Louise Lasser (April 11, 1939-July 6, 2026) was an early second banana to her husband, Woody Allen, even after their 1970 divorce. She starred in his comedies "Take the Money and Run," "Bananas," and "Everything You Wanted to Know About Sex* (But Were Afraid to Ask)." But Lasser reached celebrity of the first banana variety by starring in the 1976 satire of TV soap operas, "Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman." Produced by Norman Lear and distributed via syndication, the show ran five nights a week, portraying life in the Ohio suburb of Fernwood. Lasser's character, a housewife overloaded with consumerist messages, endured ever-wild situations of the soap variety – from marital problems, infidelity, religious cults and UFOs, to being held hostage by a mass murderer, to being institutionalized in a psychiatric ward. On top of it all, she bemoaned, "My floor has a waxy yellow buildup." In a 2013 profile for Interview magazine, Lasser said the producers asked her what she thought should happen to Mary next: "I was surprised when they asked me. I remember taking a beat and thinking, 'I think she's got to have a nervous breakdown, because you can't be this bombarded without…' Do you know what I mean? And this was equivalent to America's nervous breakdown that we were all starting to go through too fast, and you didn't know what anything meant, and nothing meant anything. … I once said that I thought she was like a survivor that lived in a world that might not be worth surviving in, you know?" "I know people think it was this very light, funny show, and it was this funny show, but the humor came from a great angst inside," she said. Though it only ran two seasons, the series developed a cult following. Lasser earned an Emmy nod for her performance, though the Television Academy was hard put in which category to list "Mary Hartman." They settled for "Special Classification of Outstanding Program and Individual Achievement." "People always say it's way ahead of its time," Lasser told Interview. "I never thought it was ahead of its time. I always thought it was of its time." Her other film and TV roles included "Slither," "Coffee, Tea or Me?," "It's a Living," "Modern Love," "Mystery Men," "Happiness," "Requiem for a Dream," and appearances on "Saturday Night Live," "Taxi," "St. Elsewhere," "Empty Nest," "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation," and "Girls," Lasser's stage credits included "Thieves," and replacing Barbra Streisand in "I Can Get it for You Wholesale."

Victor Willis A promotional photo of lead singer Victor Willis (front), of the group Village People, March 1980. | CBS via Getty Images Singer-songwriter Victor Willis (July 1, 1951-June 30, 2026) was co-founder of Village People, and co-wrote several of the disco group's greatest hits, including "Y.M.C.A.," ″Macho Man" and "In the Navy." In 1977, producers Jacques Morali and Henri Belolo, inspired by visits to gay dance clubs, put together songs for an album to be titled "Village People." Willis (who had appeared on Broadway in "The Wiz") was hired after they heard his demo tape, and he belted out such songs as "San Francisco (You've Got Me)" and "In Hollywood (Everybody Is a Star)." But once the record took off, dancers were needed for TV and live appearances, hence the ads in trade publications: "Macho Types Wanted: Must Dance And Have A Moustache." The final lineup of Village People – all very macho-looking men – featured Willis dressed as a policeman, Alex Briley as a soldier or sailor, Glenn Hughes as a leather-clad biker, David Hodo as a construction worker, and Randy Jones and Felipe Rose as a cowboy and Native American – the only two members of the group who were openly gay. "Each of us represents American images that have been around for a long time," Willis told Rolling Stone in 1979. In 1978, Village People released two albums, "Macho Man" and "Cruisin'," which featured "Y.M.C.A." The song, which Willis co-wrote, was inspired by his visit to a Y.M.C.A. in Manhattan when he moved from San Francisco to New York City. "Y.M.C.A." hit No. 2 on the Billboard chart, and No. 1 in the U.K., Canada, Japan and other countries. It was later added to the Library of Congress' National Recording Registry, and in 2021 it was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Willis left the band before they appeared in 1980's "Can't Stop the Music," a disco movie that bombed. As Village People's lineup changed, Willis returned to the group to record the 1982 album "Fox On the Box/In the Street." But he focused on a solo career. (His album "Solo Man" was released in 2015.) He also fought over the rights to his Village People songs, until a federal jury ruled in 2015 that Willis was entitled to 50% copyright of 13 of the group's songs (including "Y.M.C.A."). "I've always made a living off my (songwriting) royalties, which is the reason I was able to stay in and fight so long with the lawsuits," Willis told news.com.au in 2017. "It has cost me millions to fight this case. I've recaptured my writing credits now and I own them for life. … Now a lot of other artists are realizing they can recapture the copyrights to their songs. Other people are following in my footsteps." He then returned as the group's lead singer to record and tour, including performing his most popular song, one he insisted was not meant to be a gay anthem. "I wanted to write a song that could fit anyone's lifestyle," he said. "I'm happy the gay community adopted ['Y.M.C.A.'] as their anthem, I have no qualms with that."

Penelope Keith Actress Penelope Keith in the 1970s British sitcom "The Good Life." | Don Smith/Radio Times/Getty Images A familiar comedic presence in British sitcoms, Penelope Keith (April 2, 1940-death announced June 29, 2026) starred in the series "The Good Life" and "To the Manor Born." Her career in television, film, radio and theatre, including with the Royal Shakespeare Company, spanned decades. Beginning in the 1960s she had small roles on TV, including "The Avengers" and "The Pallisers," and starred on stage in "The Norman Conquests," before starring in "The Good Life," as the proper and snobby Margo Leadbetter, next-door neighbor to a pair of self-sufficient homesteaders who've made a farm out of their suburban tract. Keith won the first of her two BAFTA Awards for her performance. She starred for three seasons in the BBC comedy "To the Manor Born, as Audrey fforbes-Hamilton, a widowed aristocrat forced to sell off her palatial estate to a wealthy commoner. Other TV roles included "Executive Stress," "No Job for a Lady," "Moving" and "Death Comes to Pemberley," and the film "Priest of Love." On stage she won an Olivier Award for the 1976 play "Donkey's Years," and starred in "Blithe Spirit," "The Importance of Being Earnest" and "The Rivals." In 2014 Keith was made a dame for her services to the arts and charity. She told the Radio Times in 2011, "Of course, the fact that 'Manor Born' and 'The Good Life' have stayed in people's memories that long is wonderful. It's an extraordinary thing, but somehow films always date, television drama always dates, but comedy – the good comedy – seems to weather the storm."

David Clayton-Thomas David Clayton-Thomas performs with Blood Sweat & Tears in 1970. | Steve Morley/Redferns via Getty Images In the 1960s and early '70s, David Clayton-Thomas (Sept. 13, 1941-June 24, 2026) was lead singer of the band Blood, Sweat & Tears, his husky and urgent voice carrying such gold-record hits as "Spinning Wheel," "And When I Die" and "You've Made Me So Very Happy." Clayton-Thomas replaced original lead singer Al Kooper in 1968, and his debut album with the group, the eponymous "Blood Sweat & Tears," won the Grammy for album of the year. Born David Henry Thomsett in Surrey, England, and raised in Canada by his father, a pianist, he fought violently with his dad, and by his mid-teens was living on the streets. He was incarcerated for vagrancy and assault by the age of 20. But he taught himself to play a guitar left behind by another inmate, and later spent time playing clubs in Toronto. Changing his last name to Clayton-Thomas, he performed with several bands, and in the mid-'60s had a hit single with the anti-war rocker "Brainwashed." He befriended other rising stars, including Joni Mitchell and John Lee Hooker, who encouraged Clayton-Thomas to move to New York, where he was recruited to replace Hooker at the Cafe Au Go-Go in Greenwich Village, when Hooker left for a European tour. After Judy Collins brought Blood, Sweat & Tears member Bobby Colomby to the club to hear him perform, Clayton-Thomas was invited to join the band, which had started splintering following the release of their debut album, "Child Is Father to the Man," but which still had a recording contract with Columbia Records. "We rehearsed for about a week and we opened at the Cafe Au Go-Go and we started recording basically our set," Clayton-Thomas told The Wire magazine in 2020. "What we were doing at night down in the village, we'd go up to 52nd Street and record the songs in the daytime. Everything we put on that album, we played live before we recorded it. We released that album in October 1968 and by New Year's '69, it was the number one album in the world. It happened that fast." One of the biggest hits off that album was "Spinning Wheel." "It's an old theme: everything comes around, right?" Clayton-Thomas said. "I actually wrote that song about two years before I went to New York. I wrote it here in Canada and recorded it for a Canadian record company, and they heard it and they were horrified. They said, 'It's jazz. It will never sell. You can't do this.'" The band's recording of "Spinning Wheel" topped Billboard's Adult Contemporary chart and was nominated for three Grammys; the song would be covered by such artists as Sammy Davis Jr., Shirley Bassey and James Brown. After recording their second album, the group performed at the 1969 Woodstock festival, and toured Eastern Europe on behalf of the State Department. But Clayton-Thomas, burned out, left the group in 1972 to pursue a solo career. He released more than a dozen solo albums, but rejoined Blood Sweat & Tears at various times over the next several decades

Ann Blyth A studio portrait c. 1950 of actress Ann Blyth. | Screen Archives/Getty Images Her most famous film role earned her an Academy Award nomination at age 17. Actress and singer Ann Blyth (August 16, 1927-June 24, 2026) shot to stardom for her performance as Joan Crawford's unscrupulous (and murderous) daughter in the film noir "Mildred Pierce." Her career during the height of the Hollywood studio system found her acting opposite Burt Lancaster, Tyrone Power, Gregory Peck, Robert Mitchum and Paul Newman, and in the 1950s she sang opposite Mario Lanza and Howard Keel in musicals such as "The Great Caruso," "Kismet," "Rose Marie" and "The Student Prince." Born Anne Blythe in Mount Kisco, New York, she was a radio singer at age 6, and trained with the San Carlo Opera Company. At 13 she appeared on Broadway as Paul Lukas' daughter in Lillian Hellman's anti-Nazi play, "Watch on the Rhine." When the show toured in Los Angeles, Universal signed her to a contract, showcasing her in low-budget musicals like "Bowery to Broadway" and "Babes on Swing Street." Auditioning for the Warner Brothers adaptation of the James M. Cain crime novel "Mildred Pierce," Blyth screen tested opposite Crawford herself and won the role. For her performance as the scheming and amoral Veda Pierce — who slaps her mother across the face, and dares to have an affair with her new husband (Veda's stepfather!) before killing him — Blyth received an Oscar nomination for best supporting actress, one of the film's six nominations. Crawford won for best actress. "Mildred Pierce" led to more substantive and darker roles for Blyth in such films as "Brute Force," when she played her part in a wheelchair, having broken her back in a sledding accident. But she also appeared in lighter fare, like "Mr. Peabody and the Mermaid." By the end of the '50s she had stopped appearing in films to raise her family, but she occasionally worked in TV (including "Wagon Train," "The Twilight Zone," "Quincy, M.E.," and "Murder, She Wrote"), and toured in productions of "Show Boat" and "The Sound of Music." In a 2013 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Blyth was asked how she hoped she would be remembered by film fans: "That I made them happy. That would make me very happy."

Clive Davis Singer Whitney Houston and music executive Clive Davis at a party c. 1989. | Lester Cohen/Getty Images Record executive Clive Davis (April 4, 1932-June 22, 2026) had an ear for divining hits through his more-than-half-century career. In the 1960s, he signed Janis Joplin; in the '70s, he made a star of Barry Manilow; he guided Whitney Houston to seven straight No. 1 songs in the '80s; he engineered Carlos Santana's comeback in the '90s; and in the 2000s, he discovered Alicia Keys. The winner of five Grammy Awards, Davis was an indisputable icon, winning the trust of leading artists and steering musical tastes, even though, he told "Sunday Morning" in 2011, he wasn't an avid music fan as a child, and never learned how to play an instrument. He described his music career as "an accident." The son of a Brooklyn tie salesman, Davis lost both his parents to sudden illnesses within a year of each other when he was a teen. He learned an early lesson: "There was no substitute for hard work. You had to earn it. I earned every scholarship that I had to get me through law school as well as college." After studying at Harvard Law, he got a job in the legal department at CBS. Within a few years, he was tapped to be head of Columbia Records. "This was a challenge," he said, "and I poured myself into it. Not to say I had an ear, I never even thought of that, but to learn the record business as well as anybody who had ever been involved with it." At CBS Records helped nurture the careers of Billy Joel, Bruce Springsteen, and Earth, Wind & Fire. Accusations about misusing company funds led to his dismissal, and a guilty plea to tax evasion. But Davis made a stunning comeback, taking over a struggling record label, Bell, and renaming it Arista. His first release: Barry Manilow's "Mandy," which topped the Billboard chart. David signed or supported such artists as Lou Rawls, The 5th Dimension, Melissa Manchester, Gil Scott-Heron, Patti Smith, Lou Reed, The Grateful Dead, Aretha Franklin and Luther Vandross. He signed Whitney Houston when she was 19; her debut album, 1985's "Whitney Houston," sold 23 million worldwide, while her follow-up, 1987's "Whitney," made Houston the first female artist to debut an album at No. 1 on the Billboard charts. He also conceived of the Santana album "Supernatural" (1999), which went on to win nine Grammys, including album of the year. He became the first music executive to be voted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2000. Davis also launched J-Records, with such artists as O-Town and Alicia Keys, whose 2001 debut album, "Songs in A Minor," earned four Grammys. In 2002, he became Chairman and CEO of the RCA Music Group; six years later, he was named Chief Creative Officer of Sony BMG Worldwide. In his 70s and 80s, Davis was still directing the careers of such artists as "American Idol" winners Carrie Underwood and Kelly Clarkson. In 2021, when New York City was trying to recover from the COVID pandemic, Davis was asked by the city to spearhead a concert on the Great Lawn in Central Park. "We Love NYC - The Homecoming Concert" featured such artists as Santana, Manilow, Jennifer Hudson, Earth, Wind & Fire, and Jon Batiste. "We're using music to not only change the mood, but we're using music to symbolize rebirth, revival, recovery," he told "Sunday Morning" then. "And that is why it's so special." Sadly, a lightning storm shut down the concert midway, before Springsteen, Paul Simon and Elvis Costello could perform. The influential music executive who almost didn't get into the industry credits his career to a fluke: "I'm indebted to a lucky break — an accident — that brought me into music and that has given me a life of incredible fulfillment and pleasure," he said.

Alan Greenspan Alan Greenspan testifies before the Senate Banking Committee on January 26, 2000 in Washington, D.C., on his nomination for a fourth term as Chairman of the Federal Reserve. | Marshall, Liaison Agency/Getty Images As chairman of the Federal Reserve for more than 18 years, Alan Greenspan (March 6, 1926-June 22, 2026) worked with four presidents. When he left the Fed in 2006, America was in its greatest period of economic growth in its history — and Greenspan was the economy's rock star, heralded as a "maestro" and an "oracle" whose visits to Fed meetings carrying an overstuffed briefcase would lead to massive media conjectures about possible changes in economic policy. But then came the economic shocks of 2008 — a burst housing bubble, a collapse of banks, a plunge in the stock market. Greenspan told "Sunday Morning" in 2013 that one article in particular struck him: "It said basically, 'Do we economists know anything?' And it is a very legitimate question. Because if you don't know enough to capture the most extraordinary event, economic event, in all of our lifetimes, what in the world do we really know? It's like a mystery story to me. You know, how in the world did I miss it? And I said, 'I'm gonna find out why.'" He spent two years studying data and charts, and wrote "The Map and the Territory" (2013), which explored how irrational human behaviors — guided by fear or euphoria — were not factored into the Federal Reserve's computer models, but played a role in the crash that some thought should have been foreseen. "Bubbles go up very slowly as euphoria builds," Greenspan told The Associated Press. "Then fear hits, and it comes down very sharply. When I started to look at that, I was sort of intellectually shocked." A native New Yorker, Greenspan studied music at Juilliard and toured for a year with the Henry Jerome Swing Band, playing saxophone and clarinet. He accepted that he was never going to be a great musician. "I mean, I had played next to Stan Getz — I was 16, he was 15 — and I played for a year side-by-side with him in a band. And he was basically pretty much determined I was gonna become an economist!" Greenspan laughed. A disciple of libertarian philosopher Ayn Rand, Greenspan studied at New York University and Columbia and earned his doctorate from NYU. After having served as President Gerald Ford's chief economic adviser, he was named by President Ronald Reagan as chairman of the Federal Reserve in 1987. He was credited with helping restore stability after the "Black Monday" crash on Wall Street in October of that year. During his tenure at the Fed, Greenspan drew praise for presiding over an economic expansion with little inflation. He also believed financial markets could largely regulate themselves, and helped block efforts to increase federal oversight of derivatives, which allowed speculators to make bets on the market, from oil prices to mortgages. That climate proved fateful. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, assigned by Congress to investigate the 2008 crash, concluded: "More than 30 years of deregulation and reliance on self-regulation by financial institutions, championed by former Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan and others ... had stripped away key safeguards, which could have helped avoid catastrophe." Greenspan admitted he'd made a mistake in assuming that banks could regulate themselves. After leaving the Fed just weeks before turning 80, Greenspan ran a consulting business, Greenspan Associates. Retirement, he told "Sunday Morning" in 2013, was not an option: "I don't know what it means," he said. "I mean, what do we do, stop thinking?"

David Hockney A portrait of English artist David Hockney at his home in Los Angeles, 1987, alongside his 1972 painting, "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)." Acrylic on canvas. | Photo by Anthony Barboza/Getty Images; painting © David Hockney, courtesy Christie's British-born artist David Hockney (July 9, 1937-June 11, 2026) was one of the most vital artists to emerge in the era of mid-20th century pop art. Noted for his portrait and figurative works, Hockney was also recognized for his paintings of California swimming pools, landscapes, photo-collages and scenic designs for opera productions. But he had a particular affinity for portraits. Asked why, in a "Sunday Morning" interview in 2006, Hockney replied, "Well, I like people. They're rather fascinating. They're all a bit different, especially faces." Born in Radford, England, Hockney was encouraged by his parents, who frequently modeled for him. As the artist recalled, his father, using a mirror, would watch and comment on Hockney's progress: "'Is that a right color?' he'd go." After moving to the United States, Hockney fell in love with the light and lifestyle of Southern California. Collectors snapped up his work from the beginning. "They weren't very expensive — you know, $300, $500," he said. "The moment I earned a living as an artist, I felt I was rich, which I was, actually, because you're doing what you want to do. I could look at the world and interpret it and get paid for it as well. … What else would I want to do?" His portraits often displayed a sense of humor, which might explain why he usually refused to accept commissions for portraiture. "You need to be a bit of a flatterer, I think," he said, "and some people can do that. I'm not very good at that, no." One frequent subject of his was a former lover, Peter Schlesinger, featured naked in his 1966 painting "Peter Getting Out of Nick's Pool." Hockney, who was always open about being gay, said, "I don't want to live a deceitful life, you know? I mean, you're an artist, you want to be honest. You've got to be." Over the years, Hockney's lush California landscapes and cool blue swimming pools earned him an international reputation. His 1972 painting "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)" sold at auction for $90.3 million in 2018. He also experimented with "joiner photographs," creating montages of fragmented photographic details depicting an object or setting. He told "Sunday Morning" in 1984 it was to impart movement: "What it led me to believe, now, [is] that it wasn't volume that gives something life, it was time, in a way … It makes you look at it for a long time, if you fragment it. … "I think the beauty is in the looking, not in the thing itself," Hockney said. "In fact, if you can see and look, you've got life, and that's the beautiful thing."

Marjane Satrapi "Persepolis" author and filmmaker Marjane Satrapi poses during the Rome Film Festival, Nov. 16, 2012. | TIZIANA FABI/AFP via Getty Images Iranian-French cartoonist and filmmaker Marjane Satrapi (November 22, 1969-June 4, 2026) won worldwide acclaim for her graphic bildungsroman "Persepolis," which told the story of a young girl coming of age in Tehran in the midst of her country's Islamic Revolution. First published in French beginning in 2000, the multiple-volume memoir became an international bestseller, and later an Oscar-nominated animated film – one denounced by the Iranian government. Illustrated in black-and-white, "Persepolis" was the tale of a rebellious young girl growing up in a complicated, aristocratic family that opposed the Shah, but then became disillusioned with the revolution. Relatives faced execution from both sides. "I wanted to show, as an insider, how I lived it," Satrapi told "Sunday Morning" in 2008, "without wanting to make a lesson of history or of politics, or whatever. Not at all. Just to say, in my life, from my point of view, that is the way I lived the thing." Born in Rasht, Iran, and raised in Tehran, Satrapi was sent by her parents to Europe as a teenager for her education, away from the restrictions imposed upon women in her homeland. She was an art student in Strasbourg when she devised "Persepolis," despite little experience in comics. It sold millions. Satrapi was then offered the chance to turn her graphic novel into an animated film. She assembled a team to draw all the animation by hand. For her animators, she acted out all the parts, from a dog to an old man, her grandmother, and herself. She got Catherine Deneuve and her daughter, Chiara Mastroianni, to provide voices. The resulting film was nominated for an Academy Award. Living in Paris with a Swedish husband, Satrapi directed several more features (including "Chicken With Plums," "The Voices" and "Radioactive"), while also writing graphic books ("Embroideries," "Woman, Life, Freedom") and children's stories ("The Sigh," "Monsters Are Afraid of the Moon"). Despite living in exile, Satrapi remained an optimist, telling "Sunday Morning," "We don't have the right to become cynical. I want to keep the stars in my eyes, and still believe that it's possible. Human being is capable of the worst. But human being is also capable of the best."

Peabo Bryson Peabo Bryson performs at Radio City Music Hall in New York City, Sept. 13, 1991. | Ebet Roberts/Redferns via Getty Images Singer Peabo Bryson (April 13, 1951-June 2, 2026) was famed for his R&B hits, including many collaborations with Roberta Flack (such as the 1983 song "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love"). He also sang the duets "Beauty and the Beast" with Céline Dion, and, from "Aladdin," "A Whole New World" with Regina Belle, both of which won Oscars for best song (and earned Bryson two Grammy Awards). Born and raised in South Carolina, Bryson started performing with traveling revues, and appeared on Moses Dillard and Tex-Town Display's 1969 album "Now!" He then built a solo career that included "Reaching For The Sky," "Feel the Fire," "I'm So Into You," "Let the Feeling Flow," "If You're Ever In My Arms Again," and the #1 R&B hits "Show & Tell" and "Can You Stop the Rain." He also recorded with Natalie Cole ("Gimme Some Time"), Minnie Riperton ("Here We Go"), Melissa Manchester ("Lovers After All"), and Kenny G. ("By The Time This Night Is Over"). Bryson also appeared on stage in productions of "Raisin," "The Wiz" and "Porgy and Bess." In 2007 Bryson told CBS' "Saturday Early Show" that his song "Missing You" (the title track of his 20th soul album) was an emotional tour de force for him: "When you strip away everything and are left with just a piano and what God has given you, you tell a deeper story," he said. "The words for this beautiful song made me think of the two women I love the most in this world, my mother and my sister, both of whom I lost. When I sing the line 'I can't wait to see you again this side of Heaven,' it's for them. This song is for anyone that you've ever loved in a real way."

Marcia Lucas Marcia Lucas, seen with her then-husband director George Lucas, holds the Academy Award she won for editing "Star Wars," at a post-Oscar party in Los Angeles, April 4, 1978. | AP Photo Academy Award-winning film editor Marcia Lucas (Oct. 4, 1945-May 27, 2026) was married to George Lucas and worked on several of his films (along with those of Francis Ford Coppola and Martin Scorsese). She was widely credited with having "saved" "Star Wars" when it came to putting together the film's dogfight sequences in the climactic Battle of Yavin – an amalgamation of miniatures, explosions, World War II-style cockpit dialogue, a heroic mercenary, and a bit of the Force. Marcia was an apprentice editor working with the legendary Verna Fields when she met George, then a USC film student, in the late 1960s. They married, and Marcia worked as an assistant editor on George's debut feature, "THX-1138." Marcia then shared an Oscar nomination, with Fields, for editing "American Graffiti." Her views on the space fantasy "Star Wars" were particularly important to George, who leaned on her counsel when – halfway through production – she convinced him to kill off Obi-Wan Kenobi on the Death Star, a fact George hid from the studio. She also suggested Princess Leia give Luke Skywalker a kiss "for luck" before swinging over a deep chasm. She eventually took over editing duties when George expressed unhappiness with an English editor who'd started a rough cut of the film. George told Rolling Stone in 1977 that the film's final battle scene over the Death Star – fashioned after World War II movie dogfights – was extremely hard to edit: "Marcia can normally cut a whole reel – all ten minutes of the film – in one week. I think it took her eight weeks to cut that battle. It was extremely complex and we had 40,000 feet of dialogue footage of pilots saying this and that. And she had to cull through all that, and put in all the fighting as well. Nobody really has ever tried to interweave an actual plot story into a dogfight, and we were trying to do that, however successful or unsuccessful we were." Marcia shared the Academy Award for "Star Wars" with Paul Hirsch and Richard Chew, and followed with editing "The Empire Strikes Back" and "Return of the Jedi." (The Lucases divorced after "Jedi" was released.) Her counsel was also vital for other directors' work. When an early version of Steven Spielberg's "Raiders of the Lost Ark" (which George had co-written and produced) was screened, after all the congratulations, Marcia spoke up: What about Karen Allen's character, who was last seen tied to a stake with Indiana Jones when the Nazis were vanquished? A concluding scene where Indy and Marion go for a drink had been written, and yet, "They never shot it, because they didn't think they needed it," Marcia recalled in a 2017 interview. "I said, 'I don't want to leave Marion on the stake! You need to do that!" So, George flew the actors to San Francisco and shot the last-minute addition at City Hall. Marcia's other credits included Coppola's "The Rain People"; Haskell Wexler's "Medium Cool"; Scorsese's "Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore," "Taxi Driver," and "New York, New York"; and Michael Ritchie's "The Candidate."

Sonny Rollins A portrait of jazz musician Sonny Rollins dating form the 1950s. | Bob Parent/Getty Images Like his contemporaries, John Coltrane and Charlie Parker, tenor saxophonist Sonny Rollins (Sept. 7, 1930-May 25, 2026) was revered for his improvisational acuity, and his eagerness to pursue innovation in an art form that he helped define. His experimental works, captured in such recordings as 1956's "Saxophone Colossus" and his 1962 live album "Our Man in Jazz," influenced generations. He also collaborated with the greats, from Miles Davis, Dizzy Gillespie and Freddie Hubbard, to the Rolling Stones (appearing on their 1981 album "Tattoo You"). One of the leaders of the bebop era, Rollins told the Associated Press in 2007 that he found it "excruciating" to listen to what he deemed flaws in his older recordings. "I don't consider myself a musician that has learned as much as I want to learn," he said. Born into a musical family in Harlem, he hadn't even finished high school when he was invited to join Thelonious Monk's band. Soon he was recording with Miles Davis and Bud Powell. But a heroin addiction led to jail sentences, a drug treatment program – and a spiritual awakening. "I began to have a deeper philosophy of what life was about," he told the AP. "From that point on is when my consciousness awoke." After being discharged, he joined the Max Roach-Clifford Brown quintet, before recording his "Saxophone Colossus," heralding the arrival of a leading sound in hard bop. Other notable albums included "Way Out West," "A Night at the Village Vanguard" and "Freedom Suite." He also recorded music for the Michael Caine film "Alfie." Rollins referred to himself as "a work in progress," adopting new styles of performance, and frequently taking time out to hone his skills away from the stage. In 1959, he retreated from performing, spending months practicing on a walkway on the Williamsburg Bridge (to avoid annoying his Lower East Side neighbors). "It was a great experience," he told "The Early Show" in 2011. "Almost a religious experience." That long sabbatical led to his 1962 album "The Bridge." He continued to tour into his 80s, until health issues forced his retirement from playing. His 61st album, "Road Shows, Vol. 4: Holding the Stage," was released in 2016. A Kennedy Center Honoree in 2011, he won two Grammys, for best jazz instrumental album (2000's "This Is What I Do") and best jazz performance ("Why Was I Born?," recorded in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, which occurred just a few blocks from his apartment). "The thing that I am most proud of in my career is that fact that I was able to see beyond being popular and all that stuff," he told the AP in 2007, "and do what my inner self told me to do."

Ted Turner Ted Turner announces the launch of CNN in Atlanta, June 1, 1980. | Rick Diamond/Getty Images He was, in the words of his third wife, actress Jane Fonda, "a gloriously handsome, deeply romantic, swashbuckling pirate." Ted Turner (Nov. 19, 1938-May 6, 2026) was a businessman, sportsman and conservationist. Eager to take risks, and with an outsized personality and penchant for being outspoken, Turner reshaped the media landscape, and highlighted the importance of environmental protection. His early notoriety came via sports. A four-time winner of the Rolex Yachtsman of the Year award, Turner reportedly won more than 500 major sailing trophies. He was skipper of the racing yacht Courageous, whose crew won the America's Cup in a four-race sweep in 1977, earning him the nickname "Captain Courageous." In the 1970s, he bought the Atlanta Hawks and the Atlanta Braves. After the Braves suffered a 17-game losing streak, Turner put on a uniform and took over as manager. Commissioner Bowie Kuhn banned him from the field the next day. The son of the owner of several radio stations and a billboard advertising firm, Turner inherited the company after his father's death and turned a failing business profitable. He then acquired an undistinguished UHF TV station, WTCG, whose signal was too weak to even cover most of Atlanta. With an old movie library, reruns like "The Andy Griffith Show," cartoons, and broadcasts of baseball, basketball and hockey games, Turner built it into a "superstation" by making its signal available free to cable systems across the United States. Renamed WTBS, the channel joined basic cable lineups viewed by approximately five million cable subscribers. (That figure would grow to more than 90 million.) Turner's greatest television achievement was founding the Cable News Network, the first all-news-all-the-time TV channel. Born from Turner's frustration at not being able to find news on TV late at night, CNN helped establish the 24-hour cable news cycle — a revolutionary moment that transformed the industry. By the time of the 1991 Gulf War, CNN was broadcasting live from Iraq and Saudi Arabia during the early hours of the war, with the network showing images of the attack on Baghdad. In the 1980s, Turner acquired MGM/UA. Using the studio's library of more than 4,000 films, he launched Turner Classic Movies and TNT, while the Hanna-Barbera animation library led to creation of the Cartoon Network. He also purchased the film production companies New Line Cinema and Castle Rock Entertainment. (He failed in a bid to take over CBS.) His fortunes rose and fell. In 1996 he sold Turner Broadcasting System to Time Warner for $7.3 billion in stock. When AOL and Time Warner merged in 2001, Turner's stock value rose in the billions. After the merger, stock prices plummeted. "[I lost] seven or eight billion," he told "60 Minutes" in 2003. He quit his job as vice chairman, which he described as "a title without portfolio ... like the emperor of Japan." Asked what it felt like to look at CNN from the outside, Turner said, "It's difficult. But you know, you can't live in the past. You've got to live in the present and the future. And I've got plenty to do." Much of that was focused on philanthropy, conservation and habitat restoration. He owned two million acres — an amount of land larger than the state of Delaware — and turned them into living laboratories to help preserve the nation's largest bison herd, as well as elk, whooping cranes, Rio Grande Cutthroat trout, black-footed ferrets, the Bolson tortoise, and other imperiled species. To support what he termed "eco-capitalism," he opened up his ranches to tourism, and in 2002 started a restaurant chain, Ted's Montana Grill, that served bison burgers. He founded the Nuclear Threat Initiative, which advocated for non-proliferation; donated $1 billion to found the United Nations Foundation, an independent charitable organization supporting causes such as children's and women's health and human rights; and founded and sponsored the Goodwill Games, an Olympic-styled event meant to counter the boycotts of the Cold War. In addition to co-creating and co-writing "Captain Planet and the Planeteers," an animated children's series promoting care of the environment, in 1989 he funded the Turner Tomorrow Fellowship Award, which bestowed a half-million-dollar prize for an unpublished novel that promoted "creative solutions to humanity's urgent problems." "See, my life is more an adventure than a quest to make money," Turner once said. "Adventure is going out and doing something for the pure hell of it. You just want to see if you can do it, period. There's no thought of gain other than your own satisfaction."

Michael Tilson Thomas Michael Tilson Thomas conducting the USC Symphony at Bovard Hall, at his alma mater USC, Oct. 5, 2009. | Lawrence K. Ho/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images For conductor and composer Michael Tilson Thomas (Dec. 21, 1944-April 22, 2026), known for his swashbuckling charm at the podium, performing was in his blood. His paternal grandparents, Boris and Bessie Thomashefsky, were considered the "Burton and Taylor" of Yiddish theater. But while he was surrounded by art and music from birth, and received lessons at an early age from the likes of Igor Stravinksy and Jascha Heifitz, the prodigy said his parents did not want him to go into the performing arts; they encouraged him to become a scientist instead. But in high school, he found his true calling when his music teacher failed to make class one day. Thomas put down his oboe and picked up the conductor's baton. He discovered he preferred being the orchestral leader. "I didn't like practicing very much," he told "Sunday Morning" in 2025. "And I could get very good results as a conductor very quickly." At 25 he made his New York debut when he took over for an ailing conductor at a Boston Symphony concert. The "boy wonder" received early praise from his mentor Leonard Bernstein, and two years later became music director of the Buffalo Philharmonic in 1971. That same year he began conducting the New York Philharmonic's "Young People's Concerts." He also co-founded the New World Symphony, a teaching orchestra, in Miami, and was music director of the San Francisco Symphony for 30 years. In a 1984 "Sunday Morning" profile, Thomas described himself as "an adventurous romantic. I'm interested in all kinds of things. I'm interested in experimentation. I'm interested in exploration. I'm also interested very much in tradition, and this is just the way I am." Which explained Thomas' passion not just for the masters of the classical repertoire, such as Mahler, Beethoven and Gershwin, but also for contemporary composers like Steve Reich and John Adams — and rock legends James Brown, Elvis Costello and Metallica. His discography includes nearly 150 albums. Thomas also composed music; his works include pieces featuring texts by Walt Whitman, Emily Dickinson, and Anne Frank. In an extended interview with "Sunday Morning," Thomas described his function as a conductor: 'I'm kind of like the captain of a ship. So, we're on this ship together and we're on the high seas and we're traveling along and all at once we come to an island. This is a completely uncharted island, not on any map. And it's just crawling with all kinds of animals, creatures that are not described in any encyclopedia or anything anywhere. They're all completely unknown and they're making all these sounds which are completely unrecognizable. Wouldn't that be the most thrilling thing that could possibly happen? Wouldn't that be a lot more interesting than saying, 'Well, we stopped at this great island which had the most unknown duty-free shopping spot on Earth.' Wouldn't that be better? That's what I'm trying to present, to give you the opportunity to experience music in that way in this kind of discovery mode."

Ruth Slenczynska Pianist and former child prodigy Ruth Slenczynska, at age 33 (left) as she embarked on a nationwide tour in 1958; and right, at age 97. | Bettmann Archive/Getty Images; Meredith Truax/Decca Records Hailed as one of the greatest child prodigies since Mozart, Ruth Slenczynska (Jan. 15, 1925-April 22, 2026) played her first concert when she was 4. She was performing internationally at an age when most kids were learning their times tables, and was mentored by some of the 20th century's greatest virtuosos, including Sergei Rachmaninoff. After she filled in for the Russian composer at a concert when she was just 9 years old, he gave her a Fabergé egg necklace. But her musicality came at a cost. Born in Sacramento to a Polish immigrant father who'd had limited success as a violinist, she was forced by her dad to practice for nine hours a day beginning at age 3. "I wanted to be one of those kids who played," she told "Sunday Morning" in 2022. "And if I didn't practice, I was chased around the apartment with a stick, my father's magic stick. I didn't want that." She quit performing at 15 and later ran away from home. After eloping and then divorcing, she made a living teaching, and in her late 20s returned to the concert stage. She said she wanted to resume her career "as a musician, not a curiosity." Recordings followed, as did television appearances, playing duets with President Truman, and a memoir, "Forbidden Childhood," about her life as a child prodigy. Slenczynska was praised for her impeccable technique. Critics wrote of her "intellectual insight and emotional spontaneity," and her ability to convey the classical repertoire with "rhapsodic freedom." She taught at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, where she served as artist-in-residence for 23 years. It was where she met her second husband, James Kerr, a political science professor. Even after retiring from the university, she continued to give master classes and private lessons; perform internationally; and record for radio and commercial releases. Her 19th album, "My Life in Music," was issued in 2022, when she was 97. Asked by "Sunday Morning" where she is mentally when she performs a recital, Slenczynska replied, "I go to a place I can't take anybody because it's a place from where I get my music."

Alan Osmond American singer Alan Osmond c. 1974. He was the eldest of the popular family singing group The Osmonds. | Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images; Doug McKenzie/Getty Alan Osmond (June 22, 1949-April 20, 2026) was the eldest sibling of what became the popular family singing group The Osmonds. He was also a songwriter, penning such hits as "Down By the Lazy River" and "Crazy Horses." Alan and three brothers — Wayne, Merrill and Jay — were originally a boys barbershop quartet performing at state fairs in Utah. They made their first TV appearance in 1962 on "Disney After Dark," and became regulars on "The Andy Williams Show." The Osmonds went on to release 25 studio and live albums. Younger brothers Donny and Jimmy also joined the group, and later became solo artists. In the early 1970s the group hit its peak, with six gold albums and seven Top 20 hits, including "One Bad Apple," "Yo-Yo," "Down By the Lazy River," "Hold Her Tight," "Crazy Horses" and "Love Me For a Reason." As the group's songs veered from bubblegum pop to rock, Donny Osmond became a breakout star, and also teamed with sister Marie for recordings and a TV variety show, which Alan produced. In the 1980s, Alan, Wayne, Merrill and Jay regrouped as a country act, releasing "One Way Rider." Their hits included "I Think About Your Lovin.'" At the time, Alan told The Associated Press he switched from recording rock to country music because it better fit their wholesome image. "Country music really is the backbone of America," he said. "It doesn't just come and go. And we're kind of flag-wavers. You find that in the country area, too." He also helped lead Stadium of Fire, an annual July Fourth celebration in Provo, Utah, that is one of the largest in the country. Four of Alan's own children formed another group, The Osmond Boys, also known as The Osmonds Second Generation. In 1987, Alan was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and in the late '90s retreated from touring. He helped create the Children's Miracle Network, which aids children's hospitals, and with his wife Suzanne founded the humanitarian organization OneHeart. Doug Osmond, one of Alan's sons, told The AP of his dad: "I've never met anyone more positive in my life. I never once heard him complain, not once. He would say, 'I may have MS, but MS does not have me.' That was his motto and he always was worried about everyone else. ... Family always took priority and his faith was in everything he did."

Desmond Morris Desmond Morris with the chimpanzee Congo on the TV program "Zoo Time," 1956. | Desmond Morris Collection/Universal Images Group via Getty Images As a young boy, English zoologist Desmond Morris (Jan. 24, 1928-April 19, 2026) watched his father slowly die of wounds suffered during World War I. Affected by humanity's inhumanity, he became fascinated with the animal world — studying zoology and animal behavior — and art. He became a curator of mammals at the London Zoo, and a television presenter. A surrealist painter himself, Morris even gave a paintbrush to a chimpanzee named Congo. The resulting work is said to have delighted Picasso. One chimp painting sold at auction for £14,400. In 1967 Morris wrote "The Naked Ape," a look at the evolution of man and how human behavior compared to that of other primates — including sexual selection and mating habits. "I spent the first half of my life studying animal behavior," Morris told The Guardian in 2007, "and when I eventually wrote a book about human beings, I wrote about them as if I was writing about another animal species. … I hadn't any hopes for it; I didn't expect it to do anything. People say I must have known what I was doing. They think I deliberately wrote it to make a shocking bestseller, but it wasn't like that." The book was a sensation, selling more than 20 million copies, but was also criticized as being patriarchal. Nearly four dozen books followed, including "The Human Zoo," "Intimate Behavior," "Manwatching" (about body language), "The Soccer Tribe," "Catwatching and Cat Lore," "Dogwatching," and "Babywatching." There were also books on surrealist art. "I should have stuck at the art," Morris told The Guardian. "I think I had the potential to be a good artist. I still consider myself a serious artist but a very minor one, and I'm a minor artist because I've been doing too many other things. My strength is that I do lots of different things; my weakness is that I don't stick at any of them long enough."

Bob Hall Bob Hall competes in the 1978 Boston Marathon. | Frank O'Brien/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Bob Hall (Oct. 31, 1951-April 12, 2026), who lost the use of his legs from polio during childhood, became known as the father of wheelchair racing, recognized as the Boston Marathon's Wheelchair Champion three times. Hall was not the first to compete in the Boston Marathon in a wheelchair; in 1970, Eugene Roberts, who'd lost both legs in the Vietnam War, completed the course, unsanctioned, in more than six hours. But in 1975, organizers promised Hall a finisher's certificate if he could complete the 26.2-mile distance in less than three hours. His finishing time: 2:58.00. "It had nothing to do with, per se, the marathon, but it was about the inclusion," Hall told The Associated Press last year, on the 50th anniversary of his pioneering ride. "It was that I was bringing people along." Hall won again in 1977 (at 2:40:18), besting seven fellow male and female wheelchair competitors, when Boston was designated the site for the National Wheelchair Championship. Hall received encouragement along the route from marathon winner Bill Rodgers and fifth-place finisher Tom Fleming, who both slowed to encourage him. "The interaction was a sign that we were fully accepted as athletes," he said. He sued in 1978 to have wheelchair racers admitted into the New York Marathon, where it would be more than two decades before men's and women's wheelchair divisions were created. Hundreds more wheelchair athletes have followed Hall, many using racing chairs he built. In Boston this year, 50 wheelchair racers competed, along with 50 others in para and adaptive divisions. "Because of him crossing that finish line, we're able to race today. And it's evolved so much since then," five-time Boston winner and eight-time Paralympic gold medalist Tatyana McFadden told The AP last year. "It was him. It was him being brave and saying, 'I'm going to go out and do this because I believe that we should be able to race Boston Marathon just like everyone else.' So he had the courage to do that."

Pearl Fryar Pearl Fryar in his topiary garden in Bishopville, S.C. in 2017. | Jonathan Newton/The Washington Post via Getty Images "The moment you work a cut above average, you will be recognized for that," self-taught topiary artist Pearl Fryar (Dec. 4, 1939-April 4, 2026) told "Sunday Morning" in 2005. "And I was a person that wanted some recognition in my lifetime." The recognition he initially sought, after he and his wife Metra moved into a ranch house in Lee County, S.C., was to win the local garden club's Yard of the Month Award, owing to his carefully landscaped and decorated front lawn and flower beds. It turned out Fryar wasn't even eligible; his house was outside Bishopville's city limits. But he didn't give up. "Now I got to come up with some way to make them make an exception, and that's how I got into topiary," he said. Fryar, who'd never heard the word "topiary," got a three-minute lesson from the owner of a local nursery on how to prune a plant. With a gas-powered hedge trimmer in his hands, Fry

World.title: Trump envoys say Ukraine talks were "very meaningful" after Moscow visit
World.content:
President Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, said they held "meaningful discussions" and are encouraged by the talks in Kyiv, part of a trip that began in Moscow, as the latest push to end more than 4½ years of Russia's full-scale invasion continues.

Sunday marked the first time the U.S. envoys had traveled to Ukraine since Mr. Trump returned to office with a pledge to solve the conflict.

Kushner, who is Mr. Trump's son-in-law, told reporters on Sunday that the president has been following the developments of the meetings "very closely" and is working hard to "find a pathway to end this war."

"But not just to end the conflict. What President Trump's been very focused on is how do we create a framework that could actually build, lead to a durable peace," he added.

After two rounds of discussion with the U.S. officials, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the goal was a "just, fair peace" that would ensure there was "never an opportunity to resume aggression against Ukraine."
