World.title: U.S. and Iran trade attacks on ships as fighting flares up again
World.content:
U.S. and Iran trade attacks on ships as fighting flares up again

toggle caption Vahid Salemi/AP

The U.S. military on Saturday said it struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy ships were targeted by missiles, with the retaliatory attacks part of a flare-up in fighting this week following a month-long lull.

U.S. Central Command said it struck the vessels after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched two ballistic missiles at two Navy warships patrolling the sea. CENTCOM said a U.S. aircraft carrier and missile destroyer "successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks" and that no American personnel were injured.

"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours," CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement posted on social media. "We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."

Sponsor Message

Strikes between the U.S. and Iran resumed last weekend, after a month's break from the fighting, when the U.S. hit several sites in Iran in response to a threat of Iran firing sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

An Iranian oil tanker near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf, a key hub for the country's oil-export system, was one of the three vessels the U.S. struck on Saturday. A tanker in the Gulf of Oman also was hit in "multiple critical locations" and its crew had to abandon ship and another tanker near Jask was also struck, CENTCOM said.

The three Iranian oil tankers were part of a "multibillion-dollar shadow network" that funds the Iranian Revolutionary Guard and its regional proxies, CENTCOM also said in the statement.

Shadow fleets are vessels that operate outside of the official shipping system. Iran uses shadow fleets as a way to move oil because it is under sanction. The U.S. has seized Iranian vessels operating under shadow networks, including two in April.

Defense Sec. Pete Hegseth on Saturday said in a social media post that if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, "we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."

Sponsor Message

"All they have to do is not shoot at @USNavy," Hegseth wrote.

Iran's foreign ministry on Saturday condemned the U.S. strikes, saying that they are "a clear violation of Paragraph 4 of Article 2 of the United Nations Charter, constitute a war crime, and represent an overt threat to international peace and the security of commercial shipping," according to the country's state media.

Lt. Col. Ebrahim Zolfaghari also warned Iranian forces would target American military in the region "more severely than before" if the U.S. continues strikes against ships, according to Iran's state media.

Iran said Sunday it had targeted an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate confirmation from the U.S. military. Iran did not mention casualties.

NPR's Carrie Khan in Tel Aviv and Jane Arraf in Beirut contributed to this report.

World.title: Opinion: A sculpture in perpetual motion, removed
World.content:
Opinion: A sculpture in perpetual motion, removed

toggle caption Mark Schiefelbein/AP

A big blue presence has vanished from the landscape of Washington DC.

On Wednesday a crew removed a 24-foot-tall metal sculpture called Blue, by Joel Shapiro, from the grounds of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Our family turned out to say goodbye.

Blue is a giant stick figure with what seems to be four limbs, standing on what might be one leg, while the other is lifted. To walk, to leap, to dance? The upper-most limbs, which look like arms, are extended. To welcome, twirl, swing or sway?

The work was installed on that part of the Kennedy Center's grounds called The REACH, which opened in 2019. I've always thought it seemed an artful fit in that place, which before the Center became a source of controversy during the Trump presidency, abounded just about every night with music, dance, and all kinds of shows — available to the public for free.

Sponsor Message

"It's about action and risk and performance and energy," sculptor Joel Shapiro, who died last year, said in a video about Blue that was on the Kennedy Center website, "It's a celebration of possibility."

But Josef Palermo, who was let go this past March as curator of visual arts and special programming at the Kennedy Center, told the New York Times this week that Blue had been "targeted early on" for removal by the Trump administration, which might have seen something else in the sculpture. Well, isn't "seeing something else" art?

The Kennedy Center, where President Trump's supporters are now in charge, issued a statement saying, "We are deeply grateful to Joel Shapiro for the years Blue has spent animating our campus and connecting visitors to his vision."

I think part of what made Blue so engaging is that the figure in implied perpetual motion along the capital's riverfront stirred people to imagine for themselves what might have set the big blue figure to whirl, spin, stomp, or prance.

We met a man at the dismantling who works for the artist's foundation who told us that Blue will be cleaned, reassembled, and, he was sure, reinstalled in some new spot.

Sponsor Message

Maybe removing Joel Shapiro's Blue so summarily from its perch at the Kennedy Center will make people even more eager to seek out the towering figure who caused such a stir.

World.title: Elbows up or down? Why Alberta is diplomacy-first in the trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta’s top U.S. diplomat says playing nice is paying off for his province in the Canada-U.S. trade war.

Nathan Cooper, Alberta’s senior representative to the United States, told CBC’s West of Centre that compared to provinces that have taken a more aggressive approach, Alberta has come out ahead.

“I think the premier’s diplomacy-first approach has really not only been helpful for me, but certainly helpful for the province,” Cooper said.

“If we look at the impact of U.S. tariffs on the Alberta economy, we have a disproportionately low impact.”

Experts have said while Alberta’s industries are not immune to the impact of the trade dispute, they are not seeing the direct hit other provinces are. Despite the trade war, the U.S. continues to increase its imports of Canadian oil.

The comments come as Cooper, the former speaker of the Alberta legislature, spent time in Nashville, Tenn., with Premier Danielle Smith last week.

Cooper said American officials have been “significantly more responsive” to his team than some of his provincial counterparts.

Alberta is the only remaining province with no ban or retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol imports. The province’s position on that is something the Americans have shown “a real appreciation” for, Cooper said.

“I believe that that's actually translated into results for the province of Alberta,” he said.

The premier said her trip to Music City was a personal one, but she took time to meet with business and tourism leaders while there. Ahead of her trip, Smith also appeared on U.S. news networks pushing for a return to the bargaining table.

Honey or vinegar?

Not everyone has been on board with Alberta’s approach.

Following Smith’s trip to Mar-a-Lago last year , she was called out for not being a part of a unified “Team Canada” response.

This summer, Premier Doug Ford pushed for Canadian leaders to take a stronger stance, and called for energy exports to be cut off to the U.S.

Smith’s predecessor, Jason Kenney, has said a modest tax on oil exports should be considered to put extra pressure on the president.

Smith has rejected both ideas and consistently said doubling down on diplomacy is a better approach.

“I think in this scenario, maybe Premier Smith is seen as a dissenting voice or not quite on script,” Evan Menzies, vice-president of Crestview Strategy said in an interview.

Premier Danielle Smith met with business and tourism leaders while on vacation in Nashville, Tenn., last week. (Danielle Smith/X)

But Menzies, who previously worked as a director of communications for Smith’s party, said things look more favourable for Alberta when you zoom out.

“If you're to look at what's bearing good fruit, Alberta's efforts seem to be bearing some good fruit.”

Smith’s too-friendly-to-resist approach contrasts against Ontario Doug Ford’s aggressive advertising and insult slinging .

Cole Hogan, a strategic communications advisor at Alberta Counsel who has worked on Ford and Kenney campaigns, said the divergent tactics make sense considering domestic priorities.

“Ford's approach, while it makes a lot of people feel good … it hasn't garnered the same results that Smith's approach has here in Alberta.”

“They both have different political goals in doing so — they have different industries to serve.”

Separation anxiety

All this comes amid a looming election in Alberta on whether to hold a binding referendum on separation — something U.S. officials are increasingly waking up to.

It's been used by representative Andy Harris to trumpet renewed calls for a 51st state and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as a sign of disunity and failed trade talks.

On the ground, Cooper said the referendum isn’t frequently raised in his meetings with U.S. officials.

“At the end of the day, one of my key jobs is to try to determine the difference between signal and noise and do what I can to get people focused on the big issues that are impacting our province.”

World.title: 'We really weren't prepared for that': Torrential rain batters Cape Breton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A torrential downpour dumped more than 200 millimetres of rain on parts of Cape Breton over the weekend, destroying roads, culverts and bridges while triggering local states of emergency across three counties.

Nova Scotia RCMP say a 46-year-old Cape Breton woman reported missing Saturday morning was found dead later in the day in a flooded area of Richmond County.

First responders recovered the woman's body around 2:30 p.m. AT on Saturday near Kempt Road in Cleveland, N.S. Search crews initiated the response after her vehicle was discovered parked near her residence on the far side of a flooded bridge.

RCMP stated the death is not considered suspicious, though police did not elaborate. When asked whether the death was related to the flooding, police had no comment.

Richmond County Warden Lois Landry says she has never seen rain like this, comparing the destruction to hurricane damage.

"I think what struck me was [seeing] trees down on properties and across roads," she said. "And we really weren't prepared for that."

WATCH | Cape Breton battered by torrential rainfall as local states of emergency in effect: State of emergency declared in 3 Cape Breton counties after storm, flooding | Duration 4:12 Three counties in Cape Breton have declared local states of emergency due to severe flooding and widespread damage. Some areas got more than 200 millimetres of rain this weekend. The alerts from each county were jointly released on Saturday. The storm washed out roads and caused power outages across the region.

She said residents were expecting a typical rain event like those the island sees multiple times a year, but instead faced an unprecedented weather event.

She is not the only one who thinks so.

"We've never experienced anything to this size and effect," said Terry Doyle, CAO for Port Hawkesbury, N.S. "And certainly, that's what I'm being told by others as well."

Doyle spoke Sunday from an emergency response co-ordination centre where representatives from Victoria, Inverness and Richmond counties and the province are gathered. A state of emergency was declared Saturday for those three counties.

An RCMP vehicle drives through water from a brook that overflowed on Route 4 near South Side River Bourgeois, Richmond County. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

Doyle said the bulk of the damage is in Richmond County, around Bras d'Or Lake, where floodwaters have washed out numerous roads, bridges and driveways.

Emergency Management Minister Kim Masland said it's difficult to give residents a timeline for repairs, as officials are assessing damage and more rain is expected to fall.

Municipal leaders are urging residents to stay home so emergency crews can safely repair infrastructure.

Inverness County Warden Bonny MacIsaac echoed that plea, warning drivers that covered roads may be structurally unstable beneath the water. Anyone who must travel should check provincial road conditions at 511 first, she added.

Widespread washouts have left some residents stranded. Amanda Mombourquette, councillor for Richmond County District 4, expressed concern for vulnerable residents cut off from emergency services and essential groceries.

Part of the West Bay Road washed out at St. Georges Channel, about 25 kilometres west of St. Peter's, N.S. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

Nova Scotia Power's outage map showed more than 1,000 customers provincewide without power as of Sunday morning, primarily in Chéticamp, down from 5,000 earlier in the day.

Coun. Claude Poirier, who represents Chéticamp on Inverness County council, said the local Legion and fire department have opened comfort centres so residents can charge devices or get hot drinks.

Cape Breton municipalities have established a toll-free support line at 902-625-7888 for residents to report non-emergency storm issues.

In a statement posted to social media Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the federal government is ready to provide any needed support and is in contact with provincial officials.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Counter-tariffs won't just affect the cost of goods for Canadians. They'll hit the trailers moving them too
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians bracing for billions of dollars in counter-tariffs won't just see prices rise on American aluminum, toilet paper, furniture and more — but on the very semi-trailers hauling those goods into and around the country.

Ocean Trailer, the largest retailer of semi-trailers in Western Canada, is waiting on a $45-million order of 600 trailers from U.S. manufacturers.

The company is rushing to get as many over the border before a 25 per cent Canadian counter-tariff on trailers, and scores of other items, takes effect on Tuesday.

"The extra cost, the 25 per cent, is well above our profit margin on a trailer, so we would have no choice but to pass that along to the customer," said Mack Keay, Ocean Trailer's chief operating officer, told CBC News from Vancouver.

The federal government announced dollar-for-dollar countermeasures will take effect at 12:01 a.m. on Tuesday on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods , in response to the latest round of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump's administration.

Keay said it's possible Ocean Trailer may be able to cancel some of its order, which was expected to flow in trailer by trailer until the end of the year, but it's on the hook for the trailers that are already in the process of being fabricated in the U.S.

The ones the company can't get into Canada by Sept. 8 will have to be parked somewhere in the U.S. or sold to American-based retailers, and Keay said he wouldn't get back what he paid for them.

Industry 'very much concerned'

Ocean Trailer isn't alone.

The head of the Manitoba Trucking Association said the vast majority of semi-trailers in Canada come from the U.S.

"I know a number of members that currently have trailers on order and are very much concerned about the cost of those trailers, because they ordered them before the counter-tariffs," said executive director Aaron Dolyniuk.

"I don't know that they'll be able to afford to pay 25 per cent more for them when they get here."

Dolyniuk said many businesses that rely on those trucking companies to ship product are also "rushing to get things north of the border before the [counter-]tariffs come on."

"I was talking to one member late last week … [who] said normally, they hauled two loads for this one customer northbound, and they wanted 15 this week," he said.

A variety of types of semi-trailers are towed along Canadian roadways, but the two most common are called dry vans and refrigerated vans.

The latter, also known as "reefer" vans, haul groceries, pharmaceuticals and other items that need temperature-controlled conditions during transport to avoid spoilage.

Dry van trailers are used to haul everything from kitchen appliances to car and machine parts, paper products, furniture, televisions, canned goods and other non-perishable items.

'This is not going to be OK'

There are just two semi-trailer manufacturers in Canada — one based in Ontario that doesn't manufacture reefer van trailers and another in Quebec which does, along with making dry vans, flat fright vans and other specialty trailer types.

Neither would have the capacity overnight to absorb the increased demand for trailer orders or rentals from Canadian trucking companies following counter-tariffs.

Ocean Trailer's Keay said Canada's domestic manufacturing capabilities are less than half of what the trucking industry would need to meet demand.

At the industry level, the potential added costs from counter-tariffs are eye-watering.

The average cost across trailer varieties is about $75,000, said Keay. A 25 per cent tariff would drive that closer to $95,000.

Each of the seven Ocean Trailer branches from Manitoba to B.C. is bringing in one or two trailers per day, either associated with orders from trucking companies or to be added to the company's rental fleet, said Dallas Senebald, the branch manager for the Winnipeg office.

"This is not going to be OK. Not just us not being OK, the industry is not going to be OK," said Senebald, whose Winnipeg office employs 40 people.

"There will be a shortage of trailers, which then increases demand, increases the cost of the trailers, and that gets filtered down right to consumer goods that are needed to be shipped."

If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt. - Aaron Dolyniuk, Manitoba Trucking Association

Senebald said trends in semi-trailer sales can be unpredictable year to year, depending on supply and demand of goods that need shipping.

One year, a larger corporate customer might order 100 trailers for purchase, and then none the next year, said Senebald. The Winnipeg branch might bringing in 300 to 400 trailers one year, and 80 the next, he said.

The variability is one reason the industry relies on a mixed model. Ocean Trailer has about eight suppliers — seven in the U.S. and one in Mexico, said Senebald.

On top of being the largest retailer of semi-trailers west of Ontario, it's also the largest business for rentals.

In the short term, Canadian trucking companies may turn to rentals as they hold off on buying U.S. trailers that cost them 25 per cent more due to counter-tariffs, said Senebald — and that's a concern.

"Demand for rentals is going to skyrocket so much so that we probably won't have enough to fulfil customer needs," he said.

"Saying no to customers repeatedly is never a good thing. Eventually, they stop calling."

The trucking association's Dolyniuk said the depth of pain felt will ultimately depend on how long the tariff war goes on.

"If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt within the trucking sector and outside of it," he said.

World.title: How Prince Harry and Meghan's return to Britain is setting off 'shockwaves'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hello, royal watchers and those intrigued by what's going on inside the House of Windsor. This is your deep dive into royal news and analysis. Reading this online? Sign up here to get this delivered to your inbox.

After Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, stepped back as working members of the Royal Family and settled in California in 2020, there was little to suggest they would want to return to the United Kingdom any time soon.

So it came as a considerable surprise when word broke that Harry, Meghan and their two children were on their way back and would settle outside London for an extended period.

"It seems so counterintuitive and so contradictory to everything that they have said since the moment they left," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

But now they're back, and even though there has been much telegraphing of the idea that Harry and Meghan are not going to be working royals again, the move carries broader implications for both the institution of the monarchy and other members of the Royal Family.

"Regardless of whatever their reasons are, their return creates massive shockwaves," Vovk said.

WATCH | Prince Harry and Meghan returning to U.K.: Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K. | Duration 2:06 Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are moving back to the United Kingdom with their children, Buckingham Palace has confirmed. The couple will remain non-working royals and live as private citizens.

"What does this mean for Harry and Meghan as a couple? What does this mean for Harry and Meghan and their children as a family unit? How will this impact relations with the rest of the Royals?

"How will the monarchy respond to this? How will the British public respond to this? How will in particular the tabloid and the predatory media respond to this? How will Harry engage with the media in light of his wins and losses in court over the past year regarding media intrusions?"

Harry and Meghan have their supporters and detractors, and as much as they have stepped back from official royal duties, what they do and say continues to draw attention.

"They may not be working royals, but they're still members of the Royal Family," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said in an interview.

"Harry is the son of the King at the end of the day, and he will never not be the son of the King."

For the monarchy, Harry and Meghan's return could divert attention from day-to-day activities of the House of Windsor.

WATCH | Reaction in London to Harry and Meghan's return: Londoners react to Prince Harry and Meghan’s move back to U.K. | Duration 2:25 The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly returning to Britain this month – six years after they quit royal duties and relocated to the U.S. While details around the decision behind their shift are unknown, the British public has mixed feelings about the move.

"Officially, nothing changes," Prescott said. "But clearly, Harry will get attention wherever he goes, whatever he does, and so there is a sort of risk of that being a distraction from the work of the monarchy."

To avert that, Prescott sees a need for "some element" of communication between Buckingham Palace and Harry and Meghan.

Vovk sees their return as potentially a new "crisis point" for the monarchy.

"It all depends on how things are handled on both sides. We know the palace is going to — and they've already taken the position — that [Harry and Meghan are] not working royals, 'we won't be commenting on their lives now that they're back.'

"So a lot will depend on how Harry and Meghan proceed."

How they proceeded over the past few years — in what became a visible estrangement from the wider Royal Family — included several instances of pointed criticism of the monarchy and the family itself, whether through their interview with Oprah Winfrey , a Netflix docuseries or publication of Harry's memoir Spare .

Prince Harry, right, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, left, walk along the boardwalk after meeting volunteer first responders from Bondi Surf Bathers Life Saving Club during a visit to Bondi Beach, Australia, on April 17. (Jonathan Brady/The Associated Press)

More recently, there has been no public criticism, and with King Charles, there appears to have been some rapprochement.

Harry, Meghan and their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, visited with the King and Queen Camilla privately when they were in the U.K. last month, prior to word breaking of their return.

"You can imagine at the personal level [King Charles] would want to see his son and the children, as I assume Camilla would at one level," Prescott said.

"But … Harry did single Camilla out for criticism in [Spare] and … that dynamic would be interesting to know more about, how Camilla views all this."

There is, however, no sense that Harry's estrangement from his elder brother, Prince William, has thawed in any way. Much media speculation since the return has focused on how William and his wife, Catherine, Princess of Wales, will be feeling about it.

"We're probably not going to hear a word about anything from them because anything that is said, people will jump on, people will try to read into it," Vovk said.

Prince Harry, left, and Prince William, right, stand during the unveiling of a statue they commissioned of their mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, on what would have been her 60th birthday, in the Sunken Garden at Kensington Palace in London, on July 1, 2021. (Dominic Lipinski/The Associated Press)

For William, Prescott suggested, there could be a risk that there would come a point when — particularly if Charles is seen to be a bit more forgiving — that the lack of contact with his brother could start to look "quite surly and sulky."

"At some point, you may have to just let bygones be bygones and just move on and not hold a grudge for forever and a day."

The return also spawns numerous questions around issues that have been at the heart of some of Harry's most vocal grievances, whether over actions of the media — particularly the tabloids — or security for him and his family.

Still, it seems likely that whatever Harry and Meghan do will draw headlines, fuel much conversation on social media and continue to divide opinion.

"Anything that they do creates a public response because whether people like them or people hate them … there is clearly something about them that still activates public opinion," said Vovk.

He sees multiple reasons for that, one of the biggest being Harry is the younger son of the late Diana, Princess of Wales.

People who have felt like they connected with Harry after his mother's death in 1997 have continued to feel that connection, said Vovk. He likens Harry to "a reflecting mirror that has a billion different reflecting facets on it, because there are so many millions and millions of people who take an interest in him."

"It says more about us … consuming celebrity culture than it does necessarily about Harry personally."

A new royal face on Canada's $20 bill

The portrait of King Charles is seen on the new Canadian $20 note at its unveiling in Ottawa on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Canadians just got their first glimpse of King Charles on the $20 bill. Our CBC friend Natalie Stechyson had this report:

It's official — Canada has a new $20 bill.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem unveiled the new, vertical bill featuring a portrait of King Charles on Thursday in Ottawa. It's the first Canadian bank note to feature Charles , whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.

In a news conference, Macklem called the unveiling "historic." It's been more than 70 years since a new monarch appeared on a Canadian bank note. The late Queen Elizabeth first appeared on the bank's inaugural $20 note in 1935 as a young princess, Macklem added.

Two years later, in 1937, the bank's bilingual series featured King George on most of its bills. By 1954, with its landscape series , every note carried the portrait of Queen Elizabeth, until now.

The new bill is also historic because it "features security technologies never before used on a Canadian bank note," Macklem said.

"Our new $20 note is both visually stunning and more secure than ever."

Tiff Macklem, governor of the Bank of Canada, holds the new Canadian $20 note featuring the portrait of King Charles as he speaks during its unveiling in Ottawa on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

The new note is polymer, predominantly green and vertical in orientation.

The Canadian National Vimy Memorial remains on the back. Charles is centred on the front.

The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.

In a news release , the bank explained that the portrait of Charles is surrounded by a floral and leafy tapestry "inspired by the King's lifetime dedication to the environment."

Also on the front are provincial and territorial floral emblems representing the 13 provinces and territories. A circular window, which the bank explains is visible from both sides of the note, "features plants that are culturally significant to Indigenous Peoples in Canada."

As for security features, the note has a purple security stripe that includes elements that "spin, transform and pulse" when the note is moved, the bank said. This makes the bill "easy to check and hard to counterfeit."

WATCH | New $20 bill unveiled: Bank of Canada governor unveils new $20 bill | Duration 1:10 Governor of the Bank of Canada Tiff Macklem calls the new vertical $20 bill featuring King Charles 'visually stunning and more secure than ever.'

"The new $20 note reflects important parts of who we are as Canadians, honouring our Commonwealth roots and our ties with international allies," Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in the news release.

"It honours our constitutional traditions through the portrait of His Majesty King Charles III and recognizes the service and sacrifice of Canadians through the Vimy Memorial, a symbol that continues to resonate across generations."

The Bank of Canada has previously noted that the $20 bill is its most-circulated currency.

The government announced that King Charles would replace his mother on Canada's currency during his coronation celebration in 2023. The first Canadian coins bearing the image of the King began circulating that December.

Back to royal work

Queen Camilla, centre, meets local schoolchildren during a visit to Spellow Hub Community Library in Liverpool, England, on Friday. (Peter Byrne/The Associated Press)

This time of year has a back-to-school, back-to-work, holidays-are-over feel to it, and that seemed to be the case for some senior royals this week, too.

After a traditional summer break at Balmoral in Scotland, King Charles and Queen Camilla had a noticeably busier roster of engagements over the past few days.

They were at the British Museum in London on Wednesday evening to view the historic Bayeux Tapestry .

Other engagements included Charles meeting the Pakistani national cricket team at Clarence House. Camilla was at the Royal Academy of Dance , and had engagements that focused on her literary interests in Liverpool on Friday.

On Thursday evening, Camilla also made a surprise appearance at an event that celebrates "the enduring power of literary correspondence," Buckingham Palace said.

Camilla read out loud a letter that was written by Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother after the death of her husband King George VI in 1952.

Queen Camilla, right, meets with members of staff and volunteers during her visit to the Ebony Horse Club to mark the youth charity and community riding centre's 30th anniversary on Thursday in London. (Henry Nicholls/Getty Images)

The notable uptick in royal engagements early in September is a change from the reign of Queen Elizabeth, who stayed much longer at Balmoral each summer.

"It's a slight modernization of … the royal calendar," said Prescott, who noted that there was a time when it was more based on the ecclesiastical calendar.

"The Queen just followed that rhythm of decades gone past, whereas [now] it's just more typical that September is a fully working month."

There is also, Prescott said, a sense that Charles likes his royal work, "so is perhaps, in a sense, itching to get back."

William to represent Charles at royal funeral in Norway

Charles, centre, then Prince of Wales, and Norwegian King Harald, second from left, arrive for a wreath-laying ceremony at the National Monument in Oslo on March 20, 2012. Harald died on Aug. 28. (Berit Roald/Scanpix Norway/AFP/Getty Images)

After the death last week of King Harald V of Norway , King Charles offered condolences and praised the late Scandinavian monarch for his " unwavering dedication," guiding his country "through times of great change with warmth and humility."

Charles also noted "close historical and family ties" between the U.K. and Norway, "with Britain one of the first countries to recognize Norwegian independence and establish diplomatic relations in 1905."

At Harald's funeral on Wednesday in Oslo, Charles will be represented by his son and heir, Prince William, Buckingham Palace announced Saturday. Princess Anne will also attend in a private capacity as godmother to the new Norwegian king, Haakon VII.

Who would represent the Royal Family in Oslo had been a matter of some curiosity.

"Everyone's asking me: 'Who will the Windsors send to the funeral?' because that is quite … significant," Vovk said.

"Over the last … 20 years, the Windsors have not done a great job in terms of participating in the royal community at things like funerals, investitures, those sorts of ceremonials."

King Harald, centre, arrives at Westminster Abbey in London on Sept. 19, 2022, for the state funeral service for Queen Elizabeth. (Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty Images)

One possibility for attending Wednesday's funeral was Prince William. Prescott noted that tradition has held that the British heir to the throne attends such occasions.

Still, there has been some inconsistency around all of this.

"When Elizabeth the Second died, we … sort of just assumed that the kings and queens of everywhere else would come, and so there's a bit of unevenness there in that relationship," Prescott said.

Harald's funeral will be held in Oslo Cathedral. Other royals expected to attend include King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima of the Netherlands , King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium and Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko of Japan.

Headlines have also focused on the Norwegian royal family since Harald's death, given the presence at a related event earlier this week of his disgraced step-grandson, Marius Borg Hoiby, and the expectation that he will be at the funeral .

Hoiby, who was convicted of rape in June, is the son of Harald's daughter-in-law, now Queen Mette-Marit, from a relationship prior to her marriage to now King Haakon. Hoiby is appealing his conviction and has received permission to attend the funeral.

Royally quotable

"The Bayeux Tapestry — or the Canterbury Embroidery, as it might just have been called — recounts a conflict. Yet here it is today, nearly a thousand years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."

— King Charles, during a speech on Wednesday at a viewing of the Bayeux Tapestry Exhibition at the British Museum. The fragile tapestry that depicts the 1066 Norman conquest of England is on loan from France for the 10-month exhibition.

King Charles, second from right, and Queen Camilla, centre, accompanied by French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel, view the Bayeux Tapestry Exhibition at the British Museum on Wednesday in London. (Richard Pohle/Getty Images)

Royal reads

A senior equerry to King Charles and Queen Camilla who captured widespread attention online is to step down from his role supporting the Royal Family. [The Independent]

Sarah Ferguson will return to the U.K. after relocating to a Swiss chalet amid the fallout over the friendship between her and her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to reports. [The Guardian]

Amid family feuds, damaging headlines and questions about its future role, the Royal Family has spent much of the past decade managing its public image. But the importance of good royal PR dates back centuries . [The Conversation]

Princess Ingrid Alexandra has stepped into a historic new role as heir to the Norwegian throne — and appeared to pay a touching tribute to her grandmother as she stood alongside her father at his swearing-in ceremony. [Daily Mail]

World.title: Far-right AfD party takes big lead in regional German election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Alternative for Germany party has a strong lead in a regional election, but it is unclear whether it will be able to form the country's first far-right state government since the Second World War, exit polls indicated Sunday.

Alternative for Germany, or AfD, went into the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern on its own. That would overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties' refusal to work with the AfD.

A first state government would be the biggest prize in the party's 13-year history, at a time of widespread discontent with an unpopular national government that has yet to persuade voters it can get the country's sluggish economy moving. It would be at least a symbolic blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose centre-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.

The polls for ARD and ZDF public television put the AfD on around 44 per cent of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.

That was far ahead of Merz's Christian Democratic Union, which was seen polling 18.5 per cent and losing about half its support. The centre-left Social Democrats and Greens also were on course to remain in the state legislature, with around eight to nine per cent each.

WATCH | How the AfD rose to prominence in Saxony-Anhalt: How Germany’s AfD escaped the far-right fringe in Saxony-Anhalt | Duration 7:09 For the first time since the Nazi era, a far-right German political party is eyeing victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. For The National, CBC’s Marina von Stackelberg goes there to find out how Alternative for Germany (AfD) went from fringe to frontrunner.

It was unclear whether the left-wing BSW party would get the five per cent of the vote needed to win seats. The exit polls put the AfD at least marginally short of an absolute majority.

Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD's charismatic 35-year-old candidate for state governor, told ARD that "we have written history." Voters, he said, had sent a signal that "things cannot carry on like this."

He said that the unpopular Merz had been "a very good campaigner for us."

Franziska Hoppermann, the national general secretary of Merz's CDU, said that it was "a very difficult result for us."

AfD is the biggest opposition party in Germany's national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt is located.

World.title: I almost skipped my colon cancer screening, but my bottom and I survived the scope
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person column is the experience of Stephen Workman, who lives in Halifax. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

At nine a.m., my wife handed me my phone. Somebody wanted to speak with me.

“Hi, Stephen, this is Stephanie. I’m with FIT testing, Nova Scotia.”

FIT stands for fecal immunochemical test. It screens for colon cancer. The test consists of a clear plastic sheet, a tiny garden spade, a sealable container and a stout envelope. I had been avoiding the test for weeks. Finally, I thought, well, it has always been negative. I’ll just get it done.

And then some time after mailing in the test, I usually get a letter. But this time it was a phone call.

Uh-oh.

The fecal immunochemical test (FIT) is a test that can be done at home and screens for colon cancer. (Nova Scotia Health)

Stephanie kindly explained that I could have cancer, a polyp, a tumour or nothing, and would I want a colonoscopy?

I pointed out that no one wants a colonoscopy, but I would take the appointment anyway.

She described the steps required to make my colon pristine. As she told me about the pre-procedure diet (bland, colourless and fibre-free, mostly chicken and rice), starting four days before the main event, I started laughing. So much effort, so little reward.

But the thing was, I was thinking: This could really be trouble. I have Parkinson’s disease. I have lived with it for the last six years. If I have cancer, then maybe I get chemo. If I get chemo, then I get chemo brain. I already have Parkinson’s brain. Together, they have got to be a lot worse than either one alone.

When she explained that I might need wet wipes to protect my sensitive bottom from the impending onslaught, I lost it again.

“You only want to do this once,” she said.

“Oh, don’t I know,” I replied.

Did I want the scope at nine in the morning or one in the afternoon? You drink a litre of a laxative called GoLYTELY four hours before the procedure. Or Go Heavily, more accurately. I thought I would be up all night anyway.

“Nine,” I said.

Stephanie was right: get the GoLYTELY icy cold, use a metal straw to the back of your tongue, and it is tolerable.

Barely.

Since I had Parkinson’s disease and constipation, I needed a big old-fashioned double dose.

Let me tell you, this stuff works.

For the first eight to 10 hours, nothing happened.

Then it did.

And then it just kept happening.

At the hospital, little blue footprints led to the colonoscopy suite. It occurred to me this would be an excellent time to get lost, but cancer anxiety had worn me down.

And my wife was with me.

She was empathetic.

“You don’t have cancer,” she said.

Statistically correct. Actually? I wasn’t so sure.

I could tell who was waiting for a colonoscopy. They had worried looks. They were in blue gowns, sitting on hospital towels. They looked like me.

I have veins like fire hoses but when stabbed with an IV needle, they rolled around like marbles. I apologized for them to the nurse.

Ow. Ow. Ow.

IV in place, the nurse smiled and asked if I was pregnant or breastfeeding.

“Not recently,” I deadpanned.

She laughed and told me I had made her morning.

Mine, too.

In the procedure room the nurse asked if I wanted any drugs.

“Sure!”

My colonoscopist reminded me a bit of an NFL linebacker. In my sensitive state, I was aware of his shoulders. He looked me over.

“You’re a tall, slim guy. There are going to be some sharp angles. Some corners that could be a bit tough to get the colonoscope around.”

If there were corners, they were straightened out.

At first it hurt a little. Then I found myself rocked up off the bed, yelling.

“Ow. Ow. Ow. That really, really hurts.”

I was probably heard in the parkade.

Across the road.

I think the medications lowered my inhibitions. That’s my story, and I am sticking to it.

The nurse put a hand on my shoulder.

“It’s better if you just lie still and relax.”

Sure. Easy to do while a garden hose negotiates a hairpin turn. Inside your abdomen.

The last few minutes of a colonoscopy matter most. Mine were fine. And with the medications it seemed like something that happened to someone else. It ended really well, too.

“Everything looked good,” I was told.

I was so relieved.

Having one chronic progressive disease wears down your resistance to having another. The what-ifs expand geometrically.

Going all PSA for just a moment; In Canada, roughly half of colon cancer cases are diagnosed at Stage 2 or 3. And yet many eligible people still do not complete the FIT test . It takes about five minutes. It comes in a very stout envelope. It can sit on bathroom counters for weeks.

Pharmaceutical maker Sanofi sponsored the display of the "Strollin' Colon," which shows what a healthy colon looks like, how polyps develop and how they can turn cancerous at the Capitol in Sacramento, Calif., Monday, March 24, 2014. The American Cancer Society, which had an information table at the display, urges screening tests to detect colorectal cancer. (Rich Pedroncelli/The Associated Press)

I know.

Mine did, too. Put the garden spade to work.

The day after my colonoscopy, I realized that in my drug-addled state, I forgot one very important thing. So here it is.

A sincere thanks.

I am not sure I would have had the, dare I say, intestinal fortitude to complete a colonoscopy on someone like me. But I am glad my colonoscopist did.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner hold talks in Ukraine after meeting with Putin
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held "encouraging" talks in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push to end more than 4½ years of Russia's full-scale invasion.

The trip by the Americans follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, as both sides have escalated their aerial attacks. Washington's push to end the fighting has lost momentum, with the Trump administration focused for the past six months on the Iran war.

Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv. Troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilomere front line.

Following two rounds of discussion with the U.S. officials, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the goal was a "just, fair peace" that would ensure there was "never an opportunity to resume aggression against Ukraine."

He also thanked the American negotiators, who traveled by train, for coming to Kyiv, their first time in Ukraine. Zelenskyy said the next round of talks later Sunday would bring in national security advisers from Britain, France and Germany.

"We’ve had very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we’re very encouraged," Witkoff said.

Kushner, Witkoff and Zelenskyy look around St. Sophia's Cathedral prior to talks in Kyiv on Sunday. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Office/The Associated Press)

Kushner said that U.S. President Donald Trump sees it as important "not just to figure out how do we end the current war," but how do create the conditions for durable peace.

A senior Ukrainian official, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to speak publicly, said that much of the discussion was focused on "how to get through the winter and what can be done before then."

No breakthroughs in Moscow talks

Saturday's meeting in Moscow lasted more than three hours behind closed doors and ended without any major developments being announced. Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, described the talks as constructive, frank and useful, but he didn't discuss specific outcomes.

While Moscow offered its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, Ushakov said, the talks weren't purely focused on the war in Ukraine.

WATCH | Witkoff and Kushner meet with Putin in Moscow: U.S. officials in Moscow with new proposal to end Russia-Ukraine war | Duration 8:55 U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are in Moscow to discuss a new proposal aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine. Michael Bociurkiw, senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, says there is deep skepticism in Ukraine that a proposal acceptable to Kyiv will emerge.

"Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," he said.

The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, was in January when they also held talks with Putin at the Kremlin.

Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire

Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks take place. Still, the two traded fire overnight into Sunday, officials said.

Russian attacks across multiple Ukrainian regions killed one person and wounded at least 10 others overnight into Sunday, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.

In Zaporizhzhia, drone strikes killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three people, while a drone damaged an apartment building, wounding seven people, in the Khmelnytskyi region.

Ukraine's air force said Sunday that it intercepted 82 drones out of the 108 launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.

In Russia, a man was killed and a woman was seriously wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a vehicle, according to local authorities in the Belgorod border region.

The Russian Defence Ministry said Sunday that its air defences overnight shot down 258 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, the Russia-occupied Crimean Peninsula and the waters of the Black and Azov Seas.

Mixed hopes on the ground

In Kyiv on Sunday, dozens gathered for a nationwide 9 a.m. moment of silence honouring Ukraine's fallen soldiers, a daily ritual held in cities across the country.

Nataliia Lipei, 67, whose son Viktor was killed in December 2022, was among those who attended. Despite a health condition, she has travelled from city to city to take part, and said she hopes the talks in Moscow and Kyiv will finally bring an end to the war.

"I hope these steps and these meetings will definitely produce results, because there has been so much bloodshed and so many deaths here that we have to stop all of this," Lipei told The Associated Press.

WATCH | Russia's drone incursions into NATO nations: Concerns grow over Russia’s incursions into NATO nations | Duration 3:41 Concerns are escalating that Moscow might trigger a direct conflict with NATO, amid repeated drone incursions on member states during the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine.

Not everyone shared her hope for the talks. Oleksandr Pastukhov, a 27-year-old video editor who joined the commemoration, was skeptical that the envoys' visit would change anything.

"We've already seen delegations like this come here before," he said. "We've seen this so-called ceasefire for three days, which ended after just a couple of hours, and now we're supposed to naively think that two people will come and change something."

In his Sunday prayer, Pope Leo renewed his appeal for peace in Ukraine and said he hopes the negotiations will bring results.

"I hope that the efforts undertaken in recent days to resume negotiations will bear concrete fruit and make way for diplomacy," he told the gathered faithful in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican.

World.title: Etsy seller's 'bruh' T-shirts were removed over a trademark complaint. He says it's trademark squatting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Sam Joseph Karam received an email from online retailer Etsy saying 11 of his T-shirt designs bearing the slang term "bruh" had been taken down for a trademark violation, he was immediately suspicious.

"It's usually one or two listings. It's not 11 in a row. So that obviously caught our attention pretty quickly," Karam said.

Karam, who owns the U.S.-based apparel company Customized Designs and sells clothing on sites like Etsy, says the platform also revoked his Star Seller badge — a mark given by the platform that means the seller provides top-tier customer service. Following that, he says he noticed an immediate drop in sales.

In the email, Etsy told Karam the shirt had been reported by someone named Malik Yawar Abbas, who holds a Canadian trademark for the term "bruh."

Karam is one of multiple Etsy sellers who told CBC News they've had items taken down from the platform after their use of the word was reported by the trademark holder. CBC News reviewed multiple emails Etsy sent to Karam and two other sellers that showed the takedowns came in response to complaints by Abbas.

A screenshot of part of an email Etsy sent to Karam, notifying him that some of his designs were taken down following a report by Malik Yawar Abbas, who holds a trademark on the term 'bruh.' (CBC)

Karam says Abbas, the trademark holder, is "squatting" on the trademark, aiming to make money by licensing the use of the word to others rather than by making a product of his own. Some legal experts say it's up to platforms and the legal system to better prevent trademarks from being used in this way.

No clothes for sale, request for payment

A trademark for the word "bruh" was issued by the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) in July 2025 in connection with selling many kinds of clothing, according to the government's trademarks database. Another trademark for the same word was recently granted to Abbas for use in advertising restaurant services.

In an email to CBC News, CIPO did not answer questions about the "bruh" trademark, but said each trademark application the office receives is "examined on a case-by-case basis."

After the listings were removed, Karam found the trademark holder's website and was surprised to find a section detailing how he protects the "bruh" trademark and directing others to license with him in order to get permission to use it.

"We didn't invent the word. the streets did. the internet did. but we realized its power," the site reads.

The site doesn't offer clothes for sale — just mock-ups of clothing and items like energy drinks using the word "bruh."

In an email to CBC News, trademark holder Abbas said those images are there to show "potential commercial applications" of the brand.

A screenshot of the website advertising the 'bruh' trademark. The website prominently advertises options to license the use of the word. (CBC)

When Karam contacted Abbas about the Etsy takedowns to see if he would withdraw his complaint, Abbas said he would if Karam agreed to a number of terms and paid him $1,000.

Karam refused, and says the signs in this case all point toward what he says is "trademark squatting."

"It's quite disheartening," Karam said. "When you have someone immediately turn around and say, 'I want $1,000, simply to go back and retract my complaint,' you know right there that they're acting in bad faith. That's my personal belief."

Abbas told CBC News via email that the $1,000 was a proposed settlement that was "part of a negotiated resolution of a disputed trademark matter. It was not paid, and no monetary settlement was concluded."

He also disagrees with the idea that he is squatting on the trademark.

"BRUH is a lawfully registered Canadian trademark being developed as a commercial licensing brand," Abbas wrote.

He has since withdrawn the complaint to Etsy, which he says he did after the 11 designs were removed and those products were no longer being offered to Canadian consumers.

But Karam says the "damage has been done."

He is currently in contact with an intellectual property lawyer and is considering taking legal action to try to invalidate the trademark on the basis of bad faith.

A screenshot of Sam Joseph Karam's Etsy listings that were reported by the holder of a Canadian trademark for the term 'bruh.' (Submitted by Sam Joseph Karam)

Bad faith trademarks can be taken down

Under a relatively new part of Canada's trademark laws added in 2019, a trademark can be invalidated if it was filed in "bad faith," explains Carys Craig, a professor at York University's Osgoode Hall Law School specializing in intellectual property law.

While cases arguing bad faith have popped up , she says this part of the law is still somewhat untested, so she's not sure what a court might decide in this case.

Craig says licensing can be a valid way of using a trademark. Overall, she says the way the "bruh" trademark is being presented on the website, along with the takedown orders that are being sought, might be enough to reach the standard of bad faith.

"We just don't quite know what that looks like yet."

Abbas told CBC News he trademarked the term in order to build a "licensing-only brand at the time when there was no BRUH-named brand in Canada," and disagrees that "protecting, enforcing or commercially developing" the brand should be characterized as bad faith.

"If there is a genuine disagreement about the validity, scope, or infringement of the registration, Canadian law provides mechanisms and forums to determine those issues," he said.

Does a trademark mean you own a word?

Despite broad use, general terms and pop culture phrases can be trademarked — it all depends on the context, according to Craig.

The point of a trademark is to differentiate the products or services of one brand from those of another, she explains. So a word like "apple" can't be trademarked to sell fruit because it's simply describing the product, but to sell computers, it works just fine.

There are some other criteria that are considered during a trademark application, but Craig says that because "bruh" isn't describing the product in this case, the word could reasonably function as a trademark.

Osgoode Hall Law School professor Carys Craig, who specializes in intellectual property law and technology, says it's up to the courts to decide if way the 'bruh' trademark is being used could be seen as bad faith. (Alexis Raymon/CBC)

But trademarking something doesn't mean you own it outright, and experts say the "bruh" clothes on Etsy might not necessarily be infringing just because they use the word.

Paula Clancy, an intellectual property law partner at Gowling WLG, says for courts to determine if there was infringement, they would look at how the alleged infringer was using the trademark — either as a source of origin, to appear as though it was from a specific brand, or in an ornamental way, as part of a design.

Shirts with phrases like "Bruh, we back," which Karam had taken down, "might well fall within those exceptions," Clancy said — meaning they might not infringe.

Despite that, Karam says Etsy didn't give him a way to appeal its decision to take the products down.

For his part, Abbas said he reported listings to Etsy when he "reasonably believed" the listings might conflict with his trademark rights, and never intended to "prevent people from using the word in ordinary speech or everyday communication."

In an email to CBC News, an Etsy spokesperson said the platform assesses and removes items when it receives proper notice of infringement and said sellers are responsible for following all laws and site rules. The spokesperson said sellers should reach out to the person who made the initial complaint if they think their listing shouldn't have been removed.

Clancy says she understands why platforms like Etsy take these trademark takedown requests seriously, but she says a policy that doesn't allow for appeals poses a challenge for sellers who are unlikely to take on the expense of going through the courts.

Testing boundaries of trademark system

Clancy says cases like this are rare in Canada.

"Usually, we see the other way around. We see the infringers using marks without authorization," she said, noting that some people will try to piggyback on the reputation of an established brand.

Intellectual property lawyer Paula Clancy says she understands why platforms like Etsy would take down products that are reported for infringement, but says those decisions could be hard for sellers to fight. (Stu Mills/CBC)

But Craig worries that because trademark disputes can be so costly, especially for small businesses, cases of trademark squatting or over-enforcement might fly under the radar more often than we think.

She also points out that despite objections from Etsy sellers, the trademark holder in this case has walked a "careful line" that could still be potentially within the bounds of the law, given they were granted the trademark rights and licensing trademarks is allowed.

"This is really testing the sort of boundaries of that trademark system and exploiting some of the … policy weaknesses or loopholes within the system," Craig said.

She says tighter rules might be needed to prevent these kinds of situations. More care might be required in the initial stages of issuing trademarks, she says, especially when it comes to zeitgeist-y phrases where there might be more incentive to try to corner them.

Easier processes for challenging possible bad-faith trademarks, and changes to online marketplaces that allow sellers to appeal trademark takedowns, might also help, according to Craig.

She called it a "worst case scenario" to be in a place where everything is protected, nothing is actually litigated and "everything is automatically taken down as soon as a trademark owner claims their rights."

World.title: Judge orders Colombia’s military to suspend air strikes on illegal armed groups
World.content:
A court ordered the government and the military to suspend air strikes on suspected members of illegal armed groups while studying the risk of harm to child forced recruitment victims.

In a preliminary sentence, the Bogota family court in response to a lawsuit that was filed by a civilian who claimed the State ignored its obligation to protect children when carrying out air strikes on illegal armed groups.

TO ORDER the PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC, the MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE, the GENERAL COMMAND OF THE MILITARY FORCES, the NATIONAL ARMY, the COLOMBIAN AEROSPACE FORCE, and the NATIONAL NAVY, through the appropriate channels and within the scope of their respective authorities, that, pending a decision on the merits in this constitutional protection action, they refrain from conducting offensive air operations against targets regarding which there is certain, objective, or reasonably verifiable information regarding the presence of children or adolescents recruited or used by armed groups, until the necessary precautionary and protective measures have been adopted and verified, and it has been determined, based on the available information and applicable operational protocols, that there is no less harmful operational alternative that would allow the legitimate military objective being pursued to be achieved Bogota family court

According to Radio Caracol, at least 107 minors were killed in air strikes on illegal armed groups since they were resumed by former President Ivan Duque in 2018.

The sentence comes a day after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the military killed 23 “narcoterrorists” in the deadliest air strike during the peace process that started in 2016.

The president vowed to resume bombing campaigns that were all but suspended by former President Gustavo Petro as he sought peace and demobilization talks with multiple illegal armed groups, a strategy rejected by the new far-right government.

Following the killing of at least three children in an air strike carried out in August, Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora blamed guerrilla organizations for the deaths, claiming they were recruiting children for human shields and combatants.

World.title: Colombia’s education minister resigns after less than a month
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella replaced his education minister after she resigned, claiming “an unexpected family situation.”

De la Espriella announced on social media platform X that he had accepted the resignation of the evangelical Education Minister Viviane Morales, who took office on August 7, the first day of the administration.

I bid a nostalgic farewell to my dear friend Viviane Morales. God’s designs are inscrutable, and she must leave us early to take charge of a personal situation that I sincerely hope she can resolve very soon. President Viviana Morales

In the same post, De la Espriella said he had appointed Ilva Myriam Hoyos, stressing that “I am confident that she will be an outstanding minister and that she will serve Colombia with dedication, character, and conviction.”

While in office, Morales lead the government’s Culture War in education and vowed to remove “gender ideology” from Colombia’s classrooms, and proposed a law that would allow churches to provide public education services.

Hoyos, a catholic, warned in 2016 that a peace deal between the government of President Juan Manuel Santos and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC promoted gender ideology.

The new education minister used to work with Alejandro Ordoñez, Colombia’s notoriously far-right former Inspector General and the country’s current ambassador to the Organization of American States.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.
