World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum delivers her second-year report as trade tensions simmer
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 31, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report, reflecting on the state of the nation as her second year in office draws to a close. She touted falling homicides and a stable economy, only to face a pointed rebuttal from opposition leaders who accused her administration of manipulating crime statistics and shielding officials tied to drug trafficking.

Mexico continues to grapple with security challenges on a variety of fronts, a fact underscored by a car bomb in Zacatecas Sunday night — the state’s third such attack in four days. But Mexico’s security forces remain active and on Monday claimed a high-profile target: Soldiers and marines killed Luis Enrique Barragán, alias “R5,” the accused leader of extortion against Michoacán’s avocado growers, in a shootout in Tocumbo.

Trade friction with Washington ran through much of the week. A dispute over cheese naming rights is complicating already-strained talks over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Mexico continues to push back against the threat of U.S. tariffs, and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 gathering Wednesday to press Mexico’s case against tariffs on steel, aluminum and cars.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum’s second-year report meets a sharp opposition response

President Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report Tuesday, a 67-minute address touting a 51% reduction in homicides since taking office, record foreign direct investment and a stable economy. She said her administration’s relationship with Washington “has had its challenges” but reiterated that “sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared.”

Opposition senators offered a starkly different account. PAN’s Ricardo Anaya disputed the government’s homicide figures, arguing that reclassified deaths obscure a rising toll, while PRI’s Alejandro Moreno accused the administration of an unspoken “pact” with organized crime, pointing to the unresolved U.S. extradition request for Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. Sheinbaum has said her administration won’t shield anyone who has committed a crime.

The president also used Wednesday’s press conference to accuse the Trump administration of trying to “create divisions” within her cabinet ahead of November’s U.S. midterms, calling it part of a long-standing U.S. pattern of pressuring “independent governments.” Her approval rating stood at 68% heading into the report, among the highest of any Mexican president at this point in a term, according to polling firm El Financiero. Along with the high approval rating, the newest results of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ found an almost 10-point increase in the president’s performance.

Security: Zacatecas car bomb and a cartel leader’s death

Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente — the third explosives attack in Zacatecas in four days. Authorities are investigating whether the blast was retaliation for the Saturday capture of an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) sicario. The explosion damaged 30 properties and 13 vehicles; classes were suspended and army troops deployed to the municipality.

The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The singing frog that came to symbolize midcentury Mexico
World.content:
While it may be a fine place to avoid New Orleans’ sweltering heat, Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library serves a much larger purpose as a repository of Mexico travel and tourism ephemera, including magazines, hotel brochures and highway maps.

Together, the collection offers a unique look at how the United States’ southern neighbors were constructed as attractive vacation destinations throughout the midcentury.

Mexico especially loomed large in the imagination of U.S. tourists. It was a period when, as historian Mauricio Tenorio notes, Mexico was understood as a “Brown Atlantis” — where revolutionary thought fermented, and the Pan-American Highway promised access to exotic adventures. Everyone wanted to meet Frida Kahlo and visit Teotihuacán, all while dreaming up global politics anew.

Two brochures found in the Mexican ephemera collection tell how Mexico feted itself for an international community, including the crooning amphibian that would become the country’s unofficial mascot during the time.

The singing frogs of Taxco

First is a trifold brochure from arguably Mexico’s most famous nightclub during the second half of the 20th century — Cantarranas. However, the site didn’t always host the international glitterati.

Located in the silver-mining town of Taxco, roughly 2.5 hours outside of Mexico City, the estate was initially conceived in 1538 by Hernán Cortés, who ordered its construction so that he could extract the region’s precious materials.

Dubbed Hacienda Cantarranas, – literally “singing frogs” due to the loud chorus of frogs living in the nearby area – Cortés’ son Martín de Cortés oversaw its construction, which featured large stones along a hillside. Over the years, the infrastructure took its toll on the unstable land it was built on and was ultimately abandoned in favor of a new locale.

For the next four centuries, the site was nothing more than a derelict ghost of Mexico’s colonial past. That is, until one entrepreneur saw an opportunity.

Antonio “Tony” Reyes Ramírez, who would later become Taxco’s minister of tourism, officially opened Cantarranas in 1957. Eager to capitalize on its history, Reyes Ramírez kept the name and leaned on its playful imagery in his marketing materials.

Cantarranas quickly developed a global reputation as a lively hangout throughout the 1960s and 70s, and even featured prominently in a popular television show of the time.

The brochure for Catarranas promises tourists a night of “flamenco dancing by Estela Calderón,” “Carl Brice directly from Nassau, Bahamas,” “Primitive African Drums by the owner and Manager of Cantarranas Tony Reyes,” and “The Latin American Rhythms of the great pianist Juan García Esquivel.”

The nightclub also housed several distinct spaces, including the “Twilight Room,” the “Patio,” the “Flamenco Room” and the “Mulata Room.” Newspapers of the time reported that, inside Cantarranas, “the audience moves en masse from room to room as each show finishes.”

During that same decade, the brochure from Tulane notes that Cantarranas was chosen as the backdrop for an episode of the NBC series, “I Spy,” entitled “Return to Glory,” which aired Feb. 23, 1966.

In it, Alexander Scott – played by Bill Cosby – is tipped off by U.S. intelligence to visit Cantarranas, where he rendezvouses with the wife of a deposed president of an unnamed Latin American country. Famed Mexican actress Dolores del Río plays the part of the wife, as Cosby and costar Robert Culp try to negotiate the democratic leader’s return to his home nation.

Cantarranas’ popularity continued to grow throughout the early- to mid-1970s.

A newspaper article from 1974 lists several of the club’s attractions, including “Flying Indian Men,” a discotheque called “The Psychedelic Cave,” bullfighting lessons, a piñata party, and calypso songs by Carl Brice.

However, as a new decade dawned, Cantarranas was beginning to lose its luster.

An article from 1978 reported that “Cantarranas is a little rough around the edges.” Two years later, the club was described as “the kind of place that you wouldn’t miss if you missed it. But worth it if you’re utterly bored.”

Unable to sustain itself any longer, in 1983, the Mexican state of Guerrero acquired the property and converted it into a culinary school and arts center. In 1992, it changed hands once again, this time to the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México as a school for foreign nationals.

Despite its short life, Cantarranas heralded Mexico’s midcentury miracle as its nascent legacy was beginning to be forged.

The birth of Señor Frogs

Twelve years after Cantarranas opened, another Mexican restaurateur, Carlos Anderson, was cooking up a similar concept that would come to define the Mexican resort experience well into the 21st century – Señor Frog’s.

First opened in Mazatlan in 1969, Señor Frog’s capitalized on that same midcentury swagger, with waiters slinging tequila shots and cajoling spontaneous conga lines in a neon cave. It’s unclear why Señor Frog’s succeeded where Cantarranas ultimately failed, but it did.

It wasn’t just the nightclub scene, either. The Tulane collection includes another brochure with a singing frog on it — this one from Pemex or Petróleos Mexicanos, the company formed in 1938 by the Mexican government to sell the nation’s significant oil supply.

The brochure includes maps of Mexican highways and invites travelers to explore the best routes. There is no mention of Cantarranas, or Taxco, or even nightclubs. However, at this point the singing frog had become emblematic of Mexico’s exotic sights, electric nights and cultural spectacle.

From Hacienda Cantarranas to Tony Reyes’ “Singing Frogs” bar, through a national oil company and today’s Señor Frog’s franchises, the brochure in Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library chronicles the birth of a national symbol, while documenting how tourists were meant to imagine the delights of midcentury Mexico – strange, inviting and culturally savvy, not unlike a crooning amphibian.

Kevin M. Anzzolin earned a PhD in Romance Languages and Literatures from the University of Chicago. He is the author of “Guardians of Discourse: Literature and Journalism in Porfirian Mexico,” published by the University of Nebraska Press (2024), which received an Honorable Mention from LASA-Mexico for Best Book in the Humanities in 2025. He currently teaches language and literature courses at Christopher Newport University (Virginia, USA). He also publishes in more public fora.

World.title: Is Mexican-made kombucha underrated?
World.content:
There are few drinks in history with an eccentrically bubbly origin story like kombucha.

The fermented probiotic can be traced back to China around 221 B.C. during the Qin Dynasty, when it was consumed as a “remedy for immortality” by those who considered the yeasty, naturally carbonated black tea a source of long-lasting health and vitality.

The long history of kombucha

In 414 B.C., the Smithsonian reports, the cloudy beverage was imported to Japan by a Korean doctor named Kombu, in order to treat Emperor Inkyo. To further complicate its history, Japan already had its own form of kombucha, made from kombu (brown seaweed) and cha (tea).

According to Forbes, kombucha began to spread during the global trade expansion of the 20th century, when the fermented Chinese tea variety migrated into Europe, with Russia and Germany having adopted it as “kambucha” and “kombuchaschwamm,” respectively.

In 1955, Italian piano prodigy Renato Carosone delivered a hit single, “Stu Fungo Cinese!” (translated as “The Chinese Fungus!”), which was rooted in a Chinese mushroom infusion similar to kombucha.

The drink gained mainstream popularity in China during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s, with homebrews known as “Stomach Treasure” touted as digestive tonics.

Finally, in the 1990s, kombucha entered the North American market, largely thanks to major U.S. brands like GT’s Kombucha.

In the past decade, kombucha’s ubiquity — and value — has skyrocketed as one of the fastest-growing beverage markets on the continent. Now a mainstream supermarket item, North American kombucha sales generated revenue of US $2.1 billion in 2025, with revenues expected to top US $4 billion by 2033.

Of course, the United States accounts for much of the lion’s share. But a market study revealed that Mexico is predicted to have the continent’s largest compound annual growth rate for kombucha in the coming years.

So what has taken kombucha so long to work its magic in Mexico?

Mexico as a country of many beverages — except kombucha, until recently

In my personal recollection, the Eurasian style of kombucha was never plentiful in Mexico. As a child, I could get all sorts of aguas frescas, carbonated sodas and any flavored drinks imaginable. As I grew older, that evolved into other forms of consumption (micheladas, carajillos, etc.). But I have no memory of ever seeing kombucha on a restaurant menu, at a cafe or in mercados.

Here’s my theory: With all of the other beverages that are made in, and often native to, Mexico — including tepache, a naturally fermented pineapple drink — the craft of Asian and Western kombuchas couldn’t get a foothold. In a country where you can easily get tequila, mezcal, pulque, sugar cane aguardiente, rum, atole, arroz con leche and so much more on practically every corner in any pueblo (often made by someone in the neighborhood with generations of family knowledge, ancestral practices and native ingredients at their disposal), kombucha didn’t necessarily have much demand. I’ve watched señoras prepare natural tea remedies from flowers they’ve handpicked from their gardens. But getting offered kombucha inside someone’s home? Never.

It wasn’t until the mid-to-late 2010s that I started to notice kombucha — commercially and independently bottled — as a relatively more common option around Mexico.

Kombucha in Veracruz and other states in Mexico

Near my home in downtown Xalapa (a region known for its rich and deeply rooted coffee history), all of the new-school cafes now offer kombucha, with a noticeable amount of homebrewed and locally made brands available. While recently enjoying my neighborhood on foot, I popped into a few nearby cafes — touted for their espressos, flat whites and other caffeinated brews — and was excited to see artisanal kombucha on nearly every menu. I asked the owner of Marcelo whether she has noticed a rise in kombucha’s popularity and consumption; she confirmed that within the past five years (by her estimation) kombucha has exploded with trendiness across Mexico. She even started to experiment with brewing her own batches, but after failed attempts, opted to get her supply from LindaSol Fermentería, a micro-kombuchería located a few miles from her cafe in Xalapa.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by the pickle (@thepickleofbrighton)

My personal go-to is Agua Brava, made by the chef at Bravo Pizza, a small pizzeria that opened in Xalapa two years ago. Their kombucha flavors rotate weekly and are made in-house and bottled on-site. Among other favorites that I’ve found in Veracruz are Komboocha Puerto (from the port city of Veracruz), Dominga Kombucha (from Cholula, Puebla) and Naran Fermentos (from Xalapa). Mexico City, Guadalajara, San José del Cabo and other cities are no different, offering their own unique brands like Cali Kombucha in Baja California Sur. Data and testimonials suggest that kombucha first infiltrated Mexico’s market roughly a decade ago, when Mexican-owned brands like the aforementioned Cali Kombucha and Brew Lab from Oaxaca launched their brands around 2015 and 2016, respectively.

To highlight the Mexicanization of kombucha since then, “kombucherías” are now a thing in Mexico — as evidenced in the social media reel above, made by a British tourist tasting Oaxacan kombucha in Mazunte. Spoiler: It’s “banging.”

Kombucha a la mexicana: Basil jamaica, pineapple coconut, and more

Though you won’t casually walk past a kombuchería on every corner, you’re likely to encounter a local kombucha brewer in your neighborhood, who might directly sell unmarked jugs or labeled microbatches of their SCOBY-made (Symbiotic Culture Of Bacteria and Yeast) concoctions. You’ll also find it in most grocery markets with a cosmopolitan clientele, or in small businesses that are dedicated to holistic living and organic products.

Often, the flavors have a tropical Mexican vibe: maracuyá, tamarindo, coconut, mango. Some brands add additional ingredients like ancho chile peppers, jalapeño, honey or kiwi for an extra kick of spice, sweetness or tang. Puebla’s Domingo Kombucha has a killer guayaba option — subtly effervescent, fruity and mellow. Mexico City’s Umani offers canned options including orange turmeric, Mexican pepperleaf and fig. Bruja Sana from Yucatán emphasizes herbally minty options with green, earthy additions like romero and hierba buena.

Many of Mexico’s leading kombucha brands are independent, and offer or encourage other lifestyle supplements like yoga and Pilates classes, SCOBY workshops and more. It’s far from commercial profit and mass-made consumer-targeted sales; instead, kombucha offers a doorway into a wider range of health-centered practices and mindful consumption with regional flavor.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Chile hosts Falklands trade mission despite sovereignty row
World.content:

CHILE · TRADE

Key Facts —What happened: About 25 Falklands business people will meet Chilean suppliers in Punta Arenas on September 28-29. —How big it is: Mayor Claudio Radonich says Magallanes has lost about US$300 million since 2011. —What it means: A signed contract aims to start a new sea route between Chile and the Falklands. —The catch: Chile backs Argentina’s claim to the Falklands, making this trade link politically awkward. —Who it hits: Chilean suppliers and Falklands businesses could gain, but Argentina objects to the route. —What comes next: The first ship voyage is expected in November 2026, pending approvals and demand.

A business delegation from the Falklands meets Chilean suppliers in Punta Arenas this month. The visit comes as Chile backs Argentina’s claim to the islands.

A trade mission with political weight

About 25 business people from the Falkland Islands are due in Punta Arenas, Chile, around September 26. The business round with Chilean suppliers runs on September 28 and 29.

The delegation includes Lou Ellis, deputy managing director of the Falkland Islands Development Corporation. Liam Short and Mike Summers of the Falkland Islands Chamber of Commerce are also part of the trip.

The Punta Arenas municipality is hosting the event. Mayor Claudio Radonich is a main promoter of the route.

Why Chile? A second maritime link

The goal is to establish a second commercial maritime connection between Chile and the Falklands. Montevideo is currently the islands’ only South American sea link.

Chilean shipping company Easter Island Naviera is driving the project. The first ship voyage is expected in November 2026.

This route would carry cargo and strengthen business contacts between Punta Arenas and the islands.

Argentina’s claim over the Falklands

Argentina has long claimed the Falkland Islands, which it calls the Malvinas. The islands are a British Overseas Territory, but Argentina says they are part of its territory.

Chile supports Argentina’s sovereignty claim. President Jose Antonio Kast restated that backing at a summit in Santiago on September 3.

Kast urged Argentina and Britain to resume negotiations over the islands. That makes a Chilean trade link to the Falklands politically sensitive.

The Strait of Magellan dispute

Tension began when Brigadier General Gustavo Javier Valverde, chief of the Argentine Air Force General Staff, spoke on a streaming programme. He called the Strait of Magellan, the far south, and the Drake Passage a ‘bioceanic key’.

He said Argentina must ‘maintain a presence’ there, which Chile saw as a challenge. Chile has sovereignty over the entire strait under treaties from 1881 and 1984.

Argentina’s foreign ministry, led by Pablo Quirno, later clarified its position. It said the treaties ‘are fully in force’ and are ‘considered definitive by the Argentine Republic’.

Argentina steps back

After the uproar, Argentina moved to calm things down. The foreign ministry issued a statement reaffirming its position based on the 1881 and 1984 treaties.

Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno’s statement said those agreements ‘are fully in force’. Regional media read it as an attempt to defuse friction with Chile.

Chile’s response

Chile’s president, Jose Antonio Kast, welcomed Argentina’s reaffirmation. The issue was discussed at a meeting in Santiago on September 3.

Chile’s foreign minister, Francisco Perez Mackenna, spoke on September 4. He called the link ‘a project between private parties that must comply with existing regulations.’

That statement shows Chile’s careful balancing act. It supports Argentina’s claim but allows private trade with the islands.

What the delegation hopes to achieve

The business round in Punta Arenas is part of a broader effort to boost trade between the Falklands and Chile. Local suppliers could gain new customers in the islands.

For the Falklands, a reliable shipping route to Chile would provide faster access to South American markets. It could also support the islands’ fishing and tourism industries.

The contract and its details

Easter Island Naviera and the Falkland Islands Development Corporation signed a contract made official on September 2. It is a commercial deal between a private carrier and the development body, not an agreement between governments.

The contract makes the route official, but sailing schedules and volumes are not yet set. The first voyage is planned for November 2026, subject to demand and approvals.

Argentina’s objection

Argentina’s government responded within a day of the contract. It referred to ‘unilateral illegal logistics activities’ in the disputed zone.

President Javier Milei was in Santiago on September 3 for a summit and met Kast. That evening, he addressed the nation on the Malvinas, announcing measures to discourage resource exploitation around the islands.

The economic stakes for Magallanes

Mayor Claudio Radonich says the Magallanes region has lost about US$300 million since 2011. That was when Mercosur banned Falkland-flagged vessels from its ports.

Radonich’s figure is an estimate of past losses, not a forecast of future gains. He argues the new route could help recover some of that lost trade.

Potential obstacles to the route

The route faces practical challenges, including weather and distance. The southern seas can be rough, which may affect shipping schedules.

Argentina’s government has objected to the route, and its legal framework requires permission for vessels sailing between Argentine ports and the Falklands. That could complicate operations.

What happens next

The business round in Punta Arenas will take place on September 28 and 29. After that, the shipping company will decide on the route’s feasibility.

If all goes well, the first voyage could happen in November 2026. But this depends on demand and on resolving any political issues.

Who is who in the dispute

Jose Antonio Kast is Chile’s president, in office since March 2026. He met Argentina’s Javier Milei in Santiago on September 3.

Pablo Quirno is Argentina’s foreign minister. His ministry issued the statement that calmed the Magellan row.

Brigadier General Gustavo Javier Valverde is chief of the Argentine Air Force General Staff. His remarks on a streaming show started the tension.

What the treaties actually say

The 1881 treaty set the border and gave Chile the whole Strait of Magellan. The 1984 treaty confirmed that and guaranteed free navigation.

Argentina says both are fully in force and definitive. That is why Valverde’s ‘presence’ remark caused such a stir.

The legal hurdle for ships

Argentina’s Decree 256 from 2010 requires prior permission for vessels sailing between Argentine ports and the Falklands. This could complicate the new route.

Chile is not a full Mercosur member, so the 2011 ban on Falkland-flagged ships does not apply to its ports. That is why Punta Arenas can host the link.

Voices of caution in Chile

Julio Leiva, a former commander-in-chief of the Chilean Navy, has publicly questioned the initiative. He said there will be a problem, according to regional media.

His worry shows the route is not universally welcomed in Chile. The government’s careful wording reflects that sensitivity.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is in the Falklands delegation to Chile? The delegation has about 25 members, including Lou Ellis of the Falkland Islands Development Corporation. Liam Short and Mike Summers of the Chamber of Commerce are also part of the trip. Why is the Falklands delegation visiting Chile? They are coming to Punta Arenas for a business round with Chilean suppliers. The goal is to establish a second maritime shipping route between Chile and the Falklands. What is the Strait of Magellan dispute about? Argentina’s air force chief called the strait and surrounding areas a ‘bioceanic key’ and a sovereignty issue. Chile responded that it has sovereignty over the strait under treaties from 1881 and 1984. How did Argentina react to the delegation? Argentina’s government objected to what it called ‘unilateral illegal logistics activities’. President Milei met Chile’s president in Santiago and addressed the nation on the Malvinas that evening. When will the shipping route start? The first ship voyage is expected in November 2026. The business round in Punta Arenas is scheduled for September 28-29.

World.title: Brazil: Gilmar Mendes Wants Police Staff Out of Court Chambers
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · JUSTICE

Key Facts —What happened: Justice Gilmar Mendes proposed a rule change to ban police and military staff from working in Supreme Court chambers. —How big it is: The proposal would affect all police careers and armed forces personnel, not just Federal Police delegates. —What it means: If approved, police officers could no longer serve as advisers to justices, ending a practice seen as problematic. —The catch: The proposal is not yet approved; it still needs review by a committee and a full court vote. —Who it hits: Federal Police delegates and other police and military personnel currently working in justices’ chambers. —What comes next: The justices must debate and vote on the change, but no date has been set.

Gilmar Mendes wants police and armed-forces staff out of Brazilian Supreme Court chambers. He put the proposal to the court on 5 September.

A proposal to change the rules

Justice Gilmar Mendes, a senior member of Brazil’s Supreme Court, has formally proposed changing the court’s internal rules. The change would stop police and armed forces personnel from working inside justices’ chambers as loaned or commissioned staff.

He submitted the draft on September 5, 2026. It goes first to the rules committee, then to the full court once Chief Justice Fachin lists it.

What the proposal says exactly

The draft would bar the appointment of armed-forces personnel to chamber jobs. It also covers every police force named in Article 144 of the constitution, the article that lists Brazil’s police bodies.

Those are the Federal Police, Federal Highway Police, Federal Railway Police, state civil and military police, fire brigades, and prison police. Brazil’s military police are uniformed state police, not soldiers.

The ban applies even if the person is on leave, seconded, or retired. It covers any commissioned position or function inside the justices’ chambers.

For a foreign reader the point is narrow but real. Who staffs a judge’s office shapes who sees the papers on the desk.

Brazil’s court has been arguing about exactly that for weeks.

Narrow exception for security only

The only exception would be for security duties. Even then, those personnel would be barred from participating in investigation files, case instruction, or legal advisory work.

The draft also tells the Court’s presidency to send serving police and military staff back to their own agencies. That would close out the current placements, not merely review them.

Why the practice exists

For years, Federal Police delegates have worked as advisers to justices who handle investigations. These delegates are often assigned to chambers because of their technical expertise in complex cases.

The court has said that these delegates do not exercise police powers inside the building. It frames their work as advisory and technical.

Why it is controversial now

Estado de Minas reported concerns inside the court. Some justices worry the change would weaken their own security arrangements.

No leak has been traced to any of the Federal Police delegates working in chambers. G1 reported Mendes’s complaint that chambers were turning into police stations.

Mendes has not repeated that phrase in his written proposal.

Reaction from police delegates

The National Association of Federal Police Delegates, known by its Portuguese initials ADPF, has publicly criticised Mendes’s position. It is a professional body, not the Federal Police itself.

Its president, Edvandir Paiva, called Mendes’s position lamentable on September 3, two days before Mendes filed the proposal. The association has not responded separately to the filed text.

The association argues that police delegates are not responsible for the court’s problems.

What happens next

The proposal goes first to the court’s rules committee, chaired by Justice Luiz Fux. Justices Alexandre de Moraes and Nunes Marques also sit on it, with Justice Flavio Dino as substitute.

Moraes sits on the committee that will review a proposal aimed at chambers including his own, where two Federal Police delegates work. The full court then decides once Chief Justice Edson Fachin puts it on the agenda.

No date has been set for that session. As of now, the proposal remains under internal consideration, and no vote has taken place.

What could change if approved

If the rule change is approved, police and military personnel would no longer serve as advisers in justices’ chambers. They could only be present for security duties, and even then, they could not touch case files or offer legal advice.

This would end a practice that has been common for years. Whether it eases the tension between the Court and the police is untested.

Uncertainties remain

The Court has published no full count of police or military staff in chambers. But Agência Brasil reports that Justices Moraes and Mendonça each had two Federal Police delegates as advisers.

It is also not confirmed whether the proposal will pass. The Rules Committee and the full court could modify or reject it.

Background: How the Supreme Court is organized

Brazil’s Supreme Court, known as the STF, has 11 justices. Each justice has a chamber, which is a team of advisers and assistants who help prepare decisions.

Chambers are essential because they handle thousands of cases every year. Advisers research the law, draft opinions, and manage case files.

The role of police in investigations

The Federal Police investigate federal crimes. They answer to the Supreme Court only in the narrow set of cases that court hears itself.

Those involve members of Congress or cabinet ministers.

Justices lean on police expertise in complex investigations. That is why some chambers have taken delegates on secondment from the Federal Police.

Who is affected and how

If approved, the ban would affect not only Federal Police delegates but also military police and other police careers. It would also cover Armed Forces personnel.

The draft tells the Court’s president to send those staff back to their own agencies.

A history of tension

The Supreme Court and the Federal Police have had a rocky relationship for years. Disagreements over investigations and leaks have fueled distrust.

Mendes’s proposal is the latest chapter in that story. He presents it as a matter of institutional separation.

How the Supreme Court’s internal rules work

The Supreme Court operates under its own internal rules, known as the Regimento Interno. These rules govern how justices organize their chambers and manage their staff.

Changing these rules requires a formal proposal, a review by the Rules Committee, and a vote by the full court. This process ensures that any change is carefully considered.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the proposal about? He wants to change the Court’s internal rules. Police and armed-forces personnel could no longer work as staff in justices’ chambers. Who would be affected? It would cover every police force listed in the constitution. That means Federal Police delegates, state civil and military police, and prison police. Why is this happening now? It comes during a period of open friction between the Court and the Federal Police. The friction is driven by worries about leaks and conflicts of interest, but no leak has been attributed to any individual. What is the next step? The proposal goes to the Court’s Rules Committee for an opinion. Then the full court will debate it in an administrative session, but no date has been set. Has the proposal been approved? No. It is still a proposal under internal consideration. No vote has taken place yet.

World.title: Brazil: Delegates’ Association Asks Top Prosecutor to Step Aside
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · JUSTICE

Key Facts —What happened: The delegates’ association asked Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet to step aside from the Banco Master case. —How big it is: The association says it speaks for more than 2,300 Federal Police delegates. —What it means: Gonet is reviewing a police report that also mentions him in messages. —The catch: Gonet has not formally responded to the recusal demand as of September 6. —Who it hits: The case involves Supreme Court justices and former banker Daniel Vorcaro. —What comes next: Gonet must decide whether to step aside or face growing pressure from police.

The association representing Brazil’s federal police delegates wants Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet to recuse himself from the Banco Master case.

The demand from police delegates

The Associacao Nacional dos Delegados de Policia Federal (ADPF) says it represents more than 2,300 federal police delegates. It published a note on September 5, 2026, expressing ‘indignation and concern’ over a procedure opened by Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet.

Gonet opened the procedure on the night of Friday 4 September. He used the prosecution service’s constitutional power of external control over police activity.

The procedure examines possible outside interference in the Federal Police report on Vorcaro’s contacts with Justice Alexandre de Moraes.

The delegates’ association makes three explicit demands. First, Gonet should declare himself barred from acting, and take no step in any case that names him.

Second, the procedure he instituted must be archived. The association argues it is an inadequate route to challenge a Supreme Court decision.

Third, everything found in Operation Compliance Zero must be investigated in full, “without selectivity as to the authorities involved.” That was the police raid that seized Vorcaro’s phone.

The delegates’ association is a professional body. It speaks for delegates, not for the Federal Police as an institution.

Who is Paulo Gonet

Paulo Gonet is Brazil’s Prosecutor-General, the head of the federal prosecution service, known as the Procuradoria-Geral da Republica (PGR). He brings federal cases before the Supreme Court.

The prosecution service also holds a constitutional power to review police conduct. That is what Gonet invoked here.

Gonet has asked the Supreme Court to annul the investigation that produced the report. He argues that an order to police to investigate named individuals, without a request from prosecutors and without police initiative, is null.

He has also ended talks on a new cooperation deal with Vorcaro. That is the Brazilian equivalent of turning state’s evidence.

Gonet rejected a second proposal because Vorcaro did not present new facts or sufficient proof.

O Globo and Folha de S.Paulo report that messages from Vorcaro’s phone describe attempts to draw Gonet into a prosecutors’ council election.

O Globo and Folha both note there is no sign of a crime.

The police report at the center of the dispute

Moraes used a separate internal Federal Police document to ask for an investigation of Mendonca. The police itself classifies that document as “sem valor probatorio” — without evidential value — according to Folha de S.Paulo.

A CBN report, citing Federal Police characterizations, states that the document has no decisional character and no probative value. It lacks official PF letterhead, does not bear a responsible delegate’s signature, and compiles information from unidentified sources.

Its authors rate parts of it as of “low to moderate” reliability. They say backing documents are missing.

The document says of itself that it has no probative value, according to Folha de S.Paulo. Mendonca’s allies use that to attack the basis of Moraes’s request.

Why Gonet is seen as conflicted

The delegates’ association argues that Gonet cannot supervise a case in which he is personally cited. Messages taken from Vorcaro’s phone mention Gonet, including a note about cigars and whisky, according to O Globo.

O Globo and Folha de S.Paulo report there is no indication of any crime in those messages. Gonet has not addressed their content publicly.

O Globo reports that some federal prosecutors privately see grounds for him to declare himself conflicted in the Banco Master case. These are internal conversations, not a formal public note.

Being named in seized material does not automatically bar a prosecutor under Brazilian law. Impediment and suspicion have defined statutory grounds, and it is Gonet himself who decides in the first instance whether he is barred.

The broader context: Banco Master and Operation Compliance Zero

Banco Master is a Brazilian bank at the center of a major investigation known as Operation Compliance Zero. The operation seized material, including messages from former banker Daniel Vorcaro, that exposed interactions with high-ranking officials.

The messages between Vorcaro and a contact the police believe is Justice Alexandre de Moraes are at the heart of the dispute. Justice Andre Mendonca ordered the Federal Police to produce a report on these messages.

That order led to the internal document now under scrutiny. The case has become a political and judicial battle involving the Supreme Court, the Prosecutor-General’s office, and the Federal Police.

It highlights tensions between institutions over the use of intelligence reports in judicial proceedings. The delegates’ association’s demand is part of a broader effort to defend the Federal Police’s institutional role.

What happens next

As of September 6, 2026, Paulo Gonet has not formally responded to the delegates’ association’s demand that he step aside. The PGR press office did not comment when the association’s note was published, and has not commented since.

Gonet must decide whether to step aside and archive the procedure, or to carry on. The internal debate among prosecutors about Gonet’s possible conflict of interest may also intensify.

Some prosecutors see reasons for him to step aside, but there is no formal move yet.

Gonet is one of four officials named in Peticao 16.704. Chief Justice Edson Fachin ordered them on 3 September to reply in writing within five business days.

The Supreme Court may still rule on the police report. Gonet has formally asked the court to annul the investigation that produced it.

The bottom line

The delegates’ association’s demand for Gonet to step aside is a significant development in the Banco Master case. It highlights the deep divisions between Brazil’s law enforcement and prosecution bodies.

The document Moraes relied on is described by the Federal Police as having no probative value. Mendonca’s allies say that undercuts the basis of Moraes’s request; Moraes has not responded publicly to that characterisation.

Gonet’s response, or lack of one, will be crucial. If he stays on the case, pressure from delegates and from some prosecutors is likely to continue.

For foreign readers, the case tests Brazil’s institutional checks. It also tests if a police document, deemed valueless by the force, can drive a case against a judge.

Gonet has not answered. Until he does, the situation remains fluid.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ADPF? The ADPF is the Associacao Nacional dos Delegados de Policia Federal, the national association of Federal Police delegates in Brazil. The association says it represents more than 2,300 delegates and advocates for the institutional role of the Federal Police. Why do police delegates want Gonet to step aside? The association argues that Gonet cannot supervise a case in which he is personally cited. His name appears in messages from the former banker Daniel Vorcaro. What is the police report about? It is an internal Federal Police document. It sets out messages between Vorcaro and a contact the police believe is Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Has Gonet responded to the demand? As of September 6, 2026, there is no confirmed formal response from Gonet to the delegates’ association’s demand. He has not publicly addressed the recusal request. What is Operation Compliance Zero? Operation Compliance Zero is a police operation that seized material, including messages from Vorcaro, leading to the investigation. The delegates’ association wants the facts uncovered by this operation to be fully investigated without selectivity.

World.title: Brazil: Bolsonaro Son Calls Judge a ‘Rotten Orange’
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: Flavio Bolsonaro called Justice Alexandre de Moraes a ‘rotten orange’ in early September 2026. —How big it is: The remark came during the presidential campaign, where Flavio is a candidate. —What it means: It escalates attacks on the Supreme Court while defending the institution itself. —The catch: Nikolas Ferreira, a conservative influencer, is building his own candidate network, causing friction with the Bolsonaro family. —Who it hits: It targets Justice Moraes, who oversees cases involving Bolsonaro allies. —What comes next: The right-wing camp faces internal tensions as Ferreira’s project grows.

As Brazil’s presidential race heats up, Flavio Bolsonaro attacks a top judge with a striking metaphor, while a rising conservative star builds his own network, stirring tensions on the right.

The ‘rotten orange’ remark

On September 5, 2026, Flavio Bolsonaro told reporters that Justice Alexandre de Moraes is a “rotten orange” inside the Supreme Court. He said the court must be protected, but Moraes should not contaminate the whole institution.

The phrase “rotten orange” is a direct translation of the Portuguese “laranja podre”. Flavio used it during a visit to a jail in Ponta Grossa, Parana, where former presidential aide Filipe Martins is held.

Who is Flavio Bolsonaro?

Flavio Bolsonaro is a federal senator and the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. He is running for president in the October 2026 election.

He has made attacking Justice Moraes a central part of his campaign. Moraes is a Supreme Court justice who has led investigations into alleged anti-democratic plots and misinformation.

Who is Justice Alexandre de Moraes?

Alexandre de Moraes is a justice of Brazil’s Supreme Court, known as the STF. He has become a target for many on the right because of his rulings against Bolsonaro supporters.

Flavio and his allies accuse Moraes of running a “persecution office”. Moraes’s defenders say he is protecting democracy from threats.

The context: a campaign against the court

Flavio’s remarks are part of a broader strategy to question Moraes’s legitimacy. He has also demanded that impeachment proceedings against Moraes move forward.

The remark followed a Federal Police report on Moraes’s contacts with Daniel Vorcaro, as reported by Folha de S.Paulo. Moraes disputes the report, has not been charged, and has not responded to Flavio’s remark.

Nikolas Ferreira: a rising star on the right

Nikolas Ferreira is a federal deputy from Minas Gerais state. He is a popular social media influencer with millions of followers, known for his conservative views.

Since early 2026, Ferreira has been building his own network of candidates for legislative positions. This “personal slate” aims to expand his influence within the Bolsonaro movement.

Friction with the Bolsonaro family

Ferreira joined Flavio’s campaign on August 14 and leads it in Minas Gerais. O Globo reports that his independent project has caused friction with the Bolsonaro family and allies.

O Globo describes “atritos” (frictions) between Ferreira and Flavio’s campaign team. Ferreira’s camp denies trying to undermine Flavio’s presidential bid.

A ‘cold war’ on the right?

Some Brazilian media have described the situation as a “cold war” between the Bolsonaros and Ferreira. In August 2026, Jornal de Brasília reported that allies of Eduardo and Carlos Bolsonaro attacked candidates supported by Ferreira.

They accused Ferreira’s group of giving Ferreira more space than Flavio in campaigns. Ferreira’s camp denies trying to undermine Flavio’s presidential bid.

What it means for the election

The internal tensions could affect the right-wing vote in October. Ferreira has a large following, and his endorsement is valuable.

The outcome may shape the future of Bolsonarismo after Jair Bolsonaro.

The bigger picture

The “rotten orange” comment is not just about one judge. It reflects a deeper conflict between the Bolsonaro camp and Brazil’s judiciary.

Ferreira’s move shows that the right is not a monolith. Different leaders are positioning themselves for influence beyond the Bolsonaro family.

How Brazil’s Supreme Court works

Brazil’s Supreme Court, the STF, is the highest court in the land. It reviews laws and decides cases involving top politicians.

Justices retire at 75. This makes the court a powerful and lasting institution.

The STF has broad powers to investigate and try cases. That includes alleged crimes by members of Congress and the president.

Moraes has used these powers in inquiries about fake news and anti-democratic acts. His critics say he oversteps his authority.

Why the judiciary is a campaign issue

Many Bolsonaro supporters see the courts as politically biased against them. They point to convictions and bans on their leaders.

Jair Bolsonaro himself is barred from running until 2030. The electoral court, the TSE, ruled this in 2023.

Flavio’s attacks on Moraes resonate with these voters. He promises to reform the judiciary if elected.

His opponents warn that such rhetoric undermines the rule of law. They say courts must stay independent from politics.

What the ‘rotten orange’ metaphor means

The metaphor suggests one bad element can spoil the whole group. Flavio uses it to separate Moraes from the rest of the court.

He says he wants to protect the STF as an institution. But he insists Moraes must go for the court to be trusted.

This is a careful balancing act for a presidential candidate. Flavio needs to appeal to anti-court voters without seeming anti-democratic.

Whether the strategy works is unclear.

What is not confirmed

Reports of a full “rift” in the Bolsonaro camp are not confirmed. Outlets use words like “friction” and “cold war,” but not “split.”

The exact size of Ferreira’s candidate network is unknown. No official numbers have been released.

It is also unclear how much Ferreira’s project will hurt Flavio’s campaign. Political analysts are watching closely.

What is clear is that tensions exist. The coming months will show if they grow into a real divide.

The role of social media

Social media is central to the friction between Ferreira and the Bolsonaro family. Ferreira built his following on platforms like YouTube and TikTok.

His posts reach millions of young conservatives. That reach makes him a valuable ally for any candidate.

The Bolsonaro family also has strong online presence. Eduardo and Carlos Bolsonaro often post supportive content for their father’s legacy.

How the ‘rotten orange’ phrase spread

Flavio first used the “rotten orange” phrase in early September 2026.

The phrase is catchy and easy to remember. That helps it spread among voters who distrust the court.

Critics say the phrase is disrespectful to the judiciary. Supporters see it as honest talk against an overreaching judge.

What happens next in the campaign

The election is scheduled for October 2026. Flavio and other candidates are now in the final stretch.

The coming weeks will show how the friction evolves. Both sides are likely to make strategic moves.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does ‘laranja podre’ mean? ‘Laranja podre’ is Portuguese for ‘rotten orange’. Flavio Bolsonaro used it to describe Justice Alexandre de Moraes, implying he is a corrupting influence inside the Supreme Court. Who is Nikolas Ferreira? He is a Brazilian federal deputy and social media star known for conservative content. He is building his own network of candidates, which has caused friction with the Bolsonaro family. Is there a rift in the Bolsonaro camp? Reports from O Globo and other outlets describe friction between Nikolas Ferreira and Bolsonaro family members. Whether it amounts to a full ‘rift’ is not confirmed, but tensions are real. Why is Flavio Bolsonaro attacking Justice Moraes? Flavio and his allies accuse Moraes of political persecution. Moraes has led investigations into Bolsonaro supporters, which they see as unfair. What is the Supreme Court’s role in Brazil? It is the highest court, responsible for constitutional review and high-profile cases. It has become a political battleground in recent years.

World.title: Brazil: 46% More Worried About Election Outcome Than in 2022
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ELECTION

Key Facts —What happened: Datafolha poll finds 46% more worried about the election outcome than in 2022. —How big it is: 57% say they are more determined to vote than in 2022. —What it means: Worry is split by candidate: 63% of Flavio Bolsonaro’s voters are more worried, versus 30% of Lula’s. —The catch: 32% are less willing to campaign than in 2022, against 18% more willing. —Who it hits: President Lula, who leads the first round by five points, and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. —What comes next: The first round is on October 4, with a likely runoff on October 25.

Nearly half of Brazilian voters say they are more worried about the outcome of next month’s presidential election than they were in 2022. The Datafolha survey, published on 5 September 2026, also finds 57% more determined to vote.

What the poll found

Datafolha’s survey shows 46% of Brazilians are more worried about the election result than in 2022. Another 28% feel the same, 24% are less worried, and 2% gave no answer.

The poll also found 57% are more determined to vote than in 2022. That compares with 32% who feel the same, 11% who are less determined, and 1% who gave no answer.

Worry splits by political camp. Datafolha found 63% of Flavio Bolsonaro’s voters are more worried than in 2022, while only 30% of Lula’s supporters say the same.

The same survey asked about willingness to campaign for a candidate. Only 18% said they are more willing than in 2022, while 32% said they are less willing.

How it was done

Datafolha interviewed 2,002 voters aged 16 and over in 125 municipalities on 1 and 2 September 2026. The margin of error is two percentage points, at a 95 percent confidence level.

The survey was commissioned by Folha de S.Paulo and Globo. It is registered with Brazil’s electoral court as BR-03669/2026.

For sub-groups such as a single candidate’s voters, the margin of error is four points. This matters for the partisan split, where 63% of Flavio Bolsonaro’s voters are more worried versus 30% of Lula’s.

The same survey, two releases

Folha de S.Paulo released the attitude questions on 5 September 2026. The voting-intention numbers came out on 3 September 2026.

Both sets of figures come from one survey. Datafolha interviewed 2,002 voters in 125 cities on 1 and 2 September.

The poll is registered with Brazil’s electoral court as BR-03669/2026. Folha and Globo commissioned the research.

This is not a separate attitudinal poll. It is one set of interviews, with different results released on different days.

The finding that cuts the other way

Datafolha also asked about campaigning for a candidate. Only 18% said they are more willing than in 2022.

Another 45% feel the same, and 32% are less willing. Five percent gave no answer.

That cuts against the idea that voters are anxious but engaged. Declared intent to turn out is up.

But willingness to take part in the campaign is down. The poll shows 57% are more decided to vote.

Yet 32% are less willing to campaign, per Datafolha. That gap suggests a passive electorate.

Worry splits by camp

Worry splits sharply by political camp. Datafolha found 63% of Flavio Bolsonaro’s voters are more worried than in 2022.

Only 30% of Lula’s supporters say the same. The gap mirrors a tense race.

The same survey put Lula at 38% and Flavio Bolsonaro at 33% in the first round. That five-point gap is outside the margin of error.

A runoff is closer, at 46% to 44%. That gap is within the margin of error – a technical tie.

The voting-intention numbers

Datafolha put President Lula at 38% in the first round. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro got 33%, and Augusto Cury 8%.

The five-point gap is outside the poll’s two-point margin of error. So Lula’s lead is real, not a tie.

In a runoff, Lula has 46% and Flavio Bolsonaro 44%. That two-point gap is within the margin of error – a technical tie.

Who Lula is

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has been in office since 2023. He is running for re-election with Vice President Geraldo Alckmin.

Lula governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010. He helped found the Workers’ Party in 1980.

He returned to power in 2023 after defeating Jair Bolsonaro. The party confirmed his candidacy in August 2026.

Who Flavio Bolsonaro is

Flavio Bolsonaro is a senator for Rio de Janeiro, in office since 2019. He is running for the Liberal Party with Alfredo Gaspar as his running mate.

He is the candidate because his father is ineligible. Former President Jair Bolsonaro is imprisoned over the attempted coup.

Where each candidate is strongest

Earlier Datafolha releases from August 2026 show clear patterns. Lula leads among women and poorer voters.

Flavio Bolsonaro leads among evangelical voters. These findings come from separate Datafolha releases, not the September survey.

The same August releases found 30% of voters back a candidate mainly to stop another winning. That anti-vote dynamic may shape the race.

These patterns help explain the tight runoff. Lula’s strength with women and the poor offsets Flavio Bolsonaro’s edge with evangelicals.

How to read a poll like this

A margin of error means the true number likely sits within that range. A five-point gap is outside a two-point margin, so it is a real lead.

A two-point gap is inside that margin, so it is a technical tie. Brazilian institutes must register polls with the electoral court before publishing, to keep the process transparent.

What to watch next

The first round is set for October 4. If no candidate tops 50% of valid votes, the top two face a runoff on October 25.

Datafolha will release more surveys in coming weeks. Each new poll’s margin of error and sample size matter for judging reliability.

Datafolha’s latest poll had a two-point margin of error. It surveyed 2,002 voters in 125 cities on September 1 and 2.

The poll is registered with Brazil’s electoral court as BR-03669/2026. Folha de S.Paulo and Globo commissioned the research.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Datafolha? Datafolha is a Brazilian polling firm linked to the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo. It conducts regular surveys on politics and social issues. How many people were interviewed for this poll? Datafolha interviewed 2,002 voters aged 16 and over in 125 cities. The interviews were conducted face-to-face on 1 and 2 September 2026. What is the margin of error? The margin of error is two percentage points either way, at a 95 percent confidence level. For sub-groups such as a single candidate’s voters, it is four points. When was the poll conducted and published? Fieldwork was on 1 and 2 September 2026. Folha de S.Paulo published the results on 5 September 2026, and the poll is registered as BR-03669/2026. Does this poll predict the election winner? No. These are the attitude questions from a survey that also measured voting intention. The voting-intention numbers were released separately on 3 September.

World.title: Venezuela: Cisneros Heirs Say State Seized Oil Stake
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

VENEZUELA · OIL

Key Facts —What happened: The Cisneros heirs say Venezuela seized their 40% stake in Petrodelta, an oil venture. —How big it is: The family claims losses of about US$2 billion in rights and investments. —What it means: It would end the Cisneros heirs’ role in Venezuelan oil, a rare private stake. —The catch: The link to Delcy Rodriguez and the Trump administration is a single-source claim, not confirmed. —Who it hits: The heirs of Oswaldo Cisneros, who are separate from the Grupo Cisneros media house. —What comes next: The family is complaining publicly, but no legal action is confirmed.

The heirs of Oswaldo Cisneros, a separate branch from the media empire, say Venezuela stripped them of their oil stake. A Spanish report ties the loss to Delcy Rodriguez and the Trump administration, but that remains unconfirmed.

Who are the Cisneros heirs?

The Cisneros heirs are the family of Oswaldo Cisneros Fajardo, a cousin of Gustavo Cisneros. Gustavo ran Grupo Cisneros, the media empire behind Venevision and Univision.

Oswaldo’s branch built separate businesses in telecom and bottling. They are not part of Grupo Cisneros, which has no role in this dispute.

The heirs hold their oil assets through a Dutch firm called DP Delta Finance B.V. That firm owns 40% of Petrodelta, a joint venture with Venezuela’s state oil company PDVSA.

PDVSA, short for Petroleos de Venezuela SA, holds the other 60%. The stake was bought in 2016 from Harvest Natural Resources, a Texas company.

That purchase came with a joint venture already in place.

What El Espanol reports

El Espanol, a Spanish newspaper, reported on September 6 that the Cisneros heirs lost their stake in six oil fields. The story is by journalist Laura Ojea.

The fields are operated by Petrodelta. El Espanol says the process was driven by Delcy Rodriguez’s government and backed by the Trump administration.

Delcy Rodriguez is Venezuela’s interim president. The report frames the loss as part of a larger political deal with the United States.

No major international outlet has independently confirmed that account. The Rio Times has not verified it either.

What Bloomberg reports

Bloomberg reported on August 18 that the heirs of Oswaldo Cisneros accused Venezuelan authorities of confiscating their oil rights. Diario Las Americas relayed that reporting two days later.

Bloomberg said the government revoked the rights on grounds of non-compliance. The stated reason was that the venture failed to meet investment and production plans.

Bloomberg reported that the assets were then reassigned to a U.S. firm, Pacific Coast Energy Co. Bloomberg dates the revocation to early 2026.

EnergiesNet, an industry publication, reports a tighter sequence. It says proceedings opened in May, the rights were revoked in June, and the fields went to Pacific Coast Energy in July.

The loss itself is reported by Bloomberg.

The six fields and the geography

The six fields are El Salto, Temblador, Uracoa, Isleno and Bombal in Monagas state, and Tucupita in Delta Amacuro. They lie in the Monagas Sur area.

Bloomberg described the rights as covering drilling in the Orinoco Belt. But the named fields sit outside that belt, in a different region.

The Orinoco Belt is an extra-heavy-crude zone along the Orinoco river in eastern Venezuela. Monagas Sur is a separate, mature oil area to the north of it.

The distinction matters for understanding the assets. The heirs’ stake is in conventional fields, not the belt’s extra-heavy crude.

The Trump connection

El Espanol links the Cisneros loss to a broader oil deal. That deal is between the Trump administration and Delcy Rodriguez.

The pact was announced on August 28, about ten days after the family went public. Trump said the United States had secured majority control of 65 billion barrels of proven reserves.

The reported terms are narrower. The U.S. takes 20% of output at cost, and the Defense Department holds a 35% stake in the joint venture.

The operator is North American Blue Energy Partners, led by Alejandro Betancourt. EnergiesNet reports that Betancourt also brokered the Pacific Coast Energy contract.

El Espanol’s link between the Cisneros loss and the Trump-Rodriguez pact is not confirmed by other outlets.

The family’s complaint

The heirs say the Venezuelan government stripped them of their rights. They made the accusation in a statement issued through DP Delta Finance BV.

They put their losses at about US$2 billion. That is their own valuation, reported by Bloomberg.

It includes roughly US$700 million of crude already produced. It also includes US$100 million of unpaid services through March.

DP Delta’s legal adviser, Juan Domingo Alfonzo Paradisi, told Bloomberg the government ‘initiated the revocation and is responsible for the confiscation.’

The family has not announced any court action. Its complaint has so far been made through statements to the press.

Who is Pacific Coast Energy Co.?

Pacific Coast Energy Co. is a small California operator with heavy-crude experience. It is led by CEO Klaus Hasbo and had raised about US$800 million before the award.

EnergiesNet reports the fields were handed over by administrative action, not a competitive tender. EnergiesNet reports the contract was brokered by Alejandro Betancourt, a Venezuelan businessman.

Betancourt also heads North American Blue Energy Partners, the operator in the U.S.-Venezuela pact. That connection ties the two deals together.

The Rio Times asked Pacific Coast Energy for comment and had no reply by publication.

The broader oil deal context

The Trump-Rodriguez oil pact is real and widely reported. Trump has said it grants U.S. control over a significant share of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

Delcy Rodriguez defended the deal on TV in late August. She said benefits are endless, claiming it would earn Venezuela over US$209 billion yearly.

The deal is controversial inside Venezuela. Critics say it hands over national wealth to a foreign power.

Supporters argue it is the only way to revive the country’s collapsing oil industry. El Espanol argues the Cisneros case is an early casualty of that strategy.

What it means for Venezuela’s oil sector

If the Cisneros loss is confirmed as part of the broader deal, it would signal a major shift. In this one case, assets went from a local private holder to a U.S. firm.

The government puts output at about 1.23 million barrels a day. Independent estimates are lower, at 1.1 to 1.2 million.

That is far below the peak of more than 3 million barrels a day in the late 1990s. The new deal aims to reverse that decline with U.S. investment.

But it may come at the cost of local business interests. Analysts say the case could scare off other foreign investors.

The analyst David Moran Bohorquez told EnergiesNet that a contract here can be revoked by administrative decision. It can then be handed to another operator within weeks.

Any foreign investor, he said, will wonder if the same could happen to them.

How the oil industry works in Venezuela

Venezuela’s oil industry is dominated by PDVSA, the state-owned company. For upstream oil production, private firms can only operate through joint ventures with PDVSA.

These ventures are common in the Orinoco Belt, where heavy oil requires special technology. But they also exist in mature areas like Monagas Sur.

The oil ministry revoked DP Delta’s rights on grounds of non-compliance, according to Bloomberg. DP Delta says the procedure was arbitrary and that it was given no hearing.

The government has not published the revocation decision. The loss is reported by Bloomberg from documents and people familiar with the matter.

What comes next

The Cisneros heirs are speaking publicly about their losses. No legal action is confirmed.

The Venezuelan government has not responded to the El Espanol report. The Rio Times asked for comment and had no reply by publication.

Observers will watch for any official statements from Caracas or Washington.

The family may seek international arbitration or legal remedies. Such cases can take years and often end in confidential settlements.

For now, the Cisneros heirs’ oil era appears over. The broader political and economic consequences are still unfolding.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the Cisneros heirs? The Cisneros heirs are the family of Oswaldo Cisneros Fajardo, a cousin of Gustavo Cisneros. They are separate from Grupo Cisneros, the media empire, and hold their oil assets through DP Delta Finance B.V. What did the Cisneros heirs lose? According to El Espanol, they lost their stake in six Petrodelta oil fields. Bloomberg reports the family says it lost rights and investments worth about US$2 billion. Is the claim about Delcy Rodriguez and Trump confirmed? No. The link is a single-source narrative from El Espanol, not confirmed by other outlets. Bloomberg attributes the revocation to Venezuelan authorities citing non-compliance. What is the Trump-Rodriguez oil deal? It is a pact announced on August 28, giving U.S. majority control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan reserves, according to Trump. The reported terms include 20% of output at cost and a 35% Defense Department stake. What did the Cisneros heirs say? They accuse Venezuelan authorities of stripping them of their oil rights and investments. They claim losses of around US$2 billion.

World.title: Casas Bahia Is Named in the Sao Paulo Tax Credit Investigation
World.content:
BRAZIL · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened São Paulo prosecutors named the retailer as a beneficiary of an alleged tax credit scheme.

— Who is investigating The economic crimes unit of the São Paulo state prosecution service runs the case, known as Operation Parallel Tax Office.

— The catch The company is named as a beneficiary, not charged as a defendant, and says it has had no formal notification.

— Why it matters The retailer is already in court-supervised recovery, where creditor confidence decides whether a plan survives.

— What is alleged Investigators are examining manipulation of state value-added tax credits inside the tax administration.

— What comes next Prosecutors decide whether to charge anyone beyond the officials already under investigation.

Named as a beneficiary is not the same as charged. For a retailer already in court-supervised recovery, the distinction is the whole story.

Downtown São Paulo. The investigation centres on the state tax administration rather than on any single company. (Photo: “Avenue and the downtown skyline of São Paulo” by Wilfredor, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Casas Bahia has been named in a São Paulo corruption investigation. State prosecutors cite the retailer as a beneficiary of an alleged tax credit scheme.

The case is run by the economic crimes unit of the state prosecution service. It has been publicly identified as Operation Parallel Tax Office.

The alleged scheme involves manipulation of state value-added tax credits. Those credits sit inside the São Paulo state finance secretariat.

The company is not a criminal defendant. It says it has not been officially notified of any investigation against it.

What Named as a Beneficiary Means

In Brazilian practice, prosecutors may identify a company that gained from a scheme without charging it. That is what has happened here.

The distinction is legal, not cosmetic. A defendant answers a charge, while a named beneficiary answers questions.

It can become a charge later. It can also stay exactly where it is.

Reporting the two as the same thing would overstate the record. So far Casas Bahia is in the second category.

A tax sealing notice on a shuttered stall on Rua 25 de Março in São Paulo. Tax enforcement is a constant presence in the city’s commerce. (Photo: “Operação Setembro na 25 de Março (36336345304)” by Agência Brasil Fotografias, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

The Investigation Itself

The target of the case is the state tax administration. Investigators are looking at how credits were granted and reduced.

Value-added tax credits are worth real money to large retailers. A company with thin margins and high turnover lives on them.

That is why the case reaches beyond the officials involved. Any company that received an unusual credit becomes a line of enquiry.

The rail operator Rumo opened its own internal inquiry as the same case widened. It was named earlier in the process.

Why the Timing Is Difficult

The retailer is in court-supervised recovery, Brazil’s equivalent of Chapter 11. It filed in August owing about US$3.3 billion.

Recovery plans depend on creditors believing the company will exist in two years. Investigations do not help that arithmetic.

None of this is a finding against the company. It is simply the worst possible moment to be named in anything.

How the Retailer Got Here

Brazil’s instalment retail model depends on cheap funding and steady jobs. Neither has held since 2023.

The chain is one of Brazil’s best-known household names. It sells furniture and appliances on instalment credit to lower-income buyers.

That model works when interest rates are low and employment is stable. Brazil’s benchmark rate has been high for three years.

The company has been shrinking stores and staff since 2023. A court ordered it to rehire workers in August after a dismissal round.

What the Company Says

The company says it has received no official notification. It has not been asked to respond to a charge.

It has not disputed that its name appears in the case file. Its position is that being mentioned is not being accused.

That is a narrow line to hold in public. It is also, on the current record, accurate.

What to Watch on the Guatemala Bodies Count

The first marker is whether prosecutors charge any company at all. So far the defendants are officials.

The second is the recovery plan vote. Creditors decide, and they read the same headlines.

The third is whether other retailers are named. A tax credit scheme rarely benefits only one buyer.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Casas Bahia charged in the São Paulo tax case?

No. Prosecutors have named the retailer as a beneficiary of an alleged tax credit scheme at the state tax office, but it is not a criminal defendant and says it has not been formally notified.

What is the investigation about?

The economic crimes unit of the São Paulo state prosecution service is examining alleged manipulation of state value-added tax credits inside the state finance secretariat, in a case known as Operation Parallel Tax Office.

Why does this matter for the company?

Casas Bahia filed for court-supervised recovery in August owing about US$3.3 billion. Recovery plans depend on creditor confidence, and an investigation makes that harder to hold.

Sources: Ministério Público de São Paulo, Estadão, Valor, Folha de S.Paulo, Mercado e Consumo, Rio Times.

World.title: Armed Gangs Strip Metal From Chile’s Copper Train Wagons
World.content:
CHILE · MINING

Key Facts — What happened Organised gangs are attacking copper trains crossing the desert in northern Chile and stealing metal in transit.

— How they do it Attackers jump from moving trucks onto wagons and throw copper slabs of about 80 kilograms to accomplices.

— The escalation Security analysts describe the groups as quasi-paramilitary, carrying firearms and wearing body armour.

— The catch The trains run through empty desert, so a response can be an hour away even when an alarm is raised.

— Who it affects Chile is the world’s largest copper producer, and rail is how the metal reaches the Pacific ports.

— What comes next Miners are weighing convoy escorts and route changes, both of which raise the cost of every tonne shipped.

The thieves do not stop the train. They jump onto it, push the metal off, and let the desert do the rest.

A freight train crossing the Atacama in northern Chile. The isolation that makes these lines cheap also makes them hard to protect. (Photo: “FCAB EMD GT22CU-3 San Pedro – Ascotan” by Kabelleger / David Gubler, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)
