World.title: The annual Delhi Yamuna flood threat- why September matters?
World.content:
A year after the Yamuna inundated large parts of Delhi, the river is again flowing above the danger mark. The immediate threat may be lower this time, but heavy rain in the upper catchment could quickly change the picture, exposing how vulnerable the cityâs floodplain still remains.

That vulnerability is built into Delhiâs geography. Every monsoon, as September sets in, the city watches the Yamuna closely because even a sharp rise in the river or a sudden surge in upstream discharge can quickly put thousands living and working along the floodplains at risk.

The danger mark at the Old Iron Railway Bridge is 205.33 metres, while evacuation of vulnerable residents begins when the river reaches around 206 metres.

On September 6, the Yamuna was flowing at 205.59 metres, already slightly above the danger mark.

And it is not just the people living along the river who feel the impact. When the Yamuna rises sharply, critical roads and infrastructure can also be affected. The Loha Pul, a vital link between Central Delhi (including Kashmere Gate and Old Delhi Railway Station) and East Delhi, is among the key crossings vulnerable to rising waters during severe floods.





2025: When the Yamuna broke its banks

Last year, the warning turned into a full-blown crisis.

The Yamuna crossed the danger mark and rose above 207 metres, inundating several low-lying parts of the Capital and forcing more than 10,000 people to evacuate vulnerable areas.

The warning numbers you should know

The impact extended well beyond flooded homes. Roads and public infrastructure were affected, electricity supplies were disrupted and houses were left covered in mud and silt after the water receded.

Thousands whose livelihoods depended on the floodplain also took a hit.

Floodwaters reached the Ring Road and Outer Ring Road, disrupting traffic between Majnu ka Tilla and the Salimgarh bypass. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi stopped cremations at Nigambodh Ghat and the Geeta Colony ground because of flooding. Water-treatment infrastructure was also affected.

A major factor was the enormous volume of water released from the Hathnikund Barrage in Haryana after intense rainfall in the upper Yamuna catchment.

2026: Is Delhi facing another repeat?

A year later, attention is once again turning to the Yamuna.

The monsoon remains active, with heavy rain reported in parts of Delhi and northern India. The immediate concern is not simply the riverâs current level, but how much water is being released upstream and whether intense rainfall in the catchment pushes those levels sharply higher.

The Yamuna has remained comparatively stable this year, despite crossing the danger mark.

2025 vs 2026 of Yamuna flood threat

Dr Shiv Singh Rawat, water expert and convener of the WalkForYamuna Campaign, said the difference becomes clearer when the upstream discharge is examined. âThis yearâs situation needs to be understood in its proper hydrological context. The maximum discharge released from Hathnikund Barrage during this year was around 64,000 cusecs, which is significantly below an extreme flood situation. That helps explain why Delhi experienced a much less severe river-flood situation than in 2025.

â

But that relative stability offers no guarantee.

The India Meteorological Department has warned of isolated heavy rainfall over Haryana, Chandigarh and Delhi from September 10-12.

Fairly widespread rain, accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning, is also likely over Uttarakhand from September 6-12, while rainfall disturbances are expected over Himachal Pradesh.

For Delhi, what happens upstream can matter as much as what happens within the Capital itself.

A spell of intense rainfall in the upper catchment can send a surge downstream, leaving communities along the floodplain with limited time to respond.

The flood threat does not end with the water level

The relatively stable Yamuna this year may have given Delhi a temporary reprieve, but the underlying vulnerability remains.

The floodplain is not simply vacant land beside the river.

It acts as a natural buffer during floods, helps recharge groundwater and performs an important ecological function.

Know how a Yamuna flood unfolds in Delhi

âThe 2-km-stretch on both sides of Yamuna acts as a buffer for floods, restores groundwater balance and acts as an organic filter. However, excess rain will create flooding in Delhi, and sanitation is not adequate to handle floods in the Capital,â says environmentalist Kavita Ashok.

Rawat warns that the greater danger could emerge gradually through construction and development. âThe concern is that areas outside the most restrictive floodplain zones could gradually become corridors for permanent construction, infrastructure and commercial riverfront activity,â he says.

âThat would undermine the very floodplain functions that protect the city.â

The question, therefore, is not only whether the Yamuna will rise this September. It is whether Delhi is becoming more or less vulnerable when it does.

Living with the Yamuna

For families living along Delhiâs floodplain, the monsoon is not simply a season of heavy rain. It is a recurring threat of displacement.

When the river rises, families may have to move their belongings, livestock and essentials to higher ground with little warning.

Delhi Yamuna Floodplain (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

The granddaughter of Ramu Sahni, who lives with his family near the Yamuna floodplain, told TOI that residents donât receive any advance warning.

âWe receive no warning on time. We see the rise in the water level of Yamuna and ourselves decide to shift to the roads with all our belongings. The authorities then notice the crowd on the roads and help us with tents.â

Sahni, who came to Delhi from Bihar in search of employment many years ago, says the relief arrangements have also changed.

âEarlier, they used to provide us with some ration and water in tents but now the situation has changed,â he says. âI donât live here for free, I pay rent.â

Houses built around Delhi Yamuna Floodplain (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

For many residents, simply relocating permanently is not an easy option.

Their lives are tied to the floodplain through work, transport, markets and social networks. When the water recedes, they return.

âWe return back here when the water recedes after 2 months. This is all we have. I run a rickshaw, we are mostly ragpickers. Where will we go?â

That cycle of evacuation, waiting, returning and rebuilding has become part of life for many families.

Animals: The overlooked victims

For families with livestock, evacuation is even more complicated.

Leaving home is one thing. Moving buffaloes, cattle, calves and other animals to safety is another. Stray animals are even more vulnerable, particularly when rising water cuts off their escape routes.

Buffaloes in the river | Fencing installed (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)

Sahni says livestock is not simply property for floodplain families, it is their livelihood. âPeople usually take their buffaloes with them on the roads.

How will they earn? Now they have installed fencing around a small Yamuna pond here. How will buffaloes go there? They need to be there for survival. If a flood comes right now, there is no way we can rescue them immediately as there is only a small route to travel.â

When asked who rescues stray animals during floods, he had no clear answer.

PETA India told TOI that animals stranded during floods can face exhaustion, dehydration, hunger, injury and drowning, making rapid rescue and access to food, clean water and veterinary care critical.

âThe biggest challenge when trying to reach animals in emergency situations is getting to them in the first place. Access may be cut off by rising water, for instance,â said Sachin Bangera of PETA India.

During last yearâs floods, PETA Indiaâs Rapid Response Team arranged a boat to rescue dogs stranded in flooded areas and at risk of drowning.

âAnimals who are left chained are the most vulnerable because they cannot escape, or they become exhausted and drown,â Bangera said.

Aditi Bakshi, Animal Welfare Advocate and Specialist - Government and Public Policy at Mercy For Animals, says the problem goes deeper than rescue.

âMany people are forced into an impossible choice by a system that gives them no option. Rescue boats and relief camps do not take animals. When the administration tells a family to evacuate and will not let them bring their cow, their pigs, or their two goats, the family has to choose between their childrenâs safety and the animalâs life.â

She argues that flood preparedness must explicitly include animals.

According to Bakshi, Delhi lacks a comprehensive operational framework covering animal evacuation, including a nodal officer, mapped animal shelters, pre-monsoon fodder stocks, evacuation protocols for large animals and regular drills. âA plan that has never been drilled is not a plan; it is a document,â she says.

Delhiâs real test: Preparing before the next flood

For Delhiâs floodplain residents, the Yamuna may rise for only a few days.

The disruption can last months.

That makes flood preparedness about far more than issuing warnings once the river begins to rise.

âRelief must be immediate, but rehabilitation must be humane and sustainable. People should not have to repeatedly rebuild their lives every monsoon,â says Dr Heera Lal Patel, IAS.

During a flood emergency, he says, authorities need to provide clear information, accessible evacuation routes, transport and safe shelters.

Vulnerable families cannot be expected to organise an evacuation on their own.

Rawat argues that Delhi needs scientifically determined, risk-based floodplain zoning.

âThe real measures of success are: how many people are taken out of high-risk locations, flood-storage capacity restored and new encroachment prevented.â

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

For companion-animal guardians, PETA India recommends identifying safe locations where pets will be accepted, keeping an emergency kit ready, and ensuring animals are microchipped or wear collars with updated contact details.

But the larger challenge is institutional.

The Yamunaâs rise is predictable. The exact scale and timing of a flood may not be.

For communities living beside the river, that distinction can mean the difference between having time to evacuate and scrambling for safety as the water arrives.

And every September, Delhi faces the same question: when the Yamuna rises again, will the city be better prepared, or will thousands once again be forced to leave their lives behind?

World.title: Satya Niketan: building collapse exposes a student hub grappling with housing crisis
World.content:
Hours after a five-storey building housing a boys’ hostel collapsed in Satya Niketan near Delhi University’s (DU) South Campus, killing two students, the spotlight has returned to a neighbourhood that has become one of the Capital’s largest hubs for outstation students. With its location on Ring Road, direct access to the South Campus metro station and proximity to several DU colleges, Satya Niketan has helped bridge the gap between the number of students and affordable housing.

Of the seven colleges around the South Campus, Shri Venkateswara College, Jesus and Mary College, Maitri College, ARSD College, Ram Lal Anand College, Motilal Nehru College and Aryabhatta College, only two have hostel facilities. Shri Venkateswara College has around 175 hostel seats, while Maitri College has just 27, leaving many students to rely on private paying guest (PG) accommodations in the neighbourhood.

Most of the colony’s original residents have moved away, giving way to matchbox-sized apartments converted into PG accommodations, not all of which comply with civic regulations. In the aftermath of the building collapse, civic authorities removed PG signboards across the neighbourhood as part of an enforcement drive.

Despite its crumbling infrastructure, students pay around ₹13,000 a month for a shared room with three meals a day in the colony’s narrow lanes lined with cafés, dhabas, gyms and coaching centres. By comparison, the annual cost of studying at a DU college ranges from ₹15,000 to ₹80,000, depending on the course and college.

A different sight

Sunny Gupta, who grew up in the colony, said 25 years ago there were only a handful of PG accommodations and a few commercial establishments.

“It was mostly a residential area. Due to the nearby colleges and the lack of hostels on college campuses, residential houses gradually gave way to PG accommodations, along with cafés and commercial establishments. Only a handful of the original residents continue to live in the area,” he said.

The building collapse, however, has brought renewed attention to how the colony has transformed amid the student housing crisis.

Students said that high demand allows PG owners to pack tenants into cramped rooms with little or no ventilation. “PG owners have a take-it-or-leave-it attitude because they know there is huge demand. They raise prices on a whim because they know no bed will go empty. In some rooms, the beds are placed inches apart,” said Gitika Jha, an outstation student.

According to preliminary reports, construction work was under way in the basement of the building that collapsed to expand its capacity. “Every year, a new batch of students comes to DU looking for a place close to college. They are new to the city, and Satya Niketan lures them with its convenience. Most girls move out in their second year once they know the city better and factor in travel time to college,” said Prachi Goyal, who spent two years in a PG near the collapsed building.

World.title: ABVP members clash with police during protest outside MCD headquarters over building collapse
World.content:
The Delhi police on Sunday detained at least 15 members of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) after they allegedly broke through the gates of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) headquarters while staging a dharna on Sunday evening. The protesters sought the resignation of the MCD Commissioner in connection with the collapse of a five-storey building housing a boys’ hostel in Satya Niketan, in which four persons were killed.

According to a police statement, around 150–200 ABVP members gathered near the Civic Centre to protest against the building collapse.

“The protesters entered the Civic Centre through Gate No. 5 and sat outside the main building, raising slogans and protesting against the functioning of the MCD. Subsequently, some protesters attempted to forcibly enter the main Civic Centre building, resulting in jostling with police personnel. Around 15 people were detained and taken to Kamla Market police station, where action under the Delhi Police Act is being initiated. The remaining gathering was dispersed by the police. The situation is presently under control.”

Speaking on the incident, ABVP national general secretary Virendra Singh Solanki said, “The Satya Niketan incident is deeply tragic and alarming. There must be an impartial probe into this collapse, strict action against those responsible, and immediate justice for the affected students. Accountability must be fixed for officials who failed to ensure student safety, and the MCD Commissioner should resign immediately.”

Stepping up demands

The protests come ahead of the Delhi University Students’ Union (DUSU) election later this month, with organisations stepping up demands for accountability in student accommodations across the Capital.

National Students’ Union of India president Vinod Jakhar said, “It is extremely painful to see students suffering like this. Several students were trapped under the debris, and every minute was critical. The police arrived nearly an hour after the incident and the NDRF around two hours later. This raises a very serious question: if emergency agencies take hours to respond when students’ lives are at risk, who will take responsibility?”

The Delhi State Committee of the Students’ Federation of India also staged a protest at the Delhi Secretariat, demanding a comprehensive safety audit of PGs and student accommodations and strict action against illegal and unsafe constructions.

“The absence of effective regulation and accountability has allowed unsafe buildings and exploitative PG and building mafias to proliferate across student residential areas.”

World.title: Satya Niketan building collapse: students turn to phones to look for missing friends
World.content:
While 12 people were located and rescued from the rubble after the Satya Niketan building collapse, a search continued till late on Sunday night for several others whose whereabouts remained unknown, with friends and families awaiting information.

Students across Delhi University (DU) shared names and photographs and made calls to trace missing friends. Sagar of Motilal Nehru College sought help tracing two friends who lived in the collapsed paying guest (PG) accommodation.

Students from nearby colleges also joined rescue efforts, helping remove bricks and debris before heavy machinery arrived. They later formed a human chain with the police to clear the road for earthmovers.

At Durgabai Deshmukh South Campus Metro station, around 400 metres from the collapse site, Saavy, DU president of the All India Students’ Association, scrolled through WhatsApp messages about missing students.

‘Sharing names, photos’

“We have already received eight such requests. People are calling and sending photographs and names of people who are missing. We have been receiving these messages on our helpline numbers,” she said.

One message read, “He is my friend who lives in the PG that collapsed. His phone is switched off, and I have no information about him… please, if anyone gets any information about him, kindly message me.”

Students video-called friends, asking them to search the rubble and surrounding areas and sharing photographs to help trace those missing. Requests came from families unable to contact loved ones.

Conflicting information was circulating about Yuvraj, with college authorities saying he was safe with his family in Madhya Pradesh, while others claimed he had died.

“We are trying to contact Yuvraj,” said Unnayan, another student involved in the efforts.

Aditya and Pawan Kumar were among the other names being circulated.

Those seeking information were asked to contact Nirali at 9974945558, Saavy at 9871751355 or Arpit at 8887731669.

World.title: CJP demands accountability over South Delhi hostel collapse; Dipke questions PM
World.content:
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Sunday (September 6, 2026) demanded accountability and a safety audit of all paying guest (PG) hostels in Delhi after a five-storey hostel building collapsed in the city's Satya Niketan area, leaving five dead and several trapped.

CJP founder and convenor Abhijeet Dipke criticised the government's priorities over educational infrastructure, saying students were being forced to live and study in unsafe conditions even as political establishments received attention and resources.

A CJP team led by its organisation co-in-charge and north zone lead Deepak Baliyan and national joint secretary Balakrishna Shukla reached the collapse site near Delhi University's South Campus and joined residents and emergency personnel in the rescue efforts.

Mr. Dipke, in a post on X, questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi over student safety, pointing out that Mr. Modi visited Delhi University a day earlier and invoked the term "dimagi naxal" in his political speech, but spoke little about the condition of educational infrastructure.

"Today, a hostel building in South Campus has collapsed, with students feared trapped under the debris. The number of casualties is still unknown," Mr. Dipke said.

"How long must students be made to pay the price for failing infrastructure?" he asked, demanding safe classrooms, hostels, and basic dignity for students.

"Adivasi students are dying in tribal belts due to a lack of care and support, and even students studying in the national capital are not safe," Mr. Dipke said.

"Is that really too much to ask?" he said, asking whether the Prime Minister would visit DU again and explain how the collapse happened.

Rescue operations were underway at the collapsed building, named Hostel Daze by its owners.

The CJP said its volunteers would remain at the site to assist families and monitor the rescue operation until all students are accounted for.

The outfit also demanded a swift inquiry into municipal oversight of student accommodations in the area and a safety audit of PG hostels across Delhi.

The on-ground CJP team said that even before emergency services arrived, the residents had begun rescue efforts with bare hands.

According to locals, the building had around 15 rooms, with two to three students staying in each, and construction or repair work was underway in the basement.

Many of the hostel residents are from Kerala, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and are enrolled at Motilal Nehru College, Atma Ram Sanatan Dharm College and Sri Venkateswara College, located across the road.

Residents also raised concerns about the structural safety of other buildings in the locality, where several residential properties have been converted into student PG accommodations.

Mr. Dipke also referred to the curtailment of Union Minister Amit Shah's visit to Goa after the news of the building collapse.

"While grand BJP Bhavans are being built across states, students are being forced to study and live in unsafe and inadequate infrastructure. This is not merely a question of buildings; it is about the future and safety of India's young people," Dipke said.

He called on the government to prioritise safe schools, functional hostels and quality educational infrastructure over "grandiose political establishments".

Mr. Shah, who is on a three-day tour to Goa, visited the party office at Chimbel village near Panaji and inaugurated it. While the event was underway, Chief Minister Pramod Sawant announced its curtailment due to a building crash in the national capital.

World.title: Moderate rain leads to waterlogging in parts of city
World.content:
Mderate rainfall on Saturday morning again led to waterlogging in various parts of the national capital, with residents wading through knee-deep water and traffic slowing to a crawl. Chief Minister Rekha Gupta conducted a surprise inspection of waterlogged areas near Sadbhavna Park in east Delhi and directed officials to deploy pumps to clear accumulated water.

The Chief Minister emphasised that all departments concerned must work with “complete promptness and coordination” to ensure Delhi residents do not face inconvenience due to rainfall.

Waterlogging was reported from several key locations, including National Highway 48 near Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport, Mahipalpur, and Sangam Vihar.

On Saturday morning, Delhi Police said in a post on X that due to “continuous heavy rainfall, severe waterlogging” was affecting traffic movement on Road No. 210, particularly between Rotary Chowk-DJB Chowk/Office and towards Omaxe in Dwarka.

Several parts of the city, including the international and domestic terminals of the Delhi airport, witnessed heavy waterlogging on Friday as well.

In light of the upcoming BRICS summit next week on September 12 and 13, senior officials from the Delhi government also inspected the route from Bharat Mandapam, where the summit is set to take place, to IGI Airport to identify any potential issues.

“Light to moderate rain accompanied by thunderstorm/lightning occurred at most places and heavy rain at isolated places over Delhi during the past 24 hours,” the Meteorological Department (IMD) said in a statement.

The Safdarjung weather station, which is considered the city’s representative observatory, recorded 37.3 mm of rainfall in 24 hours ending 8.30 a.m. on Saturday and 29.8 mm of rainfall from then till 5.30 p.m., officials said.

Light to moderate rainfall is expected on Sunday as well, according to the IMD.

Rain batters Gurugram

In Gurugram, heavy rain provided a much-needed relief from the humid conditions, but it also caused significant waterlogging in several areas, halting the city’s usual pace.

Traffic remained slow from Sarhaul Border to Rajiv Chowk, with 36 mm of rainfall recorded within just one hour.

Roads become ponds after a short spell of rain: Cong.

The Congress on Saturday said the party is worried that waterlogging, bad roads, traffic jams and rain water entering the Delhi airport in the run-up to the BRICS summit will tarnish the country’s image.

General secretary (organisation), Delhi unit, Anil Bhardwaj alleged, “After a brief spell of rain, Delhi gets submerged, roads become ponds and there are traffic jams for long hours. If the Delhi government fails to find a permanent solution to the waterlogging problem, it will tarnish the image of the country’s capital during the BRICS summit in front of the whole world.”

World.title: Make Delhi ‘Deregulation Capital’, investors urge CM at startup meet
World.content:
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Sunday held a dialogue with leading entrepreneurs and investors on the Delhi Startup & Incubation Policy 2026, aiming to support over 10,000 startups and generate more than 4 lakh jobs.

The meeting was organised by the Department of Training & Technical Education, Government of Delhi, to obtain direct inputs and suggestions from the industry and startup community to further strengthen the policy and build a robust, dynamic and entrepreneurial ecosystem in the national capital.

During the interaction, industry representatives suggested that the State government should become the first major customer for startups. They also urged the State to develop public AI infrastructure and data sandboxes for deep-tech and GovTech companies.

A statement from the CMO said: “Representatives from the industry and startup ecosystem suggested that considering Delhi’s existing strengths and capabilities, the city should work towards becoming the country’s ‘Deregulation Capital’ by enhancing the availability of land and workspaces for startups, rationalise FAR and circle rates, and create a more conducive business environment.”

Responding to the suggestions, the Chief Minister said the government is committed to make Delhi India’s startup and innovation capital, adding that Delhi has talented youth, strong educational institutions, technological capabilities, a large market, and the presence of leading industries, making it a natural hub for startups and innovation.

Ms. Gupta said that under the Delhi Startup & Incubation Policy, 2026, the Government is undertaking concrete initiatives to provide necessary support and opportunities to startups, including the establishment of incubation centres in colleges of Delhi University and schools. “The government’s objective is to create an enabling and supportive environment where young people receive encouragement for their ideas, innovation gets the right platform, entrepreneurs receive the necessary support, and startups generate new employment and economic opportunities,” the CM said.

World.title: The political cost of unconditional cash transfers
World.content:
Since 2020, Unconditional Cash Transfer (UCT) schemes have become an important electoral strategy in India, particularly to attract women voters. Some examples of such schemes include the Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thittam in Tamil Nadu, the Lakhsmir Bhandar in West Bengal, and Gruha Lakshmi Yojana in Karnataka. Yet, despite increasing the amount of cash before the 2026 elections, some governments which implemented these schemes were defeated. One possible explanation for the loss could be the political cost associated with UCTs.

UCT schemes are well-intentioned as they provide financial support to women. They partially advance SDG (Sustainable Development Goal) 5.4, which calls for a recognition of women’s unpaid domestic and care work. According to the Ministry of Finance’s latest Economic Survey, States are expected to spend about $18 billion on UCTs in 2025-26, much of it targeted towards women.

Critics, however, argue that these schemes function as electoral “freebies.” Their financing often requires expenditure switching or larger fiscal deficits, and reduces resources available for productive investments, including employment generation and self- employment programmes. Moreover, once households become dependent on UCTs, withdrawing them is difficult as political parties encourage competitive welfarism.

DATA | The cost of unconditional cash transfers

Targeting challenges

A fundamental challenge in targeted UCT programmes is beneficiary identification. Since governments cannot directly observe incomes for most workers in the informal sector, they rely on proxy indicators such as land ownership, electricity consumption, or household assets. This inevitably produces both inclusion errors (benefits reaching ineligible households) and exclusion errors (eligible households being left out). These targeting errors, whether real or perceived, can impose significant political costs.

The Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thittam scheme illustrates this challenge. Although the ruling party at the time promised ₹1,000 per month to all women-headed households before the 2021 election, fiscal constraints led the government to restrict eligibility based on income, land ownership, and other criteria when the scheme was launched in September 2023. Initially, about 1.13 crore women were covered. Following widespread complaints from women who believed they met the eligibility criteria, another 16.94 lakh beneficiaries were added in December 2025. The scheme cost ₹13,807 crore in 2025-26.

Despite the expansion, dissatisfaction persisted. Many women who considered themselves unfairly excluded reportedly became even more aggrieved when eligible beneficiaries received an advance payment of three months’ entitlement along with a special summer relief payment. Although the precise electoral impact cannot be measured, even modest shifts in voter preferences can influence outcomes in closely contested constituencies.

Similarly, the Lakshmir Bhandar scheme, which was introduced in 2021 to provide monthly assistance to women, faced allegations for including non-residential citizens. Although benefits were increased before the 2026 election, the incumbent government lost power. Maharashtra’s Mukhya Majhi Ladki Bahin Yojana and Karnataka’s Gruha Lakshmi Scheme also faced inclusion and exclusion errors respectively.

In Focus Podcast | Cash transfers for women: Do they challenge gender norms on unpaid care work?

These experiences highlight an important feature of targeted welfare programmes. Political costs arise not only from actual errors but also from perceived ones. Individuals who fail to satisfy official eligibility criteria may nevertheless believe that they have been treated unfairly. Likewise, households that legally qualify may be perceived as undeserving because they appear relatively affluent. Such perceived targeting errors can be as politically consequential as actual administrative mistakes.

This reveals an inherent tension between economics and politics. Economics favours targeted programmes so that scarce public resources reach those most in need. Politics, however, rewards broader inclusion because voters evaluate governments not only by the benefits they receive but also by those they believe were unfairly denied. Consequently, targeted UCT programmes carry an unavoidable political cost.

Conditional cash transfers and other incentive-based welfare programmes offer a more sustainable alternative. Linking benefits to socially desirable outcomes produces broader developmental gains. Tamil Nadu’s Midday Meal Scheme illustrates this principle. Since participation depends on school enrolment, self-selection reduces grievances.

The broader lesson is that welfare programmes tied to education or other desirable behaviours can achieve developmental objectives with lower political costs. In contrast, UCTs remain inherently vulnerable to inclusion, exclusion, and perceived targeting errors.

These political costs should be recognised alongside their economic and social benefits when designing future welfare policies

K. R. Shanmugam is Former Director, Madras School of Economics and Economic Consultant to GoTN. Sankarganesh Karuppiah is Indian Revenue Services Officer

World.title: Kochi Metro Officers Association seeks serving IAS official as KMRL managing director
World.content:
The Kochi Metro Officers Association (KMOA) has written to Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan seeking the appointment of a serving IAS officer with experience in infrastructure projects as the managing director (MD) of Kochi Metro Rail Limited (KMRL).

The association said such an appointment would ensure effective coordination between KMRL and the State and Central governments, district administration, local bodies, government departments, national and international funding agencies, and other stakeholders. This would help transform the metro agency into a model urban mobility institution in the country, it said.

The KMOA’s demand comes in the wake of the end of Loknath Behera’s tenure as KMRL MD in August and the District Collector being given additional charge of the post temporarily.

World.title: KP CM Sohail Afridi says he won't leave Sindh without holding Karachi rally
World.content:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Sunday said he would not leave Sindh without holding a planned PTI gathering in Karachi, as his convoy made its way to the city.

The KP CM, accompanied by PTI’s provincial President Junaid Akbar, has been on a five-day public mobilisation campaign in Sindh for the party’s September 27 nationwide protest for the release of its founder Imran Khan and his immediate medical treatment at Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital.

Earlier in the day, the KP chief minister addressed party supporters in Tando Allahyar and Hyderabad, complaining that authorities were creating hurdles in his convoy’s route.

Speaking to reporters at night while en route to Karachi, Afridi said he would stay in Sindh until he held a rally in the provincial capital.

“If we cannot reach Karachi today, God willing, we will hold the rally tomorrow; if not tomorrow, then the day after.

“I will not take a single step out of Sindh without launching a street movement in Karachi. I will stay here until the objective is achieved.”

Referring to Saturday’s comments by PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, the KP CM said, “We are welcomed on social media, while on the other hand, roadblocks are being erected along our route.

“I have already asked Bilawal that if he is not having all this done, then he should tell us who is doing it. Bring their names forward, then we will see what they do and what we do.

“The people of Sindh will question you, because the government and police are all under your watch. If the police are not doing this, then remove the police from the scene and let whoever is responsible come forward,” Afridi contended.

In a social media post on X, shared at around 11:15pm, PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh said the caravan would “reach Karachi in any way by defying all the hurdles”.

In a post at 9:44pm, Sheikh said, “We are present at extremely deserted, raw paths in the interior. God willing, we will definitely reach Karachi.”

In earlier posts on his X account, Sheikh said he was “clearing obstacles” that his convoy faced on Kotri bridge on the way out of Hyderabad.

Karachi’s District East police, in a statement, said that “no public gatherings, rallies or processions will be allowed around Mazar-i-Quaid”, located at Shahrah-i-Quaideen, where the PTI has planned its rally.

“If any gathering is held despite the lack of permission, legal action will be taken in accordance with the law,” it warned.

Security arrangements at Mazar-i-Quaid had been “further strengthened in view of the current threat situation”, the police statement added, noting the deployment of additional police personnel.

“Surveillance at the entry and exit points of Mazar-i-Quaid has also been further tightened.”

Routes blocked near Mazar-i-Quaid as of 10pm on Sept 6, 2026. — screengrab via Google Maps

While the Karachi Traffic Police cited “security” for closing some routes around Mazar-i-Quaid, a senior police officer told Dawn that the closures had nothing to do with the PTI rally.

The officer, who wished not to be named, said the roads leading to Mazar-i-Quaid were closed with containers as security agencies had issued a security threat.

The police officer said that the district administration had not given permission to the political party to hold a rally at the Mazar-i-Quaid because of the security threat. However, the party may hold a rally on the Super Highway at Toll Plaza or near Jail Chowrangi as there were no “restrictions” on them for holding the same at the said venues.

The senior officer said several party supporters were detained when they attempted to reach the Mazar-i-Quaid on Sunday evening.

He said around 150-200 workers of the PTI gathered, adding that the police tried to stop them but they “resorted to attacking the policemen with stones, resulting in injuries to one policeman”.

“The law enforcers resorted to shelling to disperse them,” the police officer said, adding that a few party workers were also detained during the action.

A traffic police official, who wished to remain anonymous, also told Dawn that certain roads had been blocked in the metropolis because of a “red alert” issued by law enforcement authorities.

As of 6pm, the traffic police said both sides of Shahrah-i-Quaideen had been closed to traffic for “security”.

As an alternative, traffic from Noorani Chowrangi was being diverted towards Khalid Bin Waleed Road, while traffic approaching Allah Wali Chowrangi was being diverted towards Tariq Road.

Shortly after 4pm, New MA Jinnah Road and the road near the Corridor-III parking plaza towards PP Chowrangi and Jail Chowrangi had been closed to traffic from both sides for security.

Traffic was being diverted from Saddar Dawakhana towards the Star Gate side, while traffic from Jail Chowrangi was being diverted towards Kashmir Road and Tariq Road.

Afridi assails Punjab CM in Hyderabad speech

Earlier in the day, CM Afridi addressed a huge welcome rally at Hyder Chowk in Hyderabad.

“Who does Hyderabad belong to?”, Afridi roared amidst applause from the crowd, whom he thanked for turning up to welcome him. PTI leaders Aminulalh Musakhel, Mohsin Ghulam, Faisal Mughal and Usama Hafeez were among those present.

“There are only two families ruling Pakistan – one from Sindh and the other from Punjab – but it was only PTI whose leader Imran Khan chose me, an ordinary worker, to be the KP CM,” Afridi said, referring to the PPP and PML-N.

“Tomorrow another worker is to become chief minister from PTI,” he added.

He urged youth to rise for their country and for themselves. “September 27 would mark a historic date and change the destiny of Pakistan,” he asserted, referring to the planned countrywide protest.

He assailed Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz for her recent remarks regarding other provinces and demanded an apology from her. Maryam had said on Saturday that Punjab faced a greater security threat from its neighbouring provinces than it did from India.

“Please tell us who is right,” the KP CM said, addressing the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) director general as he highlighted the military’s stance that India backed terrorist groups’ activities in Pakistan.

Accusing the Sharif family of tax evasion and having properties abroad, Afridi said, “These people were sincere neither in the past nor today and they will not be sincere tomorrow.”

Addressing the gathering, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja said that his party had faced enough cases, contending that courts’ doors have been shut on it. Raja described September 27 as the day of “true freedom” for people.

The PTI confirmed shortly after 5:30pm that the central leadership’s convoy led by CM Afridi had entered Hyderabad district.

Address in Tando Allahyar

Earlier, on his way to Hyderabad, Afridi addressed PTI workers in Tando Allahyar.

While thanking PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari for welcoming him to Sindh on social media, Afridi alleged that hurdles were being created for his convoy.

“My message for Bilawal Bhutto is that obstructions are being raised in our way,” the KP CM said, affirming that people were still with PTI despite those hurdles.

“Containers are being placed and craters are being dug,” he claimed.

“Is this being done by your [PPP] government or by someone else?” Afridi asked. “Will they host their guests in this manner?” he added.

The PTI leader urged party supporters and workers to join the planned September 27 rallies across the country.

In a video shared on X, CM Afridi said that it was “possible they might have created some hurdles in the way”, but the party convoy would defy them to reach Hyderabad, and then finally Karachi.

Thanking the people from Umerkot for their support yesterday, the PTI leader also asked the people of Hyderabad to be prepared for the PTI caravan.

“After Hyderabad, we will be in Karachi by the evening,” the KP CM declared.

In a statement, the PTI condemned the alleged blocking of its caravan travelling from Hyderabad to Karachi and also claimed its party workers in multiple cities of Sindh had been taken into custody.

The statement marked a turn from Saturday’s cordial exchange on social media between CM Afridi and Bilawal.

“On the one hand, Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari welcomes Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and PTI’s visit to Sindh on social media; on the other hand, the Sindh government, under his influence, is using the police to block roads and arrest PTI workers,” the PTI said.

It termed the alleged actions a “manifestation of the PPP’s blatant political hypocrisy and fear”. “If the PPP truly believes in democracy and political freedom, then why is it so afraid of a peaceful PTI political rally?” PTI asked.

PTI asserted that the police deployments, barriers and arrests could not prevent its party workers and the people of Sindh from exercising their political rights.

“The PTI leadership made it clear that the people of Sindh are not slaves to feudal or dynastic politics. They have the right to welcome leaders of the political party of their choice, voice their concerns and express their political opinion,” the party maintained.

It demanded that the PPP chairman direct his Sindh government to ensure “political freedom in practice”.

“If the welcome is limited to Twitter while police arrest workers on the ground, this is not democracy but political theatrics.”

The party also demanded the immediate release of all workers allegedly taken into custody in Hyderabad, Karachi and other parts of Sindh, as well as an end to any obstruction to the PTI’s political activities.

PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh, who was accompanying the KP CM, shared a video of him driving a truck, which he claimed was placed to block his convoy’s route in Tando Allahyar.

Sheikh later shared videos of what he described as the people of Hyderabad welcoming the PTI convoy.

‘Politics of tolerance’

On Saturday night, Afridi thanked Bilawal after the latter wished him the best for the rest of his visit to Sindh.

In a post on X, the PPP leader welcomed Afridi to the “city of martyrs” after the KP chief minister reached Larkana.

“Best wishes for the remainder of your tour across Sindh. We must ultimately return to a politics of tolerance, respect and coexistence, the foundation of any democracy,” Bilawal wrote.

In response, Afridi thanked him and noted that the “beauty of democracy is in freedom of politics and expression, independence of judiciary, acceptance of public mandate, an independent parliament and press being free”.

He also expressed hope that a large crowd would come out on the PTI’s call in Karachi and Hyderabad, where he is due today.

Last time Afridi was in Sindh to mobilise people for a street movement, he had initially praised the PPP-led Sindh government’s reception, saying the democratic legacy of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and Benazir Bhutto still thrived in the province. However, he had later accused the Sindh government of not upholding the honour of the ajrak and topi and criticised its treatment of its “guests”.

Ahead of Afridi’s rally in Karachi on January 11, the party had alleged that the KP CM had to face obstacles on his way to the metropolis. The party also accused the authorities of violence against its workers and supporters.

World.title: Iran warns of 'more painful response' if US launches further attacks
World.content:
Iran’s top negotiator on Sunday threatened a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes.

The exchanges of fire, which began with US raids last week, come amid a deadlock in the six-month war between the two foes.

Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the country in a bid to force it into submission.

“The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end,” said Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war.

“Any aggression against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response,” he added, in a speech carried by state media.

On Saturday, US Central Command (Centcom), which oversees American military operations in the region, said Iran had unsuccessfully fired at two American warships — an aircraft carrier and a destroyer.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said the warships had been “forced to retreat” after “suffering damage”, but Centcom said they successfully evaded the attacks.

In response, the US military said it struck three oil tankers linked to the Iranian Guards.

Centcom said it had “permanently disabled” one ship off the coast of the oil hub of Kharg Island and another near Jask, and “completely destroyed” a third vessel in the Gulf of Oman.

Video posted by the military showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.

The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, Centcom said.

Iran quickly retaliated, with the Guards saying their naval forces “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas”.

It warned ships not to attempt to transit the key trade waterway via routes unapproved by Tehran.

Early on Sunday, Iran’s IRGC also said it attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.

Centcom spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins, however, called the claim “a complete lie”.

“No US vessels have been attacked today,” he said.

‘Clinging on to power’

Centcom commander Admiral Brad Cooper had said after the exchange of strikes: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours.”

The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the attacks on its oil tankers as “illegal and aggressive actions”.

The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.

US Vice President JD Vance has gone so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war”.

Trump reiterated that view on Friday, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington.

Iranian officials have so far maintained their defiant tone, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC’s “This Week” programme on Sunday that Iran was “doing everything they can to cling on to something”.

“They know their nuclear programme’s coming to an end. Their navy has come to an end. Their air force has come to an end. They’re clinging on to power,” he said.

A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.

Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory”.

Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in the strait.

World.title: FO condemns mosque demolition in India's Uttar Pradesh, terms it part of 'drive to erase Islamic heritage'
World.content:
Pakistan on Sunday condemned the demolition of a century-old mosque in India’s Uttar Pradesh, describing it as part of an “Islamophobic and Hindutva-driven campaign to erase the Islamic heritage” in the country.

Responding to media queries regarding the demolition, Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan condemned the move and described it as “a reprehensible action against a historic Islamic place of worship”.

He recalled that the demolition of the Babri Mosque in 1992 was an “enduring symbol of this ideology of religious intolerance, prejudice and hatred”.

“Pakistan calls upon the international community to take immediate cognisance of the systematic persecution of Muslims by Indian authorities,” the statement said, highlighting the “continued desecration and destruction of their places of worship under state patronage”.

Khan called for accountability of Indian authorities for actions against the religious freedom and cultural heritage of all minorities, particularly Muslims.

According to The Indian Express, the mosque, which was located inside a Collectorate in Saharanpur, was demolished a day earlier.

The demolition came three days after a district court had dismissed an appeal against an order holding that the structure stood on government land and was unauthorised.

The September 2 order did not itself mention demolition.

The Indian Express quoted mosque staff member Tanveer Ahmed as saying that the order was for eviction, not demolition. He claimed the mosque was around 150 years old, and maintained that the land was recorded in their names.

All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen president and Hyderabad lawmaker Asaduddin Owaisi condemned the demolition and questioned whether the constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion applied to Muslims, NDTV reported.

According to Owaisi, the mosque dated back to 1911, claiming that the Collectorate itself was constructed later.

In 2024, the Akhonji mosque, which was over 600 years old, was razed to the ground without any prior notice in Delhi’s Mehrauli district. In 1992, a Hindu mob destroyed the famous Babri mosque, triggering riots that killed about 2,000 people across India, most of them Muslims.

World.title: Germany's far-right AfD emerges as landslide winner in eastern state vote
World.content:
Germany’s far-right AfD won a landslide victory in a key regional election Sunday in the ex-communist east, taking at least 44 per cent of the vote according to exit polls by two public broadcasters.

“We have made history today,” said a jubilant Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old lead candidate of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt state.

It was, however, too early to tell whether the AfD will have enough votes for an absolute majority that would allow it to govern a state alone for the first time.

The centre-right CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz came a distant second, winning around 18.5pc, according to exit polls by broadcasters ARD and ZDF.

Depending on the eventual count, the CDU’s state premier Sven Schulze would hope to still be able to form a new multi-party coalition to block the AfD from power.

All major parties have so far maintained a “firewall” of non-cooperation with the Moscow-friendly AfD, whose state branch is categorised as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.

A first-ever AfD state government would be a shock for many in Germany, which has been at pains to atone for its dark history of World War II and the Holocaust and so far kept extremist parties at bay.

The spectre of a far-right state government drew thousands of the AfD’s opponents to a rally on Saturday in Magdeburg, the regional capital, with banners saying “life is better without Nazis”.

“I’m very worried,” demonstrator Laura Saalfeld told AFP.

“Whatever the results, the atmosphere will change. Far-right sympathisers will show themselves more openly on the streets.”

Smiling face, radical agenda

Siegmund, the AfD’s telegenic top candidate, has ambitions to lead a political revolution from Saxony-Anhalt that would propel the party to national victory in 2029.

On the campaign trail, Siegmund — a former entrepreneur with a sharp undercut hairstyle and a huge social media following — has been mobbed by adoring fans, many wearing T-shirts bearing his likeness.

The party has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany as well as lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.

In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermünde.

While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting irregular migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.

The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes vows to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard, and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on the Third Reich.

In order to replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking of the population in the small state of 2.1 million people.

The German Economic Institute has warned the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.

Others have voiced fears that an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany.

The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin”, Thuringia state interior minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily.

The strong AfD win also heaps pressure on Merz, who has vowed to reboot a stagnant economy and restrict irregular immigration, but has seen his party beaten by the AfD in national surveys too.

Political scientist Wolfgang Schroeder of Kassel University said that after an AfD win in Saxony-Anhalt, “Merz’s critics will become even more vocal, and calls for better leadership will become impossible to ignore”.

World.title: NA speaker's ruling on employee records cannot restrict citizen's right to information, PIC rules
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Information Commission (PIC) has ruled that the National Assembly speaker’s decision to classify certain records cannot restrict citizens’ right to information (RTI) unless the ruling gives reasons showing that the harm from disclosure outweighs the public interest.

The PIC issued the ruling while deciding two appeals filed by journalist Saddia Mazhar against the NA Secretariat.

One of the appeals sought information about officers who had joined the NA Secretariat on deputation from January 2018 onwards, including their parent departments, grades, appointment dates, promotions and records relating to their induction into the secretariat.

The NA Secretariat had argued that minutes of meetings, official file notes and recommendations relating to the employees had been classified under the speaker’s ruling of Oct 4, 2022, issued under the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the National Assembly, 2007.

The speaker’s ruling had declared various records, including committee minutes, briefing material, working papers and certain personal records of employees, as classified for the purposes of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017.

The PIC held that the speaker, being the head of the National Assembly Secretariat, could exercise the powers under Section 7(f) of the Right of Access to Information Act, despite the provision specifically referring to the minister-in-charge of a public body.

However, the PIC stressed that such power was subject to the statutory requirements of the law.

“[The] ruling does not contain reasons as to why the harm from disclosure of information outweighs the public interest,” the PIC observed, concluding that it therefore could not operate to classify the records.

It further held that the speaker’s ruling was neither prospectively nor retrospectively operative because it failed to meet the legal criteria required for classification under Section 7(f) of the Act.

Regarding the employees’ records sought by the applicant, it noted that appointment and promotion notifications were already published in the official Gazette. It therefore found no legal basis for withholding the information.

The PIC also dismissed the secretariat’s preliminary objections regarding the non-provision of a copy of the applicant’s computerised national identity card (CNIC) and her non-appearance in person, declaring both grounds legally unsustainable under the Act.

It noted that information already published in the official Gazette or otherwise publicly accessible cannot be withheld.

The commission directed the NA’s deputy secretary, or a designated officer, to provide the applicant with a specific link to information available on the secretariat’s website and furnish certified copies of the remaining requested information, including Gazette-notified records, within 10 days of receiving the order.

The ruling also emphasised that the 2017 RTI Act takes precedence over inconsistent provisions contained in other laws under Section 25 of the Act.

In a 2025 policy brief, the Free and Fair Election Network (Fafen) noted that the RTI regime in Pakistan was stifled by institutional inertia and deep-rooted secrecy norms despite advanced legal provisions.

It had called for comprehensive legal reforms to strengthen the implementation of the RTI law.

World.title: PTI claims Hammad Azhar arrested in Punjab
World.content:
The PTI on Sunday claimed that its leader Hammad Azhar has been arrested, denouncing the action as “political vengeance”.

While police officials said they were unaware of his arrest, sources said the PTI leader was taken into custody in Multan in a case pertaining to the May 9, 2023 riots.

Replying to a query, Multan Regional Police Officer (RPO) Usman Akram Gondal told Dawn that he was unaware of any arrest and did not have any information.

According to reports circulating online, the PTI leader was handed over to the Lahore police over his alleged involvement in a May 9 case.

However, Lahore Investigation Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Muhammad Naveed said that he had no confirmation about Azhar’s arrest or handover to Lahore police.

In its statement, the PTI termed the former finance minister’s arrest “the worst example of political vengeance and fascism”.

The party demanded that Azhar be immediately presented in court if there was a criminal case against him, his fundamental and legal rights be ensured, and the “series of political vengeance be halted”.

“Hammad Azhar is being continuously targeted with retaliatory actions on political grounds. The government is recklessly using state power to suppress political opponents and silence the voice of PTI,” it alleged.

Former opposition leader in NA, Omar Ayub, also claimed on X that Azhar has been arrested.

“Strongly condemn this act,” the PTI leader wrote, alleging that the move aimed to “thwart” the party’s march planned for September 27.

Moonis Elahi, son of PTI President Parvez Elahi, said Azhar had been arrested in “various false cases”.

In April 2025, Azhar had stepped down as the president of the party’s Punjab chapter for the third time, after his two previous resignations were rejected.

Azhar reappeared in public on May 22, 2024, a year after he had gone into hiding when the state launched a crackdown against the party leadership following the violent incidents of May 9.

The PTI leader had evaded arrest by the Counter-Terrorism Department, which raided the PTI secretariat in Islamabad.

A police spokesperson said at the time that Azhar is wanted in three separate cases by the capital police, including two registered with Ramna police and one filed in 2023 with the CTD.

World.title: Scuffle in Karachi's DHA: Fresh case registered after inquiry report finds first FIR unsubstantiated
World.content:
KARACHI: A resident of Karachi’s Defence Housing Authority (DHA) has sought action against her neighbours and police personnel for allegedly beating her in a fresh case registered in connection with a scuffle outside her apartment last month, it emerged on Sunday.

The matter came to light when the CCTV footage of the physical altercation at an apartment building in DHA’s Phase 6 surfaced on social media last week. The footage showed police officials restraining a woman as another woman with a dumbbell attacked her.

However, the initial first information report (FIR) of the incident was registered against the woman who was assaulted and her brother. But an inquiry report later said that the allegations in the FIR were “not substantiated” by the findings and also recommended departmental action against police officials involved in the incident.

The report also said the first FIR should be disposed of, and subsequently, another was registered at the Darakhshan police station on September 5.

In the second FIR, a copy of which is available with Dawn, the complainant said she was a resident of a third-floor apartment in DHA, Phase 6.

The FIR quoted her as saying that on August 20 at 11:45pm, she was at her house with her brother and mother when a police officer rang the apartment’s doorbell and told her that her neighbour was calling them to the ground floor.

Shortly after, the complainant continued, her neighbour came upstairs while hurling curses and started banging on the door. “When I opened the door, she dragged me by the hair, snatched my phone, and threw it down,” she alleged.

“When my mother came out, she grabbed her by the hair as well and beat her,” the complainant claimed, adding that her neighbour then pinned her to a wall.

The neighbour then went to her apartment and came back with her daughter and some police officials and “attempted to take away our phones, […] and her daughter, who was carrying a dumbbell, hit us”, she alleged.

She further stated that she, along with her family, ran inside the house and called the police. “Meanwhile, the police officials outside broke the CCTV camera and later, the Darakhshan police broke into our house and took my and my brother’s cellphones away,” the FIR said.

The complainant sought action against the suspects for “beating me, stealing our mobile phones and damaging the security camera”.

The case was registered under Sections 147 (punishment for rioting), 148(rioting, armed with deadly weapon), 379 (punishment for theft), 427(mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees), and 337A(i) (whoever, by doing any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC).

Police official suspended

Meanwhile, Darakhshan Police Sub-Inspector Imran Khan was suspended with pay on Sunday, pending an inquiry into his conduct in the DHA scuffle case.

“He is shifted to PHQ Garden, South Zone Karachi, where he will attend daily roll call/parade, accordingly,” the suspension notice dated Sept 6 said, a copy of which is available with Dawn.

A show-cause notice issued to Imran by South Investigation Superintendent of Police (SP) Touheed Rehman Memon observed that Khan had “failed to collect the tangible evidence, video footage of the incident and conduct [an] impartial investigation purely on merit”.

His conduct reflected “a lack of professional diligence, negligence and dereliction of duty”, the notice stated, a copy of which is available with Dawn.

Appropriate punishment for the negligence could include removal from service, the notice stated.

An inquiry report into the incident had previously found that the investigating officer, identified as SIP Imran, had undertaken “no serious efforts” to collect evidence and did not independently apply his mind to investigate the case.

CCTV

In the CCTV footage of the incident, a woman can be seen rushing down a flight of stairs with a dumbbell in her hand and charging at another woman before using it to hit her.

The video also showed two individuals in what appeared to be police uniforms restraining the woman being assaulted, and a man who came up the stairs shortly after and began arguing with the woman with the dumbbell.

At one point, the man and woman being assaulted managed to go inside what appeared to be their home, following which the woman with a dumbbell and another man began banging on their door and yelling obscenities.

At the end, a man in a shalwar kameez was seen using a weapon, provided by one of the people in uniform, to smash the CCTV camera.

Inquiry report

An inquiry report, which was issued on Friday, found that the incident was sparked by a parking dispute between the mother-in-law of Korangi Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Fida Hussain Janwari and another resident.

It identified the police officials visible in the CCTV footage as constables Saqib and Haider Sultan. It further added that the plainclothes man who destroyed the CCTV camera in the footage was Constable Taimoor Ahmed, while the official who handed over his weapon for this purpose was Constable Amir Sohail.

“All were detailed for duty at the private bungalow of the Korangi SSP,” it said, adding that strict departmental action should be taken against them.

It further said that the on-the-spot arrests in the case without justifiable evidence by Darakhshan Station House Officer Rashid Ali and Assistant Sub-inspector Aftab Mangi were not justifiable and spoke of the officials’ “tilt towards the aggressive party”.

It said that the investigating officer, identified as Sub Inspector Imran, also undertook “no serious efforts” to collect evidence and did not independently apply his mind to investigate the case.

“Hence, all three officials of District South are recommended to be strictly proceeded against departmentally for miscarriage of justice,” it said.

It further said that the “lapse of supervision and lack of control over his subordinates is evident on the part of the Korangi SSP”. It called for examining his overall conduct in light of Civil Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 2020 and to take further action in this regard.

The report also said that an FIR should be registered against the SSP’s mother-in-law and her daughter and son, as well as the police officials present at the time of the incident, while the “victim family shall be encouraged to initiate legal action at free will against them”.

World.title: Police in India's Gujarat publicly beat man accused of killing partner
World.content:
Indian police publicly thrashed a man accused of beating his partner to death, local media reported on Sunday, drawing mixed reactions after footage of the flogging spread online.

Public parading and beatings of suspects by police are not uncommon in India, despite Supreme Court rulings prohibiting such treatment.

Officials said the thrashing was a response to the brutality of the alleged murder. The man, identified by police as Faizal Lakhani, was arrested in Bhavnagar, a town in Gujarat state.

Police took Lakhani on Friday to the scene of the alleged crime to reconstruct the incident. He was beaten at the site, and footage of the battering was shared widely on social media.

Videos show Lakhani’s arms restrained by ropes as a uniformed officer repeatedly struck his legs and buttocks with a bamboo baton. He was also beaten on his feet inside a bus terminal.

“We beat him to set an example that crime against women will be taken seriously and nobody else dares to commit such a crime,” police officer DP Unadkat said, according to the Times of India newspaper.

“When we do this, they fear the police,” Unadkat said, The Indian Express reported.

Some social media users praised the beating while others denounced the police officers’ actions, with several X users saying the man had yet to be found guilty of the crime.

Bhavnagar police chief Nitesh Pandey told AFP only: “I have nothing to comment.”

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment.
