World.title: Brisbane drivers using everyday items to avoid camera-issued parking fines
World.content:
Brisbane residents in parking enforcement hot spots have taken to obscuring their number plates with plastic sheets, camping chairs and dishcloths to avoid getting pinged as council rolls out a new automatic camera system.

Between its mobile enforcement vehicles, officers on foot and new static parking cameras, Brisbane City Council has handed out almost $35 million in infringement notices so far this year.

But some inner-city drivers are trying to keep one step ahead of the latest technology.

In a statement, a Brisbane City Council spokesperson said they are aware of the issue "occurring from time to time".

Cars in Newstead blocking their licence plates to avoid being detected by automatic licence plate readers. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

"Our officers can undertake patrols on foot to determine what's required on a case-by-case basis," the spokesperson said.

However, the council is unable to hand out infringement notices for obscured or altered number plates which fall under state legislation.

A spokesperson for the Queensland Police Service said vehicle number plates must be visible from 45 degrees in all directions at 20 metres.

Brisbane City Council says it does not have the power to fine drivers over obscured number plates. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

"That means that plates covered by bull bars, towbars, driving lights, faded or unreadable are all illegal," the spokesperson said.

"This also includes plates tucked up under parts of the vehicle or covered by any material."

The spokesperson said police regularly check the condition of number plates and issue a fine if they do not comply.

Illegal parking has 'big impact'

New cameras that run 24/7 targeting parking complaint hotspots were responsible for just over 8,000 of the fines issued this year.

The cameras, which target illegally parked cars in some of Brisbane's busiest corridors, were first rolled out in four hotspots in early 2025 before expanding to more than 40 locations in November.

Just two locations — Graham Street in South Brisbane and Park Road in Milton — accounted for more than 3,000 infringement notices.

The cameras target motorists stopped illegally in clearways, no stopping zones, bus zones, loading zones and on yellow lines.

In a statement, Civic Cabinet Chair for Customer Services Councillor Sarah Hutton said council wants "motorists to think twice before parking illegally".

"When a vehicle parks illegally in a clearway, no stopping zone or bus zone, it causes delays for thousands of people trying to reach their destinations," Ms Hutton said.

"Even a short stop in the wrong place can have a big impact on traffic flow and safety."

A trial of the cameras was rolled out in early 2025. (ABC News: Stephen Clarke)

In total, Brisbane City Council has issued 176,494 parking infringement notices this calendar year, coming to a total of $34,941,602.

Brisbane City Council's mobile enforcement vehicles delivered almost 100,000 infringements since January 1.

World.title: Spring showers possible for parts of Queensland
World.content:
Queenslanders lapped up sunny skies over the weekend but can expect possible showers for the east coast from Tuesday.

The Bureau of Meteorology said the state was experiencing above-average temperatures for this time of year.

Emergency services are continuing to battle fires across central and south-east Queensland, including a blaze near Gladstone that police allege was deliberately lit.

The large grassfire near Gladstone on the weekend. (Supplied: Allie Cole)

"The weather at the moment is dominated by high-pressure bridging, which is extending up to the east coast," meteorologist Denver Richter said.

"What that means is that smoke can't really escape into higher areas of the atmosphere.

"It is possible if those fires arc up a little bit that some more thick smoke will form and it's advised that people stay inside and close windows and doors if that does happen."

The high-pressure ridge is also generating heavy morning fog in parts of the state, which could linger into midway through next week.

"If you find yourself driving in fog, definitely slow down, get your fog lights on and give each other plenty of space," Mr Richter said.

People flocked to beaches on the Gold Coast to cool off. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

High-risk bushfire season

Rural Fire Service Queensland Chief Superintendent Shaun Toohey said above-average temperatures and strong winds coming off the deserts west of southern Queensland have made for a high-risk bushfire weekend.

"With those winds coming through, we're expecting them to be between 20 and 30 kilometres per hour, although that can obviously vary, with gusts exceeding those forecasts," Mr Toohey said.

He said one of his big concerns was people slashing or mowing long grassy areas, and that this weekend's winds could cause accidental sparks to get out of hand quickly.

"Those sorts of activities are best done in the late afternoon as the temperature drops and conditions ease. It's better to wait until those conditions have subsided altogether," he said.

"We're expecting to get back into a more stable environment around Monday night."

Mr Toohey said crews had been busy back-burning all winter and now additional resources were positioned in areas facing the greatest risk.

"We've made a really targeted effort to push a lot of those resources into the areas where we need them most," he said.

"It's all about focusing on those areas and making sure we're bringing in that surge capacity to help local crews get those jobs done."

Spring rainfall

Families gathered in central Queensland on Saturday for the annual Kalapa Horse Sports competition. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Showers are expected across the east coast on Tuesday and will continue until the weekend.

"Showers will initially be light, up to a few millimetres, before increasing to 3 to 10mm in the south-east, and up to 20mm on the north Tropical Coast from Thursday to Saturday due to an increase in the onshore winds," a BOM spokesperson said.

"Further inland, there will be patchy cloud through the week but no rainfall is expected."

World.title: Iran threatens 'more painful response' to any further US strikes
World.content:
Iran's top security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, has said his country will establish a "prohibited zone" near the strategic Strait of Hormuz, according to state media.

"In the coming days, a prohibited zone will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz," Mr Rezaei told state TV on Sunday.

"This zone will start from the US Navy's blockade line and include areas of the Persian Gulf. Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list [of Iran]."

Iran will also launch swifter and more forceful responses to US attacks, top negotiator Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf has said, after an exchange of fire in which Tehran targeted American warships and the US attacked Iranian tankers.

"The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end," said Mr Qalibaf in a speech carried by state media, adding that "any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response".

Saturday's attacks included the Revolutionary Guard Corps saying they targeted a US naval drone, three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and US vessels elsewhere, as well as a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) had said its forces "disabled" two Iranian oil tankers off Iran's Kharg island and "completely destroyed" an unladen Iranian crude oil tanker in the Sea of Oman.

Loading...

In its statement, CENTCOM said American warships had "successfully evaded" Iran's attacks.

Iran has largely blocked passage through the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of war on February 28.

US hits three Iranian oil tankers in new Gulf strikes The US military says it has hit three Iranian oil tankers in new strikes in the Gulf region.

Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and last month announced what it called an "economic asphyxiation" campaign on Iran aimed at strangling its already battered economy.

In his speech, Mr Qalibaf called on authorities to better manage Iranian imports to confront what he called the US campaign "seeking to paralyse the supply cycle and energy management".

On Sunday, local time, Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said Tehran was seeking to inflict economic damage on the US.

"If America wants to inflict one dollar of economic damage on Iran, it inflicts tens of dollars of damage on itself," he said.

Violence flares in Yemen

Fighting between Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in south-west Yemen killed more than 140 combatants between midday Saturday and early Sunday morning, local time, military sources have told AFP.

Two military officials with the Saudi-backed government forces told AFP that 84 of their troops were killed, mostly in missile attacks, while four Houthi military sources said 57 rebel fighters were killed in the same period.

Days-long clashes have erupted in Yemen over control of a gateway to the Red Sea in the deadliest fighting in the Arabian Peninsula country since a 2022 ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July.

Beginning on Thursday, the Houthis launched an offensive aiming to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab choke point at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

According to an AFP tally compiled using various military and medical sources from both sides of the conflict, more than 300 combatants and some civilians have been killed since the start of the Houthi assault on Thursday.

One military official with the internationally recognised government based in Aden said fighting had subsided in the early hours of Sunday morning.

AFP

World.title: 'Owe my life to you': Driver stops to pull rival out of flaming Ferrari
World.content:
A young Dutch racer is being hailed as a "superhero" after stopping on a race track to help pull a fellow competitor out of his flaming car.

The incident happened on Saturday in the China GT series in Shanghai, when 36-year-old British driver Ollie Millroy was part of a multi-car crash in his Ferrari.

The car was then engulfed in flames, and the situation was made more desperate by a lack of safety marshals in the area.

Dutch competitor Loek Hartog, 23, stopped, ran over to the flaming car and tried to help Millroy out of the driver's side door.

Unable to free Millroy, Hartog then grabbed a nearby fire extinguisher and doused the flames enough so he could then pull his rival out of the other side of the car.

"I owe my life to you," Millroy wrote on social media.

"Loek Hartog stopped instantly with no flag marshals or fire crews in sight, and risked his own life to get me out of the car. I don’t remember anything between 30 seconds before the crash and 1 hour after it, but I will remember his incredible act of bravery for the rest of my life.

"One day I will tell our three kids this story and Loek will be the biggest superhero in history in their eyes too."

Millroy said he broke five ribs, as well as his collarbone, hand, finger and sustained a bruised lung from the wreck.

Hartog wrote on social media that Millroy had nothing to thank him for, stating he wished anyone else in his position would have done the same thing.

"I wish to live in a world where this would not be considered as bravery but as instinct of others too," Hartog wrote.

"I am so thankful to have been right at the place I needed to be in space and time."

Chinese-owned news website Global Times reported that organisers of the China GT Championship will review "shortcomings" in the safety protocols of the series, among other areas of improvement.

"After the race, we will further review and investigate the accident and formulate more comprehensive plans to address shortcomings in competition organization, support, emergency response, rescue and medical services," organisers said in a statement.

World.title: Concerns new west Melbourne housing too close to pokies
World.content:
After years of sitting empty, hectares of land once the site of an explosives depot in Melbourne's west will be transformed into 500 homes.

Although the extra housing in Deer Park is welcomed, some locals are concerned that the proposal is too close to a pub with poker machines and no alternative community hub in the plan.

"It's a potential social housing disaster,'' said local resident Graeme Blore.

" My concern is the devastation poker machines are causing. Brimbank has one of the highest rates of gambling losses of any LGA in Melbourne. "

Punters lost $185 million in Brimbank LGA last financial year, more than other local government area in the state.

The Brimbank local government area has one of the highest rates of gambling losses in Victoria. ( Four Corners: Jerry Rickard)

The Deer Park Hotel, which is next to the housing development, recorded $19.5 million in gambling losses, while the Deer Park Club, less than a kilometre away, recorded a further $17 million in losses.

"That's over $100,000 a day, every single day of the year," Mr Blore said.

He has campaigned against the plans for years.

Now, for the first time in his 70 years he has joined a political party, the fledgling West Party.

Cost of gambling harm in Victoria reaches $14 billion The social cost of gambling in Victoria, such as bankruptcy, loss of productivity at work, mental ill-health, and divorce, has reached $14 billion, a new study has found.

The new party has a plan to crackdown on poker machines if they win influence at this November's state election.

"We are not about outlawing altogether,'' Werribee candidate Paul Hopper said.

"We just see a much fairer and more equitable system for the people of Victoria, and we think these addictive features need to be dealt with and minimised."

Mr Hopper previously ran as an independent in the last Werribee contest.

The West Party wants to remove elements of poker machines such as alarms that make losses sound like win, as well as changing the rate pokies can spin.

Complex policy area

Treasury collects $1.5 billion in pokies taxes every year, while the social impact of problem gambling in Victoria, of which pokies is the biggest contributor, was estimated to be $14 billion.

The political issue is usually championed by minor and non-government parties.

But the Labor government under Daniel Andrews made a shock announcement in 2023 that it would pursue a scheme forcing punters to preset how much they were willing to lose.

Punters would require a card to play.

It was hailed as a major step forward by advocates worried about problem gambling, but was slammed by the industry.

Victoria's treasury collects $1.5 billion in pokies taxes every year. (Getty Images)

The state has since passed laws to enable the scheme's rollout and a trial has been held.

However, the wider rollout was delayed under Jacinta Allan who feared a negative campaign from clubs and pubs ahead of the November election.

The trial was also criticised for being too weak and its results are yet to be published.

The Coalition has previously questioned whether carded play would work after consulting the hotels lobby.

"Labor's carded play trial ended nine months ago, yet its results remain secret,'' a Coalition spokesperson said.

"An elected Coalition government will release the results of the trial upon coming to government. We will consider all forms of technology in evaluating the best ways to mitigate gambling harm."

Premier Ben Carroll has backed the scheme.

"These things have worked,'' Mr Carroll said on Friday.

"They have had a big, important impact, and that is why what is evidence-based we have to look at delivering on."

Victoria's political parties have different approaches to gambling reform. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The Greens want to phase out poker machines and have called for tougher bet limits in the interim.

"The Liberals want pokies to be able to take as much money from Victorians as they want, and this will kill people," Greens leader Ellen Sandell said.

"I think it's a disgraceful policy. Labor and Liberals are both in bed with the gambling lobby."

Long-time anti-pokies campaigner Reverend Tim Costello said he was please the West Party was pursuing a policy to cut harm but lamented the lack of action under the former premier.

"Labor has failed to deliver on carded play. The Liberals? They're nowhere," he said.

"They aren't even talking about this terrible addiction that transfers money from the poorest people, particularly in Labor electorates in the west, to the captains of the gaming industry.

"It is appalling for both the major parties."

World.title: Far-right party wins a German state election for the first time since WWII
World.content:
Germany's far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) has become the largest party in the state of Saxony-Anhalt following a regional election, representing the first far-right win in the country since World War II.

Exit polls from Germany's two public broadcasters, ARD and ZDF, showed the AfD had a commanding lead in the state, taking at least 44 per cent of the vote.

That constituted a jump of 20 per cent for the AfD compared with the last Saxony-Anhalt regional election in 2021.

That result means AfD could win as many as 39 seats in the state's 83-seat parliament, just shy of a majority, ARD projected.

Alternative for Germany has campaigned for a "deportation offensive" in Saxony-Anhalt. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

The centre-right CDU, which has governed the state since 2002, saw its vote share collapse to just 18.5 per cent.

Most parties, including the CDU, have long vowed not to form a coalition government with the AfD.

Behind the rise of Germany's far right Far-right party Alternative for Germany is running second in national polls. Here's how it got there.

Ulrich Siegmund, the lead candidate for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, said his party was prepared to reach out to all parties to form government.

"We have made history today," he told supporters.

"We extend a hand to all democratic forces that wish to pursue better policies."

Beyond the AfD and CDU, voters appeared split on where to place their votes, with no other party earning more than 10 per cent of the total vote.

Result draws protests, shock

The AfD party's co-leader Alice Weidel hailed an "historic" result, which had given the AfD a clear mandate to govern, but it was not immediately clear whether it would be able to form a government.

State premier Sven Schulze congratulated the AfD and acknowledged the result showed it was the strongest party.

Protesters were seen gathering on the streets of Saxony-Anhalt's capital city Magdeburg.

The AfD's breakthrough presents a challenge to Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his CDU party. (AP: Markus Schreiber)

Following the result, the CDU pledged not to cooperate with the AfD nor with the far-left, but the vote is likely to increase pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has struggled in recent polls.

Franziska Hoppermann, the national general secretary of Mr Merz's CDU, said that it was "a very difficult result for us".

Lars Klingbeil, co-leader of Germany's centre-left SPD party, said the result was "saddening" and a "turning point" for the country.

AfD policies include reducing teaching of Nazi Germany

Germany's domestic intelligence agency designates the AfD branch in Saxony-Anhalt, which Mr Siegmund is in charge of, as "right-wing extremist" with links to ethno-nationalist groups and think-tanks.

Several of Mr Siegmund's staffers and party colleagues are former members of the since-banned Neo-Nazi group Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend, or Patriotic German Youth.

But the outspoken political leader has defended his team as being full of "excellent people", adding that he is "not interested in what happened 20 or 25 years ago".

A first-ever AfD state government would be a shock for many in Germany, which has been at pains to atone for its dark history of World War II and the Holocaust and so far kept extremist parties at bay.

Mr Siegmund, the AfD's telegenic top candidate, has ambitions to lead a political revolution from Saxony-Anhalt that would propel the party to national victory in 2029.

On the campaign trail, Mr Siegmund — a former entrepreneur with a sharp undercut hairstyle and a huge social media following — has been mobbed by adoring fans, many wearing T-shirts bearing his likeness.

Ulrich Siegmund's Saxony-Anhalt branch embraces an "anti-woke" agenda. (Reuters: Thilo Schmuelgen)

The party has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany as well as lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the West decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.

In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local "Ossie pride", Mr Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermuende.

While Mr Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting irregular migrants with a "remigration and deportation offensive" from day one.

The party's "anti-woke" agenda also includes vows to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard, and to change history teaching to reduce the emphasis on the Third Reich.

In order to replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering "baby bonuses" for families to reverse the shrinking of the population in the small state of 2.1 million people.

ABC/wires

World.title: Running out of cards, Trump weighs declaring the Iran war over
World.content:
Yet again, the United States has got itself into a quagmire: a war that President Donald Trump does not know how to end, and the Iranian regime does not want to end.

The Wall Street Journal reported this week that US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth was "quietly extending troop deployments" into 2027, taken as a sign the conflict could drag on well into next year.

The Journal also reported that at the same time, Trump has been in discussions with senior aides about whether to officially declare the war over — with officials reportedly noting that the president "favours the idea".

Mission accomplished? Absolutely not.

This is quite a bizarre notion — a president declaring a war over despite both sides still firing at each other, the Strait of Hormuz still largely crippled and Iran still in possession of enriched uranium.

The main aim of the war — to ensure that Iran could never have nuclear weapons — has clearly not been achieved. Iran still has supplies of highly enriched uranium in a hidden location.

Then, once the war was underway, Trump said a key aim was regime change — that also has not happened.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is still effectively in charge in Tehran with, if anything, a more hardline leader after Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei took over from his father Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the early days of the war.

Then, as it was clear the US and Israel were not going to achieve either of those two aims, the goalpost shifted again.

The new goal was reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway used to transport about 20 per cent of the world's crude oil and gas.

That strait was, of course, open and functioning well before the US and Israel decided to go to war.

Now, only a trickle of tankers pass through as insurance companies around the world are reluctant to offer coverage.

The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz remains a sticking point in the war. (Reuters)

So now, having failed on those three aims, Trump is reportedly considering declaring the war over — and presumably claiming victory.

It all comes as the US has sought to widen its war against Iran, with new waves of strikes resuming last week and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier announcing a plan to inflict "economic asphyxiation" on the regime.

Without question, both the US and Iran are feeling pain from this war. But the political consequence for each nation is markedly distinct.

In Iran, the IRGC, having survived the shock and awe of American and Israeli military air power, is not about to yield to internal discontent over diminishing supplies of petrol, food and other goods.

But for Trump, the picture is very different. He is, to some extent, insulated from electoral consequences because he cannot run for another term — despite his taunts to the contrary.

But his Republican Party faces a different reality.

Pressure points in a protracted war

Two significant pressure points now weigh on Trump. The first is growing concern among the Republican Party and the second is growing discontent from Washington's traditional allies among the Gulf states.

As to the Republicans, this week Trump will try to rally the Trump MAGA faithful at what he has framed as "a midterm convention" in Texas.

The Dallas rally comes as Republicans face the possibility of losing control of the House of Representatives and perhaps even the Senate in the midterm elections in November.

The fact that Democrats have any chance of taking control of the Senate is itself a testament to how unpopular the Trump administration is.

Loading

The Democrats remain divided as they try to assess whether voters around the country want highly progressive candidates — like self-declared democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York — or more centrist candidates.

For the first year of the second Trump presidency, the president often demonstrated an instinctive ability to channel the frustrations and anger of his core constituency.

But that shrewd political instinct seems increasingly to be abandoning him.

The most obvious example of this came recently when he effectively declared a trade war against Canada.

Everyone but Australia reconsiders relationship with US The world is a confusing place just now. But no-one seems more confused about their place in it than Australia.

Few countries have cultural ties with the US as deep as those shared with Canada. Over decades, that relationship has become integrated in everything from trade and security to sport and culture.

According to the US Census Bureau, for 25 states, their largest customer is Canada. That is half the United States.

These are heartland states for any president: North Dakota, Montana, South Dakota, West Virginia, Maine, Idaho, Ohio, Vermont, Iowa, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Wyoming, Minnesota, Illinois, Oklahoma, North Carolina, Alabama, Kentucky, Tennessee, New Jersey, Virginia, Delaware, Maryland, Connecticut and Georgia.

US goods exported to Canada were worth $US333.6 billion ($463.4 billion) in 2025, and goods imported from Canada were worth $US381.0 billion, according to the US Census Bureau.

Thirteen US states share a border with Canada — Alaska, Washington, Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, Vermont and New Hampshire.

For these states, the flow of trucks taking goods both ways across the border is part of daily life.

And yet Trump has decided — with crucial midterm elections looming — to wreak havoc with this trade.

Mounting political pain

On top of the Iran war and several other issues, for some Republicans who represent states along the border, the new trade war could be the final straw.

I recently spoke to a Republican congressman who is a representative from one of those states, and a strong Trump supporter.

When I first met him two months ago, he was defending Trump on the Iran war and had a positive outlook towards the midterm elections. He told me he was certain the Republicans would hold the House.

But when I saw him this week, his political outlook had changed. When asked about the Trump tariffs and the Canada trade war, he shook his head.

"I just don't figure why he's done it," he said.

"It's terrible for the farmers in my state."

He said farmers and small business operators in his state were already mystified and angry with all the other pressures, particularly high petrol prices pushed up by the Iran war.

But they could not understand why a Republican president would add to the list of pain, he said.

In terms of the Iran war, the reality is that the hard men of the IRGC in Tehran can watch American cable television in real time and see a president under growing pressure — grappling with the political poison of a protracted war.

That is the central reason Iran is likely to do everything within its power to prolong this war as long as possible, into next year if need be.

The reality is that given current dynamics, Donald Trump cannot stop the war that he and Israel started.

Clearly, with Washington "quietly" extending troop deployments and Iran's leadership seemingly prepared to prolong Trump's political pain for as long as possible, this war looks set to continue into next year.

World.title: The High Court may be about to let Neo-Nazis form a racist political party
World.content:
Some of Australia's leading legal minds believe there is a significant prospect of the High Court overturning the federal government's recent ban on the nation's most high-profile Neo-Nazi group.

A victory in the nation's highest court for White Australia, also known as the National Socialist Network, could embarrass Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who in May said he was confident the new laws the government used to ban the group would withstand legal challenge.

It would also pave the way for the white supremacist group, with its sordid history of violence, criminality and racist demonstrations, to form its planned political party in a blaze of publicity.

In May, White Australia became the second group to be listed as a prohibited hate group under laws introduced in the wake of last year's Bondi Beach terror attack.

The organisation was trying to form a political party when it was outlawed by Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke.

It is now attempting to have the laws overturned on the grounds that they are unconstitutional.

Constitutional law expert Anne Twomey said the federal laws appeared to have been rushed through in January without sufficient scrutiny.

"There would be political issues if it was seen that the government had lost to the White Australia Party," she told ABC NEWS Verify.

"But on the whole, the bigger issue is does this legislation survive and how might it be used in the future?

"And how consistent is it with our democratic system as imposed and required to operate by our constitution?" she said.

NSW Labor MP and former barrister Stephen Lawrence is worried White Australia leader and convicted criminal Thomas Sewell may be about to get more undeserved publicity.

"Imagine the optics. Thomas Sewell launching the White Australia Party on the steps of the High Court after having a big win there. We would be handing these people a political gift."

Convicted criminal Thomas Sewell is the leader of White Australia. (Supplied: Channel 9)

Complicated legal arguments

The constitutional legal arguments Sewell and his White Australia Party are presenting to the High Court are complex.

Put simply, the first argument is that the federal government does not have the power to make this law.

The second is that this law breaches the implied freedom of political communication.

The third is that this law breaches the separation of powers between the government and the judiciary.

Constitutional law expert Anthony Gray said the federal government's position is also multi-layered.

"They're arguing that the harm that may be caused by a proscribed group justifies the intrusion on what otherwise would be protected political communication," he said.

Professor Twomey said there was relevant historical legal precedent from when the federal government attempted to ban the Communist Party in the 50s.

"People were profoundly shocked when the High Court held that that legislation providing for the dissolution of the Communist Party was invalid," she said.

" So, it is possible and it has happened before to the extent that the Menzies government did find its legislation was found to be constitutionally invalid by the High Court. "

ABC NEWS Verify sent questions to Mr Burke. A spokesman said the minister would not comment while the case was still ongoing.

The High Court will hear White Australia's case on September 8 and 9 in Canberra. (ABC News: Gregory Nelson)

Principle over ideology

Professor Twomey said that while the views of the White Australia Party might be distasteful to many Australians, it is not something the High Court can take into consideration.

She said the court would examine how these laws could hypothetically be used by a less democratic or authoritarian government.

"Do we really want on our statute books legislation that could be used in an abusive manner in a way that really undermines the democratic system? And so that's the bigger picture that the High Court needs to address," she said.

Professor Gray agreed that it is about legal principle rather than ideology.

"This is one of the things with freedom of speech that it's easy to defend freedom of speech for people whose views are what we call reasonable or views with which we agree," he said.

" It becomes challenging when we're dealing with an organisation that — or with people who — express views with which we may disagree. "

The Director of Public Affairs at the Australia/Israel and Jewish Affairs Council, Jamie Hyams, said he believed the legislation struck the right balance.

"So on the one hand, you want to preserve our democracy, and by not giving governments too much power, but on the other hand, you need to give governments the power to deal with threats to our democracy.

"There are safeguards in there. The government is meant to act on advice from ASIO and also has to brief the leader of the opposition on it before they bring anything in."

Australia's Neo-Nazis are still organising The leader of Neo-Nazi group National Socialist Network, Thomas Sewell, has appeared in an interview online alongside notorious US Neo-Nazi James Mason, who is listed as a terrorist entity by the Canadian government.

What happens if the government loses?

If White Australia is successful in this High Court case, it could still end up outlawed by other legal means.

Professor Gray said the federal government would likely attempt to redraft the legislation.

"That's happened in the past where the Commonwealth has been knocked back by the High Court, they've then redrafted their law, and then that was deemed to be valid," he said.

Mr Hyams said if the White Australia Party was victorious, it should not be interpreted as any kind of endorsement by the High Court.

"It will be decided very narrowly on constitutional grounds," he said.

"If the legislation is overturned, hopefully there'll be some guidance in there about how similar legislation can be brought forward that doesn't, in the opinion of the court, breach their concerns about the constitution."

The matter is set down to be heard in the High Court on September 8 and 9, with a judgment not expected for several weeks or months.

World.title: Why the RBA won’t be coming to save the property market
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeInterest rates Opinion Why the RBA won’t be coming to save the property market Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor September 7, 2026 — 5:20am

September 7, 2026 — 5:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Few people can move asset prices with their words quite like those “high priests” of finance who have been granted the power to set interest rates, the central bankers. A cryptic remark from a central banker can easily cause sharemarkets to bounce around, especially when the words come from the chair of the US Federal Reserve. RBA governor Michele Bullock has said house prices are not the main game for the central bank. Monique Westermann But this is not just something that happens in high finance. Closer to home, central bankers can have a big influence over the biggest asset class in Australia: housing. Indeed, right now, what happens to the nation’s housing market will be heavily influenced by what happens to interest rates.



If borrowing money becomes cheaper thanks to a rate cut (which is not expected until next year), that could be what eventually stops house prices from falling, for example. Or, more rate rises would surely inflict more property pain. The prospect of rate rises was one reason the Commonwealth Bank last week downgraded its forecast on property prices, tipping peak-to-trough falls of up to 13 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Affordable housing Do our pollies really want a more ‘affordable’ housing market? We’re about to find out Ross Gittins Economics Editor As Capital Economics put it last week, the outlook for Australia’s housing market “hinges on the RBA.” This makes sense, given interest rates affect how much you can borrow (which is crucial for most home buyers), and the cost of paying the money back. So, given the RBA’s actions have such a big impact on housing, how does it think about bricks and mortar when it’s setting interest rates? Should the RBA even take property into account, or should it just focus on its formal mandate of targeting inflation and “full” employment?



The short answer is that the RBA boffins at Martin Place in Sydney should not make the ups and downs of housing their main focus. There’s a reason why central banks around the world generally have a core objective, which is to keep inflation around a target. It keeps things clearer. RBA governor Michele Bullock said last month housing was not the “main game” for the central bank, which is more focused on inflation and the economy’s capacity. But although housing may not be the RBA’s main game, it is also too big to ignore, and the current housing slump helps to illustrate a wider economic dilemma facing the bank. Economists have downgraded their forecasts for the housing market amid price falls. Oscar Colman The RBA rate-setting board can’t completely leave property out of the discussion when it sits down to decide whether to move interest rates later this month – because the housing slump is an economic indicator in itself, and it shows rate hikes are already having a real impact in slowing the economy down, as intended.



Latest monthly figures show the national housing market continues to fall, and in recent weeks economists have been publishing increasingly negative forecasts for house prices. The government’s crackdown on negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions are surely a big reason for this. The policies have prompted many property investors to rethink putting money into property: that was the whole point of the changes. But interest rates are also part of the picture. In the past week, markets have been putting growing bets on not only a rate rise this month, but possibly another one later this year. Who knows if they are right, but this trend will probably dampen property buyers’ spirits even more. Will the RBA care about the housing slump when it decides whether to raise rates again? As house price falls continue, it could make the RBA less likely to raise rates again, because it would see the housing slump as evidence that its harsh economic medicine of rate hikes is working.



However, it’s more likely the RBA would probably see the downturn in housing as helpful to their objectives. Related Article Residential property Desperate agents vent online as real estate downturn bites Independent economist Saul Eslake says falling house prices could be helpful in getting inflation down in two ways. First, he says, if falling house prices eventually fed into falling new housing prices, that would help the RBA meet its inflation target. And second, if falling house prices make us feel a bit poorer and spend a bit less, this could also be welcome by the RBA. When the RBA board members sit down to discuss interest rates later this month, the housing market would have to be a big part of the discussion. The central bank doesn’t try to set house prices, but it would see house prices as a sign of how the economy’s travelling – and with prices now accelerating fast, it might give members reason to hold rates.



At the same time, however, the markets are betting Bullock’s bigger worry will be inflation, which remains outside the central bank’s 2 to 3 per cent target band. Related Article Analysis

Home loans ‘Frighteningly easy’: How fake AI payslips fuel mortgage fraud In the past fortnight, inflation and economic growth figures have been surprisingly strong, and economists are betting that will make rate hikes more likely. But more aggressive rate rises also run the risk of driving the economy into recession. Economists such as AMP’s Shane Oliver believe that despite that risk, the RBA’s most pressing problem right now is inflation, and Bullock and the board will respond by jacking up interest rates further, rather than waiting for inflation to gradually slow. “They face a difficult dilemma because they would be worried that if they go too far they would knock the economy into recession,” he says.



The fear is that if the RBA does not act decisively enough to get inflation back in the target, we run the risk of entrenching both high inflation and slow growth (known as stagflation). “They do face a choice between risking recession and risking stagflation,” Oliver says. As always, the challenge for the RBA is that interest rates are a blunt instrument. They inflict economic pain, and there’s the ever-present risk of going too far and causing a recession. Hopefully, that’s a risk that Bullock and the board can navigate. But we should not expect them to be less thorough in taming inflation for the sake of house prices. Anyone hoping the RBA will ride to the rescue of the housing market by delivering rate cuts in the short term is likely to be disappointed. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ASX set for flat start, Wall Street slips on jobs report
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set for flat start, Wall Street slips on jobs report Alex Veiga September 7, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks fell and Treasury yields rose after the government reported that employers unexpectedly added 162,000 jobs last month, a development that could increase chances that the US central bank will raise interest rates later this month. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent, though it managed to eke out a modest gain for the week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite gave back 0.3 per cent. The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower with futures on Saturday pointing to a loss of 1 point at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.05¢. A surprisingly strong increased the chances of an interest rate hike, spooking markets. Bloomberg Wall Street expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation, which has been running hot due to rising oil prices amid the US war with Iran and remains well above 3 per cent. The Fed has a stated goal of cooling inflation to a target of 2 per cent. The surprise increase in hiring last month could give the central bank’s policymakers leeway to raise the Fed’s benchmark short-term interest rate to fight inflation at their next policy meeting in less than two weeks.



“Today’s jobs report does lean toward the Fed increasing rates,” said Terry Sandven, chief equity strategist at US Bank Asset Management Group, noting, however, that a rate hike is “not a foregone conclusion.” The Labour Department reported that hiring in August far exceeded the 65,000 forecasters had expected, according to a poll by FactSet. Labour Department revisions also looked good, adding 55,000 to June and July payrolls. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1 per cent. The stronger jobs market could make matters more complicated for the Fed, which has to balance supporting job growth with fighting inflation. Raising interest rates can help tame inflation, but it can also slow economic growth as borrowing costs rise for households and businesses. Expectations for a rate hike in September increased to 60.4 per cent on Friday following the release of the jobs report, up from 49.4 per cent Thursday and from 57 per cent a week ago, according to CME FedWatch.



“Given the strength of the payroll report, a rate hike on September 16 appears increasingly likely,” according to Jeffrey Roach, chief economist for LPL Financial. “Ironically, a rate hike may generate less market volatility than another meeting in which policymakers choose to stand pat.” The government will release August inflation figures September 11, shortly before the Fed’s policymaking committee’s next meeting, which ends on September 16. The closely watched consumer price index, or CPI, which measures costs for consumers, is expected to show that inflation rose last month at a 3.4 per cent rate, the same as in July. Inflation has held stubbornly above 3 per cent for most of the year. “With the August CPI report now on deck, the question is whether the combined impact of stronger-than-expected hiring and a stiff inflation tail wind will push policymakers to the tipping point of raising rates later this month,” said Jim Baird, chief investment officer with Plante Moran Financial Advisors. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said last week at the Fed’s annual economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, that inflation had not shown sufficient improvement and that the central bank might have “more work to do,” a sign he is weighing a rate increase at the Fed’s next meeting. On Thursday, Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller said that if new data next week shows inflation is cooling, he “would be inclined” to keep the Fed’s benchmark interest rate unchanged. Should the data show hotter inflation, he would consider a rate hike.



US government bond yields, which had eased the last couple of days, rose as the bond market weighed the implications of the jobs report. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, rose to 4.78 per cent from 4.77 per cent late Thursday. It has been rising steadily throughout the year and was as low as 4.20 per cent at the beginning of 2026. The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations for Federal Reserve moves on interest rates, rose to 4.37 per cent from 4.34 per cent. It remains significantly higher for the year, though, and was as low as 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026. Meanwhile, gains in technology stocks helped limit declines in other sectors Friday. Nvidia rose 0.8 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices added 4.7 per cent, Sandisk jumped 11.9 per cent and Micron Technology gained 6.1 per cent. Lululemon Athletica sank 17.4 per cent, the biggest decline among S&P 500 stocks, after the retailer reported quarterly revenue that fell short of analysts’ estimates and lowered its fiscal full-year outlook again.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 29.11 points to 7,718.60. The Dow dropped 271.86 points to 53,414.25, and the Nasdaq lost 77.07 points to close at 26,506.99. Related Article Energy ‘The shift is now absolute’: China’s BYD says Australia just passed its EV tipping point Markets ended mixed in Europe and Asia. In energy markets, oil rose Friday, adding to a sharp run-up in prices earlier in the week as the six-month long US war with Iran intensified. Iran fired at Kuwait on Thursday in retaliation for US bombardments earlier in the week. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.8 per cent to settle at $96.28 a barrel. Benchmark US crude rose 0.2 per cent to settle at $91.48 a barrel. For the week, they are up 9.2 per cent and 9.7 per cent, respectively.



US gasoline prices will be higher this weekend than they have ever been at this time of year, according to AAA. Diesel hit an all-time high for any time of the year on Friday, soaring to an average of $US5.85 a gallon. Because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks, higher diesel prices mean higher transportation costs for a long list of everyday goods, a price shock that can impact prices for consumers. US stock markets will be closed Monday for the Labour Day holiday. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Election shockwave: Meet the smiling new leader set to bring hard-right upheaval to Germany
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeWorld elections Election shockwave: Meet the smiling new leader set to bring hard-right upheaval to Germany David Crowe September 7, 2026 — 5:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: German politician Ulrich Siegmund has surged to success with a simple promise to return his community to the more comfortable times of the past. “We want our good, old, safe Germany back at last,” was one of his most common refrains when urging voters to back him to lead the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. Voters responded with a thumping endorsement for Siegmund and the party he leads, the Alternative für Deutschland, known as the AfD. Ulrich Siegmund (centre) celebrates his likely win. Getty Images Exit polls showed the AfD gained 44.5 per cent of the vote when the polling stations closed at 6pm on Sunday (Monday AEST).



The outcome left no doubt about the will of the people, given that the next major contender won only 18.5 per cent of the vote. This result, for the Christian Democratic Union, was a brutal rebuff to the foremost conservative party in the country. It was also another sign of the way the public has turned against the CDU’s national leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, as he struggles to deliver on promises to bring better times to the country. The result was another sign of the way the public has turned against the CDU’s national leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Getty Images For Siegmund, the result looks like a mandate to form government. His promises to bring back the olden times, however, look dangerous and divisive to opponents, who believe the AfD leans so far to the right that it is akin to a Nazi party.



Siegmund, 35, a telegenic former salesman, looks nothing like the extremists of the past who have frightened voters with their black shirts and Nazi salutes. Related Article Analysis

Russia-Ukraine war As Putin’s long shadow falls across Europe, Germany’s far-right is prospering He was often photographed during the campaign with a smile on his face at campaign stops when he turned up on a blue scooter. His policies, however, offer radical change when Germany is divided over migration and national security, while suffering from slow growth and long-term threats to giant manufacturing businesses such as carmakers. The AfD agenda includes the deportation of refugees who do not have approval to stay in the country, free childcare and tax incentives to encourage larger families and boost the native population, and the restoration of trade with Russia to allow imports of oil and gas. It also wants to cut aid to Ukraine in its war with Russia; a halt to funding for public broadcasters, a ban on gay pride flags at schools, and funding cuts for teaching “woke” subjects.



With his likely victory on Sunday, Siegmund has become the most successful hard-right politician in Germany since the country formed its modern democracy from the ashes of the Second World War and the destruction of the National Socialist party and its leader, Adolf Hitler. One of Germany’s biggest magazines, Der Spiegel, called Siegmund “the most dangerous man in Germany” in a cover story in August. AP Photo/Matthias Schrader Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has labelled the AfD as an “extremist” organisation, while some of its early leaders have been exposed for their links to neo-Nazi group in the past. Asked about the murders of 6 million Jews during the Holocaust, some AfD leaders have hedged in their language rather than categorically denounce the crimes of the past. When Siegmund was asked about the Holocaust by news site Politico earlier this year, he said he could not “presume to judge” whether it was humanity’s worst-ever crime.



One of Germany’s biggest magazines, Der Spiegel, called Siegmund “the most dangerous man in Germany” in a cover story in August. Siegmund was born in Eastern Germany in 1990 and moved to Berlin in his early years where he set up a business selling household air fresheners. His first move into politics was to join the Christian Democratic Union, but he shifted to the hard right in 2014 by joining the AfD, then in an early phase when it was commonly dismissed as a minor party with neo-Nazi leanings and therefore unelectable as a major force in politics. A supporter of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds up a heart-shaped placard of Ulrich Siegmund. Getty Images The COVID-19 pandemic increased Siegmund’s profile when he became popular on social media with his complaints about social restrictions.



The election outcome is a serious blow to Merz, although not a surprise due to his poor personal polling over the past year. Siegmund described Merz as an asset for the AfD. “A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz. Every day this man is in the chancellery is one too many,” he said. The next step for the CDU is to take stock and consider whether Merz should remain leader, but the next election for the national parliament, the Bundestag, is not until 2029. The vote in Saxony-Anhalt was not a national ballot on Merz. The state, part of what was East Germany, is relatively small. There were only about 1.7 million registered voters at the election.



Even so, this is a shock for Germany. For the AfD, the next step is to form government. The country will have a hard-right government for the first time in its post-war democracy. Dismissed as a minor party for so long, the AfD is now a major force in German politics. The upheaval in Germany may have only just begun.

World.title: How four concrete slabs will turn into hundreds of inner Sydney homes
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life How four concrete slabs will turn into hundreds of inner Sydney homes Megan Gorrey September 7, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four concrete slabs languishing beside Parramatta Road in Sydney’s inner west will be transformed with hundreds of new apartments, under a Minns government plan to use surplus land for housing. The proposal would deliver 340 homes – 30 per cent of which would be social housing dwellings – across four apartment blocks up to seven storeys on the disused WestConnex dive site in Haberfield. The fenced-off concrete slabs at former WestConnex construction sites along Parramatta Road would be transformed into housing under a plan released on Monday. George Chan The fate of multiple parcels of land, taken over for the $16.8 billion motorway project and since left empty, along Parramatta Road has long prompted calls for new housing to help revive the tired strip. Lands and Property Minister Steve Kamper said the site was a prime location for housing as it was on a bus route, opposite a major supermarket and near two schools, as well as shops and essential services.



“Haberfield is exactly the sort of opportunity the [land] audit is designed to identify, a government-owned site that was no longer being used for its original purpose and can now help deliver hundreds of new homes, including social housing.” A concept image of plans to build 340 homes on a former WestConnex dive site in Haberfield. NSW government The blocks, which were used for a project office and motorway works until about 2023, were identified in the government’s long-running surplus land audit. Related Article Exclusive

Property development This plateau of concrete will soon be home to teachers and nurses Four buildings will range from three to seven storeys, with landscaped communal areas, parking spots for cars and bikes, and community and other non-residential uses fronting Parramatta Road.



Homes NSW, which is the government’s social and affordable housing agency, is asking the community to provide feedback on the proposal before a “state significant” development is lodged with the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure. Housing and Homelessness Minister Rose Jackson said the sites, near Alt and Bland streets, represented a “fantastic opportunity” to deliver sorely needed housing. “At a time when too many people are struggling to get a roof over their heads, we need to make the most of every suitable site we have, particularly in well-connected locations,” Jackson said. The Inner West Council has for years called for the state government to rezone disused WestConnex dive sites along Parramatta Road to tackle the housing shortage, support low-income and essential workers, and help revitalise the much-maligned corridor.



Last year, government developer Landcom chose a separate former WestConnex dive site on Parramatta Road in Annandale as the first to be developed under NSW’s $450 million build-to-rent scheme, enabling 220 apartments to be built for essential workers such as teachers, nurses and police at subsidised prices. The complex will also include about 350 private and affordable homes. Related Article Exclusive

NSW State Parliament Secret analysis reveals $1.4b in public land facing potential sale Kamper said of the Haberfield sites that officials were “continuing to work across government to find more sites like this and grow the pipeline of land available for housing”. The land audit was established as a means of unlocking sites – owned by departments or agencies that were unused or underutilised – for housing. In the June 2024 budget, the government estimated the scheme would deliver 21,000 private and affordable dwellings. In August, a spokesman for Kamper said that of the 77 property audit sites announced publicly by the government, five had been acquired by Landcom, eight had been purchased by Homes NSW, and 26 had been settled or exchanged on the private market.



Planning officials expect about 50,000 homes to be finished in NSW this financial year, well short of the 75,000 needed for the state to meet its five-year target to deliver 377,000 homes by mid-2029. The NSW Coalition has said the Minns government would not meet its National Housing Accord target, which it agreed with the federal government, until March 2032 – almost three years late. World.title: Rain, hail or shine: Why this school bus stop still doesn’t have a shelter
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandCity council Rain, hail or shine: Why this school bus stop still doesn’t have a shelter Felicity Caldwell September 7, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Primary students in Fig Tree Pocket have to wait for the bus in the sun and exposed to storms because there is no shelter at the stop outside their school – and the council never progressed a grant application to build one. Grandmother Milica Nikolic knows only too well the discomfort of being exposed to the elements at the stop – and with nowhere to sit. She said the bus often arrived 10 or 20 minutes late to Fig Tree Pocket State School, and once she waited 40 minutes with her grandchildren. Milica Nikolic outside Fig Tree Pocket State School, which has a bus stop with no shelter. Felicity Caldwell “There is nowhere to sit nearby, and at my age, 73, it is not easy for me to stand that long,” she said.



“With the storm season approaching, bringing rain and hail – often in the afternoon when kids, some parents and grandparents wait for the school bus – it is hard to stand in the open with an umbrella.” While there is a state government program for upgrading bus stop infrastructure around schools, Brisbane is largely missing out. Of 31 such projects across Queensland in the latest round of the $4 million School Transport Infrastructure Program, just one is in Brisbane – at Our Lady of the Assumption in Enoggera. Despite having more expressions of interest than other councils for the grants, only two Brisbane projects were progressed to the official nomination stage. Michael Berkman, the Greens MP for Maiwar, wrote to Walter Taylor ward councillor Penny Wolff in December 2025 asking if the council could install a bus shelter at the school.



When Berkman’s office followed up in February and March, Wolff’s office said the council’s transport and assets team said the request could be made via the School Transport Infrastructure Program (STIP) grants. Berkman submitted a STIP application, but Brisbane City Council, as the asset owner, did not make a nomination at the next stage, so it did not progress. Brisbane City Council says it is looking for opportunities to improve the Fig Tree Pocket bus stop. Felicity Caldwell In response to questions from this masthead, the council said bus stop upgrades were not funded through the STIP, and it was continuing to look for opportunities to improve the Fig Tree Pocket stop. This appears to contradict STIP guidelines published online, which say “installation/upgrading of bus stops on school bus routes” are among the program’s eligible works.



Related Article Exclusive

Traffic Driving past this huge Brisbane school? Here’s how fast traffic moves at drop-off time Under the STIP, anyone can submit an expression of interest – including state and non-state schools, P&Cs, a community member, road authorities, or MPs – which is then investigated by a Transport Department road safety team. The “responsible asset owner” – whoever owns the land, such as a council or school – investigates the issue behind the submission, and if deemed necessary, submits a STIP nomination, which is assessed more thoroughly before a final list of successful projects is announced. STIP projects can include new or upgraded bus stops, bikeways, paths, traffic signals, fences, pedestrian refuges, crossings, new school zones, bike racks, and stop, drop and go areas. The maximum state funding is $250,000, with the project cost usually split 50-50 with the asset owner.



Brisbane, which is home to a quarter of Queensland’s total population, received more expressions of interest than any other council area for STIP funding from July 2025 to April 2026, with 17 EOIs, according to an analysis of details released via a parliamentary question on notice. Brisbane City Council was the asset manager in 11 of the 17 EOIs. But only 12 per cent of EOIs from Brisbane – two projects – progressed to the nomination stage in tranche nine. In comparison, 63 per cent of Townsville’s EOIs progressed to the nomination stage, and 60 per cent in Cairns. Brisbane City Council has submitted just six nominations for STIP funding since 2022-23.



Across Queensland, 30 per cent of EOIs from private schools were funded, compared with 15 per cent for state schools. Related Article City council Locals pleaded for a dangerous crossing to be fixed. This isn’t what they had in mind Berkman said Brisbane residents expected the council to represent them. “Council is constantly blaming a lack of state funding for a lack of public and active transport infrastructure, but when there are grants like this on offer, they’re not even applying for them,” he said. “Is this pure laziness, or is it that the LNP-led Brisbane City Council – the biggest council in Australia – won’t even stump up a 50 per cent share for basic transport projects?”



But the council’s infrastructure chair, Ryan Murphy, said Berkman was “looking at one state government funding program and pretending it’s the only way we make the school run safer”. “That’s simply not the case,” he said. “We’re already getting on with improvements at schools like Bardon, Holland Park and Loreto [Coorparoo] outside this particular program. “We’ll use state funding when it makes sense, we’ll invest council funding where that gets the job done sooner, and we’ll keep working with school communities on what they actually need. “Parents don’t care which government program paid for an upgrade, they care about safer crossings, better access, and getting their kids to school safely.”



Bardon State School, Holland Park State High School and Loreto College all had EOIs lodged for projects under the latest STIP round that were not progressed to a nomination. The council was also working on a STIP application for Mount Alvernia College in Kedron and investigating improvements at Petrie Terrace State School – both of which had EOIs registered. The Crisafulli government committed $4 million to the program in 2025-26, according to the Queensland Transport and Roads Investment Program. The previous Labor government had budgeted $16 million for the same period before it lost the October 2024 election. The Transport Department did not respond by deadline. World.title: My suburb has both seaside serenity and a bustling downtown. No wonder developers are circling
World.content:
Wynnum has the best of both worlds, and it’s only half an hour from the city.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane is on the march. Growing to the north, south and westwards. But there’s one side of the city where geography puts a stop to the sprawl, and that’s at Wynnum – the waters of Moreton Bay providing a natural barrier. Fifteen kilometres from Brisbane’s General Post Office, and the closest geographical coastline to the CBD, Wynnum is the point where Brisbane ends. The number of times people remark on how “far away” Wynnum is has to do with the fact it feels a world away from the city, despite not being particularly far. Our three train stations (count ’em) can get you to Queen Street Mall in just 30 minutes. If you’re driving, the Gateway Bridge helps you access the northside quickly – as long as you’re happy to pay the tolls. Not being originally from Brisbane, our radar did not even register Wynnum when we were looking to buy in 2016. Wilston, Nundah, Sandgate and Woolloongabba all made the shortlist, but the relative affordability of the bayside, plus the fact it was so different from everywhere else, made the choice easy. Wynnum’s biggest asset is its five-kilometre waterfront. Morgan Roberts Daily foreshore dog walks are a balm for the soul. Morgan Roberts Wynnum feels far from the city, but it’s only 15 kilometres from the CBD. Morgan Roberts The biggest asset is that five-kilometre waterfront, which stretches through to neighbouring Manly, and onward to Lota. I’ve always found the waterfront at Wynnum the superior section, with more parkland, more parking, and fewer crowds. That said, since COVID, it’s never felt more popular, with four-legged friends, run clubs pounding the pavements, and two-wheeled Lycra lieutenants descending en masse.



This tension between the suburb’s popularity and its growth and development while trying to retain the village-like atmosphere lies at the heart of resistance to Wynnum being gazetted as a Brisbane LGA future growth corridor. On this front, it’s easy to see the wheels are already in motion. Cookie-cutter apartment buildings seem to be going up as high as developers can get approval for, all so they can catch bay glimpses. Old houses are central to the suburb’s heritage character. Morgan Roberts Wynnum residents protest outside LNP councillor Alex Givney’s office in November. William Davis An artwork by Camille Serisier on Bay Terrace. William Davis I’ve seen these changes close to home. My former neighbour, Joan, lived over the fence for more than 50 years before moving into aged care and passing away at 93. We saw her lovely home demolished and its 810-square-metre block subdivided. In its place are two oversized double-storey builds with name plaques like “Sol” slapped on. That’s progress eh? So what lifestyle is threatened by those now-permitted 15-storey buildings?



For a start, the serenity of the waterfront. I’ve often swum in the calm waters of Pandanus Beach or Breakwater Park at high tide, and enjoyed not acting my age paddling in the Depression-era Wading Pool, a cherished local landmark. Daily foreshore dog walks are a balm for my soul, and over the years I’ve had many up-close encounters with turtles, shovelnose rays, black swans, and even dolphins in the bay on glassy mornings. But while videos posted on the local Facebook page prove they’re out there, I’m still waiting for my dugong sighting. They are plastered on the Moreton Bay tourist drive road signs, so surely it’s only a matter of time. Kids cool off at Wynnum Wading Pool. Tourism and Events Queensland I’ve had many up-close encounters with the local wildlife. Morgan Roberts Wynnum Fringe has been based in Bay Terrace for the past two years. Wynnum Fringe What you’ll have no trouble seeing, though, is a gaggle of pelicans who have set up shop near the boat ramp looking for fish scraps. Speaking of fish, the best place for fish and chips is a hotly contested topic. For reference, the answer can only be Costa’s Seafood, formerly Finn’s Fish House, on the corner of Pine Street and the Esplanade. Wynnum has many preserved historical buildings, making it easy to conceive of the place as its own town before it was absorbed into the Brisbane LGA. There’s a huge mix of housing, from traditional Queenslanders, postwar homes, and ’70s-era brick-and-tile oblongs. Now we are seeing McMansions, duplexes and, yes, more apartment buildings every time you look.



The shopping precinct. Morgan Roberts Gigglefit Grammar is a well-stocked second-hand bookshop in Bay Terrace. Morgan Roberts The Waterloo Bay Hotel was built in 1889. Morgan Roberts Wynnum comprises the distinct localities of Wynnum Central, the business district; Wynnum North, near the Port of Brisbane; and the area west of the train line, but not as far as Wynnum Plaza (which is actually in Wynnum West, a distinct suburb of its own). Because of this, a certain clarification is often needed about where in Wynnum you live. More than a few times I’ve heard people say they live in Manly when in fact they’re in Wynnum, perhaps wishing to be associated with Manly’s perceived cachet, not the dagginess that sometimes attaches to Wynnum, which I’ve heard called “Logan by the Bay” (apologies to Logan). As the suburb changes, I sometimes wish I could preserve some of that dagginess. Pera Palace Ottoman Turkish restaurant is a local gem with a fitout as sumptuous as the food. Morgan Roberts

World.title: From Concord to the country: The student search for greener pastures in an AI world
World.content:
Exclusive NationalUniversity From Concord to the country: The student search for greener pastures in an AI world Sally Rawsthorne September 7, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before Annalise Magill began her studies, she had been on a farm only on holidays. “I had no real experience in agriculture before I chose my degree. I’d been on a farm in a very light capacity where I’d gone and had to look at some cows and some sheep, very much the city kid out of her depth,” Magill, 19, said. Agriculture appeals because “you get to actually be out there doing something in the real world and not sitting in an office typing away”, Annalise Magill says. As AI begins to eliminate entry-level roles and reshape the early-career landscape, Magill is among a cohort of young Australians who are turning towards a career in the $101 billion agriculture sector. The Concord High School graduate is working as a junior agriculture economist at consultancy AgEcon while she studies for a bachelor of agricultural science at the University of Sydney.



“AI is not something I had considered when I applied for my degree, but it’s definitely something that everyone is thinking about now. Agriculture jobs will never be replaced by AI – it might be able to do a monitoring map of your paddock, but it’s probably not going to sit in the tractor for you,” Magill said. Related Article Exclusive

AI Thousands of University of Sydney staff to strike over AI “I’m not having that same level of anxiety and stress about my future in an industry because I don’t feel as though it will be replaced by it.” Agriculture remains short of workers: the Australian Farm Institute says there are six jobs for every agriculture graduate. But remote work and the increased professionalisation of the sector (due to the internet) have done a lot to increase its appeal.



The end of the Millennium Drought and increased community understanding of supply chains thanks to panic buying during the pandemic have also helped the sector overcome its image problems of the past 40 years, says a 2021 paper published in International Journal of Innovation in Science and Mathematics Education. Sharon Starick, a grain and pork producer from South Australia who is chair of the Council of Rural Research and Development Corporations, agrees. Of the 20 domestic students in her cohort, Annalise Magill says that 10 are fellow city kids. Andrew Quilty Starick grew up on a wine-growing property in the Barossa and studied agricultural science at university “at a time when it was seen as an industry that wasn’t going places, wasn’t exciting” as producers suffered through drought and low commodity prices in the early 1990s. “There have been significant changes in farming, but also to the value chain, with new technology and new innovation. It’s creating new jobs that are highly skilled and highly technical,” she said.



Related Article Agriculture A breathalyser pregnancy test: How AI is sniffing out the next farming revolution Agriculture offered a wide range of roles, from working on a farm to communications, management, finance, policy, technology and research. “We actually need people from a diverse range of backgrounds, ages, genders, cultures. It brings diversity of thought to the way to approach some of the big challenges,” Starick said. AI was likely to automate repetitive jobs, she said. “But many of our roles in food and fibre production are based on judgment, creativity, problem-solving and really understanding people and their businesses. So AI will become a very useful tool.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Rome opened two new train stations. They’re must-visit attractions
World.content:
InspirationEurope Rome opened two new train stations. They’re must-visit attractions Julie Miller September 7, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s arguably no city in the world where antiquity sits more comfortably alongside modern life than Rome. Romans don’t give a second thought to sipping coffee overlooking a 2000-year-old former pagan temple or walking their dog alongside a crumbling aqueduct; in fact, turn any corner and you’re likely to stumble upon an ancient ruin, adding gravitas to the city’s nickname of the Eternal City. What we see above ground, however, is just scratching the surface, with many secrets of the ancient Roman capital still being revealed. Archaeological finds, including Roman walls and a well, remain in situ and on display. iStock In December 2025, Rome celebrated the long-awaited opening of two new stations of Metro Line C, finally bringing commuters into the historic city centre after nearly two decades of delays. But this infrastructure blow-out was not due to budgetary issues or mere incompetence – rather, it was because of ancient treasures discovered during excavation, turning line construction into a lengthy and painstaking archaeological dig. At Porta Metronia, a residential house and military barracks dating back 2000 years were discovered; while beneath the surrounds of the Colosseum, workers discovered 28 ancient wells and an original bathhouse, as well as countless artefacts from everyday life.



Rather than remove these findings in the name of progress, the decision was made to leave them in place, building the infrastructure around the digs and displaying treasures in situ, turning the stations into museums. 



Ascending the escalators at San Giovanni is like travelling through a time machine, with the atrium designed around the concept of vertical storytelling. Colour-coded timelines show the depth of excavation aligned with its corresponding historical era from Palaeolithic to modern times, highlighting important moments in Rome’s architectural history along the way. On each level, there are display cabinets showcasing artefacts unearthed during excavation: marble friezes, headless statues, imperial coins, glass perfume bottles, bronze farm implements and clay vessels. On the lowest level, there are even tree root fossils on display, evidence of a massive first century agricultural estate. The sleek new metro also provides respite from crowds above ground. iStock Heading back towards the city centre, I alight at Porta Metronia station next to the Aurelian Walls where a massive second century military barracks, consisting of more than 30 rooms decorated with frescoes and mosaic floors, was discovered, along with a grand commander’s house. This is considered one of the most significant archaeological findings of recent years, with the remains to be displayed in situ in a dedicated museum in the western part of the station. Unfortunately, the museum opening – originally slated for February 2026 – has been delayed, passing the early summer of my visit and with no actual opening date announced.



Related Article Travel tips The 25 astonishing man-made attractions every traveller should see But things take time in the Eternal City … and as we all know, Rome wasn’t built in a day. THE DETAILS RIDE

The museum-stations of Metro Line C are accessible to anyone with a valid Metro ticket, available for €1.50 ($2.45). Multi-day passes are also available and can be purchased at any station or online.
