World.title: My suburb has both seaside serenity and a bustling downtown. No wonder developers are circling
World.content:
Wynnum has the best of both worlds, and it’s only half an hour from the city.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane is on the march. Growing to the north, south and westwards. But there’s one side of the city where geography puts a stop to the sprawl, and that’s at Wynnum – the waters of Moreton Bay providing a natural barrier. Fifteen kilometres from Brisbane’s General Post Office, and the closest geographical coastline to the CBD, Wynnum is the point where Brisbane ends. The number of times people remark on how “far away” Wynnum is has to do with the fact it feels a world away from the city, despite not being particularly far. Our three train stations (count ’em) can get you to Queen Street Mall in just 30 minutes. If you’re driving, the Gateway Bridge helps you access the northside quickly – as long as you’re happy to pay the tolls. Not being originally from Brisbane, our radar did not even register Wynnum when we were looking to buy in 2016. Wilston, Nundah, Sandgate and Woolloongabba all made the shortlist, but the relative affordability of the bayside, plus the fact it was so different from everywhere else, made the choice easy. Wynnum’s biggest asset is its five-kilometre waterfront. Morgan Roberts Daily foreshore dog walks are a balm for the soul. Morgan Roberts Wynnum feels far from the city, but it’s only 15 kilometres from the CBD. Morgan Roberts The biggest asset is that five-kilometre waterfront, which stretches through to neighbouring Manly, and onward to Lota. I’ve always found the waterfront at Wynnum the superior section, with more parkland, more parking, and fewer crowds. That said, since COVID, it’s never felt more popular, with four-legged friends, run clubs pounding the pavements, and two-wheeled Lycra lieutenants descending en masse.



This tension between the suburb’s popularity and its growth and development while trying to retain the village-like atmosphere lies at the heart of resistance to Wynnum being gazetted as a Brisbane LGA future growth corridor. On this front, it’s easy to see the wheels are already in motion. Cookie-cutter apartment buildings seem to be going up as high as developers can get approval for, all so they can catch bay glimpses. Old houses are central to the suburb’s heritage character. Morgan Roberts Wynnum residents protest outside LNP councillor Alex Givney’s office in November. William Davis An artwork by Camille Serisier on Bay Terrace. William Davis I’ve seen these changes close to home. My former neighbour, Joan, lived over the fence for more than 50 years before moving into aged care and passing away at 93. We saw her lovely home demolished and its 810-square-metre block subdivided. In its place are two oversized double-storey builds with name plaques like “Sol” slapped on. That’s progress eh? So what lifestyle is threatened by those now-permitted 15-storey buildings?



For a start, the serenity of the waterfront. I’ve often swum in the calm waters of Pandanus Beach or Breakwater Park at high tide, and enjoyed not acting my age paddling in the Depression-era Wading Pool, a cherished local landmark. Daily foreshore dog walks are a balm for my soul, and over the years I’ve had many up-close encounters with turtles, shovelnose rays, black swans, and even dolphins in the bay on glassy mornings. But while videos posted on the local Facebook page prove they’re out there, I’m still waiting for my dugong sighting. They are plastered on the Moreton Bay tourist drive road signs, so surely it’s only a matter of time. Kids cool off at Wynnum Wading Pool. Tourism and Events Queensland I’ve had many up-close encounters with the local wildlife. Morgan Roberts Wynnum Fringe has been based in Bay Terrace for the past two years. Wynnum Fringe What you’ll have no trouble seeing, though, is a gaggle of pelicans who have set up shop near the boat ramp looking for fish scraps. Speaking of fish, the best place for fish and chips is a hotly contested topic. For reference, the answer can only be Costa’s Seafood, formerly Finn’s Fish House, on the corner of Pine Street and the Esplanade. Wynnum has many preserved historical buildings, making it easy to conceive of the place as its own town before it was absorbed into the Brisbane LGA. There’s a huge mix of housing, from traditional Queenslanders, postwar homes, and ’70s-era brick-and-tile oblongs. Now we are seeing McMansions, duplexes and, yes, more apartment buildings every time you look.



The shopping precinct. Morgan Roberts Gigglefit Grammar is a well-stocked second-hand bookshop in Bay Terrace. Morgan Roberts The Waterloo Bay Hotel was built in 1889. Morgan Roberts Wynnum comprises the distinct localities of Wynnum Central, the business district; Wynnum North, near the Port of Brisbane; and the area west of the train line, but not as far as Wynnum Plaza (which is actually in Wynnum West, a distinct suburb of its own). Because of this, a certain clarification is often needed about where in Wynnum you live. More than a few times I’ve heard people say they live in Manly when in fact they’re in Wynnum, perhaps wishing to be associated with Manly’s perceived cachet, not the dagginess that sometimes attaches to Wynnum, which I’ve heard called “Logan by the Bay” (apologies to Logan). As the suburb changes, I sometimes wish I could preserve some of that dagginess. Pera Palace Ottoman Turkish restaurant is a local gem with a fitout as sumptuous as the food. Morgan Roberts

World.title: From Concord to the country: The student search for greener pastures in an AI world
World.content:
Exclusive NationalUniversity From Concord to the country: The student search for greener pastures in an AI world Sally Rawsthorne September 7, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before Annalise Magill began her studies, she had been on a farm only on holidays. “I had no real experience in agriculture before I chose my degree. I’d been on a farm in a very light capacity where I’d gone and had to look at some cows and some sheep, very much the city kid out of her depth,” Magill, 19, said. Agriculture appeals because “you get to actually be out there doing something in the real world and not sitting in an office typing away”, Annalise Magill says. As AI begins to eliminate entry-level roles and reshape the early-career landscape, Magill is among a cohort of young Australians who are turning towards a career in the $101 billion agriculture sector. The Concord High School graduate is working as a junior agriculture economist at consultancy AgEcon while she studies for a bachelor of agricultural science at the University of Sydney.



“AI is not something I had considered when I applied for my degree, but it’s definitely something that everyone is thinking about now. Agriculture jobs will never be replaced by AI – it might be able to do a monitoring map of your paddock, but it’s probably not going to sit in the tractor for you,” Magill said. Related Article Exclusive

AI Thousands of University of Sydney staff to strike over AI “I’m not having that same level of anxiety and stress about my future in an industry because I don’t feel as though it will be replaced by it.” Agriculture remains short of workers: the Australian Farm Institute says there are six jobs for every agriculture graduate. But remote work and the increased professionalisation of the sector (due to the internet) have done a lot to increase its appeal.



The end of the Millennium Drought and increased community understanding of supply chains thanks to panic buying during the pandemic have also helped the sector overcome its image problems of the past 40 years, says a 2021 paper published in International Journal of Innovation in Science and Mathematics Education. Sharon Starick, a grain and pork producer from South Australia who is chair of the Council of Rural Research and Development Corporations, agrees. Of the 20 domestic students in her cohort, Annalise Magill says that 10 are fellow city kids. Andrew Quilty Starick grew up on a wine-growing property in the Barossa and studied agricultural science at university “at a time when it was seen as an industry that wasn’t going places, wasn’t exciting” as producers suffered through drought and low commodity prices in the early 1990s. “There have been significant changes in farming, but also to the value chain, with new technology and new innovation. It’s creating new jobs that are highly skilled and highly technical,” she said.



Related Article Agriculture A breathalyser pregnancy test: How AI is sniffing out the next farming revolution Agriculture offered a wide range of roles, from working on a farm to communications, management, finance, policy, technology and research. “We actually need people from a diverse range of backgrounds, ages, genders, cultures. It brings diversity of thought to the way to approach some of the big challenges,” Starick said. AI was likely to automate repetitive jobs, she said. “But many of our roles in food and fibre production are based on judgment, creativity, problem-solving and really understanding people and their businesses. So AI will become a very useful tool.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Elements of New Zealand electricity market 'really appealing' - visiting US expert
World.content:
As far as James Bushnell, professor of economics at the University of California, Davis, is concerned, New Zealand's gentailer-dominated electricity system has a lot going for it.

"Yeah, so I mean, what's challenging for me visiting New Zealand is there are lots of elements of the market here that I find really appealing."

Challenging, no doubt, because his visit comes at a time when high power prices and bumper profits have led to growing calls from MPs, business leaders and academics for the government to step in and break up the four major gentailers.

The gentailers, Contact, Mercury, Genesis and Meridian, made combined profits of around $1 billion this year.

All have electricity generation and retail arms, which is known in business as being vertically integrated.

James Bushnell. Supplied

Bushnell, who is an expert in electricity markets, has been hosted in New Zealand by the Electricity Retailers and Generators Association.

He said he was reasonably sympathetic to the vertical integration model and, when it came to a break-up, pointed to a similar exercise in California in the early 2000s that did not go well.

"So, my experience was from California in the early 2000s, where we had sort of the opposite, where there was a forced separation of the large retail entities from the suppliers or the generators, and that didn't go so well."

He said what happened was that everything became transacted on a daily spot market, which then led to severe market power in the wholesale market.

"That has always influenced my sort of perception of the vertical integration model looking around the rest of the world," Bushnell said.

Bushnell, who peer-reviewed the 2025 Frontier report on New Zealand's electricity system, said typical fluctuations in electricity supply and prices created risks when it came to investing capital, so having retail and generation arms within the same company made sense, as it could help smooth out and manage those risks.

"And so, my version of the trade-off is I think it's very helpful for a reasonably competitive wholesale market, and the arguments then come down to the retail side and how contestable retail can be, and that's sort of where I think the authorities here have really tried to focus on ways of trying to facilitate entry of smaller independent retailers. There is a lot of churn, a lot of different choices."

However, long-time critic of the gentailer model and Victoria University economist Dr Geoff Bertram said he totally disagreed with Dr Bushnell's assessment of the New Zealand market and that it was wrong to compare New Zealand with the US market.

"I flatly disagree with him. He's coming at this with the mindset of somebody who has worked in the United States and California, which is a market where there are lots of players. There is scope for competition. There are multiple generating options."

Bertram said New Zealand is a smaller market and there is effectively no competition.

"The important thing to remember about the gentailers is the reason why they are vertically integrated is not just that it's an effective way to manage risk, it certainly is that. If you're in a profit-driven model, avoiding risk is a big thing. And the benefits of avoiding that risk go entirely to the owners of the companies. In other words, there's nothing in this for consumers."

Calls to break up the gentailers have ranged in recent years from a full structural separation, whereby the power companies would have to sell their retail arms, to less comprehensive break-ups that involve the retail arm and wholesale arm being forced to operate separately while still under the same ownership structure.

Bertram, however, said the only solution is to force them to sell off their retail arms.

"There's just an overwhelming case in the New Zealand setting for breaking these companies up and not just separating them, because even if they have joint ownership, the incentive to collude in a vertically integrated way will remain there."

Bertram said he accepted that, from the point of view of brute engineering efficiency, there's always a case to be made for a vertically integrated monopoly.

But he said that only made sense when New Zealand electricity was in the hands of a non-profit monopoly.

"Once you make it a profit-oriented monopoly and you give the management the job of maximizing shareholder value, game over for competition and it's game over for consumers."

For Bushnell, however, a move away from a market-driven model would not mean cheaper power prices.

World.title: Election 2026: Political parties target supermarkets, NZ Super and more with fresh policy announcements
World.content:
The Greens are promising action over food prices. RNZ

Win for far-right party in German state election Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The election campaign is heating up, with parties announcing a raft of new policies on Sunday, less than nine weeks out from the general election.

Politicians targeted superannuation, supermarkets, climate change and the housing market in their latest announcements throughout the day.

Here's everything you need to know about politicians' latest pledges.

Greens announce 'KiwiMart' plan

The Green Party has revealed its plan to establish a publicly-owned supermarket chain to break up the duopoly and drive down food prices.

The initiative is part of its 'Affordable Kai' policy, which would cost more than $6 billion over four years.

"We're not short of supermarkets, we're short of competition," co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said.

"As experts have noted, divestment - that is, buying already existing stores - is key to breaking up the duopoly."

Plans to lure an existing chain to NZ had failed, she said, and further action was needed.

Foodstuffs and Woolworths would be forced to sell 120 stores and two distribution centres into public ownership, Swarbrick said.

That would require new legislation, she added.

Winston Peters says the cost of NZ Super for migrants is a "ticking timebomb" for the country. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

NZ First promises citizens-only superannuation

New Zealand First will restrict superannuation to citizens from 2029.

Leader Winston Peters said the cost of NZ super for migrants was a "ticking timebomb" for the country.

"How is it fair that the tax burden of supporting seniors now goes to paying for the full retirement of someone who has migrated to our country and only lived and paid taxes for sometimes less than half of the time compared to those who have worked their whole lives here?" he said on Sunday.

"If you want to get NZ Super then you need to sign up, be proud enough of New Zealand, and show full commitment to our country and become a citizen."

The party does not support other changes to entitlements or eligibility, or raising the retirement age to 67.

ACT vows to end 'political virtue signalling' over climate change

ACT leader David Seymour said the country's approach to dealing with climate change was broken and sending the country broke.

On Sunday he announced the party's plan to change that by ditching the net zero emissions target, repealing the Zero Carbon Act and cutting carbon tax if elected.

"A small trading nation can't ignore climate policy, but overdoing it backfires and puts unnecessary costs on Kiwi businesses and households," he said on Sunday.

The party's climate change spokesperson Simon Court said ACT would also seek a "better deal" for New Zealand under the Paris Agreement, regarding treatment of methane and CO2.

"If they're not prepared to be reasonable, maybe we should look at pulling out," he said.

National eyes easier path to homeownership

National has vowed to help more people buy their first home by expanding access to the First Home Loan scheme run by Kāinga Ora

It allows buyers to purchase their first home with a 5 percent deposit, rather than 20 percent which most banks require.

If re-elected, National said it would increase the income threshold so anyone earning less than $300,000 combined could access it - whether that was single or combined income.

"Right now, a junior doctor on $100,000 can't access the scheme," housing spokesperson Chris Bishop said.

World.title: Coalition returned to government in new poll, as Opportunity loses kingmaker spot
World.content:
RNZ national

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is speaking to RNZ shortly. Listen on the player above, the RNZ app or your local RNZ frequency.

The current coalition government would be returned to power based on the results of a new poll, with Opportunity unable to breach the threshold and become kingmaker.

The Qiulae Wong-led upstarts have fallen from 6.1 to 4.5 percent in the latest Taxpayers' Union-Curia Poll, bucking the trend found in other polls.

National was down two percentage points to 29 percent, and Labour down 1.9 to 25.9 percent.

ACT and the Greens were the main beneficiaries. The Greens were up 3.8 percentage points to 13.9 percent, and ACT up 3.2 to 10.5 percent.

New Zealand First was down 0.7 to 8.4 percent.

Te Pāti Māori gained 0.5 points to 2 percent. The party this year hopes to use MMP's overhang to boost the chance of removing the coalition.

Te Pāti Māori are trying to win all seven Māori seats, rather than boost their party vote. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Rounding out the party vote results were NZ Loyal (1.5 percent), Animal Justice (1.2), Women's Rights (0.7), Vision NZ (0.5) and the New Conservatives (0.5).

When it came to seats, the coalition - National, ACT and NZ First - would get 64 compared to the opposition - Labour, Greens and Te Pāti Māori - on 56. The right-leaning Taxpayers' Union's analysis assumes Te Pāti Māori would win three seats.

Opportunity would get zero on these results, being below the 5 percent threshold.

Christopher Luxon remained ahead of Chris Hipkins as preferred prime minister, down 2 percentage points to 21.2 percent. Hipkins fell 2.9 to 16.9 percent.

World.title: Meth-using, speeding driver with baby in car killed two in head-on crash
World.content:
A unlicensed driver high on methamphetamine and speeding with her baby in the car crashed into another motorist, killing herself and the other driver, a coroner has found.

Peta Kerr, a 33-year-old mother of four, was travelling on State Highway 1 south of Amberley about 5pm on 28 January 2024 with her 7-month-old child in the car.

Coroner Mary-Ann Borrowdale said, in findings released on Monday, Kerr had left Christchurch distressed after telling the baby's father Leonard Bourton she needed to leave town because she was afraid of associates who were threatening to harm her and take her baby.

Text messages showed the pair had argued acrimoniously the day before her death, throughout the night and into the early morning. The couple were living apart, but Bourton said they were engaged to be married and intended to reconcile.

Kerr was texting with Bourton during the early afternoon and told him she was moving her belongings from her Kāinga Ora flat in Addington to Amberley.

She sent a series of videos and text messages to Bourton about 2.30pm, claiming she had been assaulted but pleaded with him not to tell anyone.

He reported the assault to police, who contacted her.

She told them she was fine and wanted to be left alone.

An ambulance arrived at her flat about 4.15pm but Kerr told them to leave.

Shortly afterwards, she placed her baby in his car seat in her unregistered 2015 Volkswagen Touareg and left for Amberley.

Bryan Kerr, a 51-year-old from New Brighton and no relation to Peta Kerr, spent 28 January 2024 fishing at South Bay, Kaikōura with long-time friend Kurt Skinner.

The pair arrived in Kaikōura about 9am and fished for four hours, smoking a cannabis joint while fishing.

After cleaning their equipment, they left South Bay about 2.30pm.

Bryan Kerr was driving his 1996 Toyota Landcruiser towing a trailer with two jet-skis, while Skinner was in the front passenger seat.

As the vehicles approached one another at the Leithfield culvert, Peta's Touareg - travelling at about 117km/h - failed to take a sweeping left-hand bend and crossed the centre line, crashing head on into Bryan's Landcruiser.

Skinner described seeing the Touareg drift across the road towards them.

Peta did not appear to make any attempt to correct the vehicle back into the left lane, he said.

He yelled to Bryan, but there no time for him to take action before being hit, Skinner said.

Other witnesses confirmed Peta had crossed the centre line and drove straight into the Landcruiser and that there was nothing Bryan could have done to avoid the crash.

Both drivers were critically injured and died at the scene. Both were wearing seatbelts.

Skinner was seriously injured and taken to hospital by helicopter.

Peta's baby was also taken to hospital with minor injuries.

The driver of a third vehicle, following Bryan, tried to avoid the crash and flipped onto its side but the occupant was uninjured.

Postmortems found both drivers died from blunt force trauma consistent with the crash.

Bruises were found on Peta's body consistent with the video clip she had sent Mr Bourton following the alleged assault.

A separate police investigation into the alleged assault found no evidence one had occurred.

Testing showed Peta had a methamphetamine blood level of 3.9mg/L, which the coroner said was five-and-a-half times the "median recreational-use methamphetamine level".

The Serious Crash Unit found the road was clear and the weather fine, and neither vehicle had any fault that contributed to the crash.

Peta never held a driver's license and had also been forbidden from driving.

Bourton said Peta had poor vision and needed glasses, which might have been broken during her claimed assault, and she had not been taking her mental health medications and was exhibiting paranoia.

Coroner Mary-Ann Borrowdale said Peta's medical history included complex post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety with depression, borderline personality disorder, substance abuse with possible associated psychotic episodes, and previous suicide attempts and self-harm.

But there was no evidence Peta intended to crash, Borrowdale said.

While Peta had some history of being suicidal, the crash was caused accidentally by a combination of speed, fatigue, upset and intoxication, she said.

Borrowdale made no formal recommendations, but said Peta's actions "could easily have cost the life of her cherished baby son, in addition to that of Bryan Kerr".

Borrowdale highlighted unlicensed driving, methamphetamine use, speed, drug driving, fatigue and "emotional overwhelm".

Driving while distressed was an under-acknowledged hazard and could cause risk-taking, impulsivity, poor judgement, reduced awareness to the environment and slower reaction times, Borrowdale said.

That both drivers had consumed drugs ought to greatly concern road users and lawmakers, she said.

The coroner welcomed the new police roadside drug testing regime.

However, she noted Bryan Kerr's cannabis use played no role in the crash.

World.title: 25 years of helping preterm babies: 'There's a lot of opportunities to do things that matter'
World.content:
A study looking at the early brain development of babies born between 32 and 36 weeks gestation has found a third of participants showed abnormalities on their MRI.

Every year about 4500 babies are born prematurely in New Zealand and those rates have been rising.

Preterm babies - those born before the 37-week mark - can have life-long health challenges.

For 25 years the Liggins Institute at the University of Auckland has worked to improve the long-term health outcomes of these babies.

Liggins Research Doctor Olga Ivashkova takes a 2 year-old through a development assessment. Liz Garton

The Moderate-to-Late Preterm Babies Early Brain Development (MOPeD) study is just one of many running through the Liggins.

Rachel Koenen, 35, and her 2-year-old son Oren are participants in the study, which involves an early MRI scan and developmental progess check-ins.

She said it was a no-brainer for her to want to take part.

"If we can contribute to the body of knowledge and it doesn't harm people, you should," she said. "You never know how big of an impact the results are going to be on changing people's lives, particularly in the little one… and we need a clearer picture to inform future best practice on how we deal with premature babies."

Study lead Distinguished Professor Dame Jane Harding says the tiny babies born before 32 weeks have the highest risk, being up to 10 times more likely to have developmental problems as they grow up.

But she says 80 percent of preterm babies are born in the 32-37 week range and they are still twice as likely to have developmental problems.

Distinguished Professor Dame Jane Harding. Liz Garton

"We started this work because we were interested in how babies' brains grow," said Professor Harding. "We decided that we should look with MRI at how the babies' brains were growing and discovered to our surprise that there were quite a lot of them that had abnormalities on their MRI that we didn't expect."

More than a third - 38 percent - had changes similar to ones seen in the very early preterm babies.

"In the very preterm babies, [the changes] are associated with later risk, but we don't know what they mean in this group," said Professor Harding.

The MoPED study involves using MRI and developmental assessments to track outcomes.

Koenen said it had been a very easy process and one that had benefited them as well.

"It's all very clever the way they do it. Oren gets given a set of problems or a set of play exercises he has to work through and based on how he does they kind of gauge where he's at developmentally and if there's any concerns.

"They share back their results, which is awesome. I love seeing all the results."

She said for Oren the news had been all good. "Super reassuring to know that he's on track and he's advanced verbally. Definitely a little chatterbox."

MOPeD is just one of many studies currently running at the Liggins Institute.

The Liggins Institute Director Professor Justin O'Sullivan Supplied

Director Professor Justin O'Sullivan said discovering ways to improve long-term health outcomes was what the institute was known for

"The Liggans is named after Mont Liggans, who basically developed a really world-changing therapy, which meant that if you're born pre-term effectively, you have a chance to live. And that's a cornerstone for the institute."

In the 25 years since it opened, many other studies have changed the way medicine is practiced, such as work on magnesium sulphate which helps prevent cerebral palsy in tiny babies, and studies on a dextrose gel for treating low blood sugars, which is now first-line treatment for those babies.

There was still a lot of work to be done about preterm birth rates, but Professor O'Sullivan said the work was about more than babies.

"We're trying to personalize nutrition. We're looking at live therapeutics, like gut bug stuff," he says, "Then we're talking about the sort of genetic programs and fast tracking therapies for people when we find a genetic mutation and I don't mean by genetic engineering, but there are ways to treat them."

He said there were a lot of different projects that were really trying to push things into the future, for example the probiotics people use today were chosen in 1905.

"Sometimes we take for granted that something works just because we've done it for a long time. Just because we did it for a long time doesn't mean it's right and maybe there's a better way to do that and maybe you can have a better impact."

Another piece of work involved new probiotics for conditions like anxiety

"It's a huge problem in the population and what if it's as simple as a single capsule, right?"

He said there were also new problems coming, that staff were trying to get ahead, of such as changing weather and temperatures.

"If you get really hot when you're pregnant there can be impacts of the heat on the pregnancy through stress and various other things," he said.

"There's a lot of opportunities to do things that matter and help."

The changing climate could herald new challenges for newborn health 123RF

The Liggins Institute is currently running an appeal to raise funds for its work, but Professor O'Sullivan said donating money was not the only way people could help.

"Being a participant in the trials is an amazing thing," he said. "You're donating of yourself… to try and help others and it's an incredible thing that people do, when they do that."

Professor Harding said it was a privilege to be doing this sort of work

World.title: Elective surgeries postponed as winter illnesses surge in hospitals
World.content:
RNZ national

Elective surgeries are being postponed as the health system responds to the highest levels of demand seen in recent years.

Health New Zealand says acute care has to be prioritised.

Its national chief medical officer Dame Helen Stokes-Lampard said patient numbers are above historic winter levels.

She said the pressure is expected to continue for at least another three to four weeks - but numbers have reduced from the "exceptionally high levels" seen in August.

Earlier this year, the government put an extra $25 million towards extra beds and staff recruitment to prepare for winter.

Health NZ said at Middlemore Hospital in Auckland, they're redeploying staff and offering overtime shifts to address the high number of patients at its emergency department.

Where procedures are deferred, Stokes-Lampard said patients can be assured it will only happen when safe to do so.

"The decision to defer care is not taken lightly and all decisions are made on a case-by-case basis by clinical teams with patient safety and wellbeing as the highest priority.

World.title: Crash leaves two seriously injured, closes SH1 in Canterbury
World.content:
File image. RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

A major Canterbury highway has closed as emergency services respond to a crash north of Ashburton.

Two people were taken to hospital in a serious condition - one by helicopter and one by road.

The two-vehicle crash on the Rakaia Highway north of Ashburton happened shortly after 5am on Monday.

State Highway 1 was closed between Racecourse Road and Mitcham Road, with detours in place.

World.title: What New Zealanders are doing to try and live forever (or at least longer)
World.content: ​In the world of longevity, sleep is king, but it isn’t the only thing McNall is investing in to live a healthy life that - he hopes - is 200 or 300 years long. Or perhaps never-ending. He is part of the Don’t Die online community led by tech millionaire Bryan Johnson. Johnson is using his body as an experiment to test the latest scientific hunches - including injecting his son’s blood plasma - that could lead to an extended life and healthspan, the portion of a person’s life where they are relatively healthy.

World.title: F1 wonderkid wins from 19th, Piastri fifth as Ferrari fans left in tears
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli's magical season has continued emphatically, winning his home Italian Grand Prix from 19th in a historic triumph for the F1 drivers' championship leader.

The 20-year-old drove a near-flawless race to become the first Italian in 60 years to win in their home grand prix, beating teammate George Russell in a thrilling finish.

Max Verstappen placed third, while Lando Norris overtook Oscar Piastri on the final lap as the McLaren duo finished fourth and fifth.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc suffered a heavy crash into the barriers on the second lap, hitting the tyre wall at high speed and shattering the hearts of thousands of passionate Ferrari fans in the grandstands at Monza.

But those Ferrari fans were on their feet by the end of the grand prix, as one of their own took the chequered flag on a weekend where his championship lead was supposed to shrink.

"Unbelievable. I am so happy," Antonelli said after becoming the first Italian since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966 to win the race.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Italian GP 1. 267 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes 2. 201 — George Russell, Mercedes 3. 191 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari 4. 171 — Lando Norris, McLaren 5. 155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari 6. 127 — Max Verstappen, Red Bull 7. 116 — Oscar Piastri, McLaren

"I could never have imagined to be here today.

"We managed to pull it off, and I am really happy."

Antonelli's win from 19th is the second-furthest back a driver has started and gone on to win.

Only John Watson, from 22nd at the 1983 United States Grand Prix, has won from a lower grid spot.

Antonelli knew he was going to start from well back, with Mercedes announcing at the Dutch Grand Prix a fortnight earlier that the championship leader would have new power unit components fitted for this weekend, which would exceed his year's allocation.

With tyre degradation low, and a one-stop all but certain if there were no incidents, Antonelli got off to a flying start by jumping from 19th to 12th in the opening two laps.

Leclerc lost control of his Ferrari at the final turn of the second lap, ploughing into the barriers, knocking him out of the grand prix and bringing out a red flag.

A marshal consoles Charles Leclerc after crashing out of the Italian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Alex Bierens de Haan)

Leclerc's crash was too much for some Ferrari fans to bear, seen on the television broadcast crying and needing to be consoled.

Ferrari fan crying, consoled, after Charles Leclerc crashed out of the Italian Grand Prix. (Kayo/Fox Sports)

All drivers were able to make their mandatory tyre change, which led to leader Russell, who took that position from surprise Alpine pole sitter Pierre Gasly on lap two, with hard compound tyres to get to the end of the race.

Antonelli, who started on hards, had to use the slightly quicker but less durable mediums for the rest of the race.

Russell held the lead off the restart, Verstappen moved into second as Gasly fell down the order, and Antonelli continued to pick his way through the field.

By lap 16, Antonelli passed Verstappen and then he had the lead two laps later.

Antonelli and Russell would trade the lead over the next few laps, as Monza's powerful slipstream and the use of electrical power boosts, lead to drivers swapping positions in what has come to be called yo-yo racing.

Mercedes told their drivers to stop squabbling in a bid to distance themselves from Verstappen, who was just holding onto them.

Aston Martin's Lance Stroll stopped just off the track on lap 28, resulting in a virtual safety car being called — and the decisive moment in the race.

Mercedes kept race leader Russell out on his hards, but brought Antonelli in for new mediums.

When racing resumed, Antonelli was sixth and 15 seconds behind Russell with 24 laps to go.

With fresher tyres, Antonelli stormed back to the rear of his teammate, setting up an epic finish.

The 20-year-old went onto the gravel on lap 49 in an unsuccessful attempt to take the lead.

On the next lap, Antonelli made no mistake and made the race-winning move to the delight of the Italian crowd.

"It was quite scary in the moment [going into the gravel]," Antonelli said of his gravel trip on lap 49.

"I was like, 'maybe I lost my chance'.

"Luckily we still had the pace and managed to bring it home."

Antonelli's lead over Russell in the drivers' championship now extends to 66 points.

The mountain for Russell to win a maiden world championship this year just got steeper, and he is left with the disappointment of having his deficit extended despite starting 17 grid places ahead of Antonelli.

Asked about Mercedes's decision to leave him on track during the virtual safety car, Russell said he did not think Antonelli would be called into the pits.

"I thought we were both going to stay out, I was surprised to see him pitting," Russell said.

"In the end, it was a roll of the dice both ways.

"In the moment, the team wouldn't have known which strategy was better. It made sense to split the cars, but in the end, Kimi had great pace."

Verstappen finished third, after a terrific late battle with Piastri for the final podium spot.

The Australian, however, was unable to hold onto fourth, losing that place to his teammate Norris on the final lap of the grand prix.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton was sixth, pole sitter Gasly was seventh, and Racing Bulls youngster Arvid Lindblad placed eighth.

Franco Colapinto recovered from an early excursion into a gravel trap to place ninth for Alpine.

Japan's Yuki Tsunoda, driving for Racing Bulls while Liam Lawson fills in for the injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, claimed 10th and one championship point.

Relive all the action of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix in the blog below.

World.title: Dockers AFLW star turns ruck coach after injury to assist victory
World.content:
Injured AFLW powerhouse Mim Strom was forced to play ruck coach on the bench as the Dockers steamrolled a Monique Conti-less Richmond by 25 points on the road.

Two-time All-Australian ruck Strom was in agony at Princes Park after a tackle from Tigers midfielder Emelia Yassir in the first quarter of Sunday's clash.

Recruit Eden Zanker was first cab off the rank in the ruck, while Gabby O'Sullivan kicked three goals to help lift the Dockers to a 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) win in Indigenous Round.

Later on Sunday, Aishling Moloney finished with four goals as Geelong posted a 13.5 (83) to 7.9 (51) result to pile the misery on a winless Essendon at Kardinia Park.

Lisa Webb's Dockers (2-2) can finish the fourth week of the 12-fixture competition in the top eight, but are bracing to lose Strom for part of their finals push.

Before Sunday, Strom had played 78 consecutive matches since making her debut in 2020.

"She's been on the bench with a big smile, so she's hard to get a read on, but I'll get a medical update," coach Webb told Seven Plus at three-quarter time.

"She's been a ruck coach on the side. She's been a warrior for us, and we'll look after her."

Gabby O'Sullivan (pictured) kicked three goals as Fremantle recorded a 25-point road win over Richmond. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Richmond, which, like Fremantle, has not reached finals since 2024, drop from sixth and could finish as low as 13th with a 2-2 record.

The Tigers are unsure of how serious Conti's injury is, with the 2023 league best-and-fairest managing Achilles soreness.

The five-time All-Australian midfielder was a late withdrawal alongside Fina Dethlefsen, with recruit Georgia Stubs and Kate Dempsey returning to the side.

Youngster Isabel Bacon (24 disposals, six clearances) led the game in Conti's absence, and Olivia Wolmarans kicked two goals.

Geelong's Mikayla Bowen (left) picked up a game-high 40 disposals in her side's 32-point win over Essendon. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

The Dockers took the early advantage after three lead changes in the opening quarter, pipping the Tigers by five points thanks to a goal from O'Sullivan.

Strom's absence did little to sap Fremantle's momentum, with O'Sullivan piling on back-to-back goals as the hosts were kept scoreless in the second term.

It was much the same after half-time, with the Dockers maintaining a perfect record against the Tigers across four meetings since season six in 2022.

At Kardinia Park, scores were level at 1.1 (7) for much of the first quarter before Chantal Mason gave away a free kick for a high tackle on Maggie Johnstone in Essendon's forward-50.

Johnstone converted after the quarter-time siren for a six-point lead, but the Bombers' ascendancy did not last long after Moloney came to life.

The star Irishwoman kicked four of Geelong's six goals in the second term, while the visitors managed just two to trail by 18 points.

Geelong improved its record to 3-1 to tighten its grip on a top-four spot, leaving Essendon languishing in 16th.

Mikayla Bowen had a monster 40 disposals, while Cats star Georgie Prespakis matched older sister and Essendon veteran Maddy with 27 disposals and five clearances.

AAP

World.title: Osaka apologises to children after struggling with Achilles issue at US Open
World.content:
Naomi Osaka continued to impress with her style and staying power at the US Open on Saturday as she shrugged off a late Achilles problem to beat Belgian Elise Mertens 6-3, 3-6, 7-5 and reach the fourth round.

For her latest eye-catching walk-on look, the four-time major champion blended boardroom and locker-room aesthetics in a grey checked blazer-hoodie and wide-leg pants, putting a tailored twist on traditional pre-match attire.

She looked on course for a business-like win after the first set but was dragged into a battle in the third, where she had to fight through the Achilles niggle to advance.

"I wouldn't say it's a huge injury," Osaka told reporters. "I'd say it's this ongoing problem that I've had since the grass season.

"I don't know why it hasn't gone away. I feel I've done a lot of things in order to make it better, but maybe the time off wasn't enough. I'm not really sure what the reason is, but the medical timeout was to address that.

"You know, she massaged my leg and stuff, so that seemed to help, and gave me Tylenol."

The 28-year-old, a two-time champion at Flushing Meadows, reeled off three games in succession to take a 4-1 lead in the first set under the lights of Louis Armstrong Stadium, clinching it with a battling hold thanks to a string of booming serves.

Naomi Osaka was pushed hard by Elise Mertens (right) but eventually prevailed in a three-setter. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Osaka pushed the 23rd seed hard at the start of the next set with some heavy hitting from the baseline before pouncing with a break in the third game, only to surrender the lead by dropping the next two games.

"Honestly, I can't believe I won this match," Osaka said on court after sealing victory, thanking the crowd for the energy it provided.

"There was a certain point where I put my heart on the court and kept trying in every point. Thank you so much, but honestly, I'm shocked I won. I'm not going to lie."

After levelling the match to force a decider, Mertens capitalised on several unforced errors by a frustrated Osaka to gain the upper hand, but there would be another momentum shift in the match after a medical timeout for the Japanese player.

"I didn't play amazing and it was getting me down, sorry about my behaviour, for the little kids watching," said Osaka, who threw her racket to the floor at one point.

"This is my favourite tournament. I wanted to play well in front of you. I'm just that glad I have the opportunity to play another match.

"I thought I was going to be OK, but clearly I was shaky."

After recovering a break late on, Osaka fired a huge ace to take a 6-5 lead and revved up her forehand in the following game to complete the win and earn a meeting with Elena Rybakina in the next round.

Reuters

World.title: Swans star 'shattered' after skipper's heartbreaking knee injury
World.content:
Sydney star Tom Papley says he is "shattered" for Swans skipper Callum Mills as Mills braces to miss the club's push for an unlikely AFL premiership.

Mills's feared ACL rupture added a sour note to Sydney's remarkable 53-point qualifying final demolition of reigning premiers Brisbane at the SCG on Saturday.

Scans are expected to confirm the major knee injury for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss and has dealt with numerous untimely injuries across his 197-game career.

But Sydney have an opportunity to make amends for previous grand final losses, with a preliminary final at the SCG against either Fremantle or Geelong to come.

Papley admitted it "didn't look great" for Mills following the resilient skipper's first-quarter knee injury.

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the club amid the dramatic fallout from the events at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne last month.

"He is an amazing captain," Papley told the Nine Network of his skipper on Sunday.

"[He's] been amazing over the last few weeks.

"He puts this club on his back and wears his heart on his sleeve. It's just shattering for him.

"I'd love nothing more than to win a premiership and have him by my side, albeit he might not be there [playing].

"He deserves it more than anyone."

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Sydney were given little chance to knock off the Lions, even though they finished the home-and-away season second.

Even club chairman Andrew Pridham conceded the Swans' premiership hopes had been "torpedoed" after suspending the five players.

But all cylinders of the Swans machine fired on Saturday despite those major absences, with Errol Gulden calling the shots in the engine room as Harry Cunningham directed the defence.

Logan McDonald may have led with six goals, but Sydney enjoyed an even contribution from their forward line, with Charlie Curnow and Papley slotting five each.

Tall forward Hayden McLean's three-goal haul is set to further complicate coach Dean Cox's selection conundrum, with Joel Amartey (Achilles) nearing full fitness.

Star winger Justin McInerney is also expected to return from a hamstring strain for the preliminary final.

Errol Gulden (right) marshalled Sydney's engine room in style against Brisbane in the absence of some of his star teammates. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They should both be available … and that'll be a decision, like we do every week," Cox said of Amartey and McInerney.

Cox said Saturday's win felt like the most complete four-quarter performance in his tenure.

"With the quality of opposition that we were playing and the ability of the match-winners that they have all over the ground," Cox said.

"I was really proud when we've got some of the young kids that come into our football team to be able to execute the roles they had to play at the right time."

AAP

World.title: NRL finals schedule confirmed, Panthers claim minor premiership
World.content:
The Penrith Panthers have a fourth NRL minor premiership in the last seven seasons after battering the Wests Tigers 38-10 at Western Sydney Stadium.

Thomas Jenkins scored a first half double to join Alex Johnston on top of the NRL try-scoring charts for the year with 30 to share the Ken Irvine medal, while Casey McLean nabbed his first career NRL hat-trick.

The Wests Tigers briefly showed some life at the start of the second half, with PNG-bound via Parramatta five-eighth Jarome Luai benched by Benji Marshall after the break.

The lively Latu Fainu ensured the Tigers immediately lifted, amplifying the sense of disappointment fans must have felt at the underwhelming Luai era that had promised so much.

Penrith's victory ensures the Panthers will host the Roosters at Western Sydney Stadium on Sunday in the first week of the finals.

NRL finals schedule week 1 Friday Elimination Final: South Sydney Rabbitohs vs Newcastle Knights at Sydney Football Stadium — 7:50pm AEST Saturday Qualifying final: New Zealand Warriors vs Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium — 4:05pm AEST

Elimination final: Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks vs North Queensland Cowboys at Sydney Football Stadium — 7:50pm AEST Sunday Qualifying final: Penrith Panthers vs Sydney Roosters at Western Sydney Stadium — 4:05pm AEST

The Rabbitohs and Knights will open the weekend with their elimination final at the Sydney Football Stadium on Friday night (7:50pm AEST).

The second-placed Warriors will take on the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium on Saturday afternoon (4:05pm AEST) before the Sharks play the Cowboys at the Sydney Football Stadium that evening at 7:50pm AEST.

The Sharks had hoped to host the match at Shark Park but the 45,500-capacity Moore Park stadium got the nod.

The Cowboys will likely be without star forward Reuben Cotter, who will miss at least week one of the NRL finals after being charged for a high tackle against the Raiders.

The Maroons forward was handed a grade two careless high tackle charge for his contact on Josh Papali'i in the first hit up of the match.

Earlier, Tyrell Sloan scored a 45-metre field goal to secure the Dragons a thrilling 24-22 victory over the Parramatta Eels in Wollongong.

"I guess it's the stuff you dream about," Castleford-bound Sloan told ABC Sport after the match.

"The fans turned up … they stuck with us through a tough year and just to repay them there is the best feeling ever."
